Article.Title: Pupil Dynamics Reflect Uncertainty-Driven Adjustments of Probability Learning
Article.Authors: Greenhouse-Tucknott, A.; Foucault, C.; Buot, A.; Meyniel, F.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive learning in dynamic environments depends on the brain's ability to represent and respond to uncertainty. Changes in arousal-mediated pupil diameter provide insight into the neural basis of this process. Prior work has focused on magnitude-based inference tasks and revealed that learning is primarily influenced by the detection of change points and the corresponding modulation of arousal. In comparison, the role of arousal systems in learning contexts where changes are harder to detect, such as in probability learning, remains poorly understood. Here, we combined pupillometry with a probability learning task in which human participants estimated a hidden generative probability of stimuli that changed abruptly and unpredictably. A Bayesian ideal observer model was used to estimate trial-by-trial learning rates and two uncertainty-associated factors: change point probability (the probability that the generative process has abruptly changed) and prior uncertainty (about the current beliefs on this generative process). In line with normative theory, participants relied on prior uncertainty to adjust learning rates. Pupil analyses revealed temporally distinct representations of uncertainty, with phasic dilations tracking change point probability and tonic pupil dilations tracking prior uncertainty. Mediation analyses further indicated that both phasic and tonic pupil signals partially carried the effects of change point probability and prior uncertainty on learning, respectively. Critically, high tonic arousal weakened the coupling between phasic pupil responses and change point probability, accompanied by a reduced influence of change point probability on learning. Together, our results demonstrate that probability learning in a dynamic environment is underpinned by computationally rational integration of latent uncertainty factors and its contribution to belief updating,regulated through arousal-associated responses.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: prior uncertainty; probability learning; arousal; uncertainty; pupil dynamics; learning rate; change point detection

Article.Title: Environmental co-option of chromatin potential links prenatal hypoxia to persistent cortical circuit dysfunction
Article.Authors: Cristancho, A. G.; Joseph, D. J.; Cassidy, M. M.; Chauhan, P. S.; Gadra, E. J.; Gadra, E. C.; Zarrinnegar, D.; Rodriguez, B. N.; Marsh, E. D.
Article.Abstract: Transient prenatal hypoxia is associated with long-term neurodevelopmental impairment without overt structural brain injury, suggesting early regulatory disruptions precede detectable pathology. Whether these disruptions represent transient stress responses or redirect developmental programs remains unknown. Here, we combined single-nucleus RNA sequencing and chromatin accessibility profiling in the late-gestation mouse cortex immediately after transient hypoxia, capturing responses across more than 140,000 nuclei. Hypoxia induced a largely conserved transcriptional stress response across cell types, whereas chromatin accessibility showed more extensive, cell type-specific disruption. Developing glutamatergic neurons showed the strongest disruption of chromatin transcription coupling, with hypoxia-responsive distal regulatory regions associated with genes governing synaptic organization and neuronal excitability. Consistent with these chromatin-associated programs, juvenile offspring displayed reduced dendritic spine density and increased intrinsic excitability in cortical neurons. These results support a model in which transient hypoxia co-opts the developing epigenome's capacity to encode future transcriptional states before persistent circuit dysfunction emerges.

Article.Title: Computation or Weight Adaptation? Rethinking the Role of Plasticity in Learning
Article.Authors: Lior, G.; Shalev, Y.; Stanovsky, G.; Goldstein, A.
Article.Abstract: The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, despite divergence from their natural language training data. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: neuroplasticity; large language models; statistical learning; artificial neural networks; weight adaptation; generalization
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Neural Networks and Applications; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Domain Adaptation and Few-Shot Learning; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Topic Modeling

Article.Title: CLEAR-FORCE: A reservoir computing framework for closed-loop brain stimulation
Article.Authors: Moreno-Gris, A.; Godin, C.; Thivierge, J.-P.
Article.Abstract: Electrical stimulation of brain activity has emerged as a key therapeutic intervention for neurological diseases. The success of these approaches relies on precisely tuned stimulation parameters. A major challenge is that these parameters should ideally be adjusted in real-time based on changes in brain activity. Closed-loop controllers address this challenge by monitoring brain activity and adapting stimulation according to ongoing changes in neural dynamics. While machine learning has been helpful in this context, closed-loop controllers typically do not adapt in real-time to fluctuations in brain activity. Here, we propose a novel framework based on reservoir computing to train a closed-loop, real-time neural controller. This approach, termed CLEAR-FORCE, trains the output weights of a recurrent network based on a combination of target signals and feedback from brain activity. Two series of simulations were performed, where the controller was successful at (1) inducing neural oscillations in a population of spiking neurons and (2) suppressing pathological oscillations. This framework provides a promising avenue for the implementation of neural controllers in low-powered, real-time, and adaptive hardware that harnesses machine learning for the personalized treatment of brain disorders.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: closed-loop brain stimulation; reservoir computing; recurrent neural networks; neuromodulation; spiking neurons; low-power electronics; neural oscillations

Article.Title: Impaired Control Symptoms in Alcohol Use Disorder Show Convergent Associations Across Behavioral and Neural Markers of Inhibitory Control and Drinking Behavior
Article.Authors: Boehmer, J.; Reinhardt, P.; Bottino, M.; Baertl, C.; Arntz, F.; Hildebrandt, M. K.; Chen, H.; Thill, L.; Petzold, J.; Ritter, K.; Rapp, M.; Kiefer, F.; Bach, P.; Lenz, B.; Heinz, A.; Spitta, G.; Rosenthal, A.; Endrass, T.; Smolka, M. N.; Spanagel, R.; Henze, G.-I.; ReCoDe-Consortium, ; Marxen, M.; Walter, H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Deficits in inhibitory control are considered a central feature of alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet behavioral and neuroimaging findings have been inconsistent. One potential explanation is the marked heterogeneity of AUD, which encompasses multiple symptom dimensions that may differ in their underlying neurocognitive mechanisms. In this study, we investigated whether behavioral and neural markers of inhibitory control are associated with specific DSM-5 AUD symptom domains. Methods: A total of 589 participants (432 with non-treatment seeking AUD, 157 controls) completed a Stop-Signal Task (SST) during fMRI. Associations between DSM-5 symptom domains (impaired control over alcohol use, risky use, social problems, physical dependence) and SST performance, inhibition-related brain activation, and alcohol consumption were examined. Real-life drinking behavior was additionally assessed over 12 months using ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Results: Greater impaired control symptom severity was associated with poorer performance on go trials and diminished post-error slowing during SST. At the neural level, higher impaired control symptom severity was associated with reduced activation across fronto-insular, parietal, cingulate, supplementary motor, and cerebellar regions. In contrast, other symptom domains showed little to no associations with inhibition-related behavioral or neural measures. Higher impaired control symptom severity was associated with greater alcohol consumption across questionnaire-based and EMA-based assessments. Conclusions: In this large cohort, altered behavioral performance and recruitment of inhibition-related brain regions in the SST was selectively linked to impaired control symptoms. These findings highlight the importance of symptom-based approaches for understanding heterogeneity in addiction and may inform the development of more targeted interventions.

Article.Title: Cerebral hemodynamics and cytochrome c oxidase in hypoxic-ischemic rabbit fetuses
Article.Authors: Cortese, L.; Lo Presti, G.; Berdun, S.; Bale, G.; Kovacsova, Z.; Eixarch, E.; Gratacos, E.; Tachtsidis, I.; Durduran, T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Understanding fetal brain responses to hypoxia-ischemia is of growing interest, as it remains unclear to what extent these responses differ from those of newborns and whether developmental adaptations during gestation contribute to such differences. Materials and methods: Using a combination of broadband near-infrared spectroscopy (bNIRS) and diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS), we measured brain microvascular oxygen saturation (StO2), total hemoglobin concentration (THC), relative cerebral blood flow (rCBF), and the oxidation state of cytochrome c oxidase (oxCCO) during an acute ischemic challenge in the brains of five rabbit fetuses in utero. Simultaneous measurements were acquired from four control fetuses located in the contralateral uterine horn. Results: During the hypoxia-ischemia phase, we observed a rapid reduction of CBF (47% +/- 29%) and StO2, (from 64.7% +/- 1.5% at baseline to 40.6% +/- 2.0%) together with an increase of oxCCO (3.7 uM +/- 0.5 uM). Conclusion: The simultaneous increase in oxCCO and decrease in rCBF and StO2 during hypoxia-ischemia reveals a cerebral response pattern that differs from that commonly reported in the newborn brain. These findings support the hypothesis that unique developmental adaptations influence fetal cerebral metabolism during hypoxic-ischemic stress.

Article.Title: Default Mode Network Connectivity Is Associated with Capture by Distractors Assigned to Learned Spatial Regularities
Article.Authors: Chen, S.; Mueller, H. J.; Shi, Z.
Article.Abstract: Salient distractors interfere with visual search, but observers can learn to filter out distractors that occur frequently and in predictable locations. We examined whether within-default-mode-network (DMN) task-run connectivity was associated with distractor capture and its location-dependent modulation in task-fMRI data from two groups in which either orientation or color distractors carried a spatial-probability bias. Higher within-DMN connectivity was associated with greater distractor capture by the biased distractor dimension, which was also the most frequent distractor type, whereas capture by the unbiased dimension was essentially unrelated to connectivity. A hierarchical trial-level model also showed stronger DMN-distractor-capture coupling for the biased than for the unbiased dimension when both were evaluated under the same frequent-/rare-region weighting. DMN connectivity was also associated with spatial-probability learning, indexed by the rare-minus-frequent reaction-time difference on biased-dimension trials, but this association was closely tied to overall capture. When the physical distractor dimension was held constant, orientation showed stronger DMN-distractor-capture coupling when it carried the spatial bias; in contrast, the corresponding color comparison remained uncertain. The broader network analyses provided converging support for this DMN-distractor-capture coupling pattern. Higher DMN connectivity was thus not associated with poorer performance in general, but with less effective filtering of the distractor that the task set was tuned to suppress. This pattern is consistent with a DMN state that interferes with implementing the optimal task set.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: default mode network; attentional capture; individual differences; functional connectivity; distractor interference; visual search

Article.Title: Beyond the attractor: closed-loop stimulation design for learning multistable neural dynamics
Article.Authors: Jeon, H.; Park, I. M.
Article.Abstract: Online identification of nonlinear dynamical systems faces two challenges. Noisy, partial observations make the latent state difficult to estimate. Local attractors can also keep passive trajectories in regions that reveal little about the unknown dynamics. Both challenges commonly arise in closed-loop neural experiments where stimulation must be chosen from noisy spike counts, while neural activity may remain near a stable state unless stimulation drives it elsewhere. We address this problem by actively selecting inputs to collect informative observations during the experiment. We introduce PALDI (Planning-based Active Latent Dynamics Identification), which combines extended-Kalman state prediction, single-step Laplace state updates, blockwise Gaussian parameter updates, and finite-horizon planning. Its parameter expected-information-gain surrogate combines dynamics sensitivity with state Fisher information and discounts apparent parameter information when latent states are uncertain. We compare PALDI with nonadaptive inputs, a myopic policy, and two active baselines: the one-step D-optimal method FLEX and receding-horizon curiosity with uncertainty sampling. On a bistable Wilson-Cowan model of excitatory and inhibitory populations, PALDI approaches the true-model reference and remains strongest as the observation signal-to-noise ratio decreases or the readout geometry becomes biased. We then test identification in a spiking decision network where we use a reduced dynamics and observation model to approximate the data-generating process. PALDI reaches a median held-out prediction R2 of 0.90, close to a fitted reference, and its model gives the highest change-of-mind success among identification policies. Information-guided finite-horizon planning is a practical strategy for identifying neural circuit dynamics with closed-loop stimulation.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: finite-horizon planning; Wilson-Cowan model; expected information gain; extended Kalman filter; latent state estimation; nonlinear dynamical systems; multistability; uncertainty sampling

Article.Title: Identifying neural correlates of auditory perceptual awareness and deviance using a no-report inattentional deafness paradigm
Article.Authors: Ellinghorst, A.; Dellert, T.; Zhu, Y.; Straube, T.; Dykstra, A. R.; Schlossmacher, I.
Article.Abstract: The relationship between neural processes supporting perception, deviance processing, and post-perceptual task demands during auditory processing is not well understood. We used multitone masking and a no-report inattentional deafness paradigm to dissociate neural correlates of auditory perceptual awareness, deviance processing, and task demands. Evoked responses to physically identical target-tone pairs were recorded across three phases differing only in task instructions. In Phase A, human participants remained nave to (and thus unaware of) the target tones. In Phase B, participants were informed about (and thus aware of) the target tones. In Phase C, participants remained aware of the target tones and judged the duration of the silent gap between them, rendering them task-relevant. When participants were aware of them, target tones elicited an auditory awareness negativity and an increased positivity in the P3 window), with larger responses when target tones were additionally task-relevant. Furthermore, though largest in Phase C, deviant stimuli elicited a mismatch negativity across all task conditions, while a significant P3 to deviants was only observed in Phase C. Thus, early and late responses can be independently modulated by awareness, deviance, and task-relevance, indicating that they do not necessarily rely on shared neural mechanisms despite overlapping spatiotemporal profiles.

Article.Title: Functional and structural profiling of circulation via genetically encoded modular fluorescent probes.
Article.Authors: Vittani, M.; Lee, A. B.; Wang, X.; Hiraoka, Y.; Sasaki, D.; Konno, A.; Knak, P. G.; Kusk, P.; Nagao, M.; Courtin, J.; Putranto, M. F.; Nasu, Y.; Tsuno, S.; Ueda, K.; Osuga, Y.; Tsuboi, T.; Piganiol, A.; Bienvenu, T.; Terunuma, M.; Hirai, H.; Nedergaard, M.; Tanaka, K.; Asiminas, A.; Hirase, H.
Article.Abstract: Sustained labeling of fluids is crucial for their investigation in animal models. Here, we introduce a mouse line (Alb-mSc-ST), where blood and interstitial fluid are labeled with the red fluorescent protein mScarlet and SpyTag. The SpyTag-SpyCatcher technology is exploited to monitor circulating fluid properties by biosensors or detect blood-brain barrier disruption. This approach represents a valuable tool for studying vascular structure, permeability and microenvironment in body organs in vivo.

Article.Title: Olfactory Deficits and Structural Anomalies of the Peripheral Olfactory System in 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
Article.Authors: Roalf, D. R.; McDonald-McGinn, D. M.; Atkins, A.; Calkins, M. E.; Crowley, T. B.; Freedman, P.; Gallagher, R. S.; Mastracchio, C.; McGinn, D. E.; Moran, A.; Olson, A.; Pecsok, M. K.; Rockart, L.; Tran, O.; Zackai, E. H.; Emanuel, B. S.; Ruparel, K.; Shinohara, R. T.; White, L. K.; Schmitt, J. E.; Gur, R. E.
Article.Abstract: Background: Approximately 25% of individuals with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) develop a psychotic disorder, and the syndrome shares key neurodevelopmental features with psychosis in the general population. The olfactory system develops early in utero, providing a window into gestational disruptions relevant to psychosis risk. We hypothesized that 22q11DS would show impairments in olfactory function and structural anomalies of the olfactory system relative to psychosis spectrum (PS) youth without a known genetic syndrome and typically developing controls (TD). Methods: Participants included individuals with 22q11DS (n=101), PS (n=56), and TD (n=52). Sinonasal symptoms, odor identification, and discrimination (Sniffin' Sticks) behaviorally. Structural 3T MRI measured olfactory bulb volume, sulcus depth, and sulcus length. Sample sizes vary per analysis. Results: Relative to TD, 22q11DS showed elevated sinonasal burden (p<.001), lower odor identification (p<.001), and lower odor discrimination (p<.001). PS showed elevated sinonasal burden (p<.001) and marginally lower odor identification (p=.06), but no discrimination deficit. Olfactory bulb volume was significantly smaller in 22q11DS versus TD (p=.007, r=.39); PS showed a non-significant trend (p=.07). Olfactory sulcus depth (p=.52) and length (p=.82) did not differ across groups. Conclusions: 22q11DS is associated with elevated sinonasal burden, robust olfactory identification and discrimination deficits exceeding those of PS and reduced olfactory bulb volume. The co-occurrence of functional deficits and reduced bulb volume without sulcal anomalies may distinguish the 22q11DS olfactory phenotype from that of PS. These hypothesis-generating findings are consistent with partially dissociable neurodevelopmental mechanisms and support the utility of 22q11DS as a genetic model for psychosis risk.

Article.Title: An integrated multi-omic atlas of the choroid plexus highlights conserved molecular programs of epithelial function
Article.Authors: Dennis, E.; Tieu, E.; Fass, S. B.; Ochoa, L. F.; Li, Q.; Pigadas, N.; Davalan, W. C.; Kahn, M.; Galani, K.; Duy, P. Q.; Phan, B.; Mehta, N. H.; Cure, H. W.; Nenadovich, M.; Alper, S. L.; Chung, K.; Tsai, L.-H.; Kellis, M.; Kahle, K. T.
Article.Abstract: The choroid plexus (ChP) is a specialized epithelial tissue responsible for production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), maintenance of the blood-CSF barrier and regulation of CSF-borne signaling factors. However, despite the ChP's central role in CSF homeostasis, conserved molecular programs of ChP epithelial function across species and conditions remain incompletely defined. In this study, we integrated eight mouse and human single-cell/nucleus RNA-seq datasets to build a multi-species ChP atlas capturing major epithelial, stromal, vascular, and immune populations. Cross-dataset differential expression identified a conserved epithelial gene program encompassing ion transport, barrier function, ciliogenesis, and secretory signaling, while prioritizing understudied genes including CLIC6 and VAT1L. Co-expression network analysis resolved conserved epithelial meta-programs, and transcription factor regulatory inference identified OTX2, MSX1, and GLIS3 among conserved regulators of epithelial gene expression. We also generated a novel Visium HD spatial transcriptomic atlas of mouse fourth-ventricle ChP to orthogonally validate epithelial modules. Lastly, cross-tissue analyses revealed substantial transcriptional overlap between ChP and retinal pigment epithelium, including shared epithelial genes and OTX2-associated regulatory relationships. Together, these findings define conserved molecular programs of ChP epithelial specialization, nominate candidate regulators for functional investigation, and provide an integrated cross-species and spatial resource for studying ChP physiology.

Article.Title: Nicotinic modulation of frontal circuits breaks the cycle of attentional performance failure
Article.Authors: Nishioka, T.; Norman, K.; Garkun, Y.; Riceberg, J.; Waltrip, L.; Bicks, L.; Singh, A.; Serratelli, A.; Mankouskaya, T.; Maccario, P.; Allen, S.; Bateh, J.; Cho, C.; Caro, K.; Lopez, S.; Kawatake-Kuno, A.; Li, H.; Li, Y.; Wu, X.; O'loughlin, T.; Akbarian, S.; Morishita, H.
Article.Abstract: The ability to recover from consecutive failures is critical for adaptive behavior, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. In vivo screening of neuromodulatory inputs onto frontal-sensory cognitive control circuit identified a frontal cholinergic mechanism that counteracts lapses in attentional engagement following repeated errors. Cholinergic input from the basal forebrain to the frontal cortex was necessary and sufficient to restore performance after errors, specifically after repeated-but not after a single-failure. This effect was mediated by 7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in frontal-sensory cortical neurons, which sustained cortical circuit activity and frontal-sensory cortical oscillations during attentional engagement. Targeted optogenetic activation of these frontal-sensory neurons disrupted cycles of attentional performance failure and reinstated behavioral performance in a mouse model of neuropsychiatric syndrome. These findings reveal a circuit-level mechanism of cholinergic control that confers cognitive resilience under conditions of persistent failure.

Article.Title: Astrocytes in the Dentate Gyrus Shift the Equilibrium from Pattern Separation to Pattern Completion and Inhibit Fear Extinction
Article.Authors: Wang, M.; Kambali, M.; Nagarajan, R.; Lyu, J.; Kuan, H.-Y.; Yu, X.; Rudolph, U.
Article.Abstract: Pattern separation and pattern completion are core hippocampal computations linked to memory interference and overgeneralization in many neuropsychiatric disorders and to mnemonic discrimination deficits in neurodegenerative conditions. Astrocytes are increasingly recognized as important integrators and modulators of neuronal activity as many studies have shown changes in animal behavior and neural circuits induced by manipulation of astrocytic activity. The role of astrocytes in the dentate gyrus for learning and memory is, however, largely unknown. To investigate the functional significance of astrocytic activity in the dentate gyrus, we expressed the calcium extruding pump hPMCA2w/b (CalEx), resulting in inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity, the Gq-coupled receptor hM3Dq, or the Gi-coupled receptor hM4Di, allowing chronic activation of Gq- and Gi-dependent pathways by a designer drug, in dentate gyrus astrocytes. Our main finding is that inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity by CalEx resulted in improved pattern separation and impaired pattern completion. In -vivo calcium imaging revealed that CalEx expression in astrocytes altered the neuronal activity pattern in dentate gyrus neurons with an overall inhibitory effect. This suggests that in the dentate gyrus astrocytes promote the activity of these neurons. Furthermore, chronic activation of hM4Di resulted in impaired between-session fear extinction while chronic activation of hM3Dq resulted in impaired within-session fear extinction and improved pattern separation learning over multiple days, suggesting that activation of astrocytic activity enhances mechanistically separable forms of fear extinction in a Gq- or Gi-pathway-specific manner. Our findings reveal that dentate gyrus astrocytic calcium shifts the balance between pattern separation and pattern completion towards pattern completion and thus modulates an essential neuronal functional output of the dentate gyrus. Chronic activation of astrocytes inhibits fear extinction, and thus also affects management of memory interference. Our findings imply that astrocytic modulation may be beneficial to treat cognitive deficits in disorders in which overgeneralization is a problem.

Article.Title: Motor effort biases perceptual decisions through later-stage evidence accumulation rather than early sensory-attentional processing
Article.Authors: Cui, N.; Smeets, J. B. J.; van Beers, R. J.; Duncan, D. H.; van Wijk, B. C. M.
Article.Abstract: Motor effort has been shown to bias perceptual decisions toward less effortful choices, but it remains unknown whether this bias already takes effect during the early stages of decision formation through preparatory attentional allocation or sensory processing, or during later-stage evidence accumulation preceding response execution. This study investigated when motor effort becomes integrated into decision formation by focusing on the temporal evolution of neural processing during perceptual decision-making. While 64-channel EEG was recorded, twenty-four healthy adults performed an orientation discrimination task in which two Gabor patches appeared simultaneously in the left and right visual hemifield and decisions were reported using two pressure-sensitive response buttons requiring different levels of force. We found that motor effort modulated EEG activity at both the preparatory and later decision stages: pre-stimulus alpha power was reduced over the occipito-parietal cortex contralateral to the low-effort option, and mean centro-parietal positivity (CPP) amplitude preceding response execution was greater over centro-parietal cortex for low-effort choices, while leaving early sensory representations intact as indicated by no differences in P1 or N1 amplitude following stimulus onset. Trial-by-trial CPP amplitude preceding response execution increased with the likelihood of selecting the low-effort option, whereas the pre-stimulus alpha modulation was not associated with behavioral decision bias. These findings suggest that motor effort biases perceptual decisions primarily during later-stage evidence accumulation, thereby providing insight into the neural basis of embodied perceptual decision making.

Article.Title: Understanding neural circuit principles for representation learning through joint-embedding predictive architectures
Article.Authors: Mohammadi, A. G.; Halvagal, M. S.; Zenke, F.
Article.Abstract: Whether tracking prey or evading a predator, an animal's survival depends on both identifying objects in the environment and anticipating how they will move. To guide behavior, the brain must therefore extract information about object identities and their dynamics from entangled sensory inputs. How it accomplishes this feat remains an open question. Classical predictive coding theories propose that this ability arises by comparing predicted sensory signals with actual inputs and reducing the associated prediction errors. While such models capture important aspects of cortical computation, they typically focus on faithfully predicting sensory input and do not explicitly address how abstract, untangled representations of objects and their dynamics emerge solely through experience. Here, we develop a theory of representation learning in neural circuits that shifts the focus from prediction in the input space to prediction in representation space, without relying on external supervision or labeled data. Specifically, we introduce recurrent predictive learning (RPL), a recurrent joint-embedding predictive architecture inspired by self-supervised learning, that learns abstract representations of object identity and their dynamics and predicts future object motion from continuous sensory streams. While local learning rules alone can learn invariant object identity, we find that capturing object dynamics requires a circuit that explicitly generates and minimizes internal prediction-error signals. Crucially, the model learns sequence representations that resemble successor-like representations observed in the human primary visual cortex. The model also develops abstract sequence representations comparable to those reported in the macaque prefrontal cortex. Finally, we demonstrate a hierarchical version of RPL and discuss possible mappings onto cortical microcircuits. Our work establishes a circuit-centric theory framework that provides new perspectives on how the brain may acquire an internal model of the world through experience.

Article.Title: ISL1 is required for the terminal differentiation and maintenance of Starburst Amacrine Cells
Article.Authors: Santana Agreda, Y. C.; Wright, K. M.
Article.Abstract: During mammalian nervous system development, multipotent progenitor cells differentiate into hundreds of distinct neuronal subtypes. Neuronal subtype terminal differentiation is regulated by transcription factors that directly control the acquisition and maintenance of terminal identity. Using the mouse retina as a model system, we show that the transcription factor ISL1 is required for the terminal differentiation and maintenance of starburst amacrine cells (SACs), the sole cholinergic neuron subtype in the retina. We conditionally deleted Isl1 selectively from amacrine and horizontal cell precursors, allowing us to assess its cell-autonomous role in SAC development without disrupting its critical function in bipolar cell and retinal ganglion cell development. We find that ISL1 is not required for initial SAC specification but is required for their terminal differentiation. Isl1-deficient SACs retain a GABAergic amacrine cell identity but fail to adopt many SAC-specific features including expression of genes required for cholinergic transmission. In the absence of ISL1, SACs fail to migrate properly, with both OFF- and ON- SACs localizing to the inner nuclear layer. Deletion of Isl1 from post-migratory SACs at later stages of development revealed that it is also required for maintaining SAC identity and proper dendrite stratification. Loss of Isl1 from SACs ultimately caused abnormal development of the direction selective circuit. Together, these findings establish that ISL1 is required for the induction and maintenance of SAC-specific identity from a generic amacrine state.

Article.Title: Astrocyte-Specific dsRNA-ADAR1 Signalling Links Innate Immunity to Complement Activation in Parkinson Disease
Article.Authors: Liu, Y.; Halliday, G.; Fu, Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Dysregulated innate immune activation is a key feature of Parkinson disease (PD), but the upstream triggers and cell-type-specific mechanisms remain unclear. Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) has emerged as a potential driver of innate immune responses. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1), particularly its interferon-inducible p150 isoform, edits dsRNA to limit aberrant immune activation. Whether this dsRNA-ADAR1 axis contributes to neuroinflammation in PD in a cell-type-specific manner is unknown. Methods: We performed immunofluorescence on post-mortem cingulate cortex tissue from PD cases and controls to localise dsRNA, ADAR1 p150 and pathological alpha-synuclein protein. We integrated these findings with single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from three independent human brain datasets. An eight-module gene scoring framework was applied to assess dsRNA processing, sensing, and downstream innate immune pathways in neurons and astrocytes. Results: In PD cortex, the proportion of dsRNA-positive astrocytes was higher than in controls, whereas neuronal dsRNA positivity did not differ between groups. ADAR1 p150 positivity increased in both astrocytes and neurons, and the proportion of ADAR1 p150 positive astrocytes correlated with astrocytic -synuclein burden. Transcriptomic analyses showed that neurons were enriched for dsRNA editing and processing machinery, whereas astrocytes exhibited higher expression of dsRNA sensing pathways, innate immune responses, and transposable element control. While overall pathway activity did not differ between PD and controls after covariate adjustment, network analyses revealed cell-type-specific coupling patterns. Notably, complement gene expression showed a strong and selective association with dsRNA-related pathways in astrocytes, whereas interferon and NF-{kappa}B signalling were shared across cell types. In both cell types, ADAR1-associated gene programmes were enriched for oxidative phosphorylation and PD-related pathways. Conclusions: These findings identify astrocytes as a central site of relative dsRNA accumulation and ADAR1 p150 induction in the PD cortex. The selective coupling of dsRNA sensing to complement activation in astrocytes highlights a cell-type-specific innate immune pathway that is constitutively present rather than induced by disease. Together, our protein-level and network-level findings converge on a coherent and testable model in which a constitutive astrocytic circuit is engaged by disease-associated dsRNA accumulation, with potential relevance for disease progression and therapeutic targeting.

Article.Title: Syntaxin-1 and syntaxin binding protein 1-1 are required for planarian behavior and brain regeneration
Article.Authors: Clay, K. B.; Roberts, P. A.; Lechtreck, K. F.; Roberts-Galbraith, R. H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Nervous system regeneration requires creation of new neurons and their integration into new and existing networks. How new neurons find their targets and reconnect in the environment of regenerating tissue remains a major gap in knowledge. The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea is well suited to the study of neural regeneration due to the remarkable ability of planarians to regenerate their entire body, including the nervous system. However, we have not yet been able to explore synaptogenesis in regeneration using planarians due to a lack of tools to study synapses. Here we investigate potential players in planarian synapse, focusing on the conserved syntaxin protein family, which functions in neurotransmitter vesicle fusion at the synapse. Results: We found that reduction of either syntaxin-1 (stx1) or syntaxin-binding protein 1-1 (stxbp1-1) decreased locomotion and impeded brain regeneration, specifically in synapse-rich regions. Conclusions: Our observations support STX-1 and STXBP1-1 as bona fide synapse components, providing a starting point for studies neuronal connectivity during homeostatic remodeling and regeneration.

Article.Title: Induction of interhemispheric visual plasticity by paired associative stimulation
Article.Authors: Crespi, F.; Guidali, G.; Arrigoni, E.; Bolognini, N.
Article.Abstract: Unveiling the plastic mechanisms of the primary visual cortex (V1) is crucial for understanding how visual processing can change and adapt, ultimately informing interventions to promote functional recovery following visual system damage. Paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocols can induce associative plasticity within the human V1. However, previous paradigms used full-field visual stimulation, engaging both hemispheres simultaneously, leaving unclear whether plasticity can be selectively targeted to a single visual pathway and whether it can modulate the non-stimulated hemisphere. Across three experiments in healthy participants, we investigated the neurophysiological, behavioural, and interhemispheric outcomes of a novel lateralized visual PAS protocol (vPAS). Pattern-reversal checkerboards were presented in a single visual hemifield and time-locked to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) pulses delivered over the contralateral V1. Experiment 1 assessed neurophysiological effects by recording hemifield-lateralized visual-evoked potentials (VEPs) and testing three inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs: 75, 100, and 125 ms) between vPAS-paired stimuli. Experiment 2 evaluated perceptual changes in contrast detection, while Experiment 3 examined vPAS hemispheric specificity and aftereffects on interhemispheric visuomotor transfer. Only the 75-ms ISI consistently modulated visual processing in the non-conditioned hemisphere, reducing N75 amplitude and improving contrast detection for visual stimuli presented contralateral to the TMS side. Longer ISIs were not effective. Furthermore, this protocol altered interhemispheric transfer exclusively when the left, but not the right, V1 was targeted during vPAS. In conclusion, lateralized vPAS induces timing-dependent changes beyond the stimulated cortex, suggesting that associative plasticity can engage contralateral visual circuits and modulate visual processing.

Article.Title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models
Article.Authors: Brenner, J.; Caudill, M.; Zoghbi, H.
Article.Abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

Article.Title: Large-scale all-optical electrophysiology links excitability and connectivity to circuit dynamics in vivo
Article.Authors: Qi, Y.; Parot, V. J.; Wu, X.; Plutkis, S. E.; Lavis, L. D.; Cohen, A. E.
Article.Abstract: To understand neural computations, one would like to relate circuit dynamics to neuronal intrinsic excitability and connectivity. We developed tools for large-scale all-optical electrophysiology and applied them to approximately 300 layer 1 interneurons per mouse in vivo. Across two mice, targeted stimulation and voltage imaging identified 1,469 inhibitory and 5,752 directed electrical connections among 14,312 tested pairs. Presynaptic identity was more strongly associated with inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) amplitude, whereas postsynaptic identity was more strongly associated with IPSP decay time. Gap junctional and synaptic interactions had distinct spatiotemporal kernels, with corresponding signatures in spontaneous activity. Excitability measured under optogenetic stimulus predicted spiking responses to subthreshold voltage, depolarization rate, and spike history during spontaneous firing. Genetic subtypes also showed different behavioral-state-dependent voltage-to-spike relationships despite similar population-average subthreshold voltages. These measurements link cellular properties and pairwise interactions to spontaneous circuit dynamics, establishing an approach for functional circuit mapping in vivo.

Article.Title: Primary cilia facilitate GPCR neurotransmission through the canonical cAMP cascade
Article.Authors: Fagan, R. R.; He, X. J.; Stuurman, N.; Ehrlich, A. T.; Von Zastrow, M.
Article.Abstract: The primary cilium is increasingly recognized to be a discrete site for initiating neurotransmission through G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), yet how such neurotransmission is propagated downstream remains unclear. A canonical pathway of downstream GPCR neurotransmission is the cyclic AMP (cAMP) / cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) cascade. While cAMP can be locally generated in cilia and produce important effects that are functionally compartmentalized there, neurotransmission through GPCRs must propagate to effectors outside of cilia. Thus, a prevailing current view is that ciliary neurotransmission is restricted to non-canonical, cAMP-dependent pathways. Revisiting this view, we show here that the primary cilium of striatal medium spiny neurons is a major site from which endogenous D1 dopamine receptors initiate cAMP and PKA activity elevations that propagate throughout the extraciliary cytoplasm. We also show that the primary cilium spatially aligns essentially this entire long-range signaling axis from intercalating with numerous dopaminergic axon varicosities that initiate neurotransmission to enforcing proximity with somatic PKA stores that are activated by cAMP downstream. Together, these results extend the concept of ciliary neurotransmission to dopaminergic signaling in striatal neurons and reveal that, in this system, the primary cilium facilitates rather than restricts neurotransmission through the canonical cAMP / PKA cascade.

Article.Title: Single Cell Proteomics reveals partial uncoupling of the Glycerol-3-Phosphate shuttle to compensate for Electron Transport Chain dysfunction in Alexander Disease GFAP mutations
Article.Authors: van Gelder, C. A.; Daoutsali, E.; Attour, Y.; El Baghdadi, S.; Sobrevals Alcaraz, P.; van Es, R. M.; Gulersonmez, C.; Stigter, E. C.; Vos, H. R.; Hol, E. M.; Burgering, B. M.
Article.Abstract: Alexander disease (AxD) is a rare genetic leukodystrophy caused by dominant mutations in the gene coding for the astrocytic intermediate filament protein Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP). Understanding disease mechanisms is complicated by the fact that mutant GFAP promotes further GFAP accumulation, making it difficult to distinguish mutation-specific effects from those caused by elevated GFAP levels. Here, we performed mass spectrometry-based single cell proteomics to investigate proteomic alterations associated with increasing levels of wildtype GFAP and a common AxD-causing mutant GFAP R239C. By analyzing individual cells spanning a broad range of GFAP expression levels, we separated dosage-dependent effects from mutation-specific responses. Cells expressing high levels of wildtype GFAP increasingly resembled R239C-expressing cells at the proteomic level, supporting a role for GFAP accumulation in disease pathogenesis. In contrast, mutant GFAP specifically correlated with increased mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and remodeling of the proteasome tailored toward ATP- and ubiquitin-independent degradation of oxidized proteins. Integration with proteomics data from patient-derived cortical organoids revealed increased abundance of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins and respiratory chain assembly factors without corresponding changes in mitochondrially encoded proteins, suggesting impaired electron transport chain (ETC) assembly. Consistent with this, AxD cells displayed reduced oxygen consumption, increased glycolytic activity, enhanced utilization of the cytosolic part of the glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P) shuttle, and accumulation of triacylglycerides and lipid droplets. We propose that ETC dysfunction promotes partial uncoupling of the G3P shuttle, allowing sustained regeneration of cytosolic NAD to support glycolysis while diverting G3P toward lipid synthesis and storage. By regenerating NAD through the G3P shuttle rather than lactate fermentation, AxD astrocytes may sustain glycolytic flux while preserving lactate production, an important metabolic substrate for neighboring neurons. Together, our findings identify ETC dysfunction as a central feature of AxD and suggest that metabolic adaptation through the G3P shuttle links mitochondrial dysfunction to glycolytic reprogramming and lipid accumulation. More broadly, these results provide new insight into how astrocyte dysfunction drives molecular pathways implicated in neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Optimizing Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation: The Effects of Pulse Parameters on Corticospinal Excitability
Article.Authors: Proulx, B.; Hasani, S. A.; Frechette, A.-J.; Hamel, R.; Tremblay, S.; Cote, S.; Lepage, J.-F.
Article.Abstract: Objective. Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) is a repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) protocol used in clinical settings to alleviate symptoms of psychiatric disorders. Although the pulse parameters currently used in iTBS have remained unchanged since the first treatments, recent controllable TMS devices allow for the personalization of pulse shape and duration, opening the possibility of testing the efficacy of other pulse parameters in modulating corticospinal excitability (CSE). Methods. In a repeated-measures design, changes in CSE were induced by the administration of iTBS over the left primary motor cortex under three different conditions: long bidirectional pulse (L-Bi), long quasi-unidirectional pulse (L-QU), and a control short quasi-unidirectional pulse (S-QU). We assessed TMS-induced motor evoked potentials before and up to 70 minutes after iTBS. We hypothesized that L-QU pulses would induce greater facilitation than other conditions. Results. A mixed linear model showed that all conditions induced increased MEPs compared to baseline. However, the L-Bi pulse led to a larger and more sustained MEP increase than both unidirectional pulses, while the S-QU pulse appeared less effective in modulating CSE. We observed large within- and between-subject variability in responsiveness to the iTBS protocols. Conclusion. These results suggest that L-Bi pulses in iTBS protocols are more potent than unidirectional pulses in inducing CSE changes in the cortex of healthy adults. The individual variability in response to iTBS and the potential clinical relevance of these findings are discussed.

Article.Title: Suzetrigine-evoked analgesia is potentiated by Nav1.7 null-related opioid mechanisms.
Article.Authors: Riquelme, E. V.; Didenko, O.; Gossage, S.; Isensee, J.; Hucho, T.; wood, j.
Article.Abstract: The genetic evidence for an essential role of sodium channel Nav1.7 in human pain conditions is compelling. Unfortunately, potent selective channel blockers of Nav1.7 are not useful analgesics because they have deleterious side effects, particularly on the autonomic nervous system. Here we have evaluated the downstream mechanisms induced by Nav1.7 loss in utero. Nav1.1 compensates for loss of Nav1.7 in sensory neurons and antisense Nav1.1 oligonucleotides diminish excitability in Nav1.7 embryonic null sensory neurons. Enhanced endogenous opioid signalling contributes substantially to analgesia. This is linked to altered gene expression that potentiates opioid signalling through lowered levels of proteins that terminate G-protein signalling (RGS4 and RGS8). There is also enhanced opioid drive through increased enkephalin levels linked to lowered sodium levels in Nav1.7 null neurons. Opioid signalling is the main driver of analgesia, but enhanced potassium channel expression (KCNC4 KCNK2, KCNMB2, KCNAB3) all implicated in pain control, may also contribute to the small level of naloxone-resistant analgesia. These findings suggest a potential new route to analgesia, through mimicking the events at Nav1.7 null sensory neuron terminals. Here we demonstrate potentiation of suzetrigine-evoked analgesia with RGS antagonists alone or in combination with normally inactive doses of morphine in formalin-evoked pain and CFA-induced inflammatory pain. Intriguingly, no analgesia is observed with acute pain. Cancer pain is under investigation. These data are of potential clinical interest.

Article.Title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response
Article.Authors: Yang, C.; Lombardi, V.; Uygun, D. S.; Brown, R. E.; McKenna, J. T.; Basheer, R.
Article.Abstract: Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.

Article.Title: NE52-QQ57 attenuates post-ischemia protein phosphorylation in the mouse brain
Article.Authors: Joshi, S.; Zhou, Y.; Zha, X.-m.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Cerebral ischemia induces a reduction in brain pH. GPR4, a proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptor is highly expressed in vascular endothelial cells. Pharmacological inhibition of GPR4 with NE52-QQ57 (NEQQ) reduces ischemia-induced blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and brain injury. To facilitate targeting GPR4 in vivo, it is important to better define the effect of NEQQ on post-ischemia signaling and the pharmacokinetics of NEQQ in vivo. We used Liquid Chromatography-Mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to quantify the concentration of NEQQ in serum, brain, and peripheral tissues. Results: NEQQ administration decreased the phosphorylation of PKA substrates, PKC substrates, ERK1/2, and CREB. LC-MS/MS analysis detected NEQQ in both ipsilateral and contralateral hemisphere of the brain at 5 h and 24 h after reperfusion, demonstrating that NEQQ crosses the BBB. In peripheral tissues, NEQQ exhibited highest level in kidney and lowest in the heart. In sham controls, average serum concentrations were ~4 and 0.9 g/g at 5 and 24 h, respectively. Following tMCAO, ipsilateral brain exhibited higher levels as compared to the contralateral side at 5 h while the difference diminished at 24 h. Conclusions: NEQQ attenuated the ischemia-induced activation of multiple signaling pathways. NEQQ exhibited broad distribution in peripheral organs, and its brain level was sufficient for GPR4 inhibition at 24 h after injection. These findings support the use of NEQQ as a pharmacological inhibitor of GPR4-mediated signaling following ischemic stroke.

Article.Title: Therapeutic AIBP expression contributes to synaptic preservation and vision restoration against glaucomatous neuroinflammation
Article.Authors: Bastola, T.; Hwang, S.; Shen, Z.; Choi, S.-H.; Choi, S.; Jang, E.; Poudel, M.; Kim, K.-Y.; Miller, Y. I.; Weinreb, R. N.; Ju, W.-K.
Article.Abstract: Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) is the only approved treatment for glaucoma, yet retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration and vision loss often progress despite reducing IOP. Apolipoprotein A-I binding protein (AIBP) stabilizes ATP-binding cassette subfamily A member 1 (ABCA1) and promotes cholesterol efflux, thus controlling cholesterol-rich lipid rafts and restraining lipid raft-dependent Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) inflammatory signaling. In DBA/2J mice, a single intravitreal injection of AAV2-hAIBP at 5 months protected RGCs and preserved pattern electroretinogram and pattern visual evoked potential responses at 10 months, even though IOP was indistinguishable from empty-vector controls. AAV2-hAIBP preserved CaMKII and synapsin phosphorylation, restored synaptophysin and PSD95 in the inner plexiform layer, and reduced the expression of TLR4, complement C1q, IBA1, IL-1b, and IL-6 induction in Muller glia and microglia. Comparable protection was observed in microbead-induced ocular hypertension in C57BL/6 mice, both when the AAV2-hAIBP was delivered before microbead injection and when it was delivered after IOP elevation was established. Elevated IOP reduced endogenous retinal AIBP and ABCA1 expression, and AAV2-hAIBP restored both. Protection required the TLR4-binding domain, as an AIBP mutant lacking this domain failed to preserve RGCs. Conversely, AIBP knockout retinas exhibited increased CaMKII phosphorylation and reduced synaptophysin in the absence of elevated IOP. These findings identify synaptic preservation through the AIBP-TLR4 axis as an IOP-independent therapeutic mechanism and support AAV2-hAIBP as a candidate gene therapy for glaucoma.

Article.Title: From Intrinsic Topography to Cognitive Prediction: Benchmarking Approaches to Personalized Cortical Parcellation
Article.Authors: Inceler, Y. C.; Burkhardt, M.; Giessing, C.; Kristanto, D.
Article.Abstract: Personalized functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) adapts cortical parcellations to individual functional anatomy. Various methods have been proposed that differ in how they combine group-level information, spatial constraints, and individual functional data. Using the Human Connectome Project Young Adult dataset (N = 947), we compared five personalized parcellation methods and a standard group-level atlas. For each method, we calculated functional homogeneity, test-retest reliability, parcel contiguity, and inter-individual Dice overlap. Personalized parcellation methods generally yielded higher functional homogeneity and lower inter-individual Dice than the group atlas, while test-retest reliability of functional connectivity was high across methods. Parcel contiguity differed across methods: some approaches produced almost entirely contiguous parcels, whereas others frequently produced spatially disconnected components, indicating that the detection of candidate ectopic variants depends partly on the parcellation strategy. We also examined whether connectivity and topographic features were associated with and predicted general intelligence (g). Using structural equation modeling, intra-individual parcel size variability and inter-individual parcel size similarity derived from the hierarchical Bayesian method (gMSHBM) were positively associated with g, whereas no corresponding association survived correction for the other methods. Using kernel ridge regression, functional connectivity significantly predicted g, with the group atlas yielding the highest predictive accuracy, consistent with a potential advantage of cross-individual spatial correspondence for edge-wise prediction. Finally, we assessed robustness across four preprocessing pipelines. Although gMSHBM parcellations were not re-estimated, relative between-method patterns in several spatial characteristics were largely preserved. In contrast, brain-behavior associations involving time-series-derived features varied substantially with preprocessing, whereas parcel-size associations were more stable. We conclude that personalized parcellation approaches are associated with distinct trade-offs in spatial correspondence, topographic variability, and downstream predictive utility. The choice of parcellation strategy therefore affects both the properties of individualized maps and the brain-behavior information derived from them.

Article.Title: Neuropeptide Signaling Promotes Stem-Cell Driven Regeneration in Planarians
Article.Authors: Endara-Arnold, C. E.; Jenkins, J. E.; Villalobos, A. E.; Roberts-Galbraith, R. H.
Article.Abstract: Neurons and neuroendocrine cells produce neuropeptides, which act as long-range signals to modulate organismal state and physiological function. In a few cases, neuropeptides have been thought to promote regeneration, but understanding this connection has been difficult due to the relatively poor regenerative capacity of most traditional model organisms. To test whether neuropeptides drive robust regeneration, we used the highly regenerative asexual planarian flatworm as a model. We began by investigating enzymes that cleave and process pre-propeptides to produce bioactive neuropeptides. We characterized 12 putative neuropeptide-processing enzymes and identified three enzymes, prohormone convertase 2 (pc2), carboxypeptidase E (CPE), and peptidylglycine alpha-hydroxylating monooxygenase (PHM-1) that regulate regeneration through their effects on stem cell differentiation and maintenance. We then investigated 51 of the 52 known neuropeptide-encoding genes in planarians, finding that 16 of these genes promote efficient regeneration and/or stem cell function. Our work indicates that diverse neuropeptides regulate endogenous pluripotent stem cells during homeostasis and in robust regeneration. Our data supports a key role for neuropeptide signaling in planarians to promote a pro-regenerative state, which could be valuable to mimic in regenerative therapies.

Article.Title: Acoustic Context Shapes Cortical Encoding of Spectral Discrimination in Normal and Impaired Hearing
Article.Authors: Undurraga Lucero, J. A.; Stefancu, I.; Rekswinkel, M.; Simonsen, L. B.; Van Eeckhoutte, M.
Article.Abstract: The auditory change complex (ACC) provides a cortical measure of acoustic discrimination, yet the mechanisms shaping responses to spectrotemporally complex sounds remain poorly understood. We investigated how acoustic context and temporal-envelope variability influence cortical encoding of spectral contrast in normal-hearing (NH) and hearing-impaired (HI) listeners. Electroencephalography (EEG) was used to record ACCs and auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs) evoked by spectrotemporally modulated stimuli. We compared conventional spectro-temporal modulations (STMs) with a novel discrete spectro-temporal modulation (DSTM) paradigm, examined temporal roving, and evaluated cortical responses to spectral contrast in NH and HI listeners. ACCs elicited by DSTM stimuli were larger and more symmetrical across transition directions than those elicited by conventional STMs. Temporal roving markedly reduced responses to intensity changes while largely preserving responses to spectral changes, indicating a partial dissociation between intensity-driven and spectrally driven cortical discrimination. ACC responses decreased systematically with spectral contrast and were weaker and delayed in HI listeners. By contrast, ASSRs remained highly detectable and showed no systematic dependence on spectral contrast, supporting a distinction between contrast-sensitive cortical discrimination and ongoing envelope encoding. Temporal roving further enhanced separation between NH and HI listeners. ACC response strength was significantly associated with behavioural STM discrimination thresholds and explained variance beyond age and audiometric thresholds. These findings demonstrate that cortical representations of spectral discrimination are shaped by acoustic context and temporal-envelope statistics. Temporal roving attenuates intensity-driven responses while preserving spectrally driven discrimination, providing insight into cortical encoding of spectrotemporal contrast and its relationship to perceptual performance.

Article.Title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI
Article.Authors: Das, A.; Dutta, S.; Pradhan, L. K.; Chen, J.; Wang, N.; Gao, X.
Article.Abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI.

Article.Title: How aging reshapes implicit learning: behavioral and oscillatory evidence from an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm.
Article.Authors: Fricker, F.; Dornier, V.; Buzi, G.; Morantin, M.; Doidy, F.; Clochon, P.; Goujon, A.; Barbeau, E. J.; Hinault, T. T.
Article.Abstract: Most of everyday memory formation occurs without deliberate intent, yet the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding and their reorganization with age remain poorly understood. The present study investigated age-related changes in implicit learning using an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm (the Disjunctive Inference Implicit Learning Test, DIILT) in 31 younger and 35 older adults, paired with a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and a one-month delayed recognition measure. Behaviorally, younger adults rapidly acquired novel implicit associations across the learning phase, whereas older adults showed persistent reliance on familiar items and limited improvement for novel associations. Critically, both groups successfully retained novel associations after one month, with implicitly learned associations showing greater long-term stability than explicitly encoded ones regardless of age. At the neural level, younger adults exhibited early posterior theta engagement for novel compared to familiar items, which disappeared by the end of learning, consistent with novelty-driven associative encoding. Older adults showed no such theta modulation for novel items, pointing to reorganization of the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding. Theta dynamics predicted immediate recognition in younger adults but not in older adults who rather showed theta association with processing speed, suggesting an age-related shift from memory-specific binding to domain-general cognitive resource allocation, consistent with neural maintenance frameworks of cognitive aging. These findings demonstrate that implicit encoding produces durable memory traces across the lifespan but relies on reorganized oscillatory dynamics in aging, with implications for understanding how cognitive aging reshapes everyday memory formation.

Article.Title: A human model of the neurodevelopmental metabolic shift
Article.Authors: Pettit, S. N.; Kornfeld, A. T.; Morales, C.; Meffert, M. K.
Article.Abstract: The neurodevelopmental metabolic shift transitions the metabolic pathways used by neurons to generate energy in order to critically support survival, growth, and functional maturation. To better understand metabolic regulation during human neuronal development and to facilitate the study of early neurodevelopmental disorders impacting this time window, establishing a combination of effective human model systems will be required. We report that a streamlined strategy using the genetic induction of neuronal differentiation by NGN2 expression recapitulates hallmarks of metabolic reprogramming associated with neurodevelopment. The approach is refined to increase the uniformity of differentiation, allowing reproducible high-throughput assessments. We validate appropriate readouts of metabolic function, including gene expression, cellular respiration, and mitochondrial morphology, which can be combined to present a cohesive assessment of metabolic status and reliance on oxidative phosphorylation relative to glycolysis. Collectively, the strategy presented will enhance the ability of investigators to gather foundational and disease-related insights into regulatory mechanisms of the metabolic shift critical to successful neuronal differentiation.

Article.Title: Identification of Synchronously Active Cells (ISAC) to study the activity of cell assemblies
Article.Authors: Makdah, G.; Wiener, S.; Todorova, R.; Pompili, M. N.
Article.Abstract: Cell assemblies--groups of neurons that fire synchronously--are central to neuronal computation. Technological advances now permit the simultaneous recording of large neuronal populations; however, many existing cell assembly detection algorithms rely on simplified measures such as pairwise correlations, failing to capture higher-order synchrony and thereby missing a rich repertoire of assemblies present in the data. To address these limitations, we developed Identification of Synchronously Active Cells (ISAC), which performs a rigorous, iterative search across all recorded units, leveraging the full dimensionality of the dataset to detect groups that fire together above chance. Using simulated recordings with ground-truth assemblies of increasing complexity, we demonstrate that ISAC considerably outperforms currently used algorithms in identifying synchronously active cells. Finally, we show that applying ISAC to experimental recordings uncovers novel features of assembly formation and dynamics. The power and sensitivity of ISAC can thus enable insights that remain inaccessible with existing methods.

Article.Title: Intranasal L-MYC Neural Stem Cells Restore Neurovascular and Neuroimmune Homeostasis After TBI via CX3CL1 Upregulation and ICAM-1 Downregulation
Article.Authors: Enright, B.; Cheng, J. P.; Adhikarla, V.; Vasquez, I.; Yuan, Y.-C.; Bondi, C. O.; Rockne, R. C.; Kline, A. E.; Gutova, M.
Article.Abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers persistent neuroimmune and neurovascular dysfunction that contributes to secondary brain injury and limits recovery. Here, we investigated whether a single intranasal dose of LMNSC01 could reprogram neuroinflammatory and neurovascular responses post TBI and whether these effects were conserved across biological sex. Immunocompetent male and female rats underwent a controlled cortical impact (CCI) or Sham surgery and 7 days later received a single bolus dose of LMNSC01 (6 x10^6 cells/dose) or vehicle. Integrated histological and transcriptomic analyses and multiplex tissue ELISA were used to characterize injury- and treatment-associated responses. CCI induced persistent but sex-dependent transcriptional changes. Male rats exhibited prominent innate immune, adhesion, extracellular matrix, and tissue remodeling responses, whereas females demonstrated broader activation of microglial, interferon, complement, MHC/antigen presentation, and humoral/adaptive immune pathways. LMNSC01 treatment reprogrammed these distinct injury states through partially sex-specific mechanisms. In males, LMNSC01 increased endogenous immune-regulatory mediators, including Il1rn, and reduced pathways associated with adhesion and immune cell trafficking. In females, treatment decreased expression of genes related to microglial, leukocyte, MHC/antigen presentation, cytokine, and adhesion pathways, and reduced macrophage- and CD45 positive cell signatures. Despite these sex-dependent transcriptional changes, LMNSC01 produced conserved protein changes in both sexes, reducing injury associated ICAM-1 and restoring CX3CL1 proteins, proposing a novel molecular mechanism of LMNSCs modulating endothelial activation and neuron-microglia communication post injury. Our study provides further insight into sex differences in responses to injury and treatment after TBI and highlights candidate repair mechanisms, supporting further development of LMNSC01 as a minimally invasive therapy for TBI.

Article.Title: A rapid, genetically-tractable human iPSC-derived model for studying tissue-resident macrophage biology in Alzheimer's and other diseases
Article.Authors: Lee, H.; Peppler, G. B.; Sewell, M.; Münch, A.; Podlesny-Drabiniok, A.; Kim, J. J.; Orrick, J.; Marcora, E.; Goate, A. M.
Article.Abstract: Large-scale genetic and preclinical studies strongly implicate myeloid cells, particularly brain-resident macrophages, in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Efferocytic clearance of apoptotic cells and other cholesterol-rich cellular debris is a core macrophage function and represents an active area of AD research. However, human tissue-resident macrophages remain difficult to model in vitro as they acquire their transcriptional and functional identities in response to signals from their host tissue microenvironment. Many existing differentiation protocols mimic human brain macrophage developmental trajectories, but these protocols rely either on multi-step cytokine cocktails and lengthy differentiation or transduction of multiple transcription factors, both of which introduce variability and complicate genetic manipulation. To address these limitations, we developed a simplified protocol that generates high-purity (>90% CD45+CD11b+) human iPSC-derived macrophage-like cells (iMacs) from cryopreservable erythro-myeloid progenitor (EMP)-like intermediates in 19 days, including a final 7-day maturation step driven by macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) alone. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that iMacs show enrichment for phagocytic and lysosomal programs, processes integral to efferocytosis. At both the transcriptional and protein level, iMacs have higher expression of scavenger receptors such as CD36, CD163 and MRC1, and of AD risk genes such as TREM2. Functionally, iMacs show enhanced phagocytic uptake of diverse substrates relative to iPSC-derived microglia, including carboxylated latex beads, zymosan, amyloid-{beta} 1-42, and amyloid-{beta} 1-40, and exhibit expanded lysosomal mass. Robust TREM2 expression and signaling make iMacs a sensitive platform for interrogating TREM2 biology, with markedly higher phosphorylation of SYK and PLC{gamma}2 in response to TREM2 engagement compared to iPSC-derived microglia. iMacs also tolerate lipid-mediated siRNA transfection with high survival and knockdown efficiency, enabling rapid genetic perturbation of AD risk genes. Together, these features make iMacs a practical, scalable, and genetically tractable human macrophage model for studying the regulation and cell biology of core macrophage functions that are known to play critical roles in AD, aging, and other disorders.

Article.Title: What EEG doesn't see: a whole-brain MEG map of sleep spindles and slow oscillations
Article.Authors: Calvel, A.; Greenlaw, K.; Steele, C. J.; Coffey, E. B. J.
Article.Abstract: Sleep spindles and slow oscillations (SOs) are hallmarks of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, linked to memory consolidation and restorative functions. They are usually detected in one or a few scalp electroencephalography (EEG) channels with parameters that vary across studies, and serve as the reference even in magnetoencephalography (MEG), fMRI and intracranial studies. We argue that these choices filter which neural activity is captured. Nineteen young adults took a daytime nap during simultaneous MEG and EEG. Using MEG source imaging across 416 cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions, we mapped the amplitude and density of SOs (0.5-4 Hz, and 0.5-2 and 2-4 Hz separately) and of spindles (9-18 Hz, and slow, 9-12.9 Hz, and fast, 13-18 Hz, separately), and related each region's activity to a single scalp derivation (Cz-M1). Both rhythms were detected throughout the brain, including the thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, basal ganglia and cerebellum. The balance between bands varied across regions: fast spindles predominated over slow spindles along the dorsal midline, around the central sulcus and in the thalamus, slow spindles predominated in occipital cortex and the cerebellar hemispheres, and 2-4 Hz SOs were relatively most prominent in occipital cortex. Amplitude and density formed reliable but distinct maps: regions with larger fast spindles also had more of them, whereas SOs, and slow spindles once source depth was controlled, were larger where they were less frequent. More SOs were detected in every region than at Cz-M1, whereas more fast spindles were detected at Cz-M1 than in any single region. Around the SO, slow-spindle activity had the same timing at the scalp and in the sources, but the up-state increase in fast-spindle activity seen at the scalp was absent from local sources. Slow spindles were the most strongly shared events, and sensorimotor sources the most scalp-like. Thus, a single scalp derivation offers a selective and partly composite view of sleep oscillations, with implications for interpreting their functional roles and for targeting them with closed-loop auditory stimulation

Article.Title: p70 ribosomal protein S6 Kinase (p70S6K) as a potential peripheral biomarker for autistic symptoms in 16p11.2 deletion and duplication syndromes
Article.Authors: Morella, I.; Hall, J.; Butter, C.; Goldie, C.; Evans, G.; Ali, N.; Burlinson-Diaz, N.; Burkitt-Wright, E.; Caraiscos, I.; More, L.; Green, J.; van den Bree, M.; Brambilla, R.

Individuals with syndromes caused by micro-deletions and -duplications in the proximal region of 16p11.2 have increased likelihood of neurodevelopmental and mental health symptoms, as well as cardiometabolic disorder. However, considerable phenotypic variability complicates prediction of risk, disease trajectory and treatment response. The identification of biomarkers in easily accessible tissues, such as Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells (PBMCs), could help diagnosis and prognosis, yet remains an unmet clinical need. Converging evidence implicates dysregulation of ubiquitous signalling pathways, including ERK and mTOR cascades, in altered protein synthesis across NDDs of both idiopathic and genetic origin.
