We established increased psychopathology and cognitive deficits in individuals with 16p11.2 deletion and duplication syndromes, compared to sibling controls. Furthermore, we identified a significant reduction of p70 S6 kinase (p70S6K) levels in PBMCs across both genotypes compared to controls. Notably, the magnitude of p70S6K reduction correlated with the severity of autistic symptoms independent of CNV genotype. In contrast, MAPK3/ERK1 protein levels mirrored the gene dosage, showing increased expression in individuals with the duplication and reduced levels in those with the deletion. These findings suggest that peripheral alterations in p70S6K may relate to variation in autism-related traits within individuals with 16p11.2 deletion and duplication syndromes, indicating that it may repreesent a potential biomarker of autism-associated symptom severity in this genetically at-risk group.

Article.Title: The Roads Not Taken: The Neural Dynamics of Lexical Alternatives During Free Language Production
Article.Authors: Liobashevski, D.; Friedman, D.; Flinker, A.; Goldstein, A.
Article.Abstract: Human language allows multiple ways to express the same thought, raising the possibility that several lexical candidates are activated in parallel before a single word is selected for articulation. While their co-activation is assumed by computational models of word production, until recently, there has been no practical way to estimate the identity of these candidates in unconstrained speech, nor to directly probe their representation in neural activity. Here, we combined high-density electrocorticography recorded during real-world conversation with context-sensitive large language model (LLM) to characterize, for the first time, how these lexical candidates are represented in the brain. We focus on the candidates which remain unsaid, referred to as the "alternatives", by only using samples where the LLM predictions do not include the produced word. We provide evidence for three computational principles of the neural dynamics of lexical alternatives: (1) multiple lexical alternatives to each word in conversation are distinctly represented in neural activity prior to articulation; (2) the set of lexical alternatives is rapidly updated from one word to the next; and (3) alternatives to future words are represented along with alternatives to the upcoming word. Together, these findings reveal that spontaneous speech production is supported by a broad, dynamically evolving and forward-looking set of lexical alternatives, providing a neural account of how the brain prepares not only the words that are spoken, but also those that remain unsaid.

Article.Title: Pupil Dynamics Reflect Uncertainty-Driven Adjustments of Probability Learning
Article.Authors: Greenhouse-Tucknott, A.; Foucault, C.; Buot, A.; Meyniel, F.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive learning in dynamic environments depends on the brain's ability to represent and respond to uncertainty. Changes in arousal-mediated pupil diameter provide insight into the neural basis of this process. Prior work has focused on magnitude-based inference tasks and revealed that learning is primarily influenced by the detection of change points and the corresponding modulation of arousal. In comparison, the role of arousal systems in learning contexts where changes are harder to detect, such as in probability learning, remains poorly understood. Here, we combined pupillometry with a probability learning task in which human participants estimated a hidden generative probability of stimuli that changed abruptly and unpredictably. A Bayesian ideal observer model was used to estimate trial-by-trial learning rates and two uncertainty-associated factors: change point probability (the probability that the generative process has abruptly changed) and prior uncertainty (about the current beliefs on this generative process). In line with normative theory, participants relied on prior uncertainty to adjust learning rates. Pupil analyses revealed temporally distinct representations of uncertainty, with phasic dilations tracking change point probability and tonic pupil dilations tracking prior uncertainty. Mediation analyses further indicated that both phasic and tonic pupil signals partially carried the effects of change point probability and prior uncertainty on learning, respectively. Critically, high tonic arousal weakened the coupling between phasic pupil responses and change point probability, accompanied by a reduced influence of change point probability on learning. Together, our results demonstrate that probability learning in a dynamic environment is underpinned by computationally rational integration of latent uncertainty factors and its contribution to belief updating,regulated through arousal-associated responses.

Article.Title: Sparse Stimulus Generation Improves Reverse Correlation Efficiency and Interpretability
Article.Authors: Gargano, J. A.; Rice, A.; Chari, D. A.; Parrell, B.; Lammert, A. C.
Article.Abstract: Reverse correlation is a widely-used and well-established method for probing latent perceptual representations in which subjects render subjective preference responses to ambiguous stimuli. Stimuli are purposefully designed to have no direct relationship with the target representation (e.g., they are randomly-generated), a property which makes each individual stimulus minimally informative toward reconstructing the target, and often difficult to interpret for subjects. As a result, a large number of stimulus-response pairs must be gathered from a given subject in order for reconstructions to be of sufficient quality, making the task fatiguing. Recent work has demonstrated that the number of trials needed can be substantially reduced using a compressive sensing framework that incorporates the assumption that the target representation can be sparsely represented in some basis into the reconstruction process. Here, we introduce an alternative method that incorporates the sparsity assumption directly into stimulus generation, which holds promise not only for improving efficiency, but also for improving the interpretability of stimuli from subject's perspective. We develop this new method as a mathematical variation of the compressive sensing approach, before conducting one simulation study and two human subjects experiments to assess the benefits of this method to reconstruction quality, sample size efficiency, and subjective interpretability. Results show that sparse stimulus generation improves all three of these areas relative to conventional reverse correlation approaches, and also relative to compressive sensing in most conditions.

Article.Title: Clutter does not affect the spatial tuning of * category representations in human object-selective cortex *
Article.Authors: Matic, K.; Tafech, I.; Pettini, L.; Hirschhorn, R.; Görgen, K.; König, P.; Cichy, R. M.; Haynes, J.-D.; Bogler, C.
Article.Abstract: Natural vision is frequently impaired when the visual field is crowded with multiple competing objects. One way the visual system might counteract this interference is by relying on more localized object representations that are less prone to interference from objects at other locations and that are known to be prevalent also in higher-level visual cortex. If object encoding under clutter indeed uses more localized representations, then classifiers trained to recognize objects from one region of the visual field should generalize less well to other regions of the visual field in the presence of clutter compared to isolated objects. Here we tested this by measuring participants' brain signals with fMRI while they viewed objects presented either alone or within cluttered arrays. Consistent with prior work, category decoding accuracy was significantly reduced in clutter. However, we found that even classifiers trained directly on cluttered arrays generalize robustly across spatial positions, comparable to classifiers trained on isolated objects. This finding challenges the idea that clutter preferentially disrupts position-tolerant representations.

Article.Authors: Davis, E. E.; Davis, S. W.; Olsen, R. K.; Campbell, K. L.
Article.Abstract: While explicit associative memory declines with age, implicit associative memory remains preserved. Associative priming was defined as faster reaction times (behavioural associative priming) and less activation for intact than rearranged pairs at retrieval (neural associative priming). Whole-brain analyses revealed neural associative priming in occipitotemporal and frontal regions that did not differ by age. A region of interest analysis (using subject-specific masks of medial temporal lobe regions) showed that only older adults had greater posterior hippocampal activation to intact than rearranged items at test, though activation in the hippocampus did not relate to behavioural associative priming. In contrast, greater behavioural associative priming was related to greater neural associative priming in the perirhinal cortex in both age groups. Together, these findings suggest that implicit associative priming remains intact with age, possibly because it relies on additional processes outside the hippocampus such as perirhinal-dependent unitization.

Article.Title: Physics-informed neural networks for subject-specific recovery of travelling-wave structure in resting-state fMRI
Article.Authors: Taghipour L., P.; Sotero, R. C.
Article.Abstract: Resting-state BOLD fluctuations show reproducible spatiotemporal propagation that is not accounted for by conventional zero-lag functional connectivity. A soft anatomical prior derived from each subject's diffusion-tensor structural connectivity is included to encode the hypothesis that white-matter pathways constrain wave direction. The pipeline is validated on synthetic data by three simulation studies, creating the operating envelope, and then applied to 41 cognitively normal participants of the ADNI 3 cohort. A within-subject ablation showed that mean alignment between recovered wave directions and underlying white matter geometry increased by a small but statistically detectable amount when using the structural prior (one-sidedWilcoxon signed-rank, p = 0.026), with exploratory network-level effects most evident in the visual, dorsal-attention, and salience/ventral-attention networks. Article.Authors: Antony, M. S.; Miller, P. A.; Armstrong, W. P.; DiLeone, L.; Knuth, O.; Gill, M.; Luong, T.; Chamiec-Case, E.; Barik, A.; Chesler, A. T.; Lindsay, S. A.; Chee, M. J.; Jackson, A. C.

These subpopulations are distinguished by the selective enrichment of the Tacr3 and Cartpt transcripts, with each comprising approximately half of the total MCH population. However, these subpopulations remain poorly understood owing to limited genetic targeting tools. We first validated a Tacr3-Flpo mouse line for the genetic targeting of the Type I MCH subpopulation. We then generated an intersectional Type I MCH neuron reporter line to visualize Type I axonal projections. In parallel, we injected a dual recombinase mouse line with the intersectional genetic targeting viruses, Conditional Viral Expression by Ribozyme Guided Degradation (ConVERGD), and identified overlapping and distinct projections by Type I and Type II MCH neurons using fluorescence microscopy, super-resolution imaging, and high-spatial resolution fiber mapping. Article.Title: Neuronal FICD shapes motivated behavior through modulation of dopamine receptor dynamics
Article.Authors: Weaver, K. J.; Abdon, B.; Toth, B.; Jack, A.; Giblin, W.; Burgess, C. R.; Pletcher, S. D.; truttmann, m. c.
Article.Abstract: Motivated behaviors rely on dopaminergic signaling, which in turn depends on the correct folding and trafficking of receptors through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Within the ER, the AMPylase enzyme FICD acts as a molecular rheostat through its modification of the chaperone BiP, dynamically tuning the organelle's responsiveness to folding perturbations and cellular stress. While the biochemistry of FICD is well-established, its role in complex animal behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we identify FICD as a conserved contributor to the generation of motivated behavior. In Drosophila, pan-neuronal knockdown of dFic significantly reduces feeding, spontaneous locomotion, and reward-seeking behavior. These alterations occur without disrupting circadian architecture, motor capacity, or homeostatic hunger, indicating a specific loss of motivational drive. Depleting dFic within subsets of dopamine receptor-expressing (Dop1R1) neurons recapitulates these behavioral alterations. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that dFic depletion does not induce a canonical unfolded protein response, pointing to a specific post-transcriptional alteration rather than global ER stress. At the molecular level, dysregulated dFic alters the localization and abundance of Dop1R1. Finally, we demonstrate that this regulatory axis is evolutionarily conserved, as loss of FICD similarly diminishes motivated behaviors in C. elegans and mice. Together, these findings implicate FICD in the generation of motivated behavior and link dynamic control of ER proteostasis to dopamine-receptor maturation.

Article.Title: HERO: A hierarchy-aware analysis pipeline for reducing and refining whole-brain atlas-mapped cellular datasets
Article.Authors: Shipman, A. L.; Centanni, S. W.
Article.Abstract: Advances in high-throughput mesoscale microscopy and machine learning-based image analysis pipelines have made unbiased whole-brain imaging widely accessible. However, translating the resulting atlas-mapped datasets into biologically meaningful results remains a substantial barrier owing to their sheer magnitude and complex hierarchical organization. Consequently, reporting structure and analysis methods vary widely across studies, undermining rigor and reproducibility. To address this, we developed a user-friendly data reduction workflow, HERO (Hierarchy-aware Expression Region Organization), designed to perform hierarchy-aware selection, refinement, ranking, and visualization of whole-brain cell detection datasets. The workflow is customizable to specific needs, requires minimal coding experience, and outputs transparent, curated results. HERO functions as a seamless plug-in within larger-scale whole-brain cell detection analysis pipelines, providing efficient, unbiased region selection to streamline subsequent statistical analyses and comparative evaluations. Although HERO is developed with mouse cell-detection datasets, it can be applied to any atlas-mapped dataset that contains hierarchical information. Here, we applied the HERO pipeline to example cell detection datasets containing afferent cells from the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and the insular cortex (insula). HERO provided top projecting regions consistent with historical tracing studies for the BST (e.g., amygdalar and hypothalamic regions) and the insula (e.g., somatosensory, autonomic, and interoceptive regions). Furthermore, the refinement step of HERO provides additional enriched regions originally obscured in the primary ranked outputs, such as memory- and emotion-associated structures. With HEROs dynamic processing, we were able to identify top-projecting regions consistent with the literature and, additionally, find regions often obscured in these large datasets. In sum, HERO offers a standardized analysis workflow to reduce whole-brain cell-detection datasets, transforming raw regional cell counts into curated results and advancing the effectiveness, interpretability, and accessibility of whole-brain imaging in neuroscience.

Article.Title: Criticality-related dynamics accompany long-term functional decline in primary cortical MEA cultures
Article.Authors: Escobar, A.; Gil-Bea, F. J.; Rodriguez-Gomez, L.
Article.Abstract: Primary cortical neuron cultures are widely used to study network development and decline, but their long-term electrophysiological trajectories are poorly characterized. We used multi-electrode arrays to longitudinally monitor Wistar rat cortical cultures for up to ~730 days in vitro (DIV), combining activity measures with survival analysis and criticality metrics. Wells shared an early developmental phase, with mean firing rate peaking at 12-14 Hz around DIV 100-150, before diverging into two phenotypes: early-death wells, showing progressive loss of burst organization, longer inter-burst intervals, shorter bursts, and steep declines in active-electrode recruitment; and long-survival wells, which sustained organized bursting and measurable activity well beyond DIV 400, in some cases past DIV 700. Cox proportional-hazards modeling with FDR correction across thirteen candidate features identified burst duration, inter-burst interval, synchrony, mean firing rate, branching ratio, and Kappa index as significant predictors of time to network failure. Criticality metrics offered the most mechanistic insight: in early-death wells, branching ratio declined toward zero and Kappa index rose toward its upper bound as networks approached silencing. Beyond their average levels, the rate of change of branching ratio and Kappa index over recordings was the strongest correlate of survival time among all criticality metrics. Neuronal avalanche size and duration exponents and their scaling relation, remained consistent with scale-free dynamics in both phenotypes while networks were active, though avalanche occurrence rate declined progressively in early-death wells without reaching significance as an independent predictor. These results show that long-term network survival is not determined by firing rate alone, but by preserved burst organization, sustained electrode recruitment and near-critical propagation dynamics. This work offers one of the longest electrophysiological characterizations of rodent cortical cultures to date and identifies criticality-based metrics as promising tools for predicting network decline and evaluating interventions to preserve long-term neuronal function.

Article.Title: Deciphering auditory neuroprogenitor stemness for large-scale neuronal screening
Article.Authors: Rousset, F.; Pepe, L.; Sarhadi, M.; Lemeille, S.; Sgroi, S.; Oberhauser, L.; Daskalou, D.; Ilmjarv, S.; Braun, S.; Senn, P.
Article.Abstract: Sensorineural hearing loss can arise from damage to sensory hair cells, auditory neurons or their synaptic connections, with auditory neuropathy and cochlear synaptopathy highlighting the importance of neural integrity for hearing. The mammalian cochlea has limited capacity to regenerate lost auditory neurons. Understanding the molecular programs that sustain cochlear progenitor expansion and neurogenic competence could support neuronal regeneration and provide renewable models for auditory drug discovery. We previously established that WNT activation combined with dual SMAD inhibition (CHIR-DS) supports scalable expansion and neuronal differentiation of mouse auditory neuroprogenitors (ANPGs). Here, we characterize the transcriptional, chromatin and metabolic changes associated with the induced state. RNA-seq and ATAC-seq identified reduced Id1 and Id2 expression and increased accessibility at proneural basic helix-loop-helix motifs, alongside transcriptional enrichment of translation, mTOR and glucose-metabolism programs. Compared with growth-factor controls, CHIR-DS-treated ANPGs showed slight increase in glycolysis at early passage. However, after long-term expansion, both glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration were markedly enhanced. Human fetal ANPGs also responded to CHIR-DS with increased sphere growth and retained neural differentiation capacity, providing proof of concept beyond the mouse system. Finally, neurons derived from stemness-induced ANPGs (siANs) supported a 384-well reporter assay and a 2,560-compound pilot screen that nominated candidate neurite-outgrowth enhancers. Together, these findings validate the pathway basis of ANPG stemness induction, characterize the resulting molecular and metabolic state, and demonstrate human feasibility and a neuronal screening application.

Article.Authors: Schweiger, H. E.; Robbins, A.; Hernandez, S.; Moreno-Ochando, A.; Cline, I.; Doganyigit, K.; Mouzaya, M.; Hussain, K.; Pang, Z. P.; Duan, J.; Salama, S. R.; Pollen, A. A.; Bhaduri, A.; Haussler, D.; Teodorescu, M.; Mostajo-Radji, M. A.

Here we introduce PULSE, a foundation model developed using over 900 hours of high-density microelectrode array recordings of in vitro and ex vivo neural tissue. We show that this single model can address two open questions: how disease-associated variants alter network development, and how naive circuits encode information. PULSE revealed accelerated network maturation in held-out human 16p11.2-deletion organoids. It also revealed a change in network coordination shared with SHANK3 deficiency. Article.Title: Reuse of learned subtask representations during human planning
Article.Authors: Seak, L. C. U.; Luettgau, L.; Eckstein, M. K.; Moran, R.; Dolan, R. J.
Article.Abstract: The notion of a compositional reuse of previously learned problem solutions predicts that the human brain should reinstate such learned subtask representations during planning. Here, we test this in a value-ranking task implemented in an online and a magnetoencephalography (MEG) experiment, respectively. Participants first learned pairwise rankings and subsequently solved problems where these learned rankings could either be reused or required reordering. Behaviourally, in the online experiment, we show the availability of a reusable subtask structure improved accuracy, with computational modelling indicating a greater weighting of subtask-level value when participants could avail of this learnt structure. In MEG, during planning, we show enhanced reactivation of task-relevant subtask representations in the reusable condition, and particularly so early in the experiment. In a subsequent probe task, we show subtask-identity representations generalised to a novel context and that stimuli belonging to the same learned subtask manifest an increase in their neural similarity. Temporally delayed linear modelling (TDLM) revealed forward and backward sequential reactivation at a subtask level, alongside backward stimulus-level replay, with subtask sequenceness varying according to task context. The findings provide convergent behavioural, computational and neural evidence for reactivation and reuse of learnt relational structures for novel problem solving.

Article.Title: Linking anterior cingulate sulcal variability to attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder behavior
Article.Authors: Hadveck, R. F.; Paras, A.; Anctil, M.; Martinez, E.; Gallardo, C. M.; Maboudian, S. A.; Willbrand, E. H.; Weiner, K. S.
Article.Abstract: Background: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is consistently implicated in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ACC variability, including its most variable structure, the paracingulate sulcus (PCGS), has been known since the late 1800s, and since then, has been linked to cognitive control, impulsivity, and psychiatric conditions comorbid with ADHD, including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Yet, the role of the PCGS in ADHD remains unexamined at the individual level. Methods: We characterized PCGS incidence, asymmetry, and morphology in 247 children and adolescents (144 ADHD: 10.9 +/- 2.73 years old, 75% male; 103 neurotypical: 12.2 +/- 3.17 years old, 50% male) from the ADHD-200 dataset. The PCGS was manually identified in FreeSurfer cortical surface reconstructions. Morphometric measures, including sulcal length, depth, and cortical thickness, were extracted and normalized to hemisphere-wide variables. Between-group analyses tested whether PCGS presence, asymmetry, and quantitative morphology differed by diagnosis, while behavioral analyses examined associations with inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and cognitive measures. Age and gender were included as covariates. Results: Analyses revealed that, in both NT and ADHD individuals, there was significant leftward asymmetry in PCGS presence. Between groups, the PCGS was less likely to be present in individuals with ADHD in the left hemisphere. Leftward PCGS absence was also associated with significantly higher ADHD index and hyperactivity-impulsivity scores. Conclusions: These findings advance understanding of how early neurodevelopmental variation in cortical folding may serve as a structural intermediary between genetic liability and the behavioral expression of ADHD.

Article.Authors: Hope, K. T.; Zhang, Y.; Basu, A.; Luo, B.; Chassie, K.; Weiss, R. J.; Yellajoshyula, D.
Article.Abstract: Remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM), a complex structural and signaling network of the nervous system, is essential for CNS development, plasticity, and injury responses, yet how individual neural cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified Gusb-null microglia as a distinct transcriptional population enriched for a core transcriptome shared by immature and disease-associated microglia. Together, these findings establish lysosomal GAG catabolism as a pathway that links ECM remodeling to the acquisition of adult homeostatic microglial identity during CNS development.

Article.Title: Oligodendrocyte stress response as a driver of vascular dementia
Article.Authors: Merour, E.; Ghatage, T.; Corbett, C.; DeBerge, M.; Kunjamma, R.; Ian Steckler, I. S.; Heidari, M.; Sorond, F. A.; Flanagan, M. E.; Thorp, E. B.; Popko, B.
Article.Abstract: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a prevalent and devastating neurocognitive disorder characterized by profound white matter damage, yet the precise cellular mechanisms linking cerebrovascular stress to demyelination remain poorly understood. Adult HF/HBP mice exhibit progressive oligodendroglial cell loss and myelin thinning, followed by cognitive impairments, anxiety-like behavior, and memory deficits that recapitulate clinical features of VaD. Furthermore, we provide translational evidence that the ISR is activated in oligodendrocytes in human cases of cerebrovascular disease. Together, these findings reveal a critical, cell-autonomous role for oligodendroglial ISR activation during cerebrovascular stress and position this pathway as a viable therapeutic target to mitigate VaD pathogenesis.

Article.Abstract: Slowing myopia progression is central to addressing a growing public health concern. Our results show that different myopia control spectacle lenses can be compared on a common optical basis, and that their efficacy is predictable from their optical properties. This work paves the way for rational design of next-generation lenses and for adapting designs to each patient's ocular optics.

Article.Title: Recovering Hidden Neural Oscillatory Modes from Partial Observations through Delay Embedding and Perturbation
Article.Authors: Miyoshi, R.; Ogino, M.; Sekizawa, D.; Oizumi, M.
Article.Abstract: Characterising the oscillatory behaviour generated by neural interactions is central to systems neuroscience because these dynamical properties are linked to brain function. However, inferring latent neural dynamics is challenging because recordings sample only part of the system. Despite its promise, two questions remain: what dynamical information is recoverable through time-delay embedding, and how can recovery be improved? We address both questions using control theory. Our framework centres on factorising the Hankel matrix of delay-embedded observations into an observability matrix and a trajectory matrix with the form of a controllability matrix. We show that their ranks impose complementary constraints on what any delay-embedding method can recover: delay embedding can increase observability rank, while perturbation can increase trajectory rank by exciting otherwise inactive modes. We validate this framework using Hankel DMD in simulations and human electrocorticography (ECoG). In both, perturbation increased the number of fast-decaying mode estimates, whereas greater delay depth increased the number of reliably estimated modes and, in ECoG, extended their frequency range. These results clarify what partial recordings can reveal about neural dynamics and how to reveal more.

Article.Title: Crowding distorts features, not objects: structured target confusions in a 4AFC conjunction task
Article.Authors: Cass, J.; Van der Burg, E.
Article.Abstract: Visual crowding is the disruption of peripheral object identification by nearby flanking clutter. We addressed this with a 4AFC conjunction-report task in which observers reported both the orientation and the brightness of every target. We analysed the data three ways: joint accuracy, accuracy on each feature alone, and the statistical coupling between the two report channels. Orientation reports were principally impaired by orientation-similar flankers within the smallest target-flanker separations, whereas luminance reports were impaired by target-colour-similar flankers across a broader spatial range. Observed joint accuracy was closely predicted by the product of the two marginal accuracies in every condition. A complementary chi-square analysis of the full 4x4 stimulus-response matrices agreed with this conclusion at the most-crowded conditions, while revealing structured response biases that the ratio test could not detect. These biases were present at baseline and were not amplified by crowding. The conjunction errors observed under crowding therefore arose from two largely independent feature-specific failures, rather than from disruption of a representation in which the two features are bound. These results indicate that object-level crowding errors in this paradigm are the downstream signature of two independent feature-level processes rather than the breakdown of an object-level mechanism.

Article.Authors: Ipwanshek, O.; Babin, K.; Gribble, P. L.; Culham, J. C.
Article.Abstract: Virtual reality (VR) offers unique opportunities to study behaviour by allowing the visual environment to be manipulated in ways otherwise impossible in the real world. A central theoretical question is how body-related visual information shapes movement control. Given right-handers' greater dexterity with the right arm, perhaps even seeing a right arm vs. a left arm may engage sensorimotor processes associated with more precise motor control. We examined reaching performance while participants used their own right or left arm to move the manipulandum of a KINARM robot to intercept static targets. Participants wore a VR head-mounted display, calibrated to the robot's physical workspace, in which they saw either the right or left arm holding and moving the manipulandum. The 2 x 2 design allowed for independent manipulation of the controlling arm and virtual arm displayed. As expected, reaches were faster and more accurate when controlled by the right arm. More interestingly, performance was also affected by the seen arm. Participants made straighter reaches when they saw a virtual right arm than a left arm, especially for the right controlling arm. These findings show that precise motor control relies not only on the arm that is actually moved and provides proprioceptive feedback, but also on the visual identity of the arm. The ability to modulate performance using visual features in VR opens new theoretical questions and opportunities for applications such as rehabilitation.

Article.Title: Whole-brain neural substrates of behavioral variability in the larval zebrafish
Article.Authors: Manley, J.; Vaziri, A.
Article.Abstract: Animals engaged in naturalistic behavior can exhibit a large degree of behavioral variability even under sensory invariant conditions. Such behavioral variability can include not only variations of the same behavior, but also variability across qualitatively different behaviors driven by divergent cognitive states, such as fight-or-flight decisions. However, the neural circuit mechanisms that generate such divergent behaviors across trials are not well understood. To investigate this question, here we studied the visual-evoked responses of larval zebrafish to moving objects of various sizes, which we found exhibited highly variable and divergent responses across repetitions of the same stimulus. Given that the neuronal circuits underlying such behaviors span sensory, motor, and other brain areas, we built a novel Fourier light field microscope which enables high-resolution, volumetric imaging across the larval zebrafish during behavior. This enabled us to screen for neural loci which exhibited activity patterns correlated with behavioral variability. We found that despite the highly variable activity of neurons, visual stimuli were robustly encoded at the population level, and the visual-encoding dimensions of neural activity did not explain behavioral variability. This robustness despite apparent neuronal variability was due to the multi-dimensional geometry of the neuronal population dynamics: almost all neural dimensions that were variable across individual trials, i.e. the noise modes, were nearly orthogonal to those encoding for sensory information. Investigating this neuronal variability further, we identified two sparsely-distributed, brain-wide neuronal populations whose pre-motor activity predicted whether the larva would respond to a stimulus and, if so, which direction it would turn on a single-trial level. These populations predicted single-trial behavior seconds before stimulus onset, indicating they encoded time-varying internal states modulating behavior, perhaps organizing behavior over longer timescales or enabling flexible behavior routines. Our results provide the first brain-wide evidence that sensory, motor, and internal variables are represented in a highly mixed fashion across widely distributed neuronal populations and demonstrate that de-mixing each of these components at the neuronal population level is critical to understanding the mechanisms underlying the brain's remarkable flexibility and robustness.

Article.Title: State dependent modulation of optic flow-processing lobula plate cells in butterflies

Article.Abstract: Increasing experimental evidence suggests that biological systems cancel predictable components of sensory signals while maintaining sensitivity to externally induced state changes. This strategy provides task-specific sensor responses for posture, locomotion, and gaze control. A prime example is found in interneurons that respond to visual image shifts resulting from the relative motion between an animal's eyes and its visual surroundings. Such optic flow-processing interneurons, found across phyla and are particularly well characterized in Dipteran and other flying insects. We studied optic flow-sensitive interneurons in the optic lobe of the Monarch butterfly, whose large and highly contrasted wings sweep through the visual field with every wing-beat cycle, potentially obscuring interneuron output signals. Our results show baseline spiking activity increases when animals flap their wings, and individual spikes are phase-locked to the wing-beat cycle, even in the dark, when no visual motion input is available. A qualitative estimate of interneuron responses to directional wing motion through their receptive field is not sufficient to explain the recorded activity patterns. Our results suggest that an additional internal signal suppresses responses to wing-induced visual motion to support effective vision-based stabilization reflexes. These findings support the principle that self-generated signals are suppressed while sensitivity to external modulation is preserved.

Article.Authors: Stroud, J. P.; Bratsch-Prince, J.; Coles, L.; Middya, S.; Mediavilla, L.; Shamardani, K.; Zamani, P. T.; Malhotra, K. R.; Burde, T.; Kazieczko, D.; Kumar, A. S.; McDonald, J.; Dziuba, I.; Zhou, J.; Henderson, R.; Miranda, J. A.; Monje, M.; Woodington, B.; Jenkins, E. P. W.

Interestingly, lower frequency neural activity exhibited distinct, cell-line specific changes over time: GBM models exhibited decreases in low frequency neural activity whereas DIPG models exhibited increases over time. Finally, using machine learning models applied to chronic neural recordings from tumor-bearing mice treated with or without standard-of-care chemotherapy (temozolomide for GBM), we accurately predicted tumor burden as inferred through in vivo bioluminescence imaging. By fitting low-dimensional mathematical models to gamma-band neural trajectories, we could further predict individual tumor growth rates over a 5-week period with high accuracy. These results establish that pathological neural-tumor interactions can be harnessed to monitor glioma progression in vivo. Article.Title: Spanning spatial scales with functional imaging in the human brain; initial experiences at 10.5 Tesla
Article.Authors: Vizioli, L.; Knudsen, L.; Lazarova, Y. Y.; Moeller, S.; Dowdle, L.; Grant, A.; Sadeghi-Tarakameh, A.; Nothnagel, N.; Eryaman, Y.; Lagore, R.; Auerbach, E.; Adriany, G.; De Martino, F.; Faes, L.; Yacoub, E.; Ugurbil, K.
Article.Abstract: One of the most important new frontiers in the effort to improve the spatial resolution and accuracy of imaging of human brain activity is the recent development of greater than 10 Tesla magnetic fields. Here we present initial results for 10.5 Tesla Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) based functional brain imaging (fMRI) of the human brain acquired with previously unavailable or difficult to attain spatial resolutions and functional contrast. We present data obtained with nominal isotropic resolutions ranging from 0.65 to 0.35 mm for partial brain coverage for stimulus evoked responses, and 0.75 mm for whole brain coverage to capture the spontaneous fluctuations that are the source of functional connectivity measures. The increasingly higher nominal resolutions (i.e. smaller voxel volumes and dimensions) employed in image acquisition were shown to correspond to real gains in resolution using image reconstruction methods developed to minimize blurring. Existence of supralinear gains in stimulus-evoked percent signal change and major improvements in statistical significance were evident relative to 7 Tesla, the most advanced commercially available ultrahigh magnetic field platform currently employed in human brain studies. These results were feasible due to gains in intrinsic signal-to-noise ratio, BOLD contrast, and image acceleration provided by the uniquely high magnetic field of 10.5 Tesla, and the use of novel high channel count arrays to capture these gains. The results provide a preview of the potential that will be available in the new era of greater than 10 Tesla human functional imaging, particularly for mesoscale functional organizations and connectivity.

Article.Title: Progranulin deficiency promotes neuroinflammation through cathepsin B-mediated activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome
Article.Authors: Aggarwal, G.; Banerjee, S.; Bhadra, A. K.; Hwang, J. J.; Malabana, D. A. O.; Nagarajan, N.; Smith, D. M.; Kollarapu, J.; Nguyen, A. D.
Article.Abstract: Haploinsufficiency of progranulin (resulting from mutations in the GRN gene) is a major genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD), which is characterized by profound changes in personality and behavior, progressive impairments in executive function, speech, language and/or movement, TDP-43 pathology, lysosomal dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. Studies in progranulin-deficient mouse models have demonstrated the critical role of neuroinflammation in disease pathogenesis, as deletion of NF-kB or complement factors prevents FTD-associated behavioral deficits. While progranulin is known to be anti-inflammatory, the precise molecular mechanism by which its deficiency triggers inflammatory cascades remain unclear. Here, we investigate the involvement of the NLRP3 inflammasome in progranulin-deficient models, including mice, human microglial cells, and patient fibroblasts. In Grn mice, we found increased levels of several inflammasome-related proteins, including procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Similarly, GRN knockout (KO) microglia cells showed significant increases in levels of procaspase-1, NLRP3, and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Moreover, KO cells had increased NLRP3 oligomerization, suggesting that progranulin negatively regulates inflammasome assembly. We also investigated the potential link between lysosomal dysfunction and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in progranulin deficiency. We found that pharmacological inhibition of cathepsin B reduced NLRP3 inflammasome oligomerization as well as inflammatory cytokine expression in GRN KO cells. Additionally, siRNA knockdown of cathepsin B reduced levels of procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} in GRN KO cells. Finally, we found that heterozygous GRN fibroblasts exhibited similar increases in procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} levels, and these increases were corrected by treatment with an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that increase progranulin protein levels. Overall, our results demonstrate that progranulin deficiency promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activity through cathepsin B-mediated signaling, thereby establishing a mechanistic link between lysosomal dysfunction and increased inflammation. The ability of the GRN-targeting ASO to correct NLRP3-mediated inflammation highlights a promising therapeutic strategy for FTD-GRN and inflammation in other neurodegenerative disorders linked to progranulin deficiency.

Article.Title: Neurite Complexity and Plasticity Markers Track Synaptic Vesicle Density in the Living Human Brain: A Multimodal PET-MRI-EEG Study
Article.Authors: Agnorelli, C.; Peill, J.; Kurtin, D. L.; Mallon, O.; Sawicka, G.; Shatalina, E.; Godfrey, K.; Murphy, R.; Ahmad, K.; Oestreich, L. K. L.; Sumner, R.; Alberti, M.; Wall, M.; Ertl, N.; Searle, G.; Clarke, M.; Zhou, K.; Osugo, M.; Sarem, U.; Weiss, B.; Greenway, K.; Jauhar, S.; Fagiolini, A.; Carhart-Harris, R.; Matthews, P. M.; Rabiner, E.; Nutt, D.; Erritzoe, D.
Article.Abstract: Neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to reorganise its structure and function, is a transdiagnostic feature across psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases and a putative mechanism of action for pharmacological interventions. [11C]-UCBJ positron emission tomography (PET), which quantifies synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) density, offers the most direct in vivo measure of human synaptic density, but its relationship to complementary, more scalable neuroimaging measures of structural and functional plasticity remains uncharacterised. We combined [11C]-UCBJ PET, diffusion weighted imaging (DWI/NODDI), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG)-based sensory tasks (roving mismatch negativity, MMN; visual long-term potentiation, vLTP) in 18 healthy volunteers to test the relationship between synaptic terminal SV2A density and complementary structural and functional neuroplasticity measures, and whether these relationships were reproducible following pharmacological challenge with ketamine (n = 11) or N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT; n = 7). There were no statistically significant differences in PET-derived SV2A binding potential (BPND), DWI-derived neurite orientation dispersion (ODI) and structural weighted degree (SWD), EEG-derived MMN repetition suppression, and late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation, 1 to 8 days following DMT and ketamine exposure compared to baseline. BPND was coupled with ODI across cortical regions before and after pharmacological challenge, and this relationship was tighter within visual, attentional, and frontoparietal control brain networks. SWD showed a weaker, more spatially restricted association with BPND, primarily in regions belonging to the limbic and visual brain networks, but was not replicated post-drug. No consistent association was found between BPND and functional weighted degree (FWD), derived from rs-fMRI, at baseline or after pharmacological challenge. Frontotemporal BPND was positively associated with MMN repetition suppression (r = 0.61), and occipital BPND with late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation (r = 0.54), with the MMN-BPND association replicating after pharmacological challenge (r = 0.49). These findings link synaptic terminal SV2A density in the living human brain to neurite architecture and the capacity for short-term and Hebbian-like long-term synaptic plasticity, while dissociating these relationships from generic functional connectivity and magnitude of sensory-evoked responses. These data provide cross-modal validation for DWI- and EEG-derived measures as biological indices and surrogate measures of human synaptic plasticity.

Article.Title: A hippocampal digital Twin reveals latent structure in freely flying bats
Article.Authors: Lowet, A. S.; Qiu, Y.; Forli, A.; Kasuba, K. C.; Lin, Y.; Tolias, A. S.; Yartsev, M. M.
Article.Abstract: Concurrent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), large-scale neuronal recording, and behavioral tracking have enabled increasingly powerful predictive models of brain-behavior relationships. Yet predictive accuracy does not automatically yield interpretable principles of neural organization, particularly during natural behavior, where the relevant variables computed are often unknown in advance. Here, we developed a functional digital twin of the hippocampus, trained jointly on large-scale neural activity and self-directed three-dimensional flight in freely flying bats. A multimodal, multitask transformer accurately predicted both neural activity and behavior, outperformed standard approaches, and generalized across recording sessions. Interrogating the model's representations suggested a form of hippocampal generalization across self-selected trajectories that was not apparent in physical coordinates, but was plainly visible in the model's low-dimensional latent space. We confirmed this organization directly in the recorded neural activity: neurons fired at corresponding stages of spatially distinct paths connecting the same origin and destination, preserving their relative firing order even as their firing fields shifted with the path. Analysis of neuron-specific readouts further identified functional relationships among neurons that generalized from flight to waking rest and sleep, brain states never used for training, and differed systematically between the hippocampal subregions CA1 and CA3. Together, these results show how AI-based functional digital twins can complement conventional analysis by generating testable hypotheses about neural organization during natural behavior.

Article.Title: A Multiverse Approach to Brain Age Prediction: Exploring the Impact of Modality, Bias Adjustment, and Atlas
Article.Authors: Festor, J.; Smolders, L.; De Baene, W.
Article.Abstract: Brain age, an individual's age predicted from neuroimaging data, is a promising biomarker of brain health. Yet brain age estimates may depend on methodological choices within the prediction pipeline. We used a multiverse approach to systematically investigate effects of data modality, bias-adjustment method, and brain parcellation on brain-age prediction using data from 560 healthy adults (18.6-89 years) from the CamCAN dataset. Across 84 pipeline conditions, chronological age was predicted from connectivity features with elastic net regression, and performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE). A multilevel model tested the effects of the pipeline factors and their interactions; moreover, cross-atlas consistency of the most predictive connections was assessed. MAEs varied substantially across conditions (5.26-18.30 years). Modality and bias adjustment had significant effects on MAE and interacted significantly. Concatenating structural and functional connectivity performed similarly to structural connectivity alone, and structure-function coupling produced the highest MAE in most conditions. Beheshti-based bias adjustment outperformed Cole-based adjustment, while combining adjustment procedures did not consistently improve performance. Atlas choice had no main effect on MAE, its interaction with modality was significant but negligible in size, and finer parcellations did not systematically improve performance. However, the network-level features driving predictions showed limited spatial overlap across atlases, and importance was distributed over many features. Brain-age prediction is thus sensitive to methodological choices, particularly modality and bias-adjustment strategy. Atlas choice appears less important for predictive accuracy but may affect which connections appear most predictive. These findings highlight the importance of systematically evaluating analytical choices in brain-age research.

Article.Title: Targeted preoptic neuronal activation induces a hypothermic state with metabolic reprogramming and acute cerebroprotection
Article.Authors: Kamal, A.; Liu, J.; Gonzales, E. R.; Mohamad Ibrahim, K.; Zhang, F.; Abou-Antoun, T.; Skelton, H. E.; Kelly Cuenca, J.; Yuede, C.; Patti, G. J.; Shriver, L. P.; Lee, J.-M.; Norris, A. J.; Landsness, E. C.
Article.Abstract: Therapeutic hypothermia is cerebroprotective in experimental stroke but has shown limited clinical efficacy due to metabolically costly counter regulatory responses. Naturally occurring states such as torpor achieve hypothermia through coordinated regulation of temperature and metabolism are associated with cerebroprotection. Here, we tested whether selective activation of a genetically defined thermoregulatory neuronal population is sufficient to induce hypothermia after ischemic injury and whether temperature-dependent cerebroprotection is accompanied by metabolic remodeling. Using chemogenetic tools, kappa opioid receptor expressing neurons in the preoptic area were activated in mice subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion. Core body temperature, metabolism, infarct volume, and motor recovery were assessed under conditions permitting hypothermia or maintaining normothermia. Untargeted metabolomic profiling was performed on whole brain tissue collected 30 minutes after activation in the absence of ischemia. Activation of kappa opioid receptor expressing preoptic neurons induced a hypothermic state with coordinated metabolic changes, reduced infarct volume and improved acute motor outcomes. These effects were attenuated when body temperature was maintained at normothermia. Metabolomic profiling revealed coordinated alterations in nucleotide, phospholipid, and sphingolipid pathways. These findings link temperature dependent cerebroprotection to coordinated metabolic remodeling, with translational relevance for stroke.

Article.Title: Neural Representations of Visual Anagrams in Macaque Inferotemporal Cortex
Article.Authors: Yipeng, L.; Zhang, R.; Luo, J.; Zhao, Z.; Liu, X.; Gong, Z.; Jin, W.; Li, W.; Bao, P.
Article.Abstract: Visual recognition requires stable representations of object identity despite large changes in the retinal image. Yet this stability must be selective: some transformations change not only how an image looks, but also what object it appears to depict. Visual anagrams highlight this challenge: a single image can resemble two different objects at different orientations, such as an elephant and a rabbit. Here, we asked how macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex represents such transformations. We recorded large neuronal populations while presenting visual anagrams and unambiguous exemplars of their two interpretations across rotations. Neurons preferring one exemplar tended to prefer anagram orientations supporting the corresponding interpretation. At each of the two interpretation-relevant canonical angles, population responses more closely resembled those to the matching exemplar than those to the nonmatching exemplar. This matching advantage persisted when both exemplars were presented at the alternative canonical angle. Decoders trained exclusively on exemplars across rotations also tracked the shifts in anagram representations. Visual models showed anagram-exemplar alignment as well, with stronger alignment in models with greater relative shape preference. These findings suggest that transformation tolerance in IT is sensitive to what an image appears to depict, while relative shape preference is associated with similar representational organization in visual models.

Article.Title: Attentional modulation of persistent visual representations after stimulus offset is coordinated across primary visual and anterior cingulate cortices
Article.Authors: Safaryan, K.; Bhalodia, R. R.; Shenassa, J.; Golshani, P.
Article.Abstract: Flexible behavior in complex environments requires animals to infer which sensory inputs are relevant for guiding action and which need to be ignored. Yet, how cognitive control circuits apply contextual knowledge during decision-making is poorly understood. To address this question, we trained head-fixed mice on a cross-modal, context-dependent two-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) decision-making task. In this task, animals simultaneously received visual and auditory inputs, and the behaviorally relevant modality switched covertly between blocks of trials, requiring animals to infer rule changes from reward feedback alone. Mice successfully adapted their behavior after rule switches and recovered to expert performance. Using simultaneous Neuropixels recordings in the primary visual cortex (V1) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) during task performance, we found that neuronal responses in both regions showed mixed selectivity, multiplexing sensory, choice, and outcome signals. However, V1 neural responses more strongly encoded visual stimulus orientation, while ACC neural responses preferentially encoded outcome. Population decoding further revealed that V1 and ACC neurons maintained a persistent representation of task context throughout the trial, occupying a subspace approximately orthogonal to visual stimulus coding. This contextual representation strengthened progressively as mice adapted their behavior following each switch. Critically, context representations emerged in parallel in V1 and ACC, and decoding accuracies in these two regions were strongly correlated with each other and with behavioral performance across trial blocks. Orthogonal to this shared emergent and sustained context signal, visual stimulus decoding was enhanced when vision was task-relevant. This attentional enhancement in V1 occurred not only during the stimulus presentation period but also after stimulus offset. Similarly, in ACC, a persistent increase of visual stimulus identity encoding in visually relevant session blocks was present after stimulus offset. Taken together, these findings reveal a distributed, inter-areal representation of task context spanning sensory and frontal cortices, suggesting that V1 and ACC contribute to maintaining task-relevant sensory information beyond the immediate sensory response period to provide a circuit-level mechanism for cross-modal attentional control.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: anterior cingulate cortex; primary visual cortex; cross-modal attention; context-dependent decision making; attentional modulation

Article.Title: The effect of preproenkephalin gene deletion on heart function in mice
Article.Authors: Misiolek, K.; Szumiec, L.; Jasinski, K.; Kalita, K.; Kaczmarczyk-Jarosz, M.; Chroszcz, M.; Weglarz, W.; Ziolkowska, B.; Rodriguez Parkitna, J.
Article.Abstract: Enkephalins, the endogenous ligands of the - and {delta}-opioid receptors, are abundantly expressed in the nervous system and peripheral organs, including the heart. Accumulating evidence suggests that they participate in cardiac development and act as autocrine and paracrine modulators of heart activity. Here, we investigate the role of enkephalins in cardiac physiology using a newly generated mouse strain with a complete ablation of the preproenkephalin (Penk) gene. We find that, although adult mutant mice weighed less, the mutation caused no apparent changes in behavioral phenotype, no increase in anxiety-like behaviors, and only a mild reduction in locomotor activity. There was no effect of Penk deletion on heart weight or size. A comprehensive analysis of left ventricular function using MRI revealed normal basal cardiac performance, except for a significant reduction in the peak fill and ejection rates. There were no significant effects of Penk deletion on left ventricular function after {beta}1-adrenergic stimulation with dobutamine. At the same time, we observed the expected significant differences in heart size and function between male and female mice. In conclusion, our data show that enkephalins are not essential for normal heart development and have a moderate impact on adult heart function under basal conditions.

Article.Title: Auricular vagus nerve stimulation facilitates contextual fear extinction via insular-mPFC pathway without affecting reconsolidation
Article.Authors: Kuniishi, H.; Takeuchi, E.; Hashimoto, O.; Yamada, M.; Sekiguchi, M.; Matsuzaki, H.
Article.Abstract: Cervical vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) suppresses conditioned fear in rodents and may serve as an adjunct to exposure-based therapy for anxiety disorders. Non-invasive auricular VNS also reduces conditioned fear in humans, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a contextual fear conditioning paradigm, in which brief re-exposure induces reconsolidation and prolonged re-exposure promotes extinction learning in mice, we examined whether auricular VNS modulates these distinct memory processes. Auricular VNS during prolonged, but not brief, re-exposure reduced subsequent freezing, indicating facilitation of extinction learning without affecting reconsolidation. Stimulation restricted to the latter half of prolonged re-exposure, when extinction learning was underway, was sufficient to reduce subsequent fear responses. As a potential neural circuit mechanism, we focused on projections from the posterior insular cortex (pIC) to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). The pIC receives interoceptive signals, including vagal input, whereas the mPFC plays a key role in fear regulation. Auricular VNS during extinction learning increased c-Fos expression in pIC neurons projecting to the infralimbic and dorsal peduncular cortex (IL/DP) within the mPFC. Optogenetic activation of the pIC-IL/DP pathway mimicked the extinction-facilitating effect of auricular VNS, whereas inhibition blocked it. These results demonstrate that auricular VNS promotes extinction learning of contextual fear memory by activating the pIC-IL/DP circuit, providing insight into how vagal afferent stimulation engages insular-prefrontal networks to modulate fear.

Article.Title: ZFP36 is a post-transcriptional regulator of the P2X4 receptor in myeloid cells
Article.Authors: Gilabert, D.; Ahmadi, N.; Gentil, L.; Linck, N.; Charmes, V.; Rassendren, F.; Ulmann, L.
Article.Abstract: P2X4 is an ATP-gated purinergic receptor upregulated in spinal microglia after peripheral nerve injury, where it plays a key role in neuropathic pain. Yet, the molecular mechanisms controlling P2X4 expression remain incompletely understood. To address this question, we examined P2X4 mRNA expression and translation in spinal microglia following nerve injury. While total P2X4 mRNA levels remained unchanged, ribosome-associated P2X4 mRNA increased, revealing a previously unrecognized level of translational regulation. We therefore investigated whether the RNA-binding protein ZFP36 (tristetraprolin), a well-established regulator of inflammatory mRNAs, controls P2X4 expression. Our results demonstrate that the P2X4 3'UTR strongly repressed reporter and protein expression and that ZFP36 emerged as a negative regulator of P2X4 mRNA. This regulation involved phosphorylation-dependent signaling through p38 MAPK and 14-3-3. Moreover, ZFP36 knockdown increased P2X4 protein expression, while manipulation of ZFP36 phosphorylation altered P2X4-dependent ATP-evoked calcium responses. Together, these findings identify ZFP36 as a previously unrecognized post-transcriptional regulator of P2X4, extending its role beyond inflammatory mediators to a functional purinergic receptor. They reveal post-transcriptional control of receptor availability as a novel regulatory layer linking myeloid cell state to purinergic responsiveness and provide a new framework for understanding microglial P2X4 regulation in neuropathic pain.

Article.Title: Selective Auditory Attention Decoding with a Two-Node Wireless EEG Sensor Network
Article.Authors: Geirnaert, S.; Ding, R.; Bertrand, A.
Article.Abstract: Objective. Selective auditory attention decoding (sAAD) enables neuro-steered hearing devices by identifying the attended speaker in a multi-speaker environment from neural activity recorded with electroencephalography (EEG). Despite algorithmic progress, practical deployment remains constrained by a lack of wearable, unobtrusive, and fully wireless EEG acquisition solutions. We therefore evaluate whether reliable sAAD can be achieved under the realistic hardware constraints of a wireless EEG sensor network (WESN) of miniaturized, galvanically isolated EEG sensor nodes. Approach. We use a WESN of two synchronized, compact around-ear EEG sensor nodes worn bilaterally. Each node provides four local EEG channels derived from five pre-gelled electrodes, including a local reference. Sample-wise wireless synchronization of data from both nodes enables joint processing as an eight-channel EEG. On a newly recorded dataset, we apply correlation-based stimulus decoding, followed by hidden Markov model (HMM)-based post-processing. Main results. Stimulus decoding achieves an average sAAD accuracy of 69.24% on 60s decision windows, comparable to previously reported wired around-ear EEG systems that measure long-distance scalp potentials. HMM-based post-processing further improves this to a steady-state accuracy of 77.17% with an average simulated attention switch detection time of 32.79s. Combining sensor nodes at both ears outperforms single-ear configurations, primarily through redundancy rather than complementary spatial information. Finally, a fixed bipolar configuration using four electrodes per ear, yielding three channels, suffices to maintain performance. Significance. These results demonstrate the practical feasibility of sAAD using a fully wireless, galvanically isolated around-ear WESN and establish a realistic performance benchmark under practical hardware constraints.

Article.Title: Separation, isolation, and membrane lipid profiling of selectively vulnerable and resilient neurons
Article.Authors: Sadek, M.; Yokomizo, M.; Williams, E.; Wieckiewicz, N.; Owusu Kwarteng, D.; Das, S.; Bennett, R. E.; Gomez-Isla, T.; Maesako, M.
Article.Abstract: Certain neurons are more susceptible to pathogenic stressors and degenerate, while others remain resilient in neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms underlying this cell-to-cell heterogeneity in neuronal vulnerability remain unclear, primarily due to challenges in isolating vulnerable and resilient neurons to characterize their properties. In this study, we report the development of a novel cell-labeling method utilizing two cell-impermeable dyes to identify vulnerable and resilient neurons in culture, which are subsequently separated and isolated via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). As a proof-of-concept of a mechanistic study, we conducted lipidomic analysis to determine whether the lipid composition of membranes differs between vulnerable and resilient neurons to oxidative stress. This simple but unique method sets the groundwork for investigating the molecular underpinnings of selective neuronal vulnerability, which could inform new diagnostic strategies and therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.

Article.Title: Hypoxia Disrupts Multiple Processes Supporting Spatial Navigation
Article.Authors: McKeown, D. J.; Bahnson-Wright, H. M.; Caldwell, T.; Marks, M.; Marshall, G. R.; Newton, H.; Stenholm, D.; Young, M.; Angus, D. J.; Schinazi, V. R.
Article.Abstract: Hypoxia impairs cognitive function, yet its effects on navigation and intrinsic brain activity remain poorly understood. This study investigated whether a continuous exposure to hypoxia (CH) or an intermittent exposure to hypoxia (IH) differentially influence navigation performance and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) in healthy young adults. Seventy-two participants completed sham (FiO2 = .209) and hypoxia (FiO2 = .13) sessions during either a one hour of CH or IH intervention. Navigation was assessed using the Spatial Performance Assessment for Cognitive Evaluation (SPACE), while resting-state EEG was recorded before and after the intervention in a subset of participants (n = 40). EEG spectra were parameterised into periodic (alpha and beta power and central frequency) and aperiodic (exponent and offset) components. Aligned rank transform (ART) analyses of variance examined effects of hypoxia and intervention group, while linear regression determined whether reductions in peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) predicted changes in navigation or EEG. Hypoxia impaired multiple components of navigation, increasing path integration distance error and egocentric pointing angle error irrespective of intervention group, while mapping accuracy was preferentially impaired following IH and perspective taking performance following CH. Hypoxia also reduced alpha and beta power, beta central frequency, and aperiodic exponent, while aperiodic offset and alpha central frequency remained stable. The reduction in aperiodic exponent was primarily evident following IH, suggesting that the temporal pattern of oxygen delivery may influence specific neurophysiological responses. Contrary to our hypothesis, SpO2 reduction did not predict individual differences in navigation performance or EEG activity. These findings demonstrate that brief, moderate hypoxic exposure can disrupt allocentric and egocentric components of spatial navigation while selectively altering periodic and aperiodic features of intrinsic brain activity.

Article.Title: Dual Roles of Interferon-γ Receptor in Somatostatin Interneurons at Baseline and During Inflammation
Article.Authors: Rezaei, S.; Tomoda, T.; Marcotte, M.; Prevot, T. D.; Banasr, M.; Bansal, Y.; Ezzeddine, A.; Guan, A.; Vieira, E.; Sibille, E.
Article.Abstract: Background: Neuropsychiatric disorders such as major depressive disorder show converging evidence of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) dysfunction, including consistent reductions in somatostatin (SST) interneuron markers. SST interneurons are selectively vulnerable to inflammation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a pro-inflammatory cytokine implicated in mood and anxiety disorders, signals through the IFN-{gamma} receptor (IFNGR), which is expressed in neurons. We tested whether IFNGR signaling in SST interneurons regulates anxiety-like and cognitive behavior and prevents inflammation-induced molecular deficits. Methods: We generated mice with conditional deletion of IFNGR from SST cells and assessed anxiety-like behavior using elevated plus maze and working memory using Y-maze at baseline and after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced inflammation. Expression of SST-related, neurotrophic, synaptic, and glial markers was quantified. Results: At baseline and after LPS-induced inflammation, IFNGR deletion in SST cells increased anxiety-like behavior without affecting working memory. In control mice, LPS reduced Sst (p=0.0006), neuropeptide Y (Npy) (p=0.0022), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) (p<0.0001), and synapsin 1 (Syn1) (p=0.0150); these reductions were not significant in mice lacking IFNGR in SST cells. Knockouts also showed lower baseline Bdnf, Syn1, Gephyrin (Gphn), and allograft inflammatory factor 1 (Aif1, encoding Iba1) than controls. Conclusions: IFNGR signaling in SST cells plays a dual role: supporting normal behavior and molecular homeostasis while mediating LPS-induced molecular deficits. These findings link immune signaling to the GABAergic dysfunction implicated in major depressive disorder and suggest IFNGR signaling in SST cells may regulate cortical microcircuit integrity at baseline and during inflammatory challenge.

Article.Title: Dizocilpine-derived K2060 exhibits enhanced blockage at NMDA receptors with impaired Mg2+ block and provides strong protection against audiogenic seizures
Article.Authors: Kolcheva, M.; Netolicky, J.; Misiachna, A.; Rybalko, N.; Zahumenska, P.; Doderovic, J.; Pakhomova, A.; De Sanctis, C. V.; Schneider, G. K.; Hemelikova, K.; Rehakova, K.; Kortus, S.; Turecek, R.; Korabecny, J.; Soukup, O.; Ladislav, M.; Horak, M.
Article.Abstract: Background and Purpose: Voltage-dependent Mg2+ block is a defining feature of the GluN1/GluN2 subtype of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs). These Mg2+-dependent effects were absent or markedly reduced at the GluN1/GluN2A-N615S and GluN1/GluN2A-N615K receptors. In addition, K2060 showed slower unbinding and greater trapping than memantine. In hippocampal slices from GluN2A-N615S mice, K2060 exhibited enhanced but slower onset inhibition than memantine and ketamine. Conclusions and Implications: Impaired Mg2+; block removes a physiological constraint on the action of NMDAR blockers. K2060 exhibited the most favourable pharmacological profile, supporting its further evaluation for studies with NMDAR hyperfunction models. Article.Title: Exploratory Proteomics of Brain Extracellular Vesicle Enriched Preparations After LPS Challenge and miRNA Associated Vesicle Administration
Article.Authors: Brown, K.; Wang, Y.; Shan, Z.; Bi, L.
Article.Abstract: We used brain extracellular vesicle (EV) proteomics to identify protein responses to acute neuroinflammation and an EV-based microRNA intervention. Rats received vehicle, intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS), or LPS followed by an intravenous EV formulation containing anti-inflammatory microRNAs (miRNAs). Brains were collected 24 h after LPS or vehicle administration, and three independently processed animal-derived EV-enriched preparations per group were analyzed by label-free proteomics. Across all nine samples, 953 protein groups had complete normalized abundance measurements. Compared with vehicle controls, LPS exposure was associated with 227 exploratory protein changes, comprising 95 increases and 132 decreases at nominal P < 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change >= log2(1.5). Increased proteins were enriched for translation-related annotations, whereas decreased proteins were enriched for plasma-membrane annotations. These LPS-associated changes did not remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction at a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of q < 0.05. Following treatment, 119 of the 227 candidates were closer to control abundance on the log2 scale; 23 candidates also showed nominal treatment-versus-LPS differences. Lamb2 and Ptgfrn were the two proteins that differed significantly between treated and LPS-only animals after FDR correction, identifying them as priorities for further validation. Nevertheless, 174 proteins differed significantly between treated animals and vehicle controls, and analysis across the measured proteins did not demonstrate an overall shift toward control values. Thus, the intervention was associated with specific protein responses, but treated animals retained substantial differences from controls. This study identifies candidate markers for investigating treatment responses in brain EV-enriched preparations and demonstrates the value of examining individual proteins alongside broader proteomic changes. Independent validation is needed to determine their functional relevance and distinguish miRNA-specific effects from contributions of the administered EV carrier.

Article.Title: Intrastriatal injection of amplified Lewy body dementia (LBD) fibrils in mice results in accumulation of fibrils with LBD structure and neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Bagade, A. V.; Miller, R.; Dearborn, J. T.; Basore, K.; Summers, B.; Readnour, B.; Koelling, M.; O'Shea, J.; Wright, E. R.; Dhavale, D. D.; Kotzbauer, P. T.

We amplified fibrils from mouse brain tissue 5 mpi and collected single-particle cryo-EM data. High resolution 3D structural information could not be obtained because of the lack of helical twist, but comparison of the cryo-EM 2D class averages with those derived from amplified fibrils prepared from human LBD tissue revealed multiple matching classes, indicating that the Lewy fold is maintained in the fibrils that accumulate in mouse brain tissue. Article.Title: Postprandial hypertriglyceridemia activates microglia to promote satiety via an ASC dependent signaling.
Article.Authors: Salvi, J.; Nedelec, E.; Leret, L.; Lienard, F.; Landre, T.; Ben Fradj, S.; Garcia, V.; Gigot, V.; Patris, B.; Pires, V.; Polizzi, A.; Sanchez, C.; Gautier, T.; Guillou, H.; Heurtaux, T.; Petrilli, V.; Blouet, C.; Heneka, M. Article.Abstract: Reactive microglia are commonly considered neurotoxic and detrimental for brain functioning. These results reveal that microglia engage an immune signaling pathway to rapidly alert the neural circuits and activate an anorectic response that limits overconsumption of dietary fat. Unexpectedly, this regulatory process is sexually dimorphic, present in males only. Furthermore, we found that the postprandial microglial reaction is bypassed during obesity, providing a new therapeutic target to treat maladaptive eating disorders.

Article.Title: Integration of Neuroimaging and Histopathology in a Squirrel Monkey Model of Spontaneous Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy and Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities
Article.Authors: Wadghiri, Y. Z.; Khan, S.; Soliman, M. T.; Szabo, J.; Murray, A.; Patel, A. G.; Kingsley, C.; Swain, J.; Nehete, P. N.; Veraart, J.; Mulholland, M. M.; Hopkins, W. D.; Wisniewski, T.; Scholtzova, H.
Article.Abstract: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a prevalent cerebrovascular pathology in AD and contributes to amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), a major complication of current anti-amyloid immunotherapy. In contrast, white matter R2* showed an initial increase followed by a late-life reversal, likely reflecting age-related changes in myelin integrity, tissue microstructure, and tissue water content. MRI-histopathology correlation linked T2*-w MRI hypointensities to CAA-positive iron-laden vessels associated with perivascular inflammation and, in some cases, hemosiderin deposits. Here we confirmed the occurrence of ARIA-H and ARIA-E events in geriatric animals. SQMs provided a valuable opportunity to examine the underlying pathology of spontaneous ARIA-E, revealing distinctive tissue signatures associated with its manifestation. ARIA-E hyperintensities were characterized by reactive gliosis and BBB disruption, whereas more advanced lesions exhibited perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and evidence of myelin and axonal injury. Article.Title: Adaptive co-transmission shapes sensory encoding and behavior
Article.Authors: Cuentas-Condori, A. A.; Kumar, S.; Agoba, P.; Chanaba-Lopez, P.; Diaz Garcia, M.; Colon-Ramos, D.
Article.Abstract: Co-transmission expands the chemical repertoire of neurons, but whether coexisting neurotransmitters can be independently organized and remodeled by experience to control distinct aspects of behavior remains unclear. Sensory experience differentially regulates the two systems: animals trained to prefer higher temperatures exhibit increased VGLUT/EAT-4 abundance, whereas those trained to prefer lower temperatures exhibit increased VAChT/UNC-17 abundance. The two transmitters also make distinct, context-dependent contributions to goal-directed navigation. Glutamatergic transmission promotes movement toward the learned thermal preference, whereas cholinergic transmission restrains continued migration beyond it. Analysis of locomotor trajectories further reveals that the two transmitters differentially regulate reorientation decisions across regions of the thermal gradient. Together, these findings identify adaptive co-transmission, a form of synaptic plasticity in which coexisting neurotransmitter systems are differentially organized and regulated by experience, and make distinct, context-dependent contributions to behavior.

Article.Title: Hyperglycaemia reversibly disrupts circadian behaviour in mice
Article.Authors: Lloyd, M.; Ni, G.; Hu, K.-T.; Foster, R. G.; Ashcroft, F. M.; Jagannath, A.; Vasudevan, S. R.
Article.Abstract: Disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms are among the most common features of diabetes, and are known to raise the risk of developing the disease. Whether the relationship also runs the other way, with diabetes itself disrupting the clock, has remained unresolved. Using an inducible mouse model of diabetes, in which hyperglycaemia can be induced and then reversed within the same animal, we show that elevated blood glucose is a reversible cause of circadian disruption. Raising blood glucose reduced the amplitude of circadian rest-activity rhythms by 50%, in proportion to the degree of hyperglycaemia, and shortened the free-running period of the clock. Restoring normoglycaemia reversed both effects. Diabetic animals had a delayed phase of activity onset, i.e. later chronotype, and re-entrained more slowly after a simulated jet lag. However, phase shifting to nocturnal light pulses was intact, suggesting normal photic responses. Brain glucose and O-GlcNAcylation, a nutrient-sensitive protein modification, were both elevated in diabetic animals, showing that peripheral hyperglycaemia reaches the brain and alters its metabolic state, and providing a molecular readout of that exposure. Together, these findings establish that a peripheral metabolic state is a reversible determinant of circadian rest-activity behaviour, completing a bidirectional link between blood glucose and the clock and arguing that the two must be treated together rather than in isolation.
