Article.Title: Computational Evaluation of tDCS Montage Separability and Dose Coverage for Practice-Specific Mindfulness Experiments
Article.Authors: Bruschi, D. L.; Schiavi, A.; Joseph, I.
Article.Abstract: A practice-specific stimulation experiment requires candidate montages that differ in regional electric-field exposure without sacrificing interpretable target dose. We evaluated this requirement for transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) montages intended to test focused-attention and open-monitoring mindfulness practices. Four focused-attention candidates and six open-monitoring candidates formed 24 pairs, evaluated with SimNIBS 4.6 in 20 existing anatomical head models at a linearly scaled current of 2 mA. Outcomes were regional 99th-percentile field magnitude, a normalized double-dissociation index (DDI), suprathreshold overlap, and individual dose coverage. Eighteen pairs passed four recorded progression criteria, but only five also met a post hoc requirement that both intended regional contrasts be positive in at least 80% of heads. A positive DDI alone concealed a reversed salience-region contrast in one conventional comparison. The nominated F3-centered 4-by-1 ring paired with F8-Fp2 sponges (FA-05 x OM-02) produced both directional preferences in 20/20 heads, with median DDI 1.561 and median suprathreshold Dice 0.000. The conventional F3-Fp2 and FT8-FCz sponge pair (FA-02 x OM-07) produced both preferences in 19/20 heads, with DDI 0.627 and Dice 0.186. Both anatomical targets reached the operational 0.20 V/m floor in 11/20 versus 20/20 heads, respectively. ROAST 4.0, with ring placement held fixed, supported both nominations but exposed dose disagreement. Across conductivity sensitivity draws, directional separability persisted more consistently than absolute dose. These results establish a regional separability-dose trade-off within the tested candidate set and show why a summed contrast cannot substitute for a directional conjunction. They support selection of a discriminating experiment, not whole-network selectivity, physiological efficacy, or a validated treatment.

Article.Title: Braintree: An agentic framework for in-silico vision neuroscience
Article.Authors: Deb, M.; Wang, R.; Dipani, A.; Ratan Murty, N. A.
Article.Abstract: Vision neuroscience has many of the ingredients needed to conduct experiments entirely in-silico. We need AI systems that can reason over scientific knowledge, generative methods for creating precisely controlled stimuli, image-computable models that can predict neural responses with increasing accuracy, and tools that can analyze and interpret data. Here we take the first step toward making a vision neuroscience experiment end-to-end computable. We introduce Braintree, an agentic framework that can autonomously run multi-experiment studies directly with in-silico models of human visual cortex. Given a hypothesis, Braintree can reason over the current literature, design an experiment, build a stimulus set from algorithmically manipulated or synthesized stimuli, run the experiment on candidate brain encoding models, analyze the responses and then use the results to design even stronger tests. The entire loop runs autonomously and can accept human input at any stage. We evaluated Braintree on three increasingly open-ended scientific problems. First, Braintree reproduced published findings using their original stimuli and then asked whether the same effects could be replicated with entirely new stimulus sets that it constructed. Second, it designed new experiments to find stimulus dimensions that could drive two brain regions differently, even when those regions otherwise had similar response profiles. Third, it searched for experiments that could tell competing models of the same brain region apart. Experiments discovered using just two models also exposed differences across a much broader set of models, suggesting that Braintree had found more general dimensions along which brain models disagree. Braintree can augment the capabilities of a vision neuroscientist as a verifier for existing hypotheses, a test-bed for new ideas, and/or a tool for generating stimuli that can discriminate between competing hypotheses or models of the brain. Braintree shows how AI agents and brain models can work together to make in-silico vision neuroscience experiment computable, allowing vision scientists to explore many more experiment conditions and identify the most informative ones to test on the human brain.

Article.Title: A Thermodynamic Theory of Axon Guidance: Navigation Through High-Entropy Signaling States
Article.Authors: Wadsworth, W. G.
Article.Abstract: Precise neural circuit formation requires growth cones to integrate multiple, sometimes competing, guidance signals into persistent yet adaptable movement. Here, we propose a theoretical framework that recasts axon guidance as a thermodynamically regulated computation. An artificial neural network, trained on in vivo genetic data and associated outgrowth patterns, maps the microstates of a localized guidance signaling network to macroscopic outgrowth behaviors. Using the trained model, we simulated axon pathfinding through extracellular gradients of molecular cues and created dynamic entropic landscapes. These results reveal that growth cones navigate high-entropy ridges that preserve plasticity. Navigation along these ridges supports persistent extension, whereas turning and branching occur near boundaries between competing entropic macrostates, consistent with transitions in the cytoskeletal machinery that controls growth-cone movement. More broadly, the framework proposes that robust biological patterning can emerge from microscopic variability when signaling networks operate near boundaries between competing behavioral states.

Article.Title: Decoupling of spontaneous and evoked activity in locus coeruleus neurons: early synaptic and ion-channel remodeling in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
Article.Authors: Zhao, B.; Li, M.; Yi, L.; Li, J.
Article.Abstract: The locus coeruleus (LC) is among the earliest brain regions affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the mechanisms underlying its early vulnerability remain poorly understood. Clarifying synaptic and intrinsic dysfunction in LC noradrenergic (NE) neurons is essential to determine how noradrenergic circuit failure contributes to prodromal AD. We combined whole-cell patch-clamp recordings with quantitative immunofluorescence to examine synaptic transmission, firing properties, voltage-gated currents, and synaptic organization in LC/NE neurons from young 3xTg mice prior to substantial neurodegeneration. Young 3xTg mice exhibited reduced excitatory and enhanced inhibitory synaptic input onto LC/NE neurons. Consistent with these functional shifts, structural analysis revealed decreased densities of VGLUT2, PSD95, and paired VGLUT2-PSD95 puncta, alongside increased VGAT, gephyrin, and paired VGAT-gephyrin puncta. Despite this net synaptic suppression, LC/NE neurons displayed elevated spontaneous firing rates but a markedly reduced capacity to generate spike output during sustained depolarization. Voltage-clamp recordings revealed a diminished total voltage-gated K current density alongside reduced voltage-gated Na current density, without significant shifts in their voltage-dependence or kinetics. These biophysical alterations provide a mechanistic basis for the divergent firing phenotype: reduced K current; conductance likely facilitates spontaneous pacemaker activity, whereas diminished Na current; current constrains repetitive, input-driven spike generation. Together, these findings demonstrate that LC/NE neurons undergo coordinated synaptic and ion-channel remodeling during prodromal AD. This unique decoupling of spontaneous baseline activity from stimulus-evoked excitability may impair dynamic noradrenergic modulation, positioning early LC cellular dysfunction as a candidate driver of network instability and a novel therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Neonatal Delivery of Exon Skipping Therapeutics Maximizes Brain Dystrophin Rescue in the Mdx52 Mouse Model of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
Article.Authors: VACCA, O.; Doisy, M.; Nagy, C.; Saoudi, A.; Phongsavanh, X. M.; Le Coz, O.; Vaillend, C.; Goyenvalle, A.
Article.Abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, resulting in the loss of dystrophin expression. Beyond progressive muscle degeneration, nearly half of patients exhibit cognitive and behavioral impairments, highlighting the need for effective central nervous system (CNS) therapies. In this study, we investigated whether neonatal delivery could maximize brain dystrophin rescue in mdx52 mice using exon 51 skipping strategies. We compared systemic and intracerebroventricular (ICV) delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO-51) and an AAV9-mediated U7snRNA approach (scAAV9-U7-Ex51), administered neonatally. Neonatal intravenous ASO-51 induced widespread but transient exon skipping, resulting in limited brain dystrophin restoration. ICV administration markedly increased CNS exon skipping but did not overcome the limited persistence of ASO, leading to progressive loss of exon skipping and dystrophin rescue. In contrast, neonatal ICV delivery of scAAV9-U7-Ex51 achieved robust, widespread, and sustained exon 51 skipping throughout the brain, including the hippocampus, cortex, and cerebellum, resulting in 20-50% restoration of Dp427 expression. These findings demonstrate that early CNS-directed delivery enhances brain dystrophin restoration and establish AAV-U7-mediated exon skipping as a promising strategy for addressing CNS comorbidities in DMD.

Article.Title: Motor Evoked Potentials in Preclinical Models of Spinal Cord Injury and Stroke in Rodents: A Systematic Review.
Article.Authors: Shahid, R.; Cooke, D.; Balbinot, G.
Article.Abstract: Motor Evoked Potentials (MEPs) serve as an invaluable tool for assessing corticospinal tract (CST) integrity and motor pathway function in preclinical models of spinal cord injury (SCI) and stroke. Despite their diagnostic and prognostic utility, substantial methodological variability persists across studies, complicating interpretation and cross-study comparisons. This systematic review synthesizes MEP acquisition and interpretation protocols from 83 rodent SCI and stroke studies published since 2015, aiming to outline common practices, identify sources of variability, and highlight methodological gaps. Our analysis reveals a predominance of SCI models and a focus on hindlimb MEPs, employing diverse stimulation protocols including transcranial electrical stimulation (TES), direct cortical stimulation (DCoS), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Anesthetic approaches are notably heterogeneous, representing a potentially large source of variability in MEP acquisition. Amplitude and latency, often measured jointly, emerged as the most frequently reported MEP parameters. Critically, MEPs bridge cellular and molecular changes to observable behaviour by reflecting the integrated functionality of neural cell populations and their circuits. However, a lack of standardization in reporting, particularly for secondary electrophysiological features and stimulation intensity, hinders reproducibility. We emphasize the necessity for standardized protocols for stimulation, electrode positioning, and data analysis, particularly the use of comprehensive recruitment curves. Adopting these best practices will enhance the transparency, comparability, and translational potential of MEP methodology in advancing our understanding and treatment strategies for neurological disorders.

Article.Title: Effort experience as a driver of behavioral modulation in Caenorhabditis elegans
Article.Authors: Arbid, R.; Rabinowitch, I.
Article.Abstract: Effort is typically studied as a cost that influences choice, motivation, or persistence, but less is known about whether effort embedded within ordinary behavior can itself leave a trace that alters subsequent behavior. We developed a Caenorhabditis elegans paradigm in which animals reached the same food source under low or high effort conditions and were then tested in various behavioral contexts. Prior high effort enhanced subsequent food approach, generalized to more demanding tests including aversive barrier crossing, and persisted for at least 1 h but was lost by 24 h. The effect was distinct from food deprivation and was accompanied by context-dependent changes in locomotor dispersal rather than a uniform increase in activity. A monoamine screen implicated tyramine signaling. High effort also reduced ongoing activity in the tyraminergic RIM interneurons and enhanced the AWC OFF sensory response. These findings identify effort as a behaviorally consequential component of ordinary experience and suggest that ongoing behavior can generate internal state changes that may recursively influence future behavior.

Article.Title: Title: Unilateral loss of tyrosine hydroxylase in adult midbrain dopaminergic neurons reveals reduction to neuregulin1 in rat model of acute dopaminergic dysfunction
Article.Authors: Greer, L. K.; Harr, A. E.; Hoffman, A. F.; Jämsä, A. J.; Airavaara, M.; Lupica, C. R.; Harvey, B. K.
Article.Abstract: Dopamine, produced primarily in the midbrain, is required for movement and reward-based signaling all throughout life. Loss of dopaminergic function can result in changes to motor systems, mood, motivation, and cognition. Dopaminergic cell death or dopaminergic hypofunction are implicated in a variety of diseases including synucleinopathies, neuropsychiatric disorders, and substance use disorders. Loss of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and subsequent dysregulation of dopamine signaling in striatum are implicated to varying degrees in all synucleinopathies. By the time patients present with motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease, the most common synucleinopathy, >30% of DANs are lost in the SNpc because of ongoing degeneration for years prior to diagnosis. Studying the early consequences of dopamine loss is critical to understanding mechanisms of dopamine depletion disease progression and identifying biomarkers for earlier diagnosis so that effective treatment can ensue. Here, we created a model of dopamine loss in adult rats to study early transcriptional changes following loss of dopamine synthesis. We used CRISPR to knock out tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting enzyme for dopamine synthesis, in the adult rat midbrain through injection of Th guide RNAs into transgenic rats expressing Cas9 nuclease specifically in dopamine transporter positive neurons and performed single nucleus RNA sequencing on midbrain and dorsal striatal tissue. Two weeks after injection, we measured a 90% loss of TH and dopamine in the midbrain, but striatal TH and dopamine were unaffected. Despite preceding striatal dopamine loss, our data identified alterations to genes involved in synaptic signaling, organization, and function in both midbrain and striatal neurons. We found the neurotrophic factor, neuregulin1, to be significantly reduced in dopaminergic neurons, which may account for transcriptional changes in surrounding cells that precede detectable reductions to striatal dopamine. These data establish a new rat model of adult TH loss and identify early transcriptional consequences of dopamine loss in the adult midbrain after normal development, providing potential biomarkers for early-stage dopamine loss in PD, synucleinopathies and related disorders of dopamine depletion.

Article.Title: Open Dataset of Developmental Timelines for Corresponding Milestones in Mice, Rats, and Humans
Article.Authors: Amici, E.; Grimson, R.; Vazquez-Borsetti, P.
Article.Abstract: Translating developmental time across species is essential for the appropriate design and interpretation of preclinical neurodevelopmental research, yet no open, unified resource currently integrates high-quality developmental milestone data for mouse, rat, and human. Here we present a curated, open-access dataset of general and neurodevelopmental milestones spanning these three species, expanding a previously published rat--human database with newly compiled mouse data. Following a systematic literature search, 783 records covering 371 unique developmental milestones were extracted, standardized to days after fertilization, and validated through a structured curation and quality-control process. Exploratory analyses indicated that the developmental relationship between humans and rodents is markedly non-linear, with milestones becoming increasingly dispersed as development progresses. The observed pattern is consistent with the quarter-power model with an additive constant identified in a companion modeling study. Accordingly, applying a quarter-power transformation to human DAF substantially improved the linearity of developmental trajectories across species. Comparison of body and brain milestone clusters showed no detectable differences in scaling relative to humans, in line with similar underlying rules for somatic and neural development between rodents and humans. The dataset, together with its documented curation methodology, provides a transparent and extensible resource for cross-species developmental translation and a useful tool for informing the generation of animal models.

Article.Title: Perceptual similarity representations beyond the sensory cortex
Article.Authors: Moharramipour, A.; Jin, Z.; Su, N.; Ge, Y.; Matsuda, T.; Shibata, K.; Kwok, S. C.; Lau, H.
Article.Abstract: It is commonly thought that information supporting conscious perception is primarily represented in sensory cortices, whereas association cortex encodes more abstract, task-dependent information. However, this impression may partly stem from difficulties in experimentally assessing the functions of association areas characterized by mixed selectivity and complex spatial topography. Here, we combined repetition-suppression (RS) and multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to extract richer information from human fMRI. With this approach, we asked whether association regions represent the perceptual similarity structure among color stimuli, although this perceptual similarity information was task-irrelevant in the experiment. Our analysis revealed such representations beyond the visual cortex, in lateral prefrontal, and parietal regions. We further demonstrated an electrophysiological complement to the fMRI findings by applying the same approach to local field potentials recorded in the macaque dorsomedial parietal cortex. Our findings suggest that higher-order areas beyond the visual cortex may play a key role in subjective color perception.

Article.Title: Psychopharmacological Effects of Cannabidiol in Rodent Models of Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review of Behavioral Outcomes, Neurobiological Mechanisms, and Methodological Quality
Article.Authors: Domingues, B. R. R.; Felix, G. S.; Bezerra, M. F. L.; Medeiros, P.; de Freitas, R. L.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, as well as restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior. Although increasing evidence suggests that cannabidiol (CBD) may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for ASD, the preclinical literature remains fragmented, with substantial variability in experimental models, treatment protocols, CBD formulations, and reported outcomes. This systematic review (PROSPERO registration: CRD420251177933) aimed to critically evaluate the psychopharmacological effects of CBD in rodent models of ASD, with an emphasis on behavioral outcomes, underlying neurobiological mechanisms, and methodological quality. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, with a final sample of 14 articles. Due to the substantial heterogeneity across studies, a qualitative synthesis of results was performed using the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) approach. Overall, CBD and CBD-based preparations produced beneficial effects across multiple ASD-relevant behavioral domains. Enhanced social interaction, reductions in repetitive behaviors, anxiety-like responses, and cognitive impairments were observed in specific models. Neurobiological analyses revealed modulation of the endocannabinoid system, restoration of excitation/inhibition balance, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, and transcriptional regulation. Positive outcomes were observed across pharmacological, genetic, and maternal immune activation models, suggesting that CBD acts on convergent neurobiological pathways implicated in ASD pathophysiology. Despite these promising findings, important limitations were identified, including substantial heterogeneity in experimental protocols and methodological limitations, such as insufficient reporting of randomization, blinding, and allocation concealment procedures, as well as the underrepresentation of female animals. This review synthesizes behavioral, neurobiological, and methodological evidence on CBD and CBD-based preparations in rodent models of ASD, highlighting its therapeutic potential and the need for more rigorous, standardized preclinical investigations that directly compare isolated CBD with its formulations and combinations.

Article.Title: Predictive Grid Cell Coding Does Not Require Explicit Planning
Article.Authors: Sinha, A.; Fasehun, O. C.; Redman, W. T.
Article.Abstract: Predictive grid cells, a recently discovered functional class of neurons in medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), exhibit grid-like tuning, not with respect to where an animal currently is, but where it will be. Such coding, which is disjoint from standard grid cell coding, appears consistent with the hypothesis that MEC supports predictive computations for goal-directed navigation. However, given that existing predictive coding theories have been used to understand standard grid cells, it remains unclear what the functional significance of predictive grid cells is. Furthermore, the extent to which predictive grid cells are generally present in MEC is unknown. To address these open questions, we analyze data from rodent electrophysiology recordings and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). In an independent, previously recorded MEC dataset, we find evidence of predictive grid cell coding when the animal is awake and exploring an open field environment, suggesting that they are a general feature of rodent MEC. In RNNs trained to path-integrate, which have previously been shown to develop units with grid-like representations, we also find units with predictive grid-like representations, even though the RNNs are not trained with a predictive objective. We validate the predictive grid tuning of these units by finding that they exhibit significant future path-dependence, even when controlling for the same allocentric spatial position. In addition, we find that band-like units, which have been found to play an important role in maintaining path-integration in the RNNs, exhibit greater predictive grid tuning than expected by chance. These results lead us to hypothesize that predictive grid cells are a property of the underlying grid cell circuit. We test this by looking for signatures of predictive grid coding in the MEC electrophysiological data collected during sleep, finding evidence in one recording. Collectively, our results challenge the idea that predictive grid cells must necessarily be used for explicit prediction and planning, and instead may be involved in shaping the population level activity of grid cells.

Article.Title: A male-specific neural circuit for appetitive thirst in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Wang, B. P.; Zhang, X.; Shastry, S.; Kaur, G.; Fatima, N.; Wolf, F. W.
Article.Abstract: Thirst is the brain representation of the need to restore water balance. While environmental and interoceptive sensory neurons that assess water availability and status are known, the central brain representation of thirst that determines behavior in Drosophila is less well understood. In turn, NPF-M neurons release the neuropeptides sNPF, NPF, and DH31 to promote thirsty water seeking and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to inhibit it. NPF-M neurons regulate multiple motivated behaviors, including appetitive and consummatory thirst, food foraging, and courtship, driven by distinct input neurons. NPF-M neurons output to appetitive and aversive dopaminergic, mushroom body ongoing behavior integration center, and navigation circuits. This circuit exhibits similarities to those for hungry food foraging and courtship. NPF-M and Janu-AstA form a network with OviIN hub neurons that are sex-independent thirst neurons. We suggest that NPF-M neurons form a circuit branch that funnels male-specific information to tune motivated behavior.

Article.Title: THE BILE ACID RECEPTOR TGR5 MODULATES HIPPOCAMPAL NEURAL STEM CELL STATE AND AGEING
Article.Authors: Kaushik, D.; Dugam, P.; Sarkar, G.; Kumar, B. A.; Patel, S. K.; Pydi, S. P.; Yadav, P. N.
Article.Abstract: Ageing locks hippocampal neural stem cells (NSCs) into deeper quiescence and inflammation-driven senescence, which are also associated with impaired cognition. The bile-acid receptor TGR5, a member class I G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), is expressed in cultured hippocampal NSCs and in SOX2-positive cells of the adult sub granular zone, yet its role in NSC homeostasis is unknown. In this study we show that TGR5 selective agonist, TC-G 1005, expanded the NSC pool without forcing neuronal differentiation. Primary NSCs treatment with TC-G 1005 increased BrdU incorporation and PCNA in a concentration-dependent manner, and both responses were lost after TGR5 knockdown. TGR5 agonism in differentiating cultures increased nestin, left doublecortin (DCX) unchanged and suppressed MAP2 expression, preserving stemness rather than neuronal commitment. The agonist also released BMP4-imposed quiescence, lowering FOXO3a and restoring phospho-EGFR and ASCL1, and reopened autophagic flux, with less p62 and LC3-II, fewer LAMP2 puncta and more Beclin-1. Furthermore, activation of TGR5 suppressed IL-6 induced p53 and p16 expression, restored proliferation and contracted the inflammatory transcriptome by more than 90%, including Cdkn2a, Cdkn2b and Cdk6. In 18-month-old mice, brain-penetrant TC-G 1005 (5 mg/kg, subcutaneously, twice daily for 28 days) expanded SOX2-positive and proliferating NSCs, reduced p16, recovered ASCL1 and improved spatial memory, without changing locomotion or generating DCX-positive neurons. Dentate gyrus-restricted TGR5 knockdown abolished these cellular effects and the rescue of spatial and social discrimination. Hippocampal proteomic analysis revealed that TC-G 1005 treated aged mice occupied an intermediate, partially rejuvenated position between young and aged proteomes, with 86 proteins shared between ageing- and treatment-responsive sets, and mitochondrial and complement C1q modules shifted toward youthful levels. TGR5 activation therefore relieves both quiescence and senescence in the aged neurogenic niche without driving neuronal differentiation. Collectively, these results suggest that TGR5 could be targeted to preserve cognition in ageing by rejuvenating the hippocampal stem-cell niche.

Article.Title: Cortex-wide single-cell activity mapping in freely moving mice
Article.Authors: Guo, C.; Xie, M.; Qiu, G.; Lu, J.; Liu, Y.; Qu, L.; Huang, Y.; Tian, J.; Lin, J.; Guo, Z.; Zhang, B.; Zhang, X.; Zhao, J.; Liu, X.; Long, H.; Ma, J.; Zhou, B.; Ye, X.; Zhao, P.; Cao, J.; Lin, Z.; Zhang, Z.; Deng, W.; Wang, J.; Wu, W.; Wang, J.; Peng, X.; Zhao, S.; Na, S.; Li, H.; Liu, W.; Fu, Q.; Guo, Z. V.; Zhao, W.; Chen, L.
Article.Abstract: How the cortex supports complex, naturalistic behavior can be revealed only in freely moving animals. Although head-mounted microscopes promise access to the neural dynamics underlying such behavior, fundamental trade-offs among field of view, spatial resolution, device weight, and background contamination have prevented cortex-wide single-neuron recording, leaving distributed cortical coordination largely inaccessible. To meet these challenges, we introduce COMET (Cortex-wide Observational Miniature Epifluorescence Technique), a 3.75-g head-mounted mesoscope that integrates an aberration-controlled wide-field optical design, uniform high-efficiency excitation and single-coaxial power-and-data transmission with an end-to-end denoising and signal-extraction pipeline. This enables cortex-wide calcium imaging at single-cell resolution in freely moving mice. COMET captures activity from >15,000 layer 2/3 neurons per 5-min recording over fields of view up to 10 mm in diameter while preserving natural behavior. Benchmarking against benchtop two-photon microscopy demonstrates high spatial concordance of detected neurons and matched event-level calcium dynamics. We apply COMET to social interaction to quantify region-specific engagement and to an auditory trace fear-conditioning task that requires natural movement and behavioral expression, revealing time-ordered changes in regional firing-rate structure and functional connectivity preceding a global conditioned response. COMET provides an open, lightweight hardware-software framework for linking single-neuron activity to cortex-scale network dynamics during freely expressed behaviors under changing internal or external conditions.

Article.Title: A disinhibition-based model of CA1 place field sequences
Article.Authors: Green, L.; Voroslakos, M.; Buzsaki, G.; RINZEL, J.
Article.Abstract: Because of the paucity of pattern-generating recurrent excitation in the CA1 hippocampal region, place field sequences are assumed to be inherited from upstream regions. Alternatively, disinhibition may play a role in shaping pyramidal cell activity. We propose a model of CA1 activity using one layer of excitatory cells and one layer of inhibitory cells, with local excitatory-to-inhibitory connectivity, broad inhibitory-to-excitatory connectivity without recurrent excitatory connections, and broad inhibitory-inhibitory connections. The layers need not follow a topographic organization; instead they can represent sequences of place cells structured by local inhibition. Our mathematical model of CA1 neurons with data-inspired connectivity demonstrates place fields sharpened by disinhibition, mimicking a recently discovered decrease in inhibitory input within place fields and matching in vivo patterns of disinhibition. Mathematical analysis of our model suggests the importance of inhibitory-to-excitatory connections in control of place cell firing rate and sparsity. We also demonstrate that a disinhibition-based mechanism of pattern generation is more flexible without recurrent excitation than the recurrent excitation-rich CA3-like model. Finally, we demonstrate disinhibition as an efficient mechanism for internally-generated sequential activity, where the speed of sequential change depends on both input strength and inhibitory-to-excitatory connection strength. Overall, our model suggests that theta time-scale disinhibition is a foundational mechanism of self-organized sequential activity in the CA1 region, and, possibly, in other networks.

Article.Title: Regional macrophage specialization shapes intestinal neuroimmune function
Article.Authors: Warasnhe, K.; Ortiz Colmenares, J. S.; D'Ambrosio, M.; Di Lorenzo, B.; Liu, Y.; Ji, S.; Mischopoulou, M.; Wertish, N. R.; Eldesouki, M. H.; Chai, X.-y.; Jiang, J. X.; Grover, M.; Sharkey, K. A.; Beyder, A.; Farrugia, G.; Cipriani, G.
Article.Abstract: Tissue-resident macrophages adapt to local environments to support organ-specific functions, but whether their regulation differs across regions of the same organ is poorly understood. The gastrointestinal tract provides an ideal system to address this question because its anatomically distinct regions perform specialized physiological functions and contain different cellular environments. Here, we found that intestinal muscularis macrophages (MMs) exhibited distinct regional trophic requirements and neuroimmune functions across the gut. Small-intestinal MMs were highly sensitive to CSF1 neutralization but recovered robustly, whereas colonic MMs were less sensitive to CSF1 depletion yet showed limited recovery. Disruption of CSF1-dependent MMs selectively reduced nitrergic neurons and altered motility in the small intestine, whereas the colonic neuronal compartment was comparatively preserved. Csf1 was enriched in small-intestinal nNOS+ neurons, and neuron-specific Csf1 deletion reduced both MMs and nitrergic neurons and altered small-intestinal transit, with limited effects in the colon. Together, these findings reveal that macrophage trophic requirements and neuroimmune functions are regionally specialized within the intestine and identify neuronal CSF1 as a key component of the trophic relationship between nitrergic neurons and MMs in the small intestine.

Article.Title: Operator-valued free probability applied to recurrent neural networks with heterogeneity in local and global circuit structures
Article.Authors: Jiang, J.; Tian, G.; Doiron, B.
Article.Abstract: Random connectivity is a common assumption in models of recurrent neural networks, yet biological circuits combine heterogeneous synaptic connections with organization into distinct anatomical regions and functional groups. How does this global structure interact with cellular and local circuit heterogeneity to shape the dimensionality of population activity? In our work, we use operator-valued free probability to derive the covariance spectrum and effective dimension of recurrent networks with heterogeneous gains and block-structured random connectivity. This framework handles the noncommuting matrix operations through which cellular and circuit heterogeneity jointly determine population variability. We show that the linear relationship between effective dimension and firing rate uniformity persists despite global connectivity structure. At fixed total connectivity variance and with identical firing rate distributions across areas, concentrating variance within one area decreases dimension, whereas concentrating it in directed connections between areas increases dimension. Together, these results establish a mechanistic connection between circuit organization and population dimensionality, and demonstrate how operator-valued free probability unifies cellular, local, and global sources of heterogeneity in recurrent networks.

Article.Title: Eye versus hand effector-specificity in the parieto-frontal cortex and cerebellum in humans
Article.Authors: Rubino, C.; Masoudi, K.; Gallivan, J.; Crawford, J. D.
Article.Abstract: The degree and distribution of effector-specific representations for saccade and reach movements in the human brain remain unclear, partly because overlapping regional activation and the limited temporal resolution of fMRI complicate the identification of effector-dependent signals. Using a cue-separated event-related fMRI paradigm, we examined cortical and cerebellar activity across three temporally separated phases: visual target encoding, movement planning, and movement execution in 19 adults. We combined conventional univariate analyses with multivariate analyses of spatial activity patterns to characterize overlapping and distinct neural activity associated with each effector. Univariate analyses revealed widespread overlap across parieto-frontal regions, alongside effector-dependent differences in the magnitude and distribution of activation. Reach-related activity was generally more extensive than saccade-related activity, particularly during planning, while execution revealed distinct patterns of effector-preferential activation across cortical and cerebellar regions. Despite overlapping activation, multivariate analyses identified distinguishable spatial activity patterns across cortical and cerebellar regions. These findings confirm that (1) separating sensorimotor phases improves the detection of effector-preferential signals across the brain, and (2) overlapping activation during eye and hand movements does not necessarily imply equivalent neural activity patterns. Instead, multivariate analyses reveal widespread effector-dependent differences, suggesting a greater degree of spatial differentiation between saccade- and reach-related activity across the human cortex and cerebellum than conventual activation analyses alone would indicate.

Together, our findings identify the parathyroid hormonal system acts as a fine-tuning mechanism in specialized neuronal circuits allowing for hypothalamic adaptive responses to energy demands and systemic metabolic signals. Article.Title: The trade-off between fractal morphology and function of Drosophila neurons
Article.Authors: Marton, I.-B.; Pentek, B.; Ercsey-Ravasz, M.
Article.Abstract: Studying correlation between structure and function in brain networks has long been a central and compelling topic in neuroscience. Using the FlyWire project's fully digitized Drosophila melanogaster brain map, we analyzed a total number of 125330 3D skeletons of neurons from various functional super-classes and classes. By separating axonal and dendritic arbors of individual neurons we compare several morphological and topological properties, including cable length, fractal dimension, number of nodes, maximum width, and tree height. The fractal dimensions of neurons can reach up to 2.4, with dendritic arbors generally more complex than axonal ones, except in the afferent flow, where the situation is reversed. Correlating fractal dimension with cable length reveals that neurons from the same classes cluster in state space. These clusters densify and separate more clearly as we go deeper down the hierarchical annotation schema, indicating that the brain specializes fractal morphology for distinct functional classes.

Article.Title: Brain FACTs: A same-section workflow for Fiber Architecture, Cytoarchitecture and cell Types in large-scale brain sections
Article.Authors: Kooijmans, R. N.; Axer, M.; Graessel, D.; Amunts, K.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the human brain's multiscale organization requires linking cells, connections and architecture, yet conventional methods are incompatible within a single specimen, and inter-individual variability confounds cross-brain comparisons. Multiple-label immunohistochemistry for different cell types has been applied in interleaved sections but remains challenging within a single large human brain section and, has never been combined on the same tissue with 3D polarized light imaging (3D-PLI) for three-dimensional fiber architecture. Here we introduce a sequential multimodal workflow integrating 3D-PLI, multiplex chromogenic immunohistochemistry and Nissl staining on the same large human brain section, preserving each technique's quality and specificity. The method was validated on vervet monkey and Wistar rat sections. The resulting paired high-resolution images eliminate inter-subject variability and enable direct micron-scale mapping of fiber tracts relative to molecularly defined cell types, yielding previously inaccessible insights such as molecular identification of white-matter components, refined cortical layering and cytoarchitectural disambiguation.

Article.Title: Three-hinge gyri link individualized folding topology to cortical and superficial white-matter diffusion organization
Article.Authors: Chen, M.; Dong, X.; Cheng, J.; Hu, D.; Liu, T.; Zhu, D.; Li, G.
Article.Abstract: Individual differences in cortical folding are a hallmark of human brain anatomy, but what this variability reflects in the underlying tissue remains unclear. Three-hinge gyri (3HGs), where three gyral crests converge, provide an individualized higher-order folding landmark for probing this relationship. Diffusivity differences extended across the cortical ribbon, whereas anisotropy- and fiber-related differences strengthened toward and beneath the white surface. Ex vivo, diffusion measures also varied with gyral-skeleton degree, and streamlines sampled beneath 3HGs preferentially reached other 3HGs. These findings link individualized folding topology to cortical and superficial white-matter diffusion-inferred tissue properties, providing tissue-level context for understanding the microstructural correlates of individual folding variation.

Article.Title: Metabolic Cost Asymmetry as a Structural Regulariser for Recurrent Spiking Neural Networks
Article.Authors: Sotero, R.; Sanchez-Bornot, J. M.
Article.Abstract: Cortical energy expenditure is heavily dominated by synaptic transmission, with excitatory (glutamatergic) signalling demanding substantially more ATP than inhibitory (GABAergic) signalling. Yet existing trainable spiking neural networks treat energy as a generic, synapse-type-agnostic penalty. Here, we embed this fundamental glutamate/GABA cost asymmetry as a Lagrangian penalty within a surrogate-gradient learning framework, and use it to train a Dale's-law-compliant recurrent microcircuit on the Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD) benchmark. Because glutamatergic synapses are metabolically more expensive, a single scalar penalty applied uniformly to all weights automatically exerts stronger gradient pressure on excitatory pathways. We demonstrate that this differential pressure alone is sufficient to produce three major effects. First, it moves the network out of the suboptimal, inhibition-dominated regime of the unpenalised network, simultaneously improving accuracy and reducing total energy several-fold. Second, it induces an emergent pruning hierarchy in which excitatory connections are eliminated first, while inhibitory connections exhibit graded resistance. Third, it actively expands the dimensionality of the population code at moderate penalty strengths. These structural motifs remain robust across a two-dimensional sweep of five cost ratios and fifteen structural densities (75 distinct conditions). Ultimately, our results demonstrate that a single biophysical cost asymmetry, operating without auxiliary regularisers or architectural priors, is sufficient to organise sparse, pathway-specific circuit structure in recurrent spiking networks.

Article.Title: Directional coordination along the cortical hierarchy is selectively reorganized in schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Wiafe, S.-L.; Soleimani, N.; Fu, Z.; Miller, R.; Calhoun, V.
Article.Abstract: Schizophrenia has long been framed as a disorder of the cortical hierarchy. Yet, the hierarchy has been studied almost entirely as fixed anatomy, leaving its moment-to-moment expression in ongoing brain activity unmeasured. By retaining the signed lead-lag geometry that conventional connectivity measures discard, complex-valued phase synchrony resolved a dynamic directional axis of coordination in which regions reversed their lead-lag relationship over time as the brain transitioned among feedback, feedforward, and integrative regimes. The three regimes replicated across seven datasets from four independent cohorts and aligned region by region with an independently defined cortical hierarchy. Neighboring organizing principles, including propagating waves, arousal, and the principal gradient, were insufficient to explain regime identity. Within the same subjects, GABAergic sedation shifted coordination toward feedback and motor imagery toward feedforward, demonstrating that the axis reflects a manipulable property of brain dynamics rather than a statistical partition. In schizophrenia (151 patients, 160 controls), the axis reorganized selectively: feedback coordination became less persistent, integrative coordination more persistent, feedforward comparatively spared, and trajectories less diverse. These effects replicated in an independent clinical cohort (68 patients, 89 controls). The reorganization tracked positive symptom severity, and its relationship to cognition reversed relative to controls: faster convergence to equilibrium was associated with better cognition in controls and worse cognition in patients. Directional coordination therefore identifies a reproducible and controllable dynamic expression of the cortical hierarchy that is selectively reorganized in schizophrenia and linked to both symptoms and cognitive function.

Article.Title: Variabilities in the shapes of the receptive fields of simple cells in mice
Article.Authors: Meshcherina, D.; Auffarth, B.; Lindeberg, T.
Article.Abstract: Observing an object under different viewing conditions, in spite of substantial variability in the image structures when changing the distance or the viewing direction relative to the object, we can maintain the identity of the object. How does the vision system cope with this variability, that will substantially influence the receptive field responses? One hypothesis is that the receptive field family should be covariant under geometric image transformations and thereby have variabilities in the shapes of the receptive fields corresponding to the degrees of freedom of the geometric image transformations. Specifically, it has been predicted that the receptive fields should have a variability in the degree of elongation, corresponding to varying the slant angle when observing local surface patches. Such a variability has also been predicted from indirect support in terms of variabilities in the orientation selectivity properties in V1 for monkeys and cats, which by a theoretical model has been linked to variabilities in the elongation of th receptive fields. In this paper, we measure such variabilities in receptive field shapes in a more direct way, by reconstructing receptive fields from calcium imaging experiments for mice previously performed by the Allen Institute. Our findings reveal a variability in the degree of elongation that exceeds what measurement noise produces, spanning about a factor of 5, thereby showing that the predictions that were made for higher mammals with orientation maps, such as primates and cats, also apply to a species without orientation maps, with its primary visual cortex instead based on a salt-and-pepper organization of the receptive fields.

Article.Title: Synaptic microRNA dysregulation orchestrates aberrant glutamatergic transmission in a human neuronal model of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
Article.Authors: Niu, W.; Guo, J.; Ran, X.; Parker, D.; Li, X.; Yu, S.; Imes, S.; Purcell, R.; Michalski, C.; Guo, E.; Jiang, S. Y.; Xu, E.; Bassell, G. J.; Mulle, J. G.; Ousley, O. Y.; Pearce, B.; Feng, Y.; Bearden, C. E.; Walker, E. F.; Cubells, J. F.; Qin, Z.; Duncan, E.; Wen, Z.
Article.Abstract: 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome (22q11DS), the most prevalent chromosomal microdeletion disorder in humans (incidence ~1 in 4,000 live births), arises from hemizygous deletions of a 1.5-3.0 Mb region on chromosome 22. However, the mechanisms by which the 22q11.2 deletion perturbs neuronal function and drive psychotic manifestations in 22q11DS remain poorly defined. Cellular and electrophysiological analyses revealed that 22q11DS neurons exhibit hyperexcitability, reduced glutamatergic synaptic transmission, and impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity, which are pathophysiological hallmarks that may be relevant to the clinical, cognitive, and psychophysiological profiles of patients. Transcriptomic profiling of neurons and synaptosomes from 22q11DS cortical organoids uncovered dysregulated immune pathways and synaptic gene networks. Integrative mRNA-microRNA network analysis identified synergistic downregulation of hsa-miR-185-5p and hsa-miR-128-3p at synapses, driving aberrant regulation of immune and synaptic transcripts. Experimental knockdown of these microRNAs in control neurons recapitulated the molecular and functional phenotypes of 22q11DS neurons, thereby establishing a mechanistic link to synaptic dysfunction and impaired plasticity. Collectively, these findings delineate a multimodal mechanistic framework that bridges genetic vulnerability, synaptic pathology, and psychosis penetrance in 22q11DS, positioning dysregulated synaptic microRNAs as nodal regulators of neurodevelopmental networks and potential therapeutic targets.

Article.Title: Molecular anatomy of the entorhinal cortex
Article.Authors: Morello-Megias, A.; Dhulipalla, B. S.; Kahvecioglu, H. A.; Shin, J.; Joseph, S.; Aggarwal, D.; Luebke, J. I.; Rosene, D. L.; Dimovasili, C.; Roussarie, J.-P.
Article.Abstract: The entorhinal cortex (EC) is critical for episodic memory formation and is the epicenter of neurofibrillary tangle formation in Alzheimer's disease. While many features of the region appear to be conserved between rodents and primates, very little is known about the conservation of the molecular identity of EC neurons. While the well-known dichotomy between lateral and medial EC is evident in superficial layers of EC, we highlight that the medioventral region of EC forms a different population from the caudomedial section. We identify molecular correlates for the previously described parcellation of lateral EC, and show that, at least in layer IIa, subterritories of EC are not separated by abrupt borders but rather form smooth gradients. Lastly, we show that both lateral vs. medial ECIIa markers, and markers that reveal finer grain heterogeneity within ECIIa have conserved patterns of expression in macaque, highlighting the high degree of homology between the two species. Overall this molecular atlas of the mouse EC with some comparative elements is a resource for anatomically-informed molecular studies of the EC and lays the groundwork for mechanistic studies of selective neuronal vulnerability of the region in the context of AD.

Article.Title: Speech Tracking in fMRI Reveals a Distinct Response to Sentence Boundaries During Comprehension
Article.Authors: Levy-David, O.; Tikochinski, R.; Reichart, R.; Zion Golumbic, E.; Deschamps, I.; Agmon, G.
Article.Abstract: Psycholinguistic research and linguistic theory suggest that comprehending continuous speech involves segmenting it into sentences. Yet, direct neuroimaging evidence for this process remains scarce, partly because sentence boundaries coincide with acoustic, prosodic, lexical, and syntactic changes. This approach revealed sensitivity to continuously varying features of speech across multiple brain regions. Responses associated with prosodic breaks and emphasis were found in right temporal cortex, syntactic bottom-up node count in the left superior temporal sulcus, and word concreteness in the parahippocampal gyri. Critically, sentence-final words were associated with an increased activation in right temporal regions, after accounting for acoustic, prosodic, lexical, semantic and syntactic properties. These findings provide evidence for a neural response to sentence boundaries consistent with active sentence segmentation. More generally, this study demonstrates the value of continuous-regressor modelling for investigating speech comprehension with fMRI.

Article.Title: What is pathogenicity? Structural vulnerabilities lead to distinct phenotypes in a membrane protein, ATP1A3
Article.Authors: Sweadner, K. J.; Ozelius, L. J.; Domingo, A.; Mangkalaphiban, K.; Haq, I. U.; Brashear, A.; Arystarkhova, E.
Article.Abstract: Distinct protein features of pathogenic variants are illustrated here for a gene with an extraordinarily wide range of neurological syndromes: ATP1A3, the neuronal Na,K-ATPase. Vulnerable structure features produce mechanistically different consequences, from loss or gain of function to maladaptive cell biological responses. Variants in specific structural elements (glycines, prolines, and {beta}-sheets) link severe phenotype to impaired folding during biosynthesis. In contrast, impaired protein-protein interactions may result in brain malformation. Defective RNA transcripts, on the other hand, exhibit a range of benign to severe phenotypes, likely due to efficacy variability in the defensive degradation of aberrant mRNA and protein. Variant interpretation will benefit from understanding structure-specific vulnerabilities.

Article.Title: Beyond Rate: Hippocampal Phase Codes for Space and Memory
Article.Authors: Kolibius, L. D.; Hermiller, M. S.; ter Wal, M.; van der Plas, M.; Gollwitzer, S.; Walther, K.; Hopfengärtner, R.; Hamer, H.; Khazali, M. F.; Hanslmayr, S.; Bowman, H.; Jacobs, J.
Article.Abstract: Place cells and concept neurons are defined by a rise in firing rate at a particular location or for a particular person or object. Neurons without such a rise remain unlabeled, although they keep firing during the task. Such neurons could still carry information in the timing of their spikes. Hippocampal theta provides a reference for this timing. We therefore asked whether the theta phase of a neuron's spikes depends on location or on the viewed image, even when its firing rate does not. We analysed hippocampal neurons in humans navigating a virtual city, rats running on a linear track, and humans viewing images of anima ls, faces, and places. In both navigation datasets, more neurons than expected by chance fired at a consistent theta phase at particular locations. This phase tuning remained after we excluded neurons whose firing rate depended on location. In human navigation, the spike phases of these remaining neurons improved location decoding beyond the firing rates of all neurons. More phase-tuned neurons than expected by chance also fired at progressively earlier theta phases as participants passed each neuron's preferred location. This pattern resembles phase precession, which classically occurs as an animal crosses the firing-rate field of a place cell. The neurons that showed it had no firing-rate field, so their phase shift was anchored to the location defined by phase tuning alone. During image viewing, more neurons than expected by chance changed the theta phase of their spikes after a particular image appeared. This effect remained after we removed, for each neuron, the images that changed its firing rate. Spike phases alone also predicted the image category above chance. Theta-relative spike timing therefore carries in formation about location and images that firing rate alone misses. We propose that weak input changes when a neuron fires with in the theta cycle, whereas strong input also raises its firing rate.

Article.Title: A parsimonious, age-invariant, and psychometrically validated neural signature of task-control network functioning
Article.Authors: Paige, K. J.; Molloy, M. F.; Angstadt, M.; Hyde, L.; Sripada, C.; Heitzeg, M.; Weigard, A. J.
Article.Abstract: Neuroimaging has vast potential for identifying brain features that support individual and developmental differences in cognition, but challenges related to the dimensionality, unreliability, and unknown developmental properties of neuroimaging measures prevent this from being realized. We overcome these challenges by applying latent variable modeling to demand-related responses in the "task-control" frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks (FPN, DAN) within the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and Human Connectome Project. Task-control activations are well-captured by a bifactor structure with a general factor spanning FPN/DAN and network-specific factors that is remarkably invariant across middle childhood to early adolescence and largely generalizes to adulthood. Trait-state-occasion modeling reveals a general task-control trait that shows robust associations with cognitive abilities, clinical symptoms, and grades. Repeated neuroimaging substantially increases associations. Findings establish a parsimonious neural signature that generalizes across samples, is stable across development, and has broad utility for understanding developmental and individual differences in goal-directed behavior.

Article.Abstract: Dopamine signaling is crucial for motivation, movement, and learning, but has remained beyond the reach of measurement in healthy humans. Here, we measured sub-second dopamine in the olfactory epithelium of healthy humans during two reward learning tasks with distinct reward types: liquid reward during a conditioning task and monetary reward during an economic exchange game. In both tasks, as trials progress, peak dopamine transients shift from rewarding outcomes back to reward-predictive cues. In the economic game, this pattern retrains quickly when reward magnitude or reward timing is changed without warning. These findings match the time transfer characteristics and amplitude dependence of temporal difference prediction error signals. Article.Title: Aging effects on retrospective and naturalistic encoding of time and their relationship with memory.
Article.Authors: Fricker, F.; Buzi, G.; Morantin, M.; Doidy, F.; Clochon, P.; Bordas, R.; Leroy, N.; d'Argembeau, A.; van Wassenhove, V.; Hinault, T. T.
Article.Abstract: In everyday life, attention is not explicitly directed toward time. Yet, we can reconstruct how long an experience lasted from the memory traces it left behind, a process intertwined with episodic memory and subjective experience. As both memory and temporal processing change with advancing age, investigating aging effects could provide critical insights on these reconstructive processes. In this study, 31 younger (aged 24{+/-}3) and 36 older (aged 69{+/-}6) healthy adults completed two EEG sessions: 1) a resting-state recording followed by an unexpected retrospective time estimation, and 2) a video-based prospective duration estimation task where participants encoded and judged the duration of 50 naturalistic videos (2-32s) varying in eventfulness. Using a cycle-by-cycle burst analysis of alpha (: 8-12 Hz), we examined oscillatory correlates of both retrospective temporal judgement and prospective temporal processing. Behaviorally, both groups reconstructed short intervals similarly, but older adults produced longer prospective duration estimates than younger adults for longer video clips (16-32s), particularly under low-eventfulness. Regression analyses also showed that individual differences in older adults' prospective duration judgments were influenced by both their retrospective time estimation and episodic memory abilities, especially for longer videos. At the neural level, resting-state -burst dynamics were higher in older adults and predicted, with -power, longer retrospective estimates in older adults. Additionally, resting-state -burst activity predicted -burst during video encoding in both groups. Together, these findings reveal that individual -power and -burst dynamics could constitute memory-based time-tracking mechanism that aging reshapes in ways that manifest behaviorally under naturalistic conditions.

Article.Title: The vagus nerve drives cognitive function through the default mode network
Article.Authors: Yamakawa, M.; Togashi, T.; Kawagoe, H.; Shiratori, R.; Fukushima, F.; Urushihata, T.; Xie, Z.; Kayama, T.; Ikeda, G.; Xue, W.; Xiaoying, T.; Kawaoka, S.; Hongbo, W.; Maekawa, M.; Owada, Y.; Seiriki, K.; Hashimoto, H.; Konno, A.; Hirai, H.; Tsuneoka, Y.; Satoh, A.; Igarashi, H.; Iwasaki, Y.; Arimura, N.; Kuga, N.; Sasaki, T.
Article.Abstract: The afferent vagus nerve transmits interoceptive signals to the brain but a systematic understanding of how vagal signals affect brain-wide neuronal dynamics remains elusive. Here, comprehensive spatiotemporal analyses across the entire mouse brain revealed that vagus nerve stimulation activated neuronal ensembles within the default mode network (DMN). In contrast, vagal-independent mechanisms predominantly affected the salience network. The vagal-DMN association was mediated by locus coeruleus neuronal subpopulations. Selective activation or silencing of vagal-responsive DMN neuronal ensembles replicated or abolished VNS-induced enhancement of cognitive behaviors and progressive problem-solving behaviors. These findings establish a unifying framework for how the vagus nerve drives cognitive functions by engaging the DMN.

Article.Title: Grasping Under Target Size and Location Uncertainty
Article.Authors: LeBlanc, K. A.; Lacroix, A. T. D.; Benwell, J. A.; Grant, M.; Feltmate, B. B. T.; Neyedli, H. F.
Article.Abstract: Everyday actions often require movements to be planned before the exact target is known, yet most research on grasping has examined situations in which individuals reach toward a single, well-defined object. The present study investigated how grasping actions are planned under target uncertainty using a go-before-you-know (GBYK) paradigm, in which participants initiated their movement before knowing which of two potential objects would become the target. Using 3D motion capture, we examined whether peak grip aperture (PGA) was influenced by the size of a competing nontarget object. Participants grasped cylindrical objects that varied in size under two conditions: GBYK, in which target identity was revealed after movement initiation, and know-before-you-go (KBYG), in which the target was known prior to movement onset. Across two experiments, participants appropriately scaled grip aperture according to the target object in both conditions. However, during GBYK trials, PGA was influenced by the presence of a larger nontarget object. Specifically, when grasping a small target paired with a large nontarget, participants produced larger grip apertures, whereas a small nontarget did not influence grasping toward a large target. This asymmetric interference pattern is inconsistent with a motor averaging account, which predicts bidirectional shifts toward an intermediate aperture. Instead, the findings suggest that under conditions of uncertainty, grasp planning incorporates competing object information in a manner that prioritizes successful object acquisition. Together, these findings extend research on action planning under uncertainty beyond reaching and highlight the dynamic nature of grasp planning when multiple potential targets are present.

Article.Title: Convergent and Distinct Transcriptional Signatures in Suicide, Bipolar Disorder, and Major Depressive Disorder
Article.Authors: Mishra, R.; Wamalwa, A. M.; Guason, G.; Dupont, M. B.
Article.Abstract: Globally, a person dies by suicide every 40 seconds, underscoring a major global public health concern. In the United States, suicide is the second leading cause of death among individuals aged 10-34 years. Suicide is a complex, multifactorial phenomenon influenced by genetic and epigenetic factors and is strongly associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD). However, the extent to which their molecular signatures converge or diverge across disorders and brain regions remains incompletely understood. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of suicide, MDD, and BD transcriptomic studies in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible studies used human postmortem brain tissue, reported a complete genome-wide transcriptomic list of differentially expressed genes (DEG), and compared suicide decedents with psychiatric non-suicide individuals diagnosed with the same underlying disorder. Regarding BD, studies comparing affected individuals to unaffected controls were included. Single-cell and peripheral-blood studies were excluded because unavailable for suicide. Curated suicide and BD DEG datasets were integrated with a published bulk transcriptomic dataset of MDD. We identified both shared and disease-specific molecular signatures across suicide, BD, and MDD, and identified DEGs shared across brain regions and those that were region-specific. A total of 276 genes were shared across all three conditions, implicating cellular stress, hypoxia (VEGFA, ADM, NDRG1, DDIT4), immune and inflammatory signaling through TNF/NF-{kappa}B (IL1B, ICAM1, NFE2L2) and IL6-JAK-STAT3 pathways (STAT3, SOCS3, IL1R1m OSMR), complement activation (CIR, SERPiNA1, LGALS3), extracellular matrix remodeling (COL4A1, SERPINH1, PLOD2), and unfolded protein response (BAG3, WFS1, MTHFD2). Suicide-associated DEGs were prominently downregulated, and involved metal-ion homeostasis, stress responses, synaptic regulation, and circadian pathways, whereas BD showed downregulation in synaptic and vesicle-related processes alongside region-specific metabolic dysregulation. MDD exhibited changes in RNA processing, ribosomal function, and protein synthesis. Genetic integration revealed that 133 genes shared between BD and MDD had gene variants associated with the corresponding condition per GWAS. Transcription factor analysis identified 20 regulatory factors with altered activity across all three conditions despite differences in their predicted downstream targets. Overall, these findings suggest that suicide, MDD, and BD share aspects of their molecular and regulatory pathophysiology while exhibiting distinct patterns, including in a region-specific manner.

Article.Title: Autoencoder-based anomaly mapping and visualization of white matter deformation with application to glioma cases
Article.Authors: Shams, B.; Fekonja, L.; Vajkoczy, P.; Picht, T.; Aydogan, D. B.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Gliomas can alter white matter pathways, causing structural deformation and functional impairments. However, there is no method to map these structural alterations across the whole brain to support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework based on a convolutional autoencoder that learns geometry-preserving streamline embeddings for mapping structural connectivity anomalies. Methods: We trained and validated the autoencoder on 100 million synthetic streamlines and evaluated the anomaly-mapping pipeline using data from 118 healthy subjects. We analyzed how different tractography algorithms affect anomaly scores and demonstrated its feasibility in five glioma patients using multi-shell and single-shell diffusion MRI. Results: Latent-space distances strongly associated with native-space geometric distances (R2 = 0.82-0.98), supporting preserved streamline geometry in the learned embeddings. Anomaly scores varied with both the input and reference tractography methods. Patient anomaly maps showed elevated scores near gliomas and extending distally along affected pathways. These whole-brain anomaly maps were generated within minutes. Conclusion: The framework offers a practical way to quantify and visualize geometric deviations in whole-brain tractograms, providing novel insights beyond current network and microstructural analyses, with relevance to clinical applications where white matter deformation is pertinent.

Article.Title: Linguistic Context Shapes Representations in the Human Visual Cortex
Article.Authors: Li, S.; Jin, Z.; Zhang, R.-Y.; Gu, S.; Li, Y.
Article.Abstract: Language provides a way to anticipate visual scenes before they are seen, but how this context relates to visual representations across levels of abstraction remains unclear. Here, 210 hours of functional magnetic resonance imaging from eight participants performing a delayed caption-image matching task are analyzed using computational encoding, decoding, and alignment models. Caption-evoked activity carries semantic information across visual cortex, including early visual areas. Subsequent image responses vary with both the strength of caption-derived contextual representations and the discrepancy between anticipated and viewed scenes, assessed across lower-level visual and higher-level semantic features. Two functionally distinct voxel populations are identified within early visual cortex: suppression populations respond less strongly to matching than mismatching images, whereas enhancement populations show the opposite pattern. Despite their lower responses to matching images, suppression populations support comparable or better retrieval of corresponding caption-evoked responses using fewer voxels. The two populations also differ in their temporal dynamics, representational structure, and relationship to behavior. Together, these findings link linguistic context to both the strength and informational content of visual cortical responses, revealing how language-vision relationships are expressed across representational levels and two functionally distinct populations in early visual cortex.

Article.Title: Short-Term Plasticity of Contrast Surround Suppression During Repeated Psychophysical Measurement
Article.Authors: Jin, N.; Zhang, Q.; Cai, Y.
Article.Abstract: Perceptual surround suppression is commonly treated as stable within a testing session, but recent evidence for normalization reweighting suggests that suppressive interactions can be modified by recent visual input. Here, we asked whether surround suppression changes over minutes of repeated measurement and whether such change varies with stimulus and sampling conditions. Across four psychophysical experiments, we tracked contrast and motion surround suppression while varying center-surround orientation and stimulus spatiotemporal properties. With static gratings, contrast surround suppression increased early and then approached a plateau, with no evidence that this change depended on center-surround orientation. With dynamic gratings, an increase emerged only under finer temporal sampling and more sustained stimulation, and model-based analyses suggested a faster increase than with static stimulation. Motion surround suppression measured with drifting gratings showed no systematic change. Together, these findings show that contrast surround suppression can change within a single psychophysical session without a separate adaptation phase, and that its measured time course varies with stimulus and sampling conditions. The results are consistent with rapid, experience-dependent reweighting of contextual normalization.

Article.Title: Dishevelled2 Condensates control Axon Initial Segment (AIS) assembly and function through MTCL1-Dependent microtubule recruitment.
Article.Authors: Belmonte, S.; Poirault-Chassac, S.; Villagomez, J.; Isch, C.; Dorrego-Rivas, A.; Donier, M.; Chagny, E.; Renou, E.; Vacher, L.; Aubailly, N.; Moreau, M. M.; David, M.; Mondin, M.; Montcouquiol, M.; Sainlos, M.; Battefeld, A.; Sans, N.; Ezan, J.
Article.Abstract: In the epithelium, Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) signaling coordinates cellular organization along the plane of the tissue, perpendicular to the apicobasal axis. In neurons, polarity is instead expressed through the structural and molecular asymmetry that separates the axon from the somatodendritic compartment. Core PCP proteins are essential for neuronal development and function, and have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorders and epilepsy. However, their precise roles in the establishment of neuronal polarity remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify Dishevelled2 (Dvl2), a central PCP signaling scaffold, as a novel component of the axon initial segment (AIS), the proximal axonal domain that maintains neuronal polarity and initiates action potentials. We show that Dvl2 defines, both in vivo and in cultured hippocampal neurons, a proximal subdomain positioned upstream of the major AIS marker Ankyrin-G (Ank-G) and is closely associated with microtubule bundles. Dvl2 is already detected during early axon specification, suggesting that it participates in the initial organization of the proximal axon. Functional depletion of Dvl proteins disrupts AIS architecture, reduces the accumulation of Ankyrin-G and other core AIS components, and impairs the organization of AIS microtubule bundles. These structural defects translate into altered neuronal excitability, with a reduced AIS-dependent component of the action potential. Mechanistically, we identify MTCL1 as a microtubule-associated partner that recruits Dvl2 from biomolecular condensate assemblies onto microtubules. This recruitment requires the DIX and PDZ domains of Dvl2. Notably, selective intracellular binders targeting the Dvl2 PDZ domain perturb Dvl2 condensate organization and compromise AIS formation. Together, our data identify Dvl2 as an organizer of the proximal AIS and reveal a Dvl2-MTCL1-dependent mechanism coupling condensate scaffolding, microtubule organization, and neuronal excitability.

Article.Title: Concurrent anodal tDCS enhances motor learning and increases cortical TrkB phosphorylation
Article.Authors: Wang, Y.; Yu, Q.; Wen, Y.
Article.Abstract: The timing of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) relative to motor practice may influence its behavioral effects, but the accompanying molecular responses remain incompletely characterized. Here, we examined cortical current delivery, rotarod performance, and BDNF-TrkB signaling in mice receiving anodal tDCS concurrently with training or during intertrial intervals. Cortical current measurements indicated that approximately half of the applied current reached the measurement site under the experimental stimulation configuration. During four days of rotarod training, anodal tDCS concurrent with motor tasks improved performance at selected trials and increased footstep frequency, whereas stimulation delivered before or after training trials did not significantly improve performance. Preceding online anodal tDCS with cathodal stimulation provided no detectable additional behavioral benefit. Concurrent anodal tDCS increased TrkB phosphorylation in the stimulated cortex after both one and four days, without a significant increase in BDNF levels. Paused offline anodal tDCS stimulation also increased TrkB phosphorylation after one day despite lacking a detectable behavioral benefit. No significant molecular changes were detected in the sampled non-targeted brain regions. Genetic experiments revealed reduced rotarod performance in BDNF heterozygous mice at several trials and trial-dependent responses to online stimulation in BDNF-KIV mice. Together, these findings show that concurrent anodal tDCS improves rotarod performance and increases TrkB phosphorylation in the stimulated cortex. These results motivate further investigation of how BDNF-TrkB signaling interacts with task-related neural activity during stimulation.

Article.Title: Movie Watching for Individual Functional Brain Network Estimation in Adolescents
Article.Authors: Godfrey, K. J.; Grimsrud, G. J.; Ramirez, J. S. B.; Corlett, A.; Houlihan, K.; Byington, N.; Gell, M.; Kretsch, S.; Dosenbach, N. U. F.; Barch, D. M.; Gordon, E. M.; Greene, D. J.; Mueller, B. A.; Betzel, R. F.; Fair, D. A.; Conelea, C. A.; Tervo-Clemmens, B.; Nelson, S. M.

PFM requires sufficient high-quality and densely-sampled functional MRI data at the individual level that is typically acquired during the so-called resting state while passively fixating on a crosshair. Network assignments were largely conserved between crosshair fixation and movie watching, with a smaller subset of reproducible network reassignments which were overwhelmingly border shifts between neighboring networks. This suggests largely conserved global structure of functional network topography between crosshair fixation and movie watching, though border shifts can compound into variable estimates of cortical network size particularly for movie positive (language, salience, and parietal memory) and movie negative networks (default mode, action mode). Functional network assignments derived from movies and crosshair were also similarly individual-specific and consistent within common neuromodulation targets including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and somatomotor cortex. Key results were replicated in independent pediatric consortia data (Healthy Brain Network, n = 466, 6-22 years) and reproduced across independent PFM data sessions. Article.Title: Time at Home for Whom? Unequal Returns of Paid Family Leave for Infant White Matter and Language Development
Article.Authors: Lazarus, M. F.; Nelson, C. A.
Article.Abstract: Paid family leave (PFL) may give parents more time with infants, ease financial strain, and support stable routines. Although PFL has been linked to child development, little is known about neural pathways that might underpin its benefits or whether associations vary across families. Using data from 274 infants in the HEALthy Brain and Child Development Study, we examined associations of maternal and paternal PFL with language ability at 12 months and white matter microstructure at 6 months. We tested whether associations varied by the corresponding parent's education. Neither maternal nor paternal PFL was directly associated with language scores or fractional anisotropy in the left arcuate, inferior longitudinal, or uncinate fasciculus. Maternal education moderated associations between maternal PFL and fractional anisotropy in the arcuate (p = .014) and inferior longitudinal fasciculus (p = .003; n = 148). In both tracts, PFL was associated with higher fractional anisotropy only among infants whose mothers had relatively high education. No comparable pattern emerged for language, the uncinate fasciculus, or paternal PFL. Findings suggest that the neurodevelopmental correlates of PFL may depend on family resources rather than operate uniformly across families, underscoring the need to pair paid leave with additional supports and resources.

Article.Title: Neurobiological alterations and autism-like phenotype in mice following regulatory-limit exposure to fungicides in drinking water
Article.Authors: Salvador-Prince, L.; Vignon, A.; Alenda, U. G.; Lafon, P. A.; Thobois, D.; Schneider, B.; Lehmann, S.; Crozet, C.; Torrent i Mas, J.; Chaloin, L.; Vignes, M.; Laboute, T.; BECKER, J. A. J.; Le Merrer, J.; LOULIER, K.; Perrier, V.
Article.Abstract: Neurodevelopmental conditions, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorders (ASD), have increased markedly over recent decades. This rise parallels the widespread use of agrochemicals, suggesting a contribution of environmental exposures. We hypothesize that pesticide residues may disrupt brain development and promote neurodevelopmental disorders. Here, we test whether concentrations permitted in drinking water affect brain development using a maternal exposure model in wild-type mice. Exposure to a fungicide mixture at 0.3 g/L, below the current European regulatory limit of 0.5 g/L, impairs corticogenesis and is associated with alterations in synaptic function and glutamatergic signaling. Offspring exhibit delays in sensory development, reduced social interactions, and increased stereotyped behaviors. We identify the adenosine A2A receptor as a molecular target of anilinopyrimidine fungicides. Together, these findings indicate that low-dose exposure to this fungicide mixture can induce an autism spectrum-like phenotype in the offspring.
