Article.Title: Source-Decomposed Multimodal Graph Connectivity: A Temporal Mixture-Manifold Pipeline for Tracking Ischemic Injury and Treatment
Article.Authors: Park, J.
Article.Abstract: To capture the complex, dynamic network reorganization following acute focal brain injuries that standard static or unimodal neuroimaging frameworks routinely miss, we present an open, reproducible computational multimodal pipeline that integrates resting state functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) into dynamic, source-decomposed graph networks. This framework preserves sub-voxel, multi-peak distributional dynamics over time by modeling regional blood-oxygen-level-dependent signals within sliding windows using a Gaussian mixture model, with model complexity dynamically optimized. The resulting pairwise similarities define time-varying edge weights across local, nonlocal, and DTI-supported structural sources, unifying them into a multimodal connectivity manifold that precisely quantifies node strength, topological turnover, and boundary modifications. Applied to a non-human primate model of photothrombotic ischemia, the methodology revealed severe post-injury disruptions, with 66 of 144 nodes (45.8%) fundamentally altering their connectivity across localized sources. Furthermore, coupling this architecture with an Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) allowed for the continuous tracking of a tissue reversibility coordinate, yielding earlier detection of metabolic state collapse than uni-modal baselines and generating a forecast-divergence index as a rigorous early-warning signal. Extended across post-injury treatment boundaries to evaluate network recovery toward baseline, this interpretable, modality-aware framework establishes a standardized, shareable methodological foundation for tracking complex pathophysiological dynamics in neuroinformatics research.

Article.Title: Perineuronal nets in the bed nucleus of stria terminalis mediate stress-induced anxiety behaviour in adult male mice
Article.Authors: Murrall, K.; Mucha, M.; Mujmer, K.; Ten Blanco, M.; Sherlock, B.; Pawlak, R.; Mosienko, V.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety disorders affect an estimated 301.4 million people globally. However, they remain among the most challenging conditions to treat, with only around half of patients reporting a 50% or greater reduction in their symptoms. The discovery of novel and more effective treatments therefore requires a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms of anxiety at both the circuit and cellular levels. Stress induces aberrant changes in neuronal plasticity across brain regions within the anxiety circuitry including the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST). One mechanism through which synaptic plasticity is regulated is the organisation of perineuronal nets (PNNs), specialised extracellular matrix structures that are highly sensitive to stress. In rodent models, stress is associated with a reduction in PNN number and/or decreased Wisteria floribunda Agglutinin (WFA) labelling in limbic areas. However, the development of PNNs within the BNST and their role in the stress responsiveness remain largely unknown. In the current study we investigated the spatiotemporal development of PNNs within the BNST of male mice, where they first appear at P30 and continue to mature into adulthood, reaching their highest expression at P210 and specifically within the anteromedial BNST. We further showed that stress-induced anxiety is associated with a reduction in PNN number and significant changes to PNN fine structure including increased leakiness in the anteromedial BNST. Most importantly, enzymatic removal of PNNs by chondroitinase ABC in the mouse anteromedial BNST exacerbated behavioural responses to acute stress as demonstrated by increased anxiety-like behaviour. Collectively, these results highlight an indispensable role for PNNs within the anteromedial BNST in mediating a healthy emotional response to psychosocial stress.

Article.Title: Fast Generalized Longitudinal Functional Principal Components Analysis with Applications to Population-Level Neuronal Dynamics
Article.Authors: Duffy, K. A.; Pai, N.; Schneck, D.; Kozienko, G.; Zheng, L.; Xenopoulos-Oddsson, A.; Wang, J.; Johnson, L. A.; Vitek, J.; Fiecas, M.; Cui, E.
Article.Abstract: Functional data are widely collected across many fields. One approach for modeling functional data collected across repeated measures is longitudinal functional PCA (LFPCA), which allows for the decomposition of variability at multiple levels. However, existing estimation approaches for LFPCA can be computationally demanding for large or high-dimensional datasets. Here, we propose fast generalized LFPCA, a novel estimation technique that bins data along the functional domain and fits a marginal mixed model at each bin. Simulation results show that the proposed method is orders of magnitude faster than existing techniques while achieving similar accuracy, making LFPCA scalable to datasets with more densely sampled observations and larger sample sizes. We apply the proposed technique to model neuronal firing rate data both on and off deep brain stimulation (DBS) to investigate how the intervention modulates population-level neuronal activity. Our results suggest that the vast majority of between-neuron variation can be explained by four principal components, which relate to individual differences in neuronal firing as well as the arm manipulation paradigm under study. We also find that DBS significantly increases the variability of firing activity, likely driven by increased firing from a subset of neurons in response to DBS, a novel insight not obtained in previous analyses. Code to implement the proposed method and run simulation studies is included in the supplement.

Article.Title: Aging Is Associated with Reduced Topographic Differentiation Between Speaking and Silent Reading
Article.Authors: Basciano, A.; Daliri, A.; Chao, S.-C.; Rogalsky, C.
Article.Abstract: Aging affects how neural activity is organized and specialized, but its impact on neural differentiation across language tasks remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether aging influences neural differentiation during speaking and silent reading. Fifteen young adults and 15 older adults completed speaking and silent-reading tasks in a delayed-response paradigm while we collected electroencephalography (EEG) data. We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388-800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group x task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229-334 ms and 377-538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618-723 ms interval, and a group x task interaction in the 562-636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508-629 ms and 660-800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

Article.Title: Brainstem cholinergic cell loss causes slowly-developing motor impairments
Article.Authors: Udobi, K.; Aleman, V.; Lewitus, V.; Fallah, M.; Bernstein, B.; Zhang, G.; Ezeiza Ortega, M.; Konja, C.; Grossen, S.; Forcelli, P. A.; Neckel, N.; Evans, R. C.
Article.Abstract: Pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) cholinergic degeneration is a feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is difficult to isolate the symptoms and circuit alterations caused by cholinergic cell loss in PD, where multiple nuclei are simultaneously degenerating. Here we develop a novel mouse model of brainstem cholinergic cell loss to define the timeline of symptom development and map physiological adaptations within the brainstem. Mild motor symptoms, including balance and motor learning deficits reminiscent of early-stage PD, developed after cholinergic lesion with an unexpected long delay. Ex vivo whole-cell recordings showed that cholinergic cell loss increased excitatory synaptic drive onto glutamatergic PPN neurons and increased their intrinsic ability to generate sustained action potential output. In parallel, fiber photometry experiments revealed a slight increase in glutamatergic sensory responsiveness that closely tracked the delayed onset of behavioral symptoms. Together, these results reveal that brainstem cholinergic cell loss triggers the reorganization of motor-related brainstem circuits, providing critical insight into the consequences of non-dopaminergic degeneration in PD.

Article.Title: Brain-thought states during movie-watching reflect shared sensory anchors and film- and person- specific processes in association cortex
Article.Authors: Wallace, R. S.; Hardikar, S.; Ketcheson, S.; Mulholland, B.; Goodall-Halliwell, I.; Mckeown, B.; Chitiz, L.; Milham, M.; Xu, T.; Margulies, D. S.; Ho, N.; Karapanagiotidis, T.; Poerio, G.; Gonzalez-Alam, T.; Turnbull, A.; Skipper, J. I.; Bernhardt, B.; Leech, R.; Wammes, J.; Jefferies, E.; Smallwood, J.
Article.Abstract: Naturalistic paradigms such as movie-watching have transformed functional neuroimaging by capturing cognitive dynamics during rich, real-world experiences. A fundamental challenge, however, is determining whether the neural signatures identified during these experiences reflect general principles of cognition or the specific contexts in which they are measured. To address this question, we combined fMRI data from participants watching eight diverse films with continuous reports of ongoing thought. We found that the generalizability of brain-thought relationships depends on the cognitive process being recruited. Neural signatures linked to sensory processing remained robust across films, whereas those involving memory-related association networks depended on how we modelled between-film variability, indicating that cognition becomes increasingly context-dependent along the cortical hierarchy from sensory to association cortex. Within default and limbic networks, we identified two contrasting memory-related states with opposite consequences for comprehension. One, reflecting the integration of prior knowledge with ongoing experience, predicted better narrative comprehension and was revealed only after accounting for between-film variability. The other, associated with stimulus-independent thought, predicted poorer comprehension and emerged only when between-film variability was not modelled. Together, these findings establish when brain-experience relationships measured during naturalistic paradigms can generalize across contexts and when they instead reflect interactions between cognition and the specific environments in which cognition unfolds. More broadly, the consistency of a given brain-experiential association may depend less on where it occurs in the brain and more on the viewer's contextual experience: perceiving the film, drawing on memory to understand it, or drifting away.

Article.Title: Neural categorisation of rhythm in human newborns
Article.Authors: Barbero, F. M.; Lenc, T.; Gallard, A.; Jacoby, N.; Polak, R.; Varlet, M.; Foulon, A.; Moghimi, S.; Nozaradan, S.
Article.Abstract: Music is ubiquitous across cultures, and humans engage in social interactions through music from early in life. A cornerstone of these interactions is rhythm categorisation, allowing the sheer diversity of rhythmic inputs to be mapped onto internal rhythm categories. The pervasiveness of certain rhythm categories across cultures suggests that rhythm categorisation may be partially rooted in neurobiological predispositions constraining the internal representations of rhythm. However, this view appears to conflict with the diversity of music practices across cultures, which points to a role of experience in rhythm categorisation. To assess the relative contributions of neurobiological predispositions and experience, we tested 0- to 3-day-old newborns, capitalising on their minimal postnatal experience with music. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we recorded, in newborns and adults, brain responses to drum sounds whose pattern of relative interval duration ranged from isochronous to long-short rhythms (1:1 - 2:1 interval ratio). Results indicate significant categorisation in newborns's neural responses, with a representational structure that correlate with those of adults, yet with a greater degree of differentiation across rhythms. These findings reveal neurobiological predispositions enabling rhythm categorisation to be present at birth and further shaped across the lifespan, highlighting the evolutionary roots and plasticity supporting this human cultural practice.

Article.Title: NeuroMark dFNC: Transferable Dynamic-State Templates for Subject-Specific and Frequency-Resolved Chronnectomics
Article.Authors: Esfahani, M. M.; Seraji, M.; Salem, S.; Jensen, K. M.; Fu, Z.; Adali, T.; Wang, Y.-P.; Calhoun, V.
Article.Abstract: Dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) commonly identifies recurring connectivity states from resting-state fMRI, but states derived independently in each dataset lack guaranteed correspondence across studies and cannot be directly estimated in new participants. We introduce NeuroMark dFNC, which extends the NeuroMark principle of prior-guided network estimation to dynamic connectivity by using reproducible reference states as priors for estimating corresponding subject-specific states. Reference-state templates were derived from UK Biobank using windowed functional network connectivity and time-frequency moments (TFMs), with split-sample reproducibility evaluated for k-means, independent component analysis (ICA), and principal component analysis (PCA) template-generation approaches. Constrained ICA then used the templates to estimate subject-specific state patterns and continuous loadings in independent FBIRN schizophrenia and ADNI Alzheimer's disease cohorts. ICA loadings were calibrated by their contribution to reconstruction of the original feature matrix. Fractional occupancy and conditional mean dwell time were calculated from the state with the largest absolute calibrated loading at each observation. The predefined templates avoided the need for dataset-specific state discovery and post-hoc state matching. In both clinical cohorts, the analysis identified state-dependent, distributed edgewise differences and differences in selected temporal summaries. Nominal frequency-resolved findings varied across states and moment-frequency bins and were treated as exploratory. NeuroMark dFNC provides a common state space for cross-cohort comparison while retaining subject-specific connectivity patterns and continuous state expression.

Article.Title: Longitudinal associations between task-control network functioning, cognition, and the environment in early adolescence
Article.Authors: Paige, K. J.; Michael, C.; Molloy, M. F.; Kardan, O.; Angstadt, M.; Sripada, C.; Hyde, L.; Heitzeg, M.; Weigard, A.
Article.Abstract: Neural maturation in the "task-control" frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks is thought to support the development of adolescents' cognitive and adaptive functioning. Further, theory suggests that family and neighborhood contexts shape brain network development. Yet, few longitudinal studies have examined the co-development of brain network mechanisms with cognitive and adaptive functioning or with environmental factors that could shape the maturation of these mechanisms. The present study addressed these gaps. We used longitudinal data spanning late childhood (Mage=10 years) to early adolescence (Mage=12) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (n=4862). Stable and construct-valid neural signatures of task-control network functioning were estimated using longitudinal bifactor modeling of neural responses to cognitive demand during the n-back task. Multivariate latent change-score models were used to examine co-development of this signature with cognitive efficiency (drift rate from the diffusion model), teacher-reported attention problems, family conflict, and neighborhood safety. Models accounted for baseline family income. Robust reciprocal relations between task-control activation and cognitive efficiency were identified and the latent change scores for efficiency and task-control activation were positively correlated. Similar reciprocal associations were observed between cognitive efficiency and attention problems. Baseline family income predicted the rate of change in task-control network functioning. This study demonstrates that task-control network functioning co-develops with cognition, which in turn supports attentional functioning development across early adolescence. Further, findings highlight the utility of this neural signature of task-control network functioning for understanding the neural basis of cognitive development and the mechanisms through which environmental experiences shape brain and behavior.

Article.Title: Multi-parametric spectral modeling disentangles synaptic kinetics and neural excitability from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings
Article.Authors: Philippe, V.; Tombroff, L.; Akbarian, F.; De Witte, S.; Trotta, N.; Van Schependom, J.; Engelborghs, S.; Bier, J.-C.; Strauss, M.; De Tiege, X.; Wens, V.
Article.Abstract: Spectral modeling of electrophysiological recordings enables non-invasive characterization of neural excitability. However, current approaches rely on a single spectral index, limiting insight into the multiple biophysical processes underlying excitation-inhibition balance. Here, we introduce a biologically informed, multi-parametric spectral analysis that disentangles neural excitability and synaptic kinetics from recordings. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that this approach captures signatures of hyperexcitability and glutamate reuptake dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.

Article.Title: An anatomy-constrained transcriptomic screen identifies a 19-gene panel with an ordered regional similarity pattern in the human somatosensory system
Article.Authors: Boni, G. A.; Luque Hernandez, A.; Bautista Ruedas, V. I.
Article.Abstract: Neuroanatomical pathways link specialized brain regions, but whether regional transcriptomic profiles preserve relationships aligned with pathway order remains unclear. We defined candidate pathways and their available tissue representations from neuroanatomical literature, then screened 10,262 genes in the Body Index of Gene Expression (BIGE), a human microarray resource covering cells and tissues. The screen required expression across every mapped region of a route and limited single-region dominance. It identified 23 candidates in three routes with sufficient coverage; 19 met the criteria for the dorsal column-medial lemniscus (DCML) representation and formed the fixed panel. We evaluated this panel in six Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) donors across three central regional representations: an aggregate of samples assigned to the cuneate and gracile nuclei (Cu/Gr), the lateral group of nuclei, ventral division, within the dorsal thalamus (DTLv), and postcentral gyrus. The regional-order contrast compared the mean similarity of the pairs adjacent in the anatomical sequence, Cu/Gr-DTLv and DTLv-postcentral gyrus, with Cu/Gr-postcentral gyrus similarity. Both adjacent-in-order correlations were positive in all six donors; the contrast was positive in five and reached a mean of T = 0.345175 (exact sign test, P = 0.109375). The panel exceeded two distributions of 50,000 gene sets generated under comparable selection constraints (P = 0.027919 and P = 0.026579). In descriptive anatomical comparisons, it ranked third among 240 combinations and first among the target and all 16 single-region substitutions. All 50,000 one-probe-per-gene analyses retained T > 0, and broad neuronal-expression contrasts were positive in medulla, thalamus, and cortex. Spatial support depended on the null model, with stronger evidence under whole-donor surrogates (P = 0.003860) than under the primary within-compartment model (P = 0.051179). These findings identify a fixed gene panel whose regional similarity is aligned with the represented central order of the DCML system and define a specific hypothesis for prospective evaluation in an independent, anatomically resolved dataset.

Article.Title: Action-related brain dynamics during leader-follower coordination
Article.Authors: Ruuskanen, S.; Avendano-Diaz, J. C.; Hari, R.; Parkkonen, L.
Article.Abstract: Leader-follower dynamics are essential for social interaction, enabling smooth inter-personal coordination. Although neuroimaging studies have identified brain networks associated with leading and following, the dynamical brain signatures supporting these roles remain poorly characterized. Here, sixteen dyads performed a joint-improvisation mirror-game task with predefined leader-follower roles while magnetoencephalography (MEG) and hand kinematics (acceleration) were simultaneously recorded. We investigated role-specific modulations of source-space MEG activity in delta (0.54 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), and gamma (40-90 Hz) frequency bands, as well as coherence between cortical activity and movement kinematics. Compared with leaders, followers exhibited stronger theta-band activity in a cluster comprising frontal, cingulate, and sensorimotor regions, and stronger coherence between movement kinematics and occipital cortical activity, consistent with enhanced monitoring, adaptation, and reliance on visual kinematic information. In contrast, leaders showed reduced alpha-band power in sensorimotor and premotor regions, and stronger beta-band activity in occipital cortices, likely reflecting greater demands for action planning and predictive control. Our results identify complementary spectral and action-related brain signatures associated with leader-follower coordination during joint improvisation, providing new insights into the neural underpinnings of real-time interpersonal coordination.

Article.Title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Yenikapati, M. S.; Deshpande, S.; Desai, S. P.; Santine, D. D.; Roghani, A. K.
Article.Abstract: Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human. Keywords: Speech neuroprosthesis, paralinguistics, BCI, naturalistic communication

Article.Title: Pilifers provide rapid mechanosensory feedback during floral tracking in hawkmoths
Article.Authors: Anand, M.; Torres, M.; Brunton, B. W.; Daniel, T. L.; Weber, A. I.; Deora, T.
Article.Abstract: Hawkmoths expertly hover over flowers during feeding, accurately tracking floral movements even as flowers gently sway in the wind. They use visual and mechanosensory feedback to adjust their position, while their long, flexible mouthpart, the proboscis, stays inserted inside the nectar spur. Although much is known about how hawkmoths detect and process visual motion, far less is understood about how hawkmoths detect mechanical motion cues. Pilifers are hair bundles at the proboscis-head joint, well-positioned to provide feedback about floral motion. Here, we tested if pilifers could provide mechanosensory feedback essential for successful floral tracking. We computed bending at the proboscis base during floral tracking in freely flying hawkmoths and found that floral movements induce small yet significantly correlated lateral bending. Recordings from pilifer afferents showed that they respond to lateral motions of amplitudes similar to those seen in natural floral tracking behaviors. They respond to different directions and speeds of proboscis motion with an average latency of 1.9 ms. Neural tracing revealed extensive sensory arborizations in the sub-esophageal ganglion of the brain and ventral nerve cord, indicating a feedback pathway to the neck and flight motor system that enables rapid coordination of appendages and body for successful feeding.

Article.Title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
Article.Authors: Carreno Munoz, M. I.; Chehrazi, P.; Ciancone Chama, A.; Knoth, I.; Fernandes do Nascimento, S. A.; Campbell, B.; Csicsvari, J.; Chattopadhyaya, B.; Lippe, S.; Di Cristo, G.
Article.Abstract: The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.

Article.Title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways
Article.Authors: Nuttin, B.; Sans-Dublanc, A.; Chrzanowska, A.; Liu, C.; Hanson, L.; Drakaki, Z.; Luyks, R.; Bruystreen, A.; Philipon, A.; Grillet, M.; Kuhn, N.; Goncalves, P.; Montaldo, G.; Bonin, V.; Urban, A.; Farrow, K.
Article.Abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

Article.Title: Exposure to childhood adversity and adult alcohol, nicotine, and illicit drug use in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis of the German National Cohort (NAKO)
Article.Authors: Boehmer, J.; Meyer-Degering, K.; Ghadami, A.; Sreepada, A.; Bohmann, P.; Castell, S.; Feuchtinger, M.; Gottschick, C.; Grabe, H. J.; Karch, A.; Lahmann, C.; Lang, A.; Leitzmann, M.; Meinke-Franze, C.; Meyerdierks, D.; Mikolajczyk, R.; Nimptsch, K.; Obi, N.; Peters, A.; Pischon, T.; Stein, M. J.; Keil, T.; Krist, L.; Tost, H.; Heim, C. C.
Article.Abstract: Rationale: Exposure to adversity in childhood and adolescence (i.e., "early-life stress"; ELS) is a well-established risk factor for substance use. Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate associations between ELS exposure and substance use across subtypes of ELS, different substance classes, and behavioral profiles of substance use. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we examined associations between ELS exposure and substance use in a population-based sample of 172,173 adults aged 19-74 years from the German National Cohort (NAKO). ELS exposure was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Screener. Substance use included nicotine, alcohol, and illicit drug use. Associations were examined using regression models evaluating overall ELS exposure, cumulative trauma load, and ELS subtypes. Latent class analysis (LCA) was conducted to identify substance use profiles. Results: ELS exposure was associated with higher odds of smoking, greater smoking severity, heavier alcohol consumption among drinkers, and higher odds of lifetime illicit drug use. Overall, the strongest associations were observed for opioid and stimulant use. Dose-response analyses revealed higher risk with increasing numbers of ELS subtypes. Abuse-related subtypes, particularly exposure to physical and sexual abuse, consistently showed strongest independent associations across substances, whereas neglect exhibited weaker, more variable associations. LCA identified four substance use profiles, with ELS exposure predicting membership in more severe polysubstance classes. Conclusions: ELS emerged as a robust risk factor for adult substance use, underscoring the need for trauma-informed approaches in clinical practice, public health, and policy to mitigate the long-term consequences of early adversity.

Article.Title: LIF is a pro-algesic mediator in human and mouse models of arthritis-related pain
Article.Authors: Ross, R.; Li, Y.; Vlachaki Walker, J.; Ali Awadelkareem, M.; Zebochin, I.; Goodwin, G. L.; Marin, A.-C.; Trendafilova, T.; Montague, I.; Rutter-Locher, Z.; Ryan, S.; Baldeweg, F.; Freytag, K.; Condor, R.; Arridge, N.; Buckley, C. D.; Bennett, D.; Humby, F.; Kirkham, B.; Denk, F.; Taams, L.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Emerging clinical and experimental data suggest that JAK inhibitors (JAKi) are effective in reducing pain in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). We recently showed that JAK/STAT signalling cytokines, specifically IL-6, LIF and IL-11, are present in the RA joint and can act directly on human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived sensory neurons by increasing their STAT3 phosphorylation (pSTAT3) levels and expression of select pain-relevant genes. In this study, we determined that LIF is the most consequential cytokine out of the three, altering neuronal signalling, outgrowth and pain-like behaviours in in vitro and in vivo models of arthritis. Methods: Human iPSC-derived sensory neurons were stimulated with RA synovial fluid (SF) or with cytokine-treated RA synovial fibroblast conditioned media (CM) in the absence or presence of anti-cytokine antibodies. pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 levels, and gene expression patterns, were assessed by Western blot and RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq). The immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6) was assessed for LIF-induced JAK/STAT signalling in addition to neurite outgrowth assays as a functional readout of the sensory neurons. Lastly, mouse models were used to assess pain-related behaviours in vivo. Results: LIF was found to be consistently present in the SF from painful joints from individuals with inflammatory arthritis. Western blotting revealed that the addition of RA SF to iPSC-derived sensory neurons led to LIF-dependent induction of pSTAT3 and pSTAT1, while RNA-seq demonstrated that LIF alters the transcriptome of sensory neurons more prominently than IL-6 and IL-11, up-regulating signature genes related to peripheral neuron sensitization, such as TRPV1, NTRK1, BDNF, HRH1 and SCN10A. Similarly, cytokine-treated fibroblast conditioned media was shown to induce neuronal pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 and upregulate expression of BDNF, HRH1 and VGF in a LIF-dependent manner. Additionally, the immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6), which also exhibited LIF-induced pSTAT1 and pSTAT3, showed increased neurite outgrowth after axotomy when treated with LIF. Finally, in a mouse model of inflammatory arthritis, LIF was shown to be significantly increased in the affected joint. Furthermore, intraarticular injection of LIF into a healthy mouse knee resulted in increased responsiveness to painful pressure stimuli in that joint. Conclusions: Our data indicate that LIF may be a pro-algesic mediator and a possible therapeutic target to improve pain management in individuals living with inflammatory arthritis.

Article.Title: Real-Time Neurotransmitter Sensing in Midbrain Organoids Using 3D Carbon Cup Electrodes
Article.Authors: Tavares da Silva Maraschin, S.; Thongkorn, S.; Kanakkottu, S.; Rezaei, B.; Scordo, G.; Sozzi, E.; Parmar, M.; Heiskanen, A.; Keller, S. S.; Emneus, J.
Article.Abstract: Real time, chemically selective detection of neurotransmitter release in brain organoids remains a challenge due to their complex three dimensional architecture and limited optical accessibility. We introduce 3D printed carbon cup electrodes (CCEs) -pyrolyzed, multi level pillar structures - designed to confine a single organoid, increase electroactive surface area, and enable amperometric recordings of oxidizable neurotransmitters. The CCEs exhibit excellent electrochemical performance and reproducibility, supporting diffusion controlled dopamine redox behavior without interference from culture medium. Using ventral midbrain (vMB) organoids at two maturation stages (Day 30 and Day 90), we demonstrate real time detection of potassium evoked dopamine release directly from organoids. Mature organoids exhibit higher peak currents, correlating with increased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression confirmed by immunocytochemistry. Embedding organoids in Matrigel significantly attenuates dopamine signals, indicating a diffusion barrier that limits stimulant access and/or dopamine transport to the electrode. Repetitive stimulations reveal progressive depletion of dopamine stores, consistent with diminished vesicular release. Chemical perturbations using 6 hydroxydopamine and verapamil further validate the platform by producing substantial reductions in dopamine release accompanied by loss of TH neurons. These results establish CCEs as a powerful tool for label free, real-time monitoring of neurotransmission in human organoids, with potential for multiplexed sensing and integration of enzymatic detection strategies for non electroactive neurotransmitters.

Article.Title: Adolescent prodromal phenotypes of psychiatric disorders: insights from a novel DISC1-perturbed monkey model
Article.Authors: Lan, Z.; Onoe, H.; Tsukiyama, T.; Iwatani, C.; Chen, C.-Y.; Okita, K.; Ishizuka, K.; Endo, R.; Nakai, R.; Imamura, K.; Hikishima, K.; Tsuchiya, H.; Nakaya, M.; Fang, Y.; Kobayashi, A.; Shinto, Y.; Yamaguchi, R.; Matsunaga, M.; Oe, K.; Omori, K.; Ozeki, Y.; Tomoda, T.; Miura, K.; Urayama, S.-i.; Oishi, N.; Okada, T.; Tanaka, M.; Inoue, H.; Takahashi, J.; Sawa, A.; Isa, T.
Article.Abstract: Neurodevelopmental deficits frequently lead to mild but significant adolescent social and cognitive changes, representing prodromal manifestations of adult-onset psychiatric disorders in a cross-disease manner. Although experimental medicine utilizes animal models to address the mechanisms, rodent brains lack critical structures for human higher brain functions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. To fill this translational gap, we generated monkeys with an impaired DISC1 gene locus, targeting the multifunctional protein essential for neurodevelopment and involved in transdiagnostic mental health risks. Here we analyze the F0 animals by minimizing mosaicism. At ages equivalent to human adolescence, these monkeys exhibited blunted responsiveness to social stimuli and increased internal drives, mirroring altered social behaviors in the prodromal stage in humans. Resting-state functional MRI data indicated disrupted global functional connectivity and reorganization of network topology, marked by a shift in the dominance of brain hubs from prefrontal regions to sensory areas. This primate model provides a unique platform for studying psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, across the developmental trajectory.

Article.Title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
Article.Authors: Kubo, Y.; Delanois, E.; Bazhenov, M.
Article.Abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory. Net excitatory input onto this population decreased, most strongly that from older-memory populations, which allowed inputs of older memories to drive their own neurons again. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: plasticity is confined to one population, whose neurons lose inputs that are silent when they fire. The mechanism held under Dale's law, and depression of excitatory synapses alone, without any inhibitory plasticity, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation and highlight the potential for integrating human-like learning behaviors into artificial neural networks.

Article.Title: Temporal tuning of actin nucleation by the repurposed DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 encodes distinct axon guidance decisions
Article.Authors: Zerkoune, S.; Zagar, Y.; Delaroche, J.; Danicka, J.; Vougny, J.; Uthayasuthan, S.; Aureille, J.; Roche, F.; Haantjes, R.; Gomez-Bravo, C.; Baudet, S.; Denarier, E.; Zainu, A.; Bun, P.; Guillonneau, X.; Debant, A.; Baudat, F.; Nicol, X.; Pietrancosta, N.; Boudeau, J.; Andrieux, A.; Arnal, I.; Antkowiak, A.; Fassier, C.
Article.Abstract: Axon guidance is essential for neural circuit assembly and function. While much of the repertoire of guidance cues and receptors is known, its limited diversity cannot fully explain the remarkable complexity of the brain connectome. How temporally ordered, context-dependent intrinsic programs shape the diversity of axonal responses to guidance signals remains poorly understood. We reveal how non-canonical Wnt5a signalling repurposes the DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 as a downstream integrator to control retinal ganglion cell axon decision-making at the midline. We demonstrate that differential RAD51/fignl1 expression and interaction dynamics between ipsilateral and contralateral axons tunes the magnitude and temporal dynamics of F-actin nucleation, thereby encoding their trajectory choice. Our findings establish temporal control of cytoskeletal dynamics as a key determinant of axon decision-making and thereby a fundamental layer of circuit wiring. They provide a potential mechanistic framework linking mutations in the DNA repair gene RAD51 to neurodevelopmental disorders with midline guidance defects.

Article.Title: Sex shapes capillary flows and oxygen extraction in the middle-aged mouse brain
Article.Authors: Gutierrez-Jimenez, E.; Wied, B.; Lindhardt, T. B.; Mikkelsen, S. H.; Knopper, R. W.; Skoven, C. S.; Christensen, O. B.; Dashkovskyi, V.; Mrotek, F.; Rasmussen, P. M.; Andresen, M. H.; Krmpot, A.; Khatib, M. E.; Vinogradov, S. A.; Sakadzic, S.; Jensen, M. F.; Pedroza-Pacheco, I.; Postnov, D. D.; Lin, L.; Just, J.; Hansen, B.; Ostergaard, L.
Article.Abstract: Sex differences in brain aging are well documented, but their origin within the cerebrovascular hierarchy remains unclear. Here we show that cortical blood flow is higher in female than male mice at 15 months of age, at a point when an earlier sex difference in pulsatility and resistance indices has already converged, pial vessel diameter shows no difference between sexes, and estrogen levels are similar between sexes. Using an indicator-dilution and intravascular oxygen measurements using two-photon microscopy, we found that capillary transit-time heterogeneity (CTH) scales more steeply with mean transit time in females, consistent with a passively regulated capillary network, and that this is accompanied by reduced oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) without deficit in arterial oxygen delivery. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that sex differences are organized into distinct regional programs, most prominently in white matter, where a male-associated myelin and axonogenesis signature accompanies reduced white matter volume in females. These molecular and structural differences coincide with elevated hippocampal microglial reactivity and an altered spatial search strategy in females, without any detectable differences in circulating markers of stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, or immunity. Together, these findings indicate that sex differences in the aging brain are expressed at the level of capillary flow regulation and regional tissue programs rather than through bulk cerebral blood flow alone, and that elevated blood flow in females can mask, rather than reflect, adequate tissue oxygenation.

Article.Title: Diurnal Variations in the Cholinergic System of the Nucleus Accumbens
Article.Authors: Stowe, T. A.; Huang, Y.; Ferris, M.; McClung, C. A.
Article.Abstract: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) plays a critical role in reward-related behaviors, which exhibit diurnal variations. Cholinergic interneurons (CINs) are the primary source of acetylcholine within the NAc and regulate local dopamine (DA) signaling through nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs). Although there are diurnal variations in NAc dynamics, little is known about whether CIN activity and nicotinic signaling also vary across the light/dark cycle. Here, we aimed to determine diurnal variations in the NAc cholinergic system using ex vivo fast-scan cyclic voltammetry and cell-attached electrophysiological recordings in male rodents. We examined time-of-day-dependent differences in nAChR-mediated modulation of DA release, spontaneous CIN firing frequency, and firing patterns. We found that spontaneous CIN firing varied across the light/dark cycle, with increased activity during the dark cycle. Additionally, bath application of nicotine (NIC), mecamylamine (MEC), and dihydro-{beta}-erythroidine (DH{beta}E) reduced CIN firing frequency during the dark cycle, with only MEC decreasing firing frequency in the light cycle. NIC and MEC also altered CIN firing patterns during the dark cycle, whereas DH{beta}E primarily affected firing frequency. Together, these findings demonstrate diurnal variations in NAc CIN activity and reveal time-of-day-dependent differences in the effects of nAChR modulation on spontaneous firing. These results suggest that nicotinic signaling may contribute to diurnal regulation of NAc cholinergic activity, providing insight into mechanisms underlying time-of-day-dependent changes in reward circuitry.

Article.Title: Functional characterization of the 26RFa/orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamic area reveals their key role in the control of glucose homeostasis
Article.Authors: Devere, M.; Lusurier, C.; Takhlidjt, S.; Cherifi, Y.; Nedelec, E.; Benani, A.; Rosay, M.; Godefroy, D.; Arabo, A.; Lefranc, B.; Leprince, J.; Prevost, G.; chartrel, n.; PICOT, M.
Article.Abstract: Defining the nature and molecular mechanisms of the neurocircuitry controlling glucose homeostasis is crucial in understanding how alterations in these pathways promote the development of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Here, we functionally characterize a population of lateral hypothalamic neurons co-expressing the anti-hyperglycemic neuropeptides 26RFa and orexin. Using complementary chemogenetic, pharmacological and genetic approaches, including mice deficient for 26RFa, orexin or both neuropeptides, we investigated the respective contribution of each signaling system to glucose homeostasis. We found that lateral hypothalamic 26RFa neurons extensively co-express orexin, defining a distinct peptidergic population with convergent anti-hyperglycemic properties. Unexpectedly, chemogenetic activation of these neurons potentiated glucose-induced hyperglycemia despite the anti-hyperglycemic properties of both neuropeptides. To understand this paradox, we examined the transcriptional responses of the 26RFa and orexin peptidergic systems and found that neuronal activation was associated with coordinated, glycemic state-dependent downregulation of both signaling systems. Furthermore, genetic loss-of-function approaches revealed distinct contributions of the two neuropeptidergic systems, with orexin signaling mediating most of the metabolic consequences of neuronal activation, whereas 26RFa signaling is required for the dynamic regulation of orexin expression. Finally, our findings provide new insights into the functional organization of lateral hypothalamic 26RFa/orexin neurons and advance our understanding of how coordinated neuropeptidergic signaling contributes to systemic glucose homeostasis.

Article.Title: Vibrotactile stimulation on the upper back requires stronger vibration during goal-directed reaching but does not impede reaching performance
Article.Authors: Atkin, A. E.; 't Hart, B. M.; Whyne, C. M.; Tomescu, S.; Strauss, B. H.; Li, Q.; Henriques, D. Y. P.
Article.Abstract: Vibrotactile stimulation is a promising method of biofeedback, with potential applications for ergonomic posture and balance, rehabilitation, and motor learning. These applications require balancing tactile perception with motor performance and cognitive workload. In this study, participants performed a detection task, a reaching task, and a concurrent reach-and-detect task, with vibrotactile signals delivered on the hand or upper back. Sensitivity to stimuli, motor performance, and cognitive workload were compared for each task. Sensitivity was suppressed during movement, but this suppression was greater on hand compared to the upper back. Movement time was slowed by vibration on the hand but not the upper back. Mental workload and task complexity increased for the reach-and-detect task compared to the individual tasks. We conclude that vibrotactile feedback devices worn on the upper back do not impede motor performance, with only minor tactile suppression. This could be overcome by presenting highly salient or personalized feedback.

Article.Title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
Article.Authors: WU, Q.; Erickson, I.; Davidson, S.; Shonka, S.; Smith, V.; Gidi, B.; Knox, K.; Yu, T. W.; Khurana, V.; Carroll, J.; Korecka, J. A.; Barker-Haliski, M.
Article.Abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

Article.Title: Robust regulatory interplay of enhancers, facilitators, and promoters in a native chromatin context
Article.Authors: Zhou Z.; Cheng Y.; Lieberth J.; Zhang J.; Jin Y.; Li A.; Yu H.; Ozer A.; Lis J.
Article.Abstract: Enhancers are abundant and critical gene-distal cis-regulatory elements with distinct architectural features; however, a mechanistic understanding of their interactions within endogenous chromatin contexts remains challenging. Here, we developed a recombinase-mediated genome-rewriting platform to explore how a long-range human enhancer, eNMU, confers a remarkable 10,000-fold activation of its target gene, Neuromedin U (NMU), at its native locus. Our systematic dissection reveals two functionally distinct sub-elements of eNMU: the canonical autonomous enhancer e1 and the intrinsically inactive facilitator e2, which dramatically augments e1's activity. The autonomous enhancer e1 is functionally hierarchical to e2, additional facilitators, and the NMU promoter across the ∼100-kb NMU-eNMU region, and it orchestrates the formation of a 3D regulatory hub. e1 also harbors a bipartite structure: a divergently transcribed retroviral long terminal repeat (LTR) enhancer and an adjacent LTR promoter that dampens NMU expression. We explore and discuss the broader implications of our focused study for understanding enhancer regulatory mechanisms genome-wide.

Article.Title: Condensates of the chromatin regulator ANKRD11 restrict hypertranscribed genes to safeguard development
Article.Authors: Zhang T.; Li X.; Zhou W.; Li Z.; Bi J.; Ma X.; Li X.; Fan Y.; Hong Y.; Wang S.; Wang Y.; Yang L.; Chen Y.; Qin W.; Wang H.; Xi Q.; Shi S.; Liu N.
Article.Abstract: Genes that define cell identity are often highly transcribed, but how their activity is regulated to prevent pathological dysregulation remains elusive. Using a two-tiered genetic screen, we identify a network of genes regulating hypertranscribed loci, which is notably enriched for genes mutated in developmental disorders. Among these, ANKRD11, a chromatin regulator haploinsufficient in KBG syndrome, exerts progressively stronger repression on more highly transcribed genes. ANKRD11 enriches around hypertranscribed loci and forms biomolecular condensates via charge-block-patterned intrinsically disordered regions. These condensates spatially sequester elongation factors away from RNA polymerase II, thereby restricting transcription elongation. In mice, Ankrd11 loss abrogates this restriction, causing aberrant developmental gene activation, disrupted organogenesis, and embryonic lethality. Critically, KBG patient cells with ANKRD11 mutations show defective condensate formation and consequent overactivation of hypertranscribed genes. These results uncover a condensate-mediated mechanism that restricts hypertranscribed genes and suggest its disruption underlies developmental disorders such as KBG syndrome.

Article.Title: Trichoderma swollenin activates AtABCB5-dependent auxin efflux to promote plant development
Article.Authors: Lu J.; Liu J.; Jiang S.; Xu Y.; Yan Z.; Li L.; Zhang F.; Chen W.; Xu D.; Li Y.; Liu B.; Raza W.; Xuan W.; Liu D.; Shen Q.
Article.Abstract: The beneficial fungus Trichoderma enhances plant growth and stress tolerance through poorly understood mechanisms. Here, we show that Trichoderma harzianum swollenin ThSWO contributes to efficient root colonization and plant growth promotion. ThSWO traverses the plant cell wall and localizes to the plasma membrane, where it interacts with ABC transporter AtABCB5, which we establish as a bona fide auxin efflux carrier. ThSWO binding to NBD2 and R-domain faces of AtABCB5 prosmotes phosphorylation at Ser640 and Ser644, enhancing indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) efflux and triggering auxin-associated responses, including cell wall acidification, membrane potential transitions, and accelerated cytoplasmic streaming. Structure-guided substitutions at the AtABCB5-ThSWO interface differentially affected transporter binding and lateral root promotion, supporting the conclusion that host auxin transport is a primary effector target. These findings reveal a molecular mechanism by which a fungal effector co-opts host auxin transport machinery to promote plant development, with implications for microbe-assisted crop improvement.

Article.Title: An Oryza orphan gene confers trans-species drought tolerance
Article.Authors: Tu H.; Liu Q.; Ye T.; Ye Y.; Feng X.; Shen L.; Li S.; Bai S.; Liu X.; Liu X.; Wang H.; Li X.; Lin J.; Wang H.; Chen Y.; Feng Z.; Ji B.; Ding J.; Li W.; Zhang J.; Dai M.; Dong F.; Hu H.; Tang N.; Lai X.
Article.Abstract: Drought threatens crop productivity, yet enhancing tolerance often compromises yield. Abscisic acid (ABA) signaling is central to drought response, but its deep conservation can constrain adaptive flexibility. Here, we identify ROAD1 (rice orphan gene adapted for drought 1), an Oryza-specific orphan gene that confers robust drought tolerance without obvious growth defects under normal conditions. ROAD1 originated from Oryza meridionalis, and its functional allele, ROAD1C, was selected during japonica domestication. In field trials, elite rice lines carrying ROAD1C exhibited up to 34.75% higher grain yield than corresponding controls under drought. Mechanistically, ROAD1 bypasses the canonical ABA receptor-ligand complex by binding the phosphatase OsPP2C68, preventing sucrose non-fermenting 1-related protein kinases 2 (SnRK2) dephosphorylation and activating downstream responses. ROAD1 also interacts with protein phosphatase 2C (PP2C) orthologs from maize, wheat, and Arabidopsis, and heterologous expression of ROAD1C enhances drought tolerance in Arabidopsis, rapeseed, maize, wheat, and poplar. These findings reveal that an Oryza-specific orphan gene can co-opt conserved signaling for potential trans-species drought tolerance.

Article.Title: Gasdermin E couples viral pyroptosis to lethal hepatic lipid accumulation
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Zheng X.; Zhang Y.; Shang X.; Qu Q.; Li C.; Zhang X.; Jin N.; Liu W.; Li H.
Article.Abstract: Tick-borne orthonairoviruses, including the emerging wetland virus (WELV), pose a growing public health concern as cases increase, yet their pathogenesis remains unclear. Here, we show that WELV infection causes fatal liver dysfunction in patients, characterized by elevated hepatic enzymes, triacylglycerol accumulation, and hyperinflammation. WELV induces gasdermin E (GSDME)-dependent pyroptosis in hepatocytes through mitochondrial and Fas-mediated apoptotic pathways. Viral RNA activates RIG-I/CASP3-mediated GSDME cleavage, while viral nucleoprotein undergoes CASP3-dependent processing, forming a negative regulatory feedback loop. GSDME directly interacts with fatty acid synthase (FASN) and blocks K48-linked ubiquitination to inhibit FASN degradation, driving lipid metabolic reprogramming and lethal hepatic steatosis. GSDME knockout abolishes pyroptosis and metabolic dysregulation, conferring complete protection against WELV infection. Clinically approved caspase and FASN inhibitors mitigate liver pathology and improve survival in WELV-infected mice. These findings establish a pyroptosis-metabolism axis driving orthonairovirus pathogenesis, highlighting GSDME as a critical determinant of liver injury and a promising target for antiviral therapy.

Article.Title: CRISPR screens identify targets to rescue age-related T cell dysfunction in cancer
Article.Authors: Chen A.; Ji K.; Yerinde C.; Knudsen N.; Bi K.; Hao S.; Zhabotynsky V.; Martinez D.; Carmona-LaSalle T.; Taguchi K.; Xu K.; Seider E.; Schwartz M.; Zschummel M.; Nieman L.; Yates K.; Gazzaniga F.; Miller B.; Mempel T.; Manguso R.; Hacohen N.; Sen D.
Article.Abstract: Immune aging impairs T cell-mediated tumor control as well as cancer immunotherapy outcomes. The most important drivers of T cell dysfunction in aged tumors remain unknown. We performed single-cell CRISPR screens to identify Dusp5 and Zfp219 as key regulators of CD8+ T cell persistence and effector differentiation within aged tumors. Loss of Dusp5 increased extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation and globally enhanced T cell proliferation. Conversely, Zfp219 deletion induced epigenetic reprogramming and increased expression of cytotoxic molecules, enhancing antitumor immunity specifically in aging. Levels of the human ortholog ZNF219 were higher within intratumoral CD8+ T cells from older cancer patients, which correlates with worse survival following immunotherapy. Zfp219 ablation synergized with immune checkpoint inhibitors to expand effector-like CD8+ T cells, leading to tumor clearance in aged mice. Our findings highlight Dusp5 and Zfp219 as critical drivers of age-related T cell dysfunction that can be targeted to rejuvenate antitumor immunity in older cancer patients.

Article.Title: Milk osteopontin alters the infant microbiome to drive DC hematopoiesis and disease tolerance

Article.Title: A geothermal amoeba sets a new upper temperature limit for eukaryotes
Article.Authors: Rappaport H.; Petek-Seoane N.; Tyml T.; Niblo J.; Mikus F.; Gilbert N.; LaButti K.; Ani G.; MacVicar E.; Shepherd R.; de la Higuera I.; Lord S.; Dey G.; Wolfe G.; Dudin O.; Katz L.; Stedman K.; Sukenik S.; Skruber K.; Schulz F.; Dyche Mullins R.; Oliverio A.
Article.Abstract: The study of temperature limits has transformed our understanding of life's boundaries but has focused on bacteria and archaea. For decades after their discovery, no eukaryote was shown to replicate above 60°C. We isolated a geothermal amoeba, Incendiamoeba cascadensis, that divides at 63°C and is motile up to 64°C. We identified an enrichment of genes related to proteostasis and environmental sensing relative to mesophilic amoebae. Comparative RNA sequencing of I. cascadensis revealed upregulation of pathways related to proteostasis, DNA repair, and membrane trafficking at high temperatures. Predicted proteins of I. cascadensis have distinct biophysical properties, including enrichment of positively charged surface residues similar to bacterial and archaeal hyperthermophiles, which suggests a convergent mechanism for protein stability under temperature stress. Together, our findings expand our understanding of where and how life can persist.

Article.Title: Switching of transcriptional control from interferon regulatory factor 2 to interferon regulatory factor 1 drives innate immune cell activation
Article.Authors: Cadena C.; Reja R.; Bolech E.; Webster J.; Kameswaran V.; de Simone M.; Chen C.; Jiang J.; Hotzel K.; Bjornson C.; Alegre K.; Tan Z.; Elsaesser H.; Newland R.; Kelly R.; Darmanis S.; Daniel B.; Brooks D.; Deshpande I.; Newton K.; Kayagaki N.; Dixit V.
Article.Abstract: Interferon regulatory factor 2 (IRF2) is a transcription factor that prevents skin inflammation in mice and humans but, paradoxically, promotes pyroptosis by upregulating gasdermin D. How IRF2 activates some proinflammatory genes but suppresses inflammation is unclear. We show that skin inflammation in Irf2-deficient mice is driven by IRF1 activation of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). Chromatin profiling reveals that IRF1 and IRF2 occupy the same ISG regulatory sites, but as a weaker transcriptional activator, IRF2 limits ISG transcription by IRF1. Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling favors IRF1-driven transcription by inducing Irf1. In addition, IRF1 recruits the ubiquitin ligase SPOP to ISG sites, resulting in proteasomal degradation of IRF2. This shift from IRF2 to IRF1 occupancy enhances ISG transcription. Collectively, these findings define a hierarchical transcriptional circuit in which IRF2 limits IRF1 activity under homeostatic conditions but is displaced during an immune response, allowing IRF1-dependent gene programs central to innate immunity and autoinflammation.

Article.Title: Resident tissue macrophages transfer selenium transporter protein to protect pancreatic cancer from ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Guo W.; Li Z.; Chen Q.; Dunsmore G.; Jiang L.; An Z.; Fu Z.; Liu Y.; Shao Y.; Zhao S.; Wang T.; Tang H.; Zhao C.; Zhangyuan G.; Liu J.; Liu P.; Liu Z.; Qian J.; Zhang S.; Shi M.; He D.; Liu Y.; Blériot C.; Ng L.; Bai F.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), an aggressive cancer with a poor prognosis, contains resident tissue macrophages (RTMs) present before tumor onset and monocyte-derived macrophages recruited during tumor development, but their distinct roles in supporting tumor progression remain unclear. Combining single-cell profiling, spatial analysis, lineage tracing, RTM depletion, and selenium tracing, we found that RTMs preferentially localize at the tumor border, where they promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), tumor growth, and metastasis. Mechanistically, RTMs transfer the selenium transporter Selenop to EMThi tumor cells through LRP8-dependent uptake, increasing tumor-cell selenium availability, limiting lipid peroxidation, and shielding EMThi tumor cells from ferroptosis. RTM-specific Selenop deletion or tumor-cell Lrp8 disruption reduced EMT and tumor progression, whereas ferroptosis inhibition reversed the effect of RTM depletion. Human PDAC showed border-enriched SEPP1+ RTMs near EMThi tumor cells, suggesting a conserved macrophage-derived selenium niche that supports invasive tumor states and highlighting the potential for targeting RTMs or their secretory factors in PDAC.

Article.Title: A high-confidence plant mitochondrial proteome via protein correlation profiling
Article.Authors: Kim M.; Calvo S.; Nguyen K.; Rivera K.; Udeshi N.; Aphasizhev R.; Aphasizheva I.; Betsinger C.; Carr S.; Chao L.; Chen M.; Deng F.; Duraisingh M.; Fry M.; Goyal M.; Issa T.; Lian C.; Liao Y.; Luce B.; Mian S.; Paul A.; Samuelson J.; Solayman M.; Stefely J.; Vacas A.
Article.Abstract: Plant mitochondria share many features with animal mitochondria but also possess unique traits, including presence of both circular and linear mitochondrial DNA, RNA editing, a branched electron transport chain, and metabolic pathways supporting photosynthesis. An accurate mitochondrial proteome is crucial for studying these conserved and lineage-specific functions. Here, we introduce a novel approach to defining plant mitoproteomes that combines serial mitochondrial enrichment, mass spectrometry, and protein correlation profiling. This approach allows us to experimentally define a mitochondrial protein inventory of 1,462 proteins with high sensitivity and specificity. Integration of our experimental inventory with literature and microscopy validation yields the Arabidopsisthaliana MitoCarta (AtMitoCarta) atlas of 1,609 mitochondrial proteins, including 236 newly defined proteins and 147 proteins of unknown functions. A comparative analysis across eukaryotic organisms reveals that 15% of mitochondrial protein families are plant specific, including expanded pentatricopeptide repeat proteins. The AtMitoCarta inventory and the experimental workflow applicable to wild-type plants will enable comparative studies of plant mitochondria.

Article.Title: Comparative analysis of mitochondrial proteomes across the tree of life
Article.Authors: Chen M.; Stefely J.; Bardon E.; Aphasizhev R.; Aphasizheva I.; Betsinger C.; Carr S.; Chao L.; Deng F.; Duraisingh M.; Fry M.; Goyal M.; Issa T.; Kim M.; Lian C.; Liao Y.; Luce B.; Mian S.; Nguyen K.; Paul A.; Rivera K.; Samuelson J.; Solayman M.; Udeshi N.; Vacas A.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondria arose from the endosymbiosis of a bacterium with an archaea-related host cell about 2 billion years ago. To understand their origins and evolution, we compared experimentally defined mitoproteomes from the MitoCarta Tree of Life project. Across eight organisms, we identified 8,619 distinct mitochondrial proteins within 3,199 families, of which 43% lack Pfam domains. We report 33 protein families conserved in eukaryotic pathogens yet absent in humans, representing promising candidate targets for protozoan infectious diseases. Leveraging our experimentally defined mitoproteomes, we retrained a classifier based on a protein language model to predict mitoproteomes of ∼200 eukaryotes. From this expanded set, we detail the evolutionary trajectories of mitochondria, ranging from clade-specific gene family expansions to extreme mitoproteome reductions seemingly en route to complete organelle loss. Finally, we reconstruct the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) mitoproteome, revealing that LECA possessed a complex mitochondrion capable of both aerobic and anaerobic metabolism.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial proteome of Acanthamoeba delineates aerobic and anaerobic pathways dynamically regulated by oxygen
Article.Authors: Stefely J.; Deng F.; Chen M.; Nguyen K.; Luce B.; Fry M.; Guo X.; Maliaris K.; Rivera K.; Papanastasiou M.; Issa T.; Kanakapura Sundararaj B.; Root S.; Mani D.; Aphasizhev R.; Aphasizheva I.; Betsinger C.; Carr S.; Duraisingh M.; Goyal M.; Kim M.; Lian C.; Liao Y.; Mian S.; Paul A.
Article.Abstract: Acanthamoeba castellanii causes infectious blindness and resides in a key evolutionary outgroup to humans and fungi. Its divergent mitochondria are of outstanding interest due to their predicted aerobic and anaerobic functions with potential for drug targeting. However, a detailed delineation of its bioenergetic machinery, its activities, and their regulation remains lacking. Here, we integrate mitochondrial immunoprecipitation, density gradient purification, mass spectrometry, protein correlation profiling, and microscopy to generate a high-confidence inventory of the Acanthamoeba mitoproteome. The resulting AcMitoCarta contains 1,122 proteins, including 381 lacking readily identifiable homologs in human and yeast mitochondria. Complexome analysis highlights 20 macromolecular assemblies. Complementary proteomic and transcriptomic profiling reveals extensive rewiring of the organelle's bioenergetic machinery by oxygen, including induction of an anaerobic pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase-to-hydrogenase pathway under anoxia. We experimentally demonstrate that Acanthamoeba can produce H2 gas under anoxic conditions via a mitochondria-localized, oxygen-labile hydrogenase. AcMitoCarta establishes a framework for dissecting the interplay between aerobic and anaerobic energy metabolism.

Article.Title: Acanthamoeba ATP synthase structure reveals the TCA cycle is tethered to OXPHOS
Article.Authors: Fry M.; Luce B.; Stefely J.; Chen M.; Deng F.; Issa T.; Aphasizhev R.; Aphasizheva I.; Betsinger C.; Carr S.; Duraisingh M.; Goyal M.; Kim M.; Lian C.; Liao Y.; Mian S.; Nguyen K.; Paul A.; Rivera K.; Solayman M.; Udeshi N.; Vacas A.; Calvo S.; Samuelson J.; Mootha V.
Article.Abstract: Oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is a key metabolic process that couples redox energy to ATP production. While some core OXPHOS complex subunits are found across all domains of life, many have diverged or expanded across evolution-as seen in the protozoan pathogen Acanthamoeba castellanii. By integrating cryo-electron microscopy of unenriched mitochondrial lysate with mass spectrometry proteomics, we resolved the structures of endogenous mitochondrial ATP synthase (complex V), Hsp60, and respiratory complex III from Acanthamoeba. We capture Acanthamoeba ATP synthase in an IF1-inhibited state and reveal how Acanthamoeba-specific subunits and extensions stabilize the molecular machine, which includes a β subunit extension that interfaces with the peripheral stalk. Additionally, we characterize an active malate dehydrogenase (MDH) dimer structurally integrated within the ATP synthase peripheral stalk, thus revealing a direct protein tether between OXPHOS and the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Together, these findings provide structural insight into lineage-specific adaptations in Acanthamoeba that may tune protozoan metabolism.

Article.Title: Decoding mitochondrial proteomes of diverse eukaryotes
Article.Authors: Mootha V.; Calvo S.
Article.Abstract: Our textbook view of mitochondria, which has been shaped by studies in animals and yeast, fails to do justice to the organelle's broader eukaryotic diversity. While most mitochondria retain a tiny genome, the overwhelming majority of their proteins are nuclear-encoded and vary extensively across lineages. To map this diversity, the MitoCarta Tree of Life Consortium developed experimental and computational workflows to generate high-accuracy mitochondrial proteomes across diverse eukaryotes-helping to lay a foundation for comparative mitochondrial biology with broad implications for physiology, evolution, and disease.

Article.Title: SPARCS enables scalable recovery of complex image-based phenotypes for genetic screening
Article.Authors: Schmacke N.; Mädler S.; Wallmann G.; Metousis A.; Varlamova V.; Steigerwald S.; Christ S.; Bérouti M.; Harz H.; Leonhardt H.; Theis F.; Mann M.; Hornung V.
Article.Abstract: Forward genetic screening links genotype to phenotype by introducing random genetic perturbations and identifying phenotype-altering mutations. Although genome-scale screens are routine for simple phenotypes in cultured cells, extending them to complex image-based phenotypes remains challenging. Here, we present spatially resolved CRISPR screening (SPARCS), a microscopy-based platform for forward genetic screening on single-cell images. SPARCS physically isolates mutants in situ by automated laser microdissection, enabling image-based screening at unprecedented scale with multimodal hit phenotyping. We demonstrate SPARCS in genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens of autophagosome formation and activation of the immune sensor STING across 70 million cells. Via machine learning-based image analysis, SPARCS recovered most macroautophagy genes and identified GPHR as a pH-dependent regulator of STING. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics of isolated hit cells revealed endoplasmic reticulum (ER)/Golgi disruption and nominated additional STING regulators via in silico perturbation modeling. These results establish SPARCS as a scalable platform for genome-wide genetic screening of complex cellular phenotypes with a proteome-level readout.

Article.Title: A non-canonical function of glutathione to suppress ferroptosis via FSP1
Article.Authors: Han J.; Zhang Y.; Liu S.; Yang L.; Sun S.; Zhang B.; Liu A.; Zhu L.; Wang R.; Song D.; Zhuang X.; Gao Y.; Li J.; Li W.; He R.; Zhou H.; Yu L.; Feng S.; Chai R.; Chu B.
Article.Abstract: It is well established that glutathione (GSH) is mainly utilized by glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) to diminish peroxidized phospholipids and defend against ferroptosis. However, we found that GSH robustly protects a variety of GPX4 knockout (KO) cells from ferroptosis, thus indicating that there is an alternative pathway for GSH to suppress ferroptosis. By carrying out genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening, we identified that ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) is the key factor mediating the GPX4-independent protective effect of GSH. Mechanistically, FSP1 uses GSH to generate reduced ubiquinone, which scavenges oxidized lipids and suppresses ferroptosis. Inhibition of FSP1 abolishes this GSH-dependent ferroptosis protection both in vitro and in vivo. Distinct from NAD(P)H-mediated ubiquinone reduction, GSH-stimulated generation of reduced ubiquinone via FSP1 is independent of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD). Together, our work clarifies a new mechanism of GSH-mediated ferroptosis suppression, thus highlighting the potential that targeting GSH metabolism should be beneficial for ferroptosis-related diseases whether or not it is related to GPX4.

Article.Title: A spatiotemporal lifecycle atlas decodes spatial coordination in rice
Article.Authors: Jing Y.; Chen Q.; Chen Y.; Yan W.; Gui Y.; Zhong Y.; Qin M.; Zhang H.; Whelan J.; Li C.; Chen S.; Xu C.; He W.; Lv Z.; Yang F.; Chen R.; Zhang J.; Wang Z.; Xiong Z.; Liao X.; Xia K.; Wei T.; Fan L.; Yang T.; Bai Y.
Article.Abstract: How gene expression programs are coordinated across space and time to build a complete plant remains poorly understood. Here, we combine high-resolution spatial transcriptomics, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and a gap-free reference genome to build a 3D spatiotemporal atlas of rice, spanning 10 organs and 61 stages from seed to seed. Our datasets profile 851,725 nuclei and 347,640 spatial bins, defining 119 cell types and 133 subtypes across the rice lifecycle. Through multimodal integration, we reconstruct an inferred developmental trajectory graph that links cell states from the proembryo to mature organs and identifies trajectory-associated regulators. We further implicate the pleiotropic regulator OsARF1 in distinct spatial gene programs across developmental contexts. We also uncover widespread axis-associated transcriptional asymmetry, including dorsoventral endosperm programs that partition starch and protein accumulation. Collectively, this high-resolution atlas provides a spatiotemporal framework for understanding rice development and guiding future crop improvement.

Article.Title: Cancer competition for vitamin B2 creates metabolic checkpoint for T cell ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Chen H.; Li C.; Ke Y.; Wu Z.; Ou Z.; Huang N.; Lin Z.; Gao H.; Xu X.; Lu L.; Huang Z.; Bian Y.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic competition between tumors and T cells drives immune evasion, but the transporters and mechanisms remain largely elusive. Here, we establish the CareSLCs platform and identify that SLC52A3-mediated vitamin B2 (VB2) uptake is indispensable for T cell antitumor immunity. Mechanistically, VB2 deficiency impairs mitochondrial respiration and glutathione regeneration, leading to mitophagy, labile iron accumulation, and lipid peroxidation that trigger T cell ferroptosis. Unexpectedly, tumors preferentially employ SLC52A2, not SLC52A3, to scavenge VB2 and outcompete T cells. Tumor SLC52A2 ablation enhances T cell function in immunocompetent hosts without appreciably affecting intrinsic tumor growth. Clinically, high tumoral SLC52A2 correlates with T cell dysfunction and poor survival, whereas dietary VB2 intake is associated with reduced cancer risks. Thus, VB2 supplementation or SLC52A3 overexpression augments CAR-T cell antitumor efficacy. Our results suggest that tumoral VB2 competition establishes a metabolic checkpoint driving T cell ferroptosis and that enhancing VB2 uptake reinvigorates T cells to improve cancer immunotherapy.

Article.Title: STING reprogramming by estrogen promotes neutrophil extracellular trap formation and sex-biased resistance to ADC therapy
Article.Authors: Yan J.; Zhou T.; Shi S.; Mao G.; Xu J.; Zhang Y.; Zhang Y.; Sun H.; Wang Y.; Wang X.; Huang C.; Liu R.; Hu D.; Yang S.; Yu J.; Feng Y.; Xie Y.; Wang B.; Hao J.
Article.Abstract: Sex differences in cancer therapy response remain poorly understood. Using a "phase II-like preclinical trial" across 55 CLDN18.2+ pancreatic cancer patient-derived xenografts, we identify marked female-biased resistance to CLDN18.2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) therapy despite equivalent antigen expression. Mechanistically, estrogen signals through GPER1 to upregulate TRAF6, redirecting tumor-intrinsic STING signaling from IRF3-mediated interferon production toward nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) activation. This drives CXCL1 secretion, neutrophil recruitment, and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. NETs form a charged extracellular network that restricts antibody access to tumor-cell-surface antigens-a mechanism we term functional antigen shielding-reducing ADC cytotoxicity independently of antigen expression. The NET burden also correlated with poorer responses to trastuzumab, cetuximab, and enfortumab vedotin across three clinical cohorts. Pharmacologic NET disruption with sivelestat restored ADC efficacy in female mice. These findings reveal an estrogen-driven resistance mechanism with broad implications for antibody-based cancer therapy.
