Article.Title: Global and specific mechanisms stimulate mistranslation in cancer
Article.Authors: Wernaart D.; Fumagalli A.; Adhikary M.; Feng X.; Geintzer O.; Kyei-Baffour E.; Bleijerveld O.; Hoekman L.; Zwart C.; Fish A.; Giebel L.; Burylo A.; Proost N.; Körner P.; Alkan F.; Yang C.; Brouwer J.; Henriksen C.; Westhof E.; Champagne J.; van Tellingen O.; Rodnina M.; Agami R.
Article.Abstract: Tryptophan codon-specific mistranslation, in the form of ribosomal frameshifting and tryptophan-to-phenylalanine (W > F) codon reassignments (substitutants), is induced in cancer cells by the limiting level of tryptophan imposed by anti-tumour immunity. While the oncogenic mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway drives frameshifting, whether substitutants are genetically regulated remains unknown. Here we screened for genes that control W > F substitutants following interferon-γ-mediated tryptophan shortage. This screen identified ADAR1, an enzyme that converts adenosine to inosine in double-stranded RNA molecules, and FTSJ1, an enzyme that 2'-O-methylates the anticodon region of several tRNAs. We demonstrate that ADAR1 sustains expression of key players in the ribosome quality control pathway, which in turn is essential for mistranslation events. FTSJ1, in contrast, specifically drives W > F mistranslation by methylation of tRNATrp to promote its binding to WARS1 loaded with phenylalanine instead of tryptophan. As ADAR1 and FTSJ1 levels are elevated in many cancer types, we propose that cancer cells deploy global and specific mechanisms to promote mistranslation in response to anti-tumour immunity.

Article.Title: Power-law scaling of mitotic spindles with genome sizes across eukaryotes is driven by chromosome crowding
Article.Authors: Gudlin L.; Vukušić K.; Novak M.; Trupinić M.; Ljulj M.; Dundović I.; Petelinec A.; Petrušić L.; Hertel A.; van Ravesteyn T.; Trakala M.; Kops G.; Storchová Z.; Tambača J.; Pavin N.; Tolić I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Genome size varies more than 10,000-fold across eukaryotes, yet how the mitotic spindle adapts to this range remains unknown. Here we show that metaphase plate width scales with genome size following a power law with an exponent of ~1/3 across eukaryotes. Comparative analysis and a physical model reveal that this scaling arises from the linear relationship between total chromosome volume and genome size, with chromosome number playing a secondary role. The same scaling holds across ploidy levels in cell lines, patient-derived cancer organoids and meiotic systems. Physical model and acute spindle compression demonstrate that chromosome crowding generates interchromosome pushing forces that set metaphase plate width. By contrast, spindle length is regulated by microtubule dynamics, cytoplasmic forces and cell size, indicating that spindle dimensions are independently controlled. The revealed scaling law provides a robust mechanism for accommodating large genomic variation and offers insight into the evolution of open mitosis and mitotic cell rounding, as well as polyploidy tolerance in tumours and during speciation.

Article.Title: In vivo DNA damage protection during cell migration across confining embryonic tissue environments
Article.Authors: Häkkinen H.; Villaseca S.; Alhashem Z.; Hamidzadeh A.; Chomiczewski S.; Desevedavy M.; Leleux S.; Liu Y.; Becker J.; Htun M.; Gallo F.; El-Zohiry D.; Petre V.; Stefanowski K.; Franze K.; Renkawitz J.; Scarpa E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cells migrating through confined spaces can experience nuclear deformation, nuclear envelope damage and DNA lesions, but the physiological consequences of confinement in vivo remain unclear. Using the zebrafish neural crest as a model of developmental migration, we show that tissue confinement increases along the antero–posterior axis and scales with the extent of nuclear deformation. Genetic and mechanical disruption of surrounding tissues relieves confinement and restores nuclear morphology in vivo. Surprisingly, even under extreme deformation, neural crest cells exhibit nucleo-cytoplasmic leakage without nuclear envelope rupture or increased DNA damage. Instead, confinement is associated with reduced LaminB2 at the nuclear envelope. Functional perturbation of LaminB2 reveals that its depletion accelerates recovery from deformation, whereas sustained expression causes persistent nuclear distortion, identifying LaminB2 as a regulator of nuclear deformability. RNA-seq of confined trunk neural crest cells reveals broad upregulation of DNA repair pathways, suggesting that these embryonic stem-like cells are intrinsically resistant to confinement-induced mechanical stress.

Article.Title: Quantification of lipid sorting during clathrin-mediated endocytosis
Article.Authors: Lennartz H.; da Costa Nunes S.; Böhlig K.; Chhatre A.; Šachl R.; Kuhn S.; Moneta L.; Barahtjan P.; Yee Yau W.; Iglesias-Artola J.; Hof M.; Opálka L.; Modes C.; Honigmann A.; Nadler A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is a major transport route for proteins from the plasma membrane to the interior of the cell. While the recruitment of cargo proteins to clathrin-coated pits is well understood, it remains an open question whether lipids are also sorted by this process. Here, to address this question, we combined super-resolution stimulated emission depletion imaging of bifunctional lipid probes with mathematical modelling. Quantification of ten different lipid species revealed significant differences in pit partitioning, ranging from slight enrichment to moderate exclusion. We find that the lipid asymmetry in the plasma membrane is sufficient to explain the observed trend. Taken together, our findings imply that clathrin-mediated endocytosis has a minor selectivity for cytoplasmic leaflet lipids, but overall does not substantially contribute to lipid sorting compared with non-vesicular trafficking.

Article.Title: Spatially resolved multiomics of human meningeal development reveal lineage and disease dynamics
Article.Authors: To K.; Pett J.; Dufva O.; Chipampe N.; Polanski K.; Cujba A.; Roberts K.; Predeus A.; Yayon N.; Kanemaru K.; Patel M.; Horsfall D.; Li T.; Mazin P.; Cakir B.; Kapuge R.; Wilk A.; Memi F.; He X.; Solanky N.; Kayhanian S.; Mair R.; Rademaker K.; Bayraktar O.; Haniffa M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The meninges are increasingly recognized as key stromal and immune niches supporting cranial development. Here we constructed a paired single-nuclei RNA and Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin atlas of human meningeal development from 6 to 21 postconception weeks across cranial regions. By integrating spatial transcriptomics, we resolved cell types across meningeal layers. Our multiomic atlas defines gene regulatory networks underlying blood–brain barrier endothelial identity during development. Within immune compartments, the data support a yolk sac origin for meningeal myeloid lineages, including perivascular macrophages primed for barrier immunity. We present two analytical tools: Nichefinder, for spatial label transfer and proximity analysis, and cell2home, for inferring chemotactic signalling. Using cell2home, we identify interactions potentially driving B cell migration from cranial marrow into prenatal meninges. We studied trisomy 21, and observed reduced fibroblast chemokine expression with enhanced JAK–STAT signalling. Together, this work provides a developmental atlas of the human meninges and defines cellular and regulatory programs shaping early barrier immunity.

Article.Title: Cell atlas of the developing human meninges reveals a dura-like nature of meningiomas
Article.Authors: Vinsland E.; Marco Salas S.; Kapustová I.; Hu L.; Webb S.; Li X.; He X.; Nilsson M.; Haniffa M.; Barker R.; Persson O.; Raleigh D.; Sundström E.; Lönnerberg P.; Linnarsson S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The vertebrate central nervous system is enveloped by the meninges, consisting of the pia, arachnoid and dura layers. The arachnoid is hypothesized to give rise to the most common primary intracranial tumours, meningiomas. However, supporting molecular evidence is lacking. There are no effective medical therapies to treat meningiomas that are resistant to local interventions, encumbered by our limited understanding of their cellular origin. Here, to advance our understanding of meningioma biology, we generated a comprehensive reference single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlas of human fetal meninges at postconceptional weeks 5–13. We found that the meningeal layers develop concurrently, and identified an inner CDH1 -positive dura layer expressing tight-junction genes consistent with barrier function. Comparing meningiomas with fetal meninges, we show that, transcriptionally, meningioma cells resemble dura-lineage cells, and that common meningioma driver genes were expressed in the dura lineage. This raises the hypothesis that meningiomas could originate from dura-lineage cells.

Article.Title: Taxane-induced conformational changes in the microtubule lattice activate GEF-H1-dependent RhoA signalling
Article.Authors: Meiring J.; Mahapatra V.; Liu R.; Gravett M.; Morren D.; Saunders H.; Choi S.; Pelster José A.; Karhanova A.; Metallidou I.; Moore A.; Spoelstra M.; Grigoriev I.; Giono M.; Iyer S.; Stehbens S.; Díaz J.; Lansky Z.; Stecker K.; Steinmetz M.; Howes S.; Kapitein L.; Akhmanova A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Taxanes are widely used chemotherapeutic agents that perturb cell division. They also exert effects during interphase, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. Here we show that taxanes activate RhoA signalling and induce actin remodelling by releasing the RhoA activator GEF-H1 from microtubules. This taxane-induced release of GEF-H1 occurs rapidly, is independent of tubulin post-translational modifications, and can be recapitulated using purified proteins. In vitro reconstitution assays combined with analyses of microtubule structure revealed that microtubule binding by GEF-H1 is inhibited by microtubule-stabilizing ligands that expand the microtubule lattice, such as taxanes and GMPCPP, but not by others, including GTPγS and discodermolide, which stabilize a compacted microtubule lattice. Our findings demonstrate that alterations in microtubule lattice conformation can activate key signalling pathways, offering insights into the mode of action of taxanes and the possible origins of their side effects.

Article.Title: The dual-enhanced graph learning framework DePass allows paired data integration in single-cell and spatial multiomics
Article.Authors: Li W.; Jiang Y.; Zhao Q.; Xu Y.; Dai D.; Rong Y.; Zhao X.; Zhang H.
Article.Abstract: Recent sequencing advances have enabled abundant multi-omics data generation for both single-cell and spatial contexts. Integrating such multimodal data is critical for decoding cellular and tissue-level complexity. However, compared with single-modality profiling, multimodal data often exhibit higher levels of noise, and existing methods typically overlook this challenge during integration. Meanwhile, most current approaches are tailored to either single-cell or spatial data, limiting their applicability across data types. Here we present DePass, a scalable graph learning framework for paired data integration in both single-cell and spatial multi-omics. We propose a coupled enhancement-integration architecture that iteratively denoises data and improves integrated embeddings. We systematically benchmarked DePass across 6 modalities, 9 tissue types and 13 experimental platforms, demonstrating superior integration accuracy. In the in-house colorectal cancer data, DePass further uncovered immune niche substructure and spatial tumour heterogeneity at near single-cell resolution. These results establish DePass as a unified and generalizable solution for multi-omics integration across diverse biological contexts.

Article.Title: Amygdala excitability across development: mechanisms, environmental influences, and behavioral outcomes

Article.Abstract: Recent work in rodent models provides mechanistic insights into how the excitability of principal neurons is dynamically regulated to facilitate the encoding and retrieval of emotionally salient memories in the basolateral amygdala (BLA). Article.Title: The nervous system as a systemic organizer of cancer-associated cachexia
Article.Authors: Weng Z.; Cai S.; Zhu H.; Jiang L.; Zhang S.; Zhang Z.; Jiang S.
Article.Abstract: Cancer-associated cachexia (CAC) is a progressive, multiorgan wasting syndrome that critically limits treatment response and survival. In CAC, the nervous system senses, amplifies, and coordinates responses to a broad range of tumor-induced perturbations, including both direct tumor-derived factors and the resulting systemic disturbances in inflammation, metabolism, and immunity. By dysregulating central neural circuits and remodeling peripheral innervation, tumor-hijacked neural coordination drives both anorexia and multiorgan wasting, forming a self-reinforcing cachexia loop. Additionally, treatment-associated neurotoxicity further augments dysfunction across the central and peripheral nervous systems. In this review, we synthesize evidence from patient studies and animal models to examine how tumors co-opt the nervous system to systemically organize cachexia, thereby providing a pathophysiological framework for studying early disease detection, biomarker development, and mechanism-based intervention for CAC.

Article.Title: Spatial navigation and the basal forebrain in Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative diseases

Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Lewy body disease (LBD) are frequently associated with spatial navigation impairments. However, these impairments are less pronounced in frontotemporal dementia and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy. While basal forebrain degeneration occurs in all of these diseases, disruption of cholinergic pathways and related cholinergic deficits has been primarily observed in AD and LBD, and in both of these conditions, basal forebrain degeneration appears to be associated with spatial navigation deficits. In this review, we discuss current understanding of spatial navigation impairments in neurodegenerative diseases, with a particular focus on disease-related changes in the basal forebrain and their associations with impaired spatial navigation abilities in humans.

Article.Title: Beyond breathing: multimodal pathways connecting olfaction to autonomic nervous system modulation
Article.Authors: Walter M.; Puech A.; Aliyari F.; Courtiol E.; Buonviso N.
Article.Abstract: The interaction between olfaction and respiration has recently emerged as a central aspect of brain-body interactions. To date, most studies in this context, both in rodents and humans, have focused on how respiratory airflow rhythmically drives brain activity. In this review, we shift the focus to the modulatory effects of odorant molecules, which engage chemical, affective, and trigeminal pathways to elicit integrated sensory experiences and robust autonomic responses. We synthesize recent findings showing that the olfactory system, through its unique connectivity with limbic and autonomic networks, operates at the interface between exteroception and interoception. By modulating respiratory dynamics, and more generally autonomic nervous system activity, odors emerge as a multimodal signal capable of influencing brain-body interactions and supporting well-being.

Article.Title: Temporal astrocytic metabolic reprogramming gates pain chronification
Article.Authors: Park J.; Lee S.
Article.Abstract: Most experimental models of chronic pain emphasize the gradual emergence of sensory hypersensitivity, yet pain chronification can also be conceptualized as a metabolically regulated state transition. In this review, we synthesize evidence mainly from mouse and rat spinal cord and anterior cingulate cortex studies indicating that astrocytes temporally coordinate neuronal excitability, inflammatory signaling, and metabolic coupling. We propose that chronification proceeds through temporally organized astrocytic metabolic remodeling: GPCR-linked lactate-coupled signaling during acute induction, sustained glycolytic gene expression and glycogen remodeling during consolidation, and stabilization of pain-permissive astrocyte states through lactylation-linked inflammatory and chromatin regulation. By integrating these mechanisms along a temporal axis, this framework distinguishes processes that initiate chronicity from those that maintain established pain and suggests stage-specific logic for future interventions.

Article.Title: The dynamics of functional connectivity-based language lateralization across timescales
Article.Authors: Cao W.; Wang N.; Zhou K.; Xu M.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: In most individuals, language is predominantly left-lateralized, a prominent feature of human brain organization. Recent research increasingly views language lateralization as a property of distributed and interacting functional networks. In this article, we review evidence that the lateralization of functional connectivity within the language system varies in both degree and direction across multiple timescales. We propose that this connectivity-based lateralization undergoes long-term developmental, experience-dependent, and perturbation-induced reorganization, while also exhibiting short-term context-driven and spontaneous fluctuations within apparently stable patterns. Furthermore, we discuss neurobiological mechanisms that may support and constrain these dynamics. Together, these findings provide a multiscale framework for understanding how the human brain balances functional flexibility with relative stability in shaping the lateralized organization of language.

Article.Abstract: Brains synchronize interpersonally during social interaction, yet the term 'synchrony' is often used to describe phenomena with different origins and functional implications. In this article, we briefly synthesize and organize these phenomena according to their signal and coupling properties, highlighting the value of disambiguation for reproducibility, theoretical clarity, and translational impact.

Article.Title: The mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome in aging and brain diseases
Article.Authors: Shawky A.; Huang H.; Parikh D.; Morris-Blanco K.
Article.Abstract: The mitochondrial genome is a dynamic regulatory platform that extends far beyond its protein-coding capacity. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) harbors epigenetic modifications and produces diverse noncoding RNAs that influence mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis. Evidence from animal models and human studies indicates that mtDNA methylation, mitochondrial-encoded noncoding RNAs, and cytosolic release of mitochondrial nucleic acids regulate transcription, metabolism, and stress signaling. Furthermore, these mechanisms are altered in aging, neurodegenerative disease, and acute brain injury. In this review, we synthesize emerging insights into how the mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome shape mitochondrial function and serve as regulatory interfaces linking cellular stress and neuronal vulnerability in brain aging and disease.

Article.Title: Resilience and vulnerability in the midbrain dopamine system during aging
Article.Authors: McMurtrie G.; Mabry S.; Glausier J.; Rocha E.; Freyberg Z.
Article.Abstract: The midbrain dopamine system is integral to movement, reward, and motivation, and its dysfunction underlies a range of brain disorders. Age is a primary risk factor for many of these disorders, yet systematic analysis of how the dopamine system changes during healthy aging remains relatively understudied. In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. Elucidating these neuroadaptive mechanisms could offer a path toward preserving dopamine neuron function across the lifespan and potentially preventing age-related neurodegeneration.

Article.Abstract: Sleep loss heightens pain sensitivity, but the brain circuits involved remain unclear. In a recent study, Huang, Wang, Jiao, and colleagues identified a pathway connecting the retrosplenial cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and zona incerta that contributes to heightened sensitivity to mechanical stimulation and heat after sleep deprivation in male mice.

Article.Title: Molecular architecture of Cryptococcus cell walls reveals species-specific chitosan-dependent remodeling
Article.Authors: Ankur A.; Upadhya R.; Doosti M.; Ferreira D.; Miller S.; Xie L.; Hung I.; Lodge J.; Wang T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii are fungal pathogens that cause life-threatening infections, including cryptococcal meningitis. A distinctive feature of the cryptococcal cell wall is the extensive deacetylation of chitin to chitosan, a modification that is essential for virulence but whose structural role in cell-wall organization remains poorly understood. Here, we analyze the cell walls of wild-type strains of both species and their avirulent chitosan-deficient mutants, which serve as vaccine candidates. Loss of chitosan disrupted cell morphology and altered cell-wall ultrastructure, with more pronounced defects in C. neoformans . Solid-state NMR reveals that aggregated α-(1→3)-glucans form the principal rigid domain of the cell wall in both species and are closely associated with chitin microfibrils, whereas surrounding β-glucans and mannoproteins constitute a more dynamic matrix. Chitosan modulates hydration and flexibility, and its loss increases chitin exposure and triggers species-specific remodeling of the polysaccharide network. In C. neoformans , chitosan depletion increased α-(1→3)-glucan content and reduced β-glucan levels, whereas C. gattii selectively lost one α-(1→3)-glucan subtype while maintaining β-glucan levels. Although capsule production remained intact, chitosan deficiency altered glucuronoxylomannan linkage patterns and mannoprotein composition. These findings reveal how chitosan organizes cryptococcal cell-wall architecture and highlight distinct structural adaptation strategies among pathogenic Cryptococcus species.

Article.Title: Bacteroides–Escherichia interactions contribute to colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile
Article.Authors: Ambat A.; van den Berg N.; Zorrilla F.; Menon S.; Maji A.; Islam T.; Basile A.; Ghimire S.; Kalmar L.; Patil K.; Scaria J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Commensal gut bacteria are key contributors to the resilience against pathogen invasion. This is exemplified by the success of faecal microbiota transplantation in treating recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. Yet, characteristics of communities that can confer colonisation resistance and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown. Here we use a synthetic community of 14 commensal gut bacteria to uncover inter-species interactions and metabolic pathways underpinning the emergent resilience against C. difficile invasion. We challenged this synthetic community as well as faecal-matter-derived communities with antibiotic treatment and C. difficile in a continuous flow bioreactor. Using generalised Lotka-Volterra and genome-scale metabolic modelling, we identified interactions between Escherichia coli and Bacteroides/Phocaeicola sp. as key to the pathogen’s suppression. Metabolomics and targeted validation experiments revealed that fructan-derived fructooligosaccharides, vitamin B3 biosynthesis, and competition for Stickland metabolism precursors causally contribute to suppression across multiple C. difficile strains and donor backgrounds. Analysis of metagenomics data from patient cohorts and clinical trials attested the in vivo relevance of the identified metabolic pathways and the ratio between Bacteroides and Escherichia in successful colonisation resistance. The latter was found to be a stronger discriminator than commonly used alpha diversity metrics. Together, our study uncovers emergent microbial interactions in pathogen resistance with implications for rational design of bacteriotherapies.

Article.Title: Solvent heterogeneity regulates assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization
Article.Authors: Ghosh G.; Bachmann J.; Nyenhuis M.; Krüger T.; Fernández Z.; Coelho J.; Albers A.; Köyer M.; Doltsinis N.; Fernández G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Supramolecular polymers are fundamental mimics of biological assemblies with diverse functions. However, predicting monomer solubility and controlling the colloidal stability of the resulting assemblies in solution remain major challenges. As a result, their preparation commonly relies on solvent mixtures, which can generate local heterogeneities during sample processing—an effect that remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that solvent heterogeneity biases assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization, with the extent of this effect modulated by monomer structure. Using an amphiphilic Pd(II) complex as a model system, we uncover a thermally accelerated transition from kinetically controlled discrete nanostructures to thermodynamically stable supramolecular polymers in water/1,4-dioxane mixtures. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that this transformation is mediated by microscopic liquid–liquid phase separation within the mixed solvent, creating 1,4-dioxane-enriched microdomains with increased local monomer concentration. Thermal annealing enhances molecular mobility and promotes the growth and coalescence of these microdomains, facilitating the transition to one-dimensional fibers. Extending the investigation to structurally related monomers further identifies the metal center and hydrogen-bonding motifs as key design elements governing this behavior. By linking molecular design and solvent heterogeneity to pathway complexity, our findings highlight how mixed solvents can be used to control supramolecular polymerization.

Article.Title: Brown adipose tissue ankyrin-B cell-autonomously modulates lipid content and its deletion protects male mice against diet-induced obesity
Article.Authors: Aguillard A.; Ferrer I.; Chen J.; Manja K.; Tzeng J.; Naughton N.; Soderblom E.; Bartman C.; Lorenzo D.
Article.Abstract: Fatty acid (FA) availability for brown adipose tissue (BAT) thermogenesis depends in part on lipolysis of lipid droplet (LD) triglycerides. Here, we identify the membrane adaptor ankyrin-B (AnkB), encoded by the cardiometabolic disease-associated ANK2 gene, as a regulator of brown adipocyte lipid homeostasis and metabolic adaptation. BAT-specific AnkB deficiency caused excess lipid accumulation, enlarged LDs, and BAT whitening without altering mitochondrial oxidative capacity or thermogenesis in the fed state in male mice. Mechanistically, AnkB promoted basal lipolysis by recruiting hormone-sensitive lipase to LDs. However, AnkB loss compromised thermoregulation during cold exposure with fasting, linking AnkB-dependent FA release to thermogenesis under energetic stress. Unexpectedly, BAT AnkB deficiency protected male mice from high-fat diet-induced obesity (DIO), hepatic steatosis, glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance. This protection was associated with enhanced BAT mitochondrial oxidative capacity, oxidative remodeling of white adipose tissue, and increased circulating FGF21. Together, these findings establish AnkB as a previously unrecognized regulator of BAT lipid mobilization that coordinates thermogenic fuel availability with mitochondrial oxidative adaptation during metabolic stress. Ankyrin-B couples BAT lipid droplet lipolysis to thermogenic fuel availability. Its loss impairs thermoregulation during fasting but preserves fed-state thermogenesis and protects against diet-induced metabolic dysfunction.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Physiology > Adipose Tissue and Metabolism; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Biochemistry > Lipid metabolism and biosynthesis; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors

Article.Title: Permeability heterogeneity controls fluid migration and microseismicity evolution in The Geysers geothermal field, California
Article.Authors: Li L.; Zeng X.; McBrearty I.; Cui X.; Tan X.; Mao S.; Beroza G.; Tan J.; Liu J.; Segall P.; Ellsworth W.
Article.Abstract: Fracture networks directly govern the efficiency of geothermal energy extraction and play a critical role in fluid migration and microearthquake generation. Using deep learning and Markov clustering, we build a high-resolution microseismic catalog covering the past decade for The Geysers geothermal field, California. Our observations reveal distinctive clustering patterns and inferred fracture systems tightly correlated with injection operations. Source mechanism analyses and pore pressure simulations indicate that the inferred connected fracture network provides pathways for rapid and directional pore pressure diffusion, highlighting that heterogeneous permeability controls the localized migration of fluids and the associated microseismic response. Our study highlights the importance of continuous and integrated seismic monitoring for ensuring the sustainability of long-term reservoir development and exploitation. Continuous seismic observations and numerical simulations reveal that, over the past decade, fluid migration and microseismic responses at The Geysers geothermal field have been primarily controlled by heterogeneous permeability.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Mechanical Engineering > Hydraulic Fracturing and Reservoir Analysis; Energy > Renewable Energy, Sustainability and the Environment > Geothermal Energy Systems and Applications; Environmental Science > Environmental Engineering > CO2 Sequestration and Geologic Interactions

Article.Title: Decomposing multi-scale dynamic regulation from single-cell multiomics with scMagnify
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Yan X.; Shen B.; Wang H.; Tang Z.; Zang Y.; Lin P.; Zhang H.; Li Y.; Li H.
Article.Abstract: Deciphering the highly coupled regulatory circuits that drive cellular dynamics remains a fundamental goal in biology. However, capturing the multi-scale time-lagged dynamics and combinatorial regulatory logic of gene regulation remains challenging. Here we present scMagnify, a deep-learning-based framework that leverages chromatin accessibility and gene expression via Granger causality to reconstruct and decompose multi-scale gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Diverse benchmarks demonstrate scMagnify’s favorable performance. scMagnify employs tensor decomposition to identify combinatorial TF modules and their activation profiles across multiple time-lags. We applied scMagnify to human hematopoiesis and mouse pancreas development, where it recovered known lineage-driving regulators and provided further insights into the combinatorial logic underlying cell fate decisions. Furthermore, in the context of kidney injury, scMagnify’s intercellular communication module mapped key signaling-to-transcription cascades linking microenvironment cues to pathological epithelial cell changes. In summary, scMagnify provides a robust computational framework for dissecting the multi-scale regulatory logic that governs complex biological processes in development and disease. Chen and colleagues present scMagnify, a framework that uses single-cell multi-omic data to reconstruct and decompose time-lagged gene regulatory networks. The study analyses regulatory programs associated with development and disease.

Article.Title: Breaking water-structure constraints by Hofmeister effects in interfacial polymerization for polyamide membranes
Article.Authors: Tang Q.; Chen H.; Chen Y.; Wu H.; Meng X.; Jin W.; Jiang P.; Zhang Y.; Feng X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Hydration critically governs the physicochemical behavior of solutes in both the aqueous bulk and interfacial environments. As typical chaotropic Hofmeister ions, weakly hydrated anions (WHAs) can reshape hydration structures and accumulate at water–hydrophobe interfaces. Notably, WHAs paradoxically suppress the solubility of certain small-molecule monomers in water while enhancing that of chemically analogous polymers. Here, we exploit WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control to regulate polyamide-forming interfacial polymerization (IP), using the piperazine (PIP) and trimesoyl chloride (TMC) nanofiltration system as the primary model. Introducing WHAs into the aqueous phase reduces the affinity of amine monomers for water and accelerates partitioning into the reaction front in the oil phase, remarkably reinforcing IP self-limitation. Simultaneously, interfacial WHA enrichment lowers interfacial tension and, together with accelerated amine delivery, potentially intensifies transport-driven interfacial instabilities. WHAs also lower interfacial water availability, attenuating acyl chloride hydrolysis. These synergistic effects yield hollow-ridged polyamide selective layers with reduced thickness and high crosslinking density, delivering enhanced water permeance and salt rejection. Crucially, module-scale fabrication of high-performance membranes demonstrates that WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control is directly compatible with established desalination pipelines.
Article.TopicFields: Environmental Science > Water Science and Technology > Membrane Separation Technologies; Engineering > Mechanical Engineering > Membrane Separation and Gas Transport; Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Nanopore and Nanochannel Transport Studies

Article.Title: ADAM17 is a broad HIV-1 restriction factor targeted by Nef to restore Env maturation
Article.Authors: Li Q.; Li S.; Dey S.; Sun D.; Sun L.; Zheng Y.
Article.Abstract: HIV-1 uses the accessory protein Nef to enhance the infectivity of newly produced virus particles, but the host defenses counteracted by Nef remain incompletely defined. The membrane protein SERINC5 contributes to this defense but primarily restricts laboratory-adapted HIV-1 strains, suggesting that other cellular factors influence the requirement for Nef. Here we show that ADAM17, a cell-surface protein best known for cleaving inflammatory mediators, restricts both laboratory-adapted and primary HIV-1 isolates. ADAM17 acts independently of its enzymatic activity: its signal peptide, which normally directs proteins into the cellular secretory pathway, binds the HIV-1 envelope precursor gp160 and retains it in the endoplasmic reticulum. This prevents envelope maturation, transport to the cell surface and incorporation into virus particles, thereby reducing viral infectivity. Nef counteracts this restriction through a PxxP protein-interaction motif that promotes the release of ADAM17 in extracellular vesicles, reducing its abundance within cells and restoring envelope maturation. Disruption of ADAM17 in CD4-positive T-cell lines and primary human lymphocytes reduced the requirement for Nef during viral replication. These findings establish ADAM17 as a regulator of HIV-1 envelope production and show how Nef redirects host-cell trafficking to promote the formation of infectious virus particles. Here, the authors show that the cell-surface protein ADAM17 blocks HIV-1 by preventing maturation of the viral envelope protein, while the viral protein Nef counteracts this effect by redirecting ADAM17 out of infected cells.
Article.TopicFields: Immunology and Microbiology > Virology > HIV Research and Treatment; Medicine > Infectious Diseases > HIV/AIDS drug development and treatment; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Genetics > Virus-based gene therapy research

Article.Title: Molecular basis of PADI6 species-specific oligomerization in maternal regulatory complexes
Article.Authors: Li J.; Li J.; Chi P.; Zeng Y.; Liu S.; Ju S.; Huang J.; Liu Q.; Zhang Z.; Han Z.; Yan L.; Qi Q.; Ou G.; Guo L.; Wang X.; Lu Y.; Deng D.
Article.Abstract: Peptidyl arginine deiminase 6 (PADI6) is an essential maternal effector in mammalian oocytes and preimplantation embryos. Recently, we identified the conserved maternal PADI6-UHRF1-UBE2D complex (MPU). MPU, together with the subcortical maternal complex (SCMC), further forms the cytoplasmic lattices (CPLs). Here, we reconstitute the mouse MPU (mMPU) and uncover striking species-specific differences in PADI6 oligomerization. In solution, mouse PADI6 (mPADI6) undergoes further oligomerization, forming tetramers, higher-order oligomers, and filamentous assemblies. Cryo-EM analysis reveals that the N-terminal IgG domain of mPADI6 mediates this behavior. These distinct oligomerization properties alter the stoichiometric ratios of the three components during assembly of both human MPU and mMPU. Moreover, PADI6 from different species adopts distinct oligomeric states in solution, suggesting potential differences in CPL assembly mechanisms. Together, our findings define the differential oligomerization capacity of PADI6 at the molecular level and provide a critical framework for understanding PADI6-mediated maternal regulatory assemblies during early embryonic development in different species. Maternal effector PADI6 forms the MPU complex with UHRF1 and UBE2D and assembles CPLs with SCMC members in oocytes and early embryos. PADI6’s oligomerization capacity, driven by its N-terminal domain, defines species-specific MPU structure and highlights differences in CPL architecture and regulatory mechanisms

Article.Title: Baseline radiographic and microbiologic predictors of treatment outcomes in a shortened all-oral regimen for MDR/RR-TB
Article.Authors: Shen E.; Mpinda S.; Maama L.; Tamirat M.; Sebakeng P.; Oyewusi L.; LaHood A.; Trevisi L.; Romo M.; Osso E.; Rich M.; Mitnick C.; Seung K.; Franke M.; Mikanda K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract WHO-endorsed shortened, all-oral regimens have improved tolerability and outcomes for MDR/RR-TB treatment, but predictors of poor outcomes remain incompletely-characterized. We conducted a prospective cohort study (NCT05871489) of adults with bacteriologically-confirmed pulmonary MDR/RR-TB treated with a shortened, all-oral regimen in Lesotho. We evaluated baseline microbiologic and radiographic features and their associations with time-to-culture-conversion, end-of-treatment outcomes, and final post-treatment outcomes. Among 238 participants (median age 41 [IQR:31–56], 29% female, 62% with HIV), there were 27 unfavorable outcomes (20 deaths, 3 treatment failures, 4 recurrences). 142 of 148 (95.9%) with positive baseline cultures experienced conversion within four months. Fibrosis, cavitation, bilateral disease, and high smear grade were associated with delayed culture conversion and lower odds of treatment success. Bilateral disease was more strongly associated with unfavorable outcomes in those without HIV; fibrosis and high smear grade showed stronger associations among those with HIV. Cavitation with high smear grade (uOR=0.29, 95%CI:0.11–0.78; aOR=0.39, 95%CI:0.14-1.14), and severe fibrocavitary disease (multi-lobar fibrosis and at least one cavity ≥5 cm) (uOR=0.20, 95%CI:0.07–0.64; aOR=0.26, 95%CI:0.07-0.94) were negatively associated with favorable final outcomes. These findings suggest that baseline sputum and chest radiographic features—particularly in-combination—identify higher-risk patients and may inform risk-adapted strategies for shortened all-oral MDR/RR-TB regimens.

Article.Title: Rationally micropatterned antifogging hydrogels counteracting extreme condensation
Article.Authors: Park H.; Lam C.; Haechler I.; Schutzius T.; Poulikakos D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Loss of transparency due to water vapor condensation is a widespread problem across diverse applications such as windows, eyewear, displays, vehicles, and kitchenware. Conventional antifogging strategies relying on hydrophilic or hydrophobic coatings, based on chemistry and/or nano-topography, can counteract up to mild water deposition, but lose functionality at excessive condensation environments. Here, we present a passive approach, rationally micropatterning an inherently hydrophilic hydrogel to maintain high transparency under supersaturation. Guided by optics and wetting theory, and employing a diffusion model to calculate related timescales of water film formation, we engineer a wicking structure on poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate hydrogel, facilitating long-term sustainable filmwise condensation. Employing quantitative optical clarity measurements and visualization, we show that our approach clearly outperforms state-of-the-art antifogging alternatives, retaining high optical clarity even in boiling environments. Facile fabrication and superior performance establish our microstructured hydrogel as an excellent choice for sustaining transparency under extreme condensation.
Article.TopicFields: Materials Science > Surfaces, Coatings and Films > Surface Modification and Superhydrophobicity; Engineering > Aerospace Engineering > Icing and De-icing Technologies; Engineering > Mechanical Engineering > Heat Transfer and Boiling Studies

Article.Title: Size-dependent catalysis of Ru nanoparticles for selective reductive amination of PET plastic
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Shi Y.; Zhang S.; Wang J.; Meng C.; Niu X.; Diao X.; Ji N.
Article.Abstract: Converting waste polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic into high-value p-xylylenediamine (PXDA) is a revolutionary solution to alleviate energy shortages and plastic pollution. However, current catalytic methods are often limited by poor chemoselectivity due to uncontrolled reductive amination and hydrodeoxygenation capabilities. Herein, we report a precision strategy to regulate the aggregation state of Ru on nitrogen-doped carbon, enabling size-dependent control of reaction pathways in the reductive amination of PET. Ultrasmall Ru nanoclusters (~1.3 nm) favor over-hydrogenation to 1,4-cyclohexanedimethanamine, whereas larger Ru nanoparticles (~4.6 nm) promote excessive hydrodeoxygenation to p-xylene. Notably, Ru/NC-SNPs (~2.4 nm) gives a high PXDA yield of 95.5% with a low apparent activation barrier (30.8 kJ/mol) under mild conditions. Mechanistic studies indicate that Ru/NC-SNPs achieve an optimal balance between hydrogen activation and amidation activity, thereby enabling selective amidation through the controlled dehydrogenation of the amide intermediate. The catalyst also demonstrates broad applicability for post-consumer PET, mixed plastics containing PET and other polyester plastics. Techno-economic analysis and life-cycle assessments further confirm the economic viability and environmental benefits of this process. This work establishes a size-governed selectivity paradigm for Ru-based catalysts and provides a general strategy for steering competing pathways in heterogeneous reductive amination toward sustainable PET valorization. Turning waste plastic into valuable chemicals requires precise control of competing reactions. This study shows that tuning ruthenium particle size enables selective conversion of polyethylene terephthalate into p-xylylenediamine.
Article.TopicFields: Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Nanomaterials for catalytic reactions; Chemistry > Inorganic Chemistry > Asymmetric Hydrogenation and Catalysis; Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Catalysis for Biomass Conversion

Article.Title: Brassinosteroids improve nitrogen utilization by antagonizing BIN2-mediated SnRK1 activation
Article.Authors: Yao L.; Lyu J.; Qiao Y.; Zheng G.; Liu S.; Sun N.; Wang H.; Smagghe W.; Van Leene J.; Fan M.; Han C.; Bai M.
Article.Abstract: Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth and development, and is central to increasing crop yield. Brassinosteroids (BRs) and their analogs are widely used in agriculture to enhance crop yields and improve nitrogen utilization, yet the underlying mechanism remains fragmentary. Here, we demonstrate that BR conservatively improves nitrogen utilization by modulating the activity of SnRK1, an evolutionarily conserved regulator balancing carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Exogenous BR application increases plant biomass and nitrogen utilization, and enhances key nitrogen assimilation enzyme activities when photosynthesis is inhibited. Metabolomic reveals that BR restores 47.8% of metabolic alterations caused by photosynthetic suppression. Mechanistically, BIN2, a key kinase in BR signaling, interacts with and phosphorylates KIN10, the catalytic α-subunit of SnRK1, at conserved Thr175 and Ser179, thereby stabilizing KIN10. BR inhibits BIN2, promoting KIN10 degradation and thereby activating nitrate-responsive gene expression and enhancing nitrogen assimilation. These findings reveal how BR signaling enhances nitrogen utilization and offer insights for improving crop productivity and sustainability. Brassinosteroids are widely used in agriculture, but their modes of action remain incompletely understood. Here, the authors show that brassinosteroids inhibit BIN2, leading to KIN10 degradation and activation of gene expression and nitrogen assimilation enzymes.

Article.Title: Lesions of anterior cingulate cortex disrupt an electrophysiological signature of goal completion in humans
Article.Authors: Oerlemans J.; Alejandro R.; Hemelsoet D.; Genbrugge E.; Bouche K.; Defreyne L.; De Herdt V.; Holroyd C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The reward positivity (RewP) is an event-related brain potential (ERP) component associated with feedback and goal completion. Although the component is said to be generated in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), this inference is disputed because of the inverse problem. Recent intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) current source density analyses provided direct evidence that the RewP is generated in caudal ACC, specifically Brodmann areas 24c’ and 32’. To further test this hypothesis, we examined the effects of damage to frontal cortex damage on RewP amplitude. Scalp EEG was recorded from 68 stroke patients with frontal lesions while they performed a trial-and-error guessing task used to elicit a canonical RewP. Non-parametric voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping revealed that damage to Brodmann areas 24c’ and 32’ significantly attenuated RewP amplitude. These results align with evidence suggesting a single generator of the RewP in the caudal ACC, supporting the role of caudal ACC in motivation of extended behaviors.

Article.Title: Zr-based oxyhalide superionic electrolyte with self-passivating interphase stabilisation for high-voltage and fast-charging all-solid-state lithium batteries
Article.Authors: Li Z.; Mu Y.; Xia Y.; Yang T.; Yan Z.; Li Y.; Guo L.; Zeng L.; Sun X.; Wei M.
Article.Abstract: The pursuit of high-energy-density all-solid-state lithium batteries necessitates integration with next-generation high-voltage positive electrodes. However, a critical challenge lies in the intrinsic instability of most highly ionically conductive solid electrolytes, which decompose at potentials above 4.30 V vs Li+/Li, resulting in severe interfacial degradation and increased impedance. Here, we show that an amorphous Li2Zr0.625Ta0.3Cl4.2O0.9 halide electrolyte, synthesized via a non-equimolar cation-anion amorphous engineering strategy based on Li2ZrCl6, effectively overcomes this limitation. With a high ionic conductivity of 4.11 mS cm−1 at 25 °C, it enables stable high-potential cycling through kinetically stabilized operation mediated by a self-passivating positive electrode–electrolyte interphase. When paired with LiNi0.88Mn0.06Co0.06O2 positive electrode and a Li-In alloy negative electrode, the cells retain up to 81.2% of the initial capacity after 2,000 cycles at 10 C under cell cutoff voltages of 4.18 V (corresponding to 4.80 V vs Li⁺/Li). Overall, non-equimolar cation–anion amorphous engineering enables conductive, high-voltage-tolerant Zr-based halides for all-solid-state lithium batteries. High-voltage solid-state batteries require conductive, stable electrolytes for fast charging. Here, authors show that an amorphous Zr-based oxyhalide electrolyte combines high ionic conductivity with self-passivating interphases, enabling sustained cycling at high voltages.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advanced Battery Materials and Technologies; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advancements in Battery Materials; Materials Science > Materials Chemistry > Thermal Expansion and Ionic Conductivity

Article.Title: Low-Dose Glucocorticoids Adjunctive to Flow Diverter Therapy for Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysms Improve Cerebrovascular Outcomes
Article.Authors: Wen Z.; Chen X.; Tong X.; Huang C.; Huang M.; Lin J.; Xu A.; Yang H.; Zhang X.; Lin Y.; Huang J.; Ge R.; Yuan H.; Peng C.; Liu Y.; Jin F.; Su S.; Zhang X.; Li X.; Guo Z.; Lv M.; Liu A.; Duan C.; Feng X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Flow diverter (FD) implantation is standard for unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIAs), but cerebrovascular complications persist. This nested study within a prospective multicenter cohort evaluates whether short-term, low-dose glucocorticoid use is associated with cerebrovascular outcomes after FD implantation. Propensity-score matching with exact matching on UIA location yielded 1327 patients (360 glucocorticoid-treated; 967 controls). Intravenous glucocorticoids, initiated within 2 hours of the FD procedure and administered for ≥2 days, were associated with fewer in-hospital cerebrovascular events (6.9% vs. 13.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.53) and major cerebrovascular events (4.7% vs. 12.4%; aOR, 0.37). Over a median 2-year follow-up, glucocorticoid use was also associated with fewer new-onset major cerebrovascular events (3.6% vs. 8.7%; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.41) and less in-stent stenosis (7.9% vs. 13.2%; aOR, 0.55). Findings remained robust in unmatched patients on sensitivity analyses. We demonstrate that perioperative glucocorticoid regimens may reduce cerebrovascular events and in-stent stenosis in FD-treated patients, warranting randomized trials.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Neurology > Intracranial Aneurysms: Treatment and Complications; Medicine > Pulmonary and Respiratory Medicine > Cerebrovascular and Carotid Artery Diseases; Medicine > Neurology > Vascular Malformations Diagnosis and Treatment

Article.Title: Accounting for longitudinal peak quality metrics with MSstats+ enhances differential analysis in proteomic experiments with data-independent acquisition
Article.Authors: Kohler D.; Dogu E.; Bhattacharya M.; Karayel O.; Magana M.; Wu A.; Anania V.; Vitek O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mass spectrometry-based proteomics with data-independent acquisition benefits from advanced instrumentation and computational analysis. Despite continued improvements, the quality of quantification may be poor for some measurements. As the scale of proteomic experiments increases, these poor-quality measurements are challenging to characterize by hand, yet they undermine the detection of differentially abundant proteins and the downstream biological conclusions. We introduce MSstats + , a computational workflow that takes as input not only peak intensities reported by tools such as Spectronaut or DIA-NN, but also quality metrics such as peak shape and retention time, and longitudinal run order profiles of these metrics. MSstats+ translates these metrics into a single measure of quality, and downweights poor quality measurements when detecting differentially abundant proteins. The method offers a natural treatment of missing values, weighting the imputed values according to the quality metrics in the run. We demonstrate the accuracy of the resulting differential analysis in five experiments: two custom benchmarking studies with intentionally induced anomalies, a controlled mixture of proteomes, and two large-scale clinical investigations. MSstats+ is implemented in the family of open-source R/Bioconductor packages MSstats.
Article.TopicFields: Chemistry > Spectroscopy > Advanced Proteomics Techniques and Applications; Chemistry > Spectroscopy > Mass Spectrometry Techniques and Applications; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Bioinformatics and Genomic Networks

Article.Title: A CRC–MYB chromatin loop controls auxin-mediated nectary growth in Arabidopsis
Article.Authors: Iimura H.; Takahashi M.; Ohta R.; Nagamori A.; Togawa S.; Furuta Y.; Nakamura K.; Kurniawan F.; Wang X.; Kumaishi K.; Klasfeld S.; Kawakatsu T.; Ichihashi Y.; Suzuki T.; Wagner D.; Ito T.; Yamaguchi N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Floral nectaries, typically located at stamen bases, secrete sugar-rich nectar containing diverse secondary metabolites. Despite their defined position and specialized function, the mechanisms governing nectary formation remain unclear. Using publicly available single-nucleus RNA-seq data and newly generated spatial transcriptomic data, we identify a putative ordering of transcriptional states associated with nectary development and a spatial regulatory network controlling nectary growth in Arabidopsis thaliana . We further show that CRABS CLAW (CRC) is central to this network, integrating transcriptional regulation with spatial auxin transport and pathways controlling phytohormone signaling, sugar transport and terpene biosynthesis. CRC interacts with MYB21, MYB24 and MYB57 to form a complex that binds the 5′ and 3′ regulatory regions of MACCHI-BOU 4 ( MAB4 ), promoting a chromatin loop that enhances MAB4 expression and supports proper nectary size. MAB4 reinforces PIN-FORMED 1-mediated auxin transport to establish auxin maxima at the nectary tip and regulates PIN6 localization to maintain auxin gradients. These findings link transcriptional regulation and auxin transport with nectary organogenesis and metabolic function.
Article.TopicFields: Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Plant Molecular Biology Research; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Plant Gene Expression Analysis; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Plant biochemistry and biosynthesis

Article.Title: APOE ε4 carriership status enhances age-related changes in Alzheimer’s disease plasma biomarkers concentrations
Article.Authors: Rousset R.; den Braber A.; Bongers B.; Boonkamp L.; Wilson D.; Ligthart L.; Pool R.; Visser P.; van der Landen S.; de Geus E.; Teunissen C.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) plasma biomarkers are cost-effective tools to detect early stage amyloid pathology. We investigated how interactions between AD genetic risk (apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4, AD polygenic risk score (excluding APOE; PRSAD)), age, and sex affected AD plasma biomarkers concentrations in a population-based cohort. We included 5913 participants from the Netherlands Twin Register age 30 – 80 (64.1% females, 29.8% ε4 carriers) and measured plasma phosphorylated-tau-217 (p-tau217), amyloid-β−42/40 (Aβ−42/40), neurofilament light (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). We showed that the PRSAD did not associate with biomarker concentrations over age. In ε4 carriers, decreases in Aβ−42/40 became steeper after age 50, and increases in p-tau217 and GFAP became steeper after age 55 and 60 compared to non-carriers, respectively. Analyses in a separate longitudinal cohort (EMIF-AD) confirmed that p-tau217 concentration changes in ε4 carriers reflect AD pathology. These results highlight the potential of plasma biomarkers, especially p-tau217, for early detection of preclinical AD pathology. In cognitively normal individuals, the rate of change in concentrations of plasma ptau217 and Aβ−42/40 over age differs between APOE ε4 carriers and non-carriers. For p-tau217, the effect of APOE ε4 carriership is stronger in males than females.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Psychiatry and Mental health > Dementia and Cognitive Impairment Research; Medicine > Physiology > Alzheimer's disease research and treatments; Neuroscience > Neurology > Neuroinflammation and Neurodegeneration Mechanisms

Article.Title: Unlocking electric vehicle flexibility in microgrids via lightweight on-charger coordination
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Cui X.; Kang C.; Morstyn T.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: The large-scale integration of electric vehicles could provide substantial flexibility for balancing renewable energy in microgrids, yet this potential remains largely constrained by uncoordinated charging. Here, we show that on-board chargers can be transformed into intelligent agents to unlock this flexibility through distributed vehicle-grid coordination. To enable such coordination under practical hardware constraints, we develop a distributed framework that embeds edge intelligence into resource-constrained chargers for autonomous charging optimization. Validated on a high-fidelity hardware-in-the-loop platform capturing microgrid cyber-physical dynamics, experimental results demonstrate that our framework reduces memory consumption by 96.1% and communication overhead by 74.3% compared to the traditional distributed coordination scheme. Moreover, unlocking this hardware-level flexibility achieves a 10.8% profit increase over the current uncoordinated situation. Importantly, the proposed framework promises profound economic, environmental, and social benefits for the future energy landscape from 2025 to 2040. Uncoordinated electric vehicle charging strains microgrids, yet advanced control exceeds charger hardware limits. Here, the authors develop a lightweight on-charger coordination framework that unlocks vehicle flexibility with low memory and communication needs.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Electric Vehicles and Infrastructure; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Smart Grid Energy Management; Engineering > Control and Systems Engineering > Microgrid Control and Optimization

Article.Title: De novo design of lipopeptides with antimicrobial potency enabled by a chain-as-prompt deep learning framework
Article.Authors: Zhang F.; Yu X.; Wu Y.; Li L.
Article.Abstract: Antimicrobial lipopeptides (AMLPs) represent a promising solution to global antibiotic crisis, yet their precision design remains challenging due to the inability of current computational models to account for N-terminal fatty acid modification. Here we develop a deep learning-driven AMLP model for de novo design of AMLPs by integrating a chain-as-prompt mechanism with domain-adaptive transfer learning, effectively bridging the representation gap between peptide sequence and lipid-induced bioactivity. Using the AMLP model, 2657 evolutionarily selected RiPP-derived core peptide sequences from 96,911 bacterial genomes are inspiringly designed for virtual lipidation with seven N-terminal fatty acid chains (C6–C18) followed by predictive screening, generating 6197 candidate sequences. Notably, we find that both high KRH rate ( ≥ 0.3) and common fatty acid tails (C12 and C16) are also critical for further selection of candidate AMLPs, resulting in 289 sequences. Then, 46 are randomly synthesized, with 44 showing antimicrobial activities (a positive rate of 95.7%). The lead antibiotic LP630 exhibits broad-spectrum activities against typical Gram-positive, Gram-negative and mycobacterial strains by targeting multiple bacterial cell membrane components, and demonstrates potent therapeutic efficacy in murine wound infection models. Our study provides a streamlined and universal paradigm for deep learning-enabled high-throughput discovery of novel lipopeptide therapeutics. Authors present their chain-as-prompt deep learning framework, which identifies antimicrobial lipopeptides that show efficacy against drug-resistant bacterial pathogens in laboratory and animal model.
Article.TopicFields: Immunology and Microbiology > Microbiology > Antimicrobial Peptides and Activities; Computer Science > Computational Theory and Mathematics > Computational Drug Discovery Methods; Medicine > Pharmacology > Microbial Natural Products and Biosynthesis

Article.Title: Spatially resolving isomeric trisaccharides on surfaces with Orbitrap-SIMS
Article.Authors: Moloney M.; Paterson R.; Yan B.; Eyres A.; Newell C.; Vorng J.; Pirkl A.; Watts J.; Gilmore I.; Trindade G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Many biologically important molecules are structural isomers that share the same molecular mass yet differ in shape, bonding and function. This creates an ambiguity for mass spectrometry imaging (MSI), where chemically distinct species can be indistinguishable on the mass-to-charge ( m/z) scale and therefore cannot be reliably mapped in heterogeneous materials. Here we demonstrate that Orbitrap secondary ion mass spectrometry (OrbiSIMS) can provide an orthogonal contrast that enables both identification and spatial separation of isomeric molecules directly on surfaces. By exploiting structure-dependent secondary-ion dissociation and gas-phase collisional effects during ion transmission, we discriminate isomeric trisaccharides raffinose, maltotriose and melezitose and spatially resolve raffinose and maltotriose in mixtures. We benchmark these measurements against ion mobility spectrometry and observe consistent trends between OrbiSIMS transmission behaviour and ion mobility separation. These results establish OrbiSIMS as an approach for isomer-resolved MSI at surfaces and interfaces, opening opportunities to map isomeric biomolecules in complex systems where spatial distribution is central to function.
Article.TopicFields: Chemistry > Spectroscopy > Mass Spectrometry Techniques and Applications; Engineering > Computational Mechanics > Ion-surface interactions and analysis; Materials Science > Surfaces, Coatings and Films > Electron and X-Ray Spectroscopy Techniques

Article.Title: Metabolic reprogramming of macrophage-specific transketolase orchestrates angiogenesis in diabetic wounds
Article.Authors: Xiong Y.; Lu L.; Wu Q.; Wang H.; Hu H.; Zhao H.; Santos H.; Shahbazi M.; Mi B.
Article.Abstract: Diabetic wound healing is profoundly impaired by macrophage metabolic dysfunction, which compromises angiogenesis. Here, we show a macrophage transketolase (TKT) as a crucial metabolic checkpoint governing vascular regeneration in diabetes. We demonstrate that loss of TKT in macrophages accelerates amino acid and fatty acid catabolism, elevates reactive oxygen species, and disrupts endothelial cell proliferation and differentiation. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia activates the AGEs-RAGE signaling cascade through suppressing TKT expression, establishing a pathological TKT-AGEs-RAGE axis that reprograms macrophage metabolism toward dysfunction. Then, we engineer a nanozyme-integrated hydrogel patch that selectively increases TKT level in macrophages, which rebalances macrophage metabolism, reduces oxidative stress, and rescues angiogenic capacity. In a diabetic pig model, localized delivery of the nano-system markedly accelerates wound closure and vascular repair. These findings not only elucidate a macrophage-specific TKT metabolic reprogramming mechanism for enhancing angiogenesis, but also offer a potential therapeutic strategy for the clinical management of diabetic wounds. Diabetes impairs wound healing by disrupting macrophage metabolism and angiogenesis. Here, authors identify macrophage-specific transketolase (TKT) as a metabolic checkpoint and develop a nanozyme hydrogel that restores macrophage TKT to promote vascular repair in diabetic wounds.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Rehabilitation > Wound Healing and Treatments; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Clinical Biochemistry > Advanced Glycation End Products research; Medicine > Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism > Diabetic Foot Ulcer Assessment and Management

Article.Title: Optical-handedness-driven enantioselective synthesis and programmable chirality encoding of covalent organic frameworks
Article.Authors: Kim T.; Kim J.; Oh J.; Kang S.; Kim S.; Kim J.; Han M.; Kim Y.; Pak C.; Park J.; Lim H.
Article.Abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) typically require chiral precursors or catalysts to achieve asymmetry. Here, we report the enantioselective synthesis of chemically chiral COFs using circularly polarized light (CP-λ) as the sole chiral director. By exploiting the reversibility of imine condensation, a dynamic self-correction process amplifies the photonic chiral bias into long-range crystalline order without any chiral auxiliaries. Unlike conventional strategies that rely on localized chiral centers, our approach induces chirality directly within the emissive framework backbone. This structural integration results in a luminescence dissymmetry factor of 0.24, representing a substantial value for purely organic systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate spatially programmable encoding with sub-micrometer resolution, enabling the transcription of complex enantiomeric patterns into the frameworks. This methodology establishes a reagent-free platform for the manufacturing of chiral crystalline materials and advances the development of programmable photonic devices. Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) typically require chiral precursors or catalysts to achieve asymmetry. Here, the authors report the enantioselective synthesis of chemically chiral COFs using circularly polarized light as the sole chiral director.

Article.Title: Molecular chaperone-like TIGR04500 family proteins guide graspetide biosynthesis
Article.Authors: Hu L.; Huang W.; Huang J.; Zhang J.; Qiu X.; Cheng B.; Pan L.; Liu W.
Article.Abstract: TIGR04500 family proteins share architectural features with the prokaryotic chaperones trigger factor and SurA, but their functions have remained unknown. Here, we demonstrate that TIGR04500 proteins act as dedicated, non-catalytic tri-domain partners in the biosynthesis of graspetides, a family of ribosomally synthesized and posttranslationally modified peptides (RiPPs) that possess ester/amide linkages formed between residue side-chains. The partner action of TIGR04500 proteins largely depends on their distinct N-terminal domains, which can interact with family-defining ATP-grasp enzymes to form a catalytic complex. The remaining central multi-helix and C-terminal domains share structural similarities with trigger factor and SurA, and thus enable TIGR04500 family proteins to function in a manner similar to these molecular chaperones for peptide substrate recognition. Genome mining reveals a number of conserved multi helix-containing proteins/domains that could be involved in the biosynthesis of many families of RiPPs using a similar molecular mechanism, suggesting a common, chaperone-like function in RiPP biosynthesis. Graspetides are ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides. Here, TIGR04500 family proteins are shown to guide graspetide biosynthesis as non-catalytic chaperone-like partners through a likely widespread recognition mechanism.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Pharmacology > Microbial Natural Products and Biosynthesis; Immunology and Microbiology > Microbiology > Antimicrobial Peptides and Activities; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Chemical Synthesis and Analysis

Article.Title: Multimodal substrate recruitment enables CTLHMKLN1 E3 ligase to target acetylated N-, C-, and internal degrons
Article.Authors: Sepic S.; Gottemukkala K.; Du J.; Maiwald S.; Chrustowicz J.; Papadopoulou E.; Stier L.; von Gronau S.; Schulman B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The GID/CTLH family of E3 ubiquitin ligases employs several substrate receptor subunits that recruit distinct degrons, but the substrate recognition mechanisms of the CTLH MKLN1 assembly have largely remained elusive. Here, we reconstitute CTLH MKLN1 -dependent ubiquitylation of three biochemically distinct substrates – MKLN1 itself, ZMYND19, and FAM72A-recruited UNG2, and determine cryo-EM structures of each substrate bound to MKLN1. The structures reveal how MKLN1’s discoidin and Kelch β-propeller domains engage substrates through multivalent contacts. MKLN1 recruits itself through discoidin-Kelch interactions between MKLN1 dimers, forming an assembly that competes with other substrates. ZMYND19 and FAM72A each bind to MKLN1 through loops engaging the discoidin trench domain while their C-terminal Arg residues engage the MKLN1 Kelch central channel, identifying MKLN1 as an Arg/C-degron receptor. The acetylated N-terminus of UNG2 is positioned within a Y-shaped tunnel of FAM72A, defining an adaptor-mediated Ac/N-degron recognition mechanism. Thus, our data reveal how combinatorial deployment of MKLN1 discoidin and Kelch domains enable a single receptor subunit to recognize a diverse substrate repertoire, adding to a complex picture of degron recognition across the GID/CTLH family.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Ubiquitin and proteasome pathways; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Protein Degradation and Inhibitors; Materials Science > Materials Chemistry > Enzyme Structure and Function

Article.Title: Developing and benchmarking one health genomic surveillance tools for influenza A virus in wastewater
Article.Authors: Jiang M.; Wang A.; Thissen J.; Nelson K.; Pipes L.; Kantor R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Influenza A viruses (IAV) remain a persistent One Health threat, and whole-genome sequencing from wastewater offers a promising surveillance tool. However, IAV is at low abundance in wastewater, making it difficult to sequence. We benchmark four targeted enrichment methods suited for multi-subtype whole-genome IAV sequencing including custom and off-the-shelf methods. Our custom HA tiled-amplicon panel is sensitive, fast, and cost-effective, making it suitable for monitoring low-abundance seasonal variants of known subtypes, although its reliance on conserved and intact primer-binding sites limits primer design to fewer subtypes. A published universal amplicon method targets all IAV subtypes but performs poorly in wastewater due to its reliance on intact genome segments. Meanwhile, probe-capture methods are resilient to RNA degradation. In real wastewater samples, our custom probe panel recovers whole-genome signals from circulating H1N1, H3N2, H5N1, including validated H5N1 2.3.4.4b reads in samples where dPCR detection is limited. However, probe-capture is generally more costly and labor-intensive than amplicon methods. Across all four sequencing methods, two wastewater matrices, and most spike-in and endogenous virus targets, ultrafiltration-based virus concentration consistently outperforms large-volume direct extraction. Together, these benchmarking comparisons and custom panels provide needed information for implementing IAV genomic sequencing in routine wastewater surveillance.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Epidemiology > Influenza Virus Research Studies; Medicine > Infectious Diseases > SARS-CoV-2 detection and testing; Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Zoonotic diseases and public health

Article.Title: Realisation of a protected cat-qutrit manifold via engineered quantum tunnelling
Article.Authors: Kwon S.; Hoshi D.; Nagase T.; Sugiyama D.; Mukai H.; Takemura K.; Kojima R.; Zhou Y.; Watabe S.; Yoshihara F.; Tsai J.
Article.Abstract: Engineering quantum tunnelling in phase space has emerged as a viable method for creating a protected logical qubit manifold with biased-noise properties. A promising approach is to combine a Kerr nonlinearity with a multi-photon drive, resulting in a system known as a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO). In this work, we implement a three-photon KPO and explore its potential as a protected bosonic qutrit. We confirm quantum coherence by demonstrating three-photon Rabi oscillations and performing direct Wigner function measurements that reveal the formation of three-component cat-like states. Crucially, we observe a breathing-like dynamic in phase space, a characteristic feature of driven quantum systems. This dynamic arises from macroscopic temporal interference between the cat-qutrit manifold and the excited states. The frequency of resulting oscillations in the mean photon number provides a direct, time-domain measurement of the energy gap separating the qutrit from the excited states, thereby establishing an experimental hallmark of qutrit manifold protection. Furthermore, we identify a parasitic higher-order pump term as the primary mechanism constraining the mean photon number, highlighting its mitigation as a requisite for maximising protection. Our findings elucidate the basic quantum properties of the three-photon KPO and establish the first step towards its use as an alternative qutrit platform.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: Kerr nonlinearity

Article.Title: Nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate hybrid electrolyte for high-voltage lithium batteries via preemptive passivation
Article.Authors: Kim H.; Kim J.; Yang Y.; Song X.; Koo D.; Xu K.; Sun Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Achieving high energy density without compromising safety remains a significant challenge for advanced batteries. Nonflammable electrolytes can mitigate fire risk, but poor bulk and interfacial properties of such electrolytes limit their application. Here, a nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate electrolyte was developed, achieving a self-extinguishing time of ~0 s and stable cycling in both lithium metal and lithium-ion batteries under high-voltage conditions. The electrolyte comprising lithium hexafluorophosphate dissolved in dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride, fluoroethylene carbonate, and ethyl methyl carbonate at low concentration establishes a weakly solvating environment, wherein dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride and fluoroethylene carbonate preferentially contribute to stabilize the positive and negative electrodes, while working together to enhance the rate capability, low-temperature performance, and long-term cycling at high-voltage. Accelerating rate calorimetry revealed a delayed thermal runaway onset by 87 °C, correlating with Broadness Index. These findings suggest that preemptive passivation on both electrodes, when coupled with nonflammable electrolyte design, can provide a viable route toward safe, high-energy lithium batteries.

Article.Title: Confining chlorine in the cation solvation sheaths towards stable and sustainable seawater electrolysis
Article.Authors: Yu P.; Wang Y.; Zhang X.; Sun S.; Fang T.; Tao X.; Yang Y.; Liao J.; Li Y.; Niu Z.; Sun M.; Fan M.; Liu S.; Gao F.; Gao M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chlorine electro-oxidation represents the primary anode side reaction during direct seawater electrolysis, causing corrosion and permanent deactivation of catalyst and thereby insufficient stability. We report that in situ segregated fluorine can actuate the desolvation of cations and Cl − ions via strong H ∙ ∙ ∙ F bonding, leading to the formation of intimate cation-Cl − contact ion pairs that make Cl − migration toward electrode surface prohibited. Meanwhile, fluorine remaining in the cobalt-based catalyst shortens the Co–Co distance, attributable to its large electronegativity, triggering an oxide path mechanism that circumvents the nonideal scaling between OH * and OOH * during oxygen-evolving reaction. Direct seawater electrolysis (with 1 M NaOH) incorporating this catalyst achieves 1 ampere per square centimeter (A cm −2 ) at 1.7 volts and maintains at 0.5 A cm −2 and 60 °C over 2,450 hours degrading at 24.9 microvolts per hour. Our catalyst even survives repeatedly switched current densities (0.25, 0.5, and 1 A cm −2 ) for more than 1,250 hours, manifesting compatibility with fluctuating renewable electricity.

Article.Title: Coordinated control of both microtubule ends regulates mitotic spindle length
Article.Authors: Fiorenza S.; Cheeran S.; Doria E.; Tolić I.; Meraldi P.; Pavin N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The mitotic spindle is a biomechanical structure whose length must be precisely controlled to ensure faithful chromosome segregation. The treadmilling of microtubules towards spindle poles, termed poleward flux, is involved in spindle length control. However, poleward flux velocity has been shown to be both inversely and directly proportional to spindle length, a contradiction that remains unexplained by current mechanisms. Here we introduce a model which demonstrates that length-dependent regulation at both microtubule ends allows plus- and minus-end dynamics to synchronize with one another, enabling pathways of poleward-flux-based spindle length control which rectify previous results. Moreover, our model predicts that spindle length and poleward flux velocity can vary independently via simultaneous perturbations at both microtubule ends, which we validate with protein depletion experiments in human cells. Finally, we provide experimental evidence for length-dependent accumulation of proteins at microtubule minus-ends. Our results thus resolve a longstanding paradox and provide mechanistic insight into the reciprocal control of spindle length and poleward flux.

Article.Title: Precision RNAi for fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva in mice using a combinatorial unimolecular allele selective approach
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Gross K.; Cooper D.; Chaugule S.; Kim M.; Dahlke C.; Mayer E.; Kercher E.; Kim J.; Ormsby T.; Yamada N.; Caiazzi J.; Jackson S.; Rachid M.; Aronson B.; Echiverria D.; Fakih H.; Yamada K.; Lee F.; Khvorova A.; Alterman J.; Shim J.
Article.Abstract: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is a rare genetic disorder caused primarily by the ACVR1R206H mutation, resulting in debilitating heterotopic ossification triggered by inflammatory flare-ups. Here, we report a disease-modifying, allele-selective small interfering RNA targeting ACVR1R206H while preserving wildtype ACVR1 function. Docosanoic acid-conjugated ACVR1 small interfering RNA, alone or combined with one targeting the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1β, reduced heterotopic ossification in a murine model using both post-trauma and preventative strategies. Combination therapy was more effective than either pathway alone. We further developed lipophilic divalent molecules targeting both pathways in a single compound. These showed comparable muscle accumulation and efficacy to the combined monovalent forms following local and systemic administration, while enabling equimolar dosing and simplified manufacturing. Treatment suppressed inflammatory, WNT, Notch, Hedgehog, and transforming growth factor β signaling in fibroadipogenic progenitors, reducing cartilage, bone, and connective tissue formation. This work establishes a platform for disease-modifying therapies in this and other musculoskeletal disorders. Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva progressively transforms muscle and connective tissues into bone. Here, researchers developed a targeted siRNA therapy that blocks the mutant receptor and inflammation, greatly reducing abnormal bone formation in mice.
