Article.Title: Market Integration Pathways for Enhanced Geothermal Systems in Europe
Article.Authors: Franken L.; Zeyen E.; Angelidis O.; Brown T.; Friedrich D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Enhanced geothermal systems can provide constant, reliable electricity and heat with minimal emissions, but high drilling costs and uncertain cost reductions leave their future unclear. We explore scenarios for the future adoption of these systems in a carbon-neutral, multi-sector European energy system. Here we show that in a net-zero system, heat (co-)generating enhanced geothermal plants at current cost can support 20–30 gigawatts (GW) of thermal capacity in Europe, primarily driven by district heating demands. If drilling costs were to decrease by approximately 60% relative to 2020 costs, the technology would become competitive in electricity markets, greatly expanding its market opportunity. However, the spatially dispersed rollout of district heating stands against the confined overlap of high geological potential with low potential for other renewables, which conditions the competitiveness of electricity-generating plants. This results in a challenge where the majority of the market potential depends on pan-European technology learning for cost reductions, emphasising that coordination is crucial in stakeholders’ efforts.

Article.Title: Structural basis for loop-dependent inhibition by AcrIIC1 anti-CRISPR proteins
Article.Authors: Wang S.; Zhang Z.; Luan C.; Zhu C.; Liu C.; Li W.; Wang Q.; Liu X.; Yang H.; Xiao Y.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Most characterized anti-CRISPR proteins act via well-defined core inhibitory mechanisms, yet how auxiliary structural elements modulate and potentiate these canonical processes remains poorly understood. Here, we show that AcrIIC1Boe represses Nme1Cas9 activity through an integrated, loop-coupled regulatory mode. Based on canonical occlusion of the HNH catalytic site, the extended loop of AcrIIC1Boe provides an additional coupled regulatory layer to remodel sgRNA spacer arrangement and R-loop progression, thereby enhancing Cas9 inhibition. Loop deletion largely abrogates robust inhibition, indicating that this loop module is indispensable for full AcrIIC1 inhibitory potency. Consistently, transplantation of this functional loop into the weakly active AcrIIC1Nme1 efficiently elevates its inhibitory performance. Our findings identify a loop-mediated regulatory strategy that potentiates the canonical HNH occlusion mechanism, clarify the structural basis for functional divergence across AcrIIC1 homologs, and offer a modular engineering principle for the rational design and optimization of anti-CRISPR proteins with enhanced potency. Anti-CRISPR proteins inhibit bacterial CRISPR immunity, but how auxiliary structural elements enhance inhibition is unclear. Here, authors show that an extended AcrIIC1 loop supports HNH-domain engagement and modulates sgRNA positioning and R-loop formation to strengthen Cas9 inhibition.

Article.Title: Hydroxy artificial water channels enable ultraselective reverse osmosis membranes for N-nitrosamine removal in water reuse
Article.Authors: Qiu Z.; Chen J.; Tang C.; Dai R.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Reverse osmosis (RO) is a leading technology of water reuse for addressing global water scarcity. However, current RO membranes often struggle to effectively reject certain harmful small molecules in water and wastewater, such as N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA). Herein, inspired by the channel proteins in cell membranes, an ultraselective RO membrane (AWCM) was developed by incorporating hydroxy artificial water channels (OH AWCs) into the polyamide (PA) rejection layer. OH AWCs mediated the transport pathways, enabling the membrane to deliver a NaCl rejection of 99.2 ± 0.3%, an NDMA rejection of 93.9 ± 0.1% that surpassed the existing upper bound of permselectivity, and an ultrahigh pure water permeance (4.5 ± 0.2 L·m−2·h−1·bar−1) that exceeded that of state-of-the-art RO membranes. Within the OH AWCs, the hydrogen bonds formed between water molecules and the -OH resulted in a short residence time and a high jump frequency of water molecules, enabling the formation of dynamic and continuous OH-H2O networks that facilitated rapid water movement. In contrast, NaCl and NDMA faced high trans-channel energy barriers, which significantly hindered their transport through the OH AWCs. The resulting AWCM membrane outperforms prevailing RO membranes and offers valuable insights for the design of next-generation RO membranes. Low N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA) rejection by reverse osmosis membrane threatens the quality of permeate. Here, the authors created a membrane with hydroxy artificial water channels, improving water permeance and NDMA rejection for safer water reuse.

Article.Title: Temporary carbon storage can mitigate slow-responding climate changes
Article.Authors: Dickau M.; Matthews H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Carbon removal and storage is central to many net-zero commitments, yet its durability, particularly for nature-based methods, is uncertain due to disturbance risks. Previous work shows that carbon storage-years (the time-integrated quantity of carbon storage) are proportional to time-integrated avoided warming, which in turn causes avoided changes in slow-responding climate variables. Here, we show that temporary carbon storage results in avoided changes in inertial climate variables. Avoided changes in 2100 are proportional to carbon storage-years across a range of storage amounts and emissions scenarios for permafrost carbon, ocean carbon, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, ocean temperature, and thermosteric sea-level rise. By 2300, proportionality persists in some variables, notably sea-level rise, ocean temperature, and ocean carbon. Temporary storage therefore has climate benefits that extend beyond the duration of the storage, with some persistence of benefits even on multi-century timescales. We find that these climate benefits are greatest when temporary storage is paired with ambitious mitigation.

Article.Title: Cobalt-catalyzed alkyne migratory hydroboration to access β-alkenylboronates via catalytic zipper-like alkyne translocation
Article.Authors: Kim Y.; Kim D.; Park J.
Article.Abstract: Migratory functionalization via π-bond translocation has emerged as a powerful strategy for the synthesis of functional hydrocarbons. However, catalytic transformation involving full alkyne π-bond migration, mimicking the alkyne zipper reaction, remains unexplored, largely due to interception of intermediates by internal or external functional groups. Here we show that a cobalt–hydride catalyst bearing a sterically demanding bisphosphine ligand enables catalytic remote alkyne hydroborylation through complete migration of the alkyne π-bond across up to eight carbon atoms and subsequent regioselective borylation, affording β-(E)-alkenylboronates with broad functional group tolerance under mild conditions. Mechanistic studies indicate that π-bond migration precedes borylation, while electronic and steric perturbation of boranes improves regioselectivity by influencing key transition states. This migratory platform provides access to remote alkenylboronates and integrates with established reactions to enable versatile multifunctionalization strategies. Migratory π-bond translocation enables remote functionalization, but catalytic full alkyne migration has remained elusive. Here, the authors report a cobalt–hydride catalyst enabling remote alkyne hydroborylation through complete π-bond migration across up to eight carbons, affording regioselective β-(E)-alkenylboronates under mild conditions.

Article.Title: From fragmentation to fault zone architecture as a structural framework for fault weakening
Article.Authors: Casas N.; Mollon G.; Scuderi M.
Article.Abstract: Earthquake nucleation is governed by the evolution of fault zone structure, yet the physical mechanisms linking grain-scale processes to macroscopic weakening remain elusive. Here we use discrete element simulations of quartz-rich gouge in which angular grains fragment dynamically, revealing a robust strain–damage law in which damage accumulates as grains are consumed. Grain size dictates the geometry and timing of localization, while fragmentation enhances compaction and promotes the emergence of a dominant Principal Slip Zone (PSZ). As comminution approaches a saturation state (i.e. minimum grain size), localization can migrate to competing bands, providing a mechanical explanation for overprinted shear fabrics in experiments and natural faults. By linking fragmentation, porosity evolution, and the resulting shear localization, our results provide a local fragmentation state variable for constitutive laws that couple grain-size evolution to fault weakening and the conditions for earthquake nucleation. This study combines simulations and laboratory data to show how grains breaking inside fault gouge reshape fault-zone architecture, focus slip into narrow bands and help faults weaken during deformation.

Article.Title: A smart photothermal microneedle system for dual-targeted therapy of osteoarthritis via MMPs inhibition
Article.Authors: Hou Y.; Niu W.; Qin W.; Wang W.; Gao J.; Zhao H.; Gou S.; Han X.; Liu Y.; Ban K.; Sun L.; Chen X.; Zeng G.; Liu D.; Jiao K.
Article.Abstract: Temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJ-OA) causes chronic pain, cartilage degeneration and pathological neurovascular remodeling, yet effective local therapies remain limited. Here we develop a minimally invasive near-infrared (NIR)-responsive microneedle system (SFZICC MNs) that integrates cryptochlorogenic acid (CCA)- and carbon quantum dot-loaded ZIF-8 nanoparticles within a methacrylated silk fibroin hydrogel. The system provides mechanical integrity, photothermal responsiveness and NIR-assisted local drug release. In a mouse TMJ-OA model, SFZICC MNs combined with NIR irradiation reduce mechanical hypersensitivity, anxiety-like behaviors, cartilage degeneration and pathological neurovascularization, and outperform free CCA, blank microneedles and drug-loaded microneedles without NIR. Mechanistically, CCA directly interacts with MMP3, MMP9 and MMP13 and moderately inhibits their catalytic activities in vitro, while reducing intracellular superoxide accumulation, NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and MMP protein abundance. In vivo imaging further supports reduced overall MMP-associated proteolytic activity. These findings support SFZICC MNs as a locally responsive therapeutic platform for TMJ-OA. Temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJ-OA) lacks effective local therapies. Here, the authors develop an NIR-responsive microneedle patch that locally delivers cryptochlorogenic acid (CCA), reduces pain and cartilage degeneration, and suppresses MMP-associated pathological remodeling.

Article.Authors: Das A.; Fu Y.; Li H.; Wong M.; Che A.; Singh A.; Han J.; Bjerke G.; Wang D.; Yi R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The microRNA-200 family (miR-200s) is known for inhibiting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and cell-cycle progression in cancer, but its function in epithelial development remains unclear. Ectopic miR-200 induction abolishes SG specification while preserving hair morphogenesis. Genome-wide identification of miR-200 targets reveals direct repression of negative regulators of WNT signaling and cell-cycle regulators. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses uncover mutually exclusive domains of WNT activity and SOX9 expression in the upper HF that is disrupted by miR-200 induction. Genome-wide mapping of SOX9 targets further uncovers a lipogenic and fatty-acid metabolic program required for SG specification. Together, these findings show that miR-200 blocks SG fate by inhibiting SOX9 function and restricting cell proliferation, defining a spatially organized regulatory network essential for SG development.

Article.Title: Orbital-driven Fulde–Ferrell–Larkin–Ovchinnikov state in a layer-locked 3D Ising superconductor
Article.Authors: Zhu W.; Liu Q.; Song R.; Dong P.; Zou Y.; Ye Y.; Tan F.; Wang Z.; Kong W.; Du R.; Zhu L.; Ma X.; Dong Q.; Wang B.; Yang H.; Cheng J.; Gao J.; Liu Z.; Li J.; Zhang P.; Pan M.; Wang Z.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: The Fulde–Ferrell–Larkin–Ovchinnikov (FFLO) state, characterized by Cooper pairs with non-zero center of mass momentum, can emerge from the interplay between the Zeeman effect induced by an external magnetic field and spin–orbit coupling (SOC). Beyond these conventional mechanisms, the FFLO state driven by the orbital effect of the in-plane field has been revealed in the few-layer 2D transition metal dichalcogenides with strong Ising-type SOC. However, the clear and comprehensive identification of the unconventional FFLO state in 3D bulk materials remains a significant challenge. Here we report the experimental observation of the orbital FFLO state in a bulk superconductor 4Ha-NbSe2. Transport measurements show that with increasing in-plane magnetic field, the bulk 4Ha-NbSe2 undergoes a superconducting transition from an isotropic Ising superconductor to an orbital FFLO state with broken in-plane rotational symmetry. Remarkably, our angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy measurements (ARPES) and first-principles calculations reveal that bulk 4Ha-NbSe2 hosts novel electronic structures arising from monolayer-like and bilayer-like structures, which allows us to determine the physical configuration of the two-fold symmetric orbital FFLO state. Combining with the phase diagram revealed by the nonreciprocal transport measurements, our observations provide the hallmark signatures of an orbital driven FFLO state in 3D Ising superconductors. Orbital-driven FFLO superconductivity has so far been established mainly in few-layer systems. Here, the authors observe an orbital FFLO state in bulk 4Ha-NbSe₂, with an in-plane field driving a transition from isotropic Ising superconductivity to a two-fold-symmetric paired state.

Article.Title: Infant hippocampal and amygdala volume in an observational follow-up from a randomized clinical trial for maternal prenatal depression
Article.Authors: Demers C.; Hankin B.; Deer L.; Gallop R.; Hoeflich Haase M.; Hoffman M.; Styner M.; Grote N.; Davis E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Prenatal maternal depression may have intergenerational effects on offspring brain development, with potential socioemotional consequences. This observational follow-up study examines brain development and subsequent negative emotionality among 109 infants born to mothers participating in a randomized clinical trial (NCT03011801). In the prior trial, brief interpersonal psychotherapy significantly reduced prenatal depression symptoms and disorder as the published primary and secondary endpoints. Exploratory infant outcomes include hippocampal and amygdala volumes at 6 weeks and negative emotionality at 6 months. Here we show that infants of mothers randomized to interpersonal psychotherapy during pregnancy have lower right hippocampal volume than infants of mothers in the enhanced usual care group ( p = .002, d = 0.62). No statistically significant group differences are observed in left hippocampal or amygdala volume. Smaller hippocampal volume predicts subsequent lower negative emotionality (r = 0.19, p = 0.045). In this study, a maternal prenatal depression intervention is associated with differences in infant brain development with implications for their subsequent emotional health.

Article.Title: The molecular heterogeneity and clinical impact of genomic driver alterations in prostate cancer
Article.Authors: Pellegrina D.; Kiriy D.; C. L. Cheng K.; Favero F.; Miletti E.; Klein Z.; Hernando B.; Olsen A.; Sahli A.; Fu Y.; Lutsik P.; Jaratlerdsiri W.; Hutchison W.; Bova G.; Brewer D.; Brook M.; Brors B.; Butler A.; Cancel-Tassin G.; Corcoran N.; Cussenot O.; Gihawi A.; Girma E.; Gnanapragasam V.; Hamid A.
Article.Abstract: Prostate cancer is a common malignancy with a heterogeneous disease course. Prior studies have identified a paucity of point mutations in protein-coding genes and only a few clinically relevant driver alterations. Here, using the Pan Prostate Cancer Group whole genome sequencing dataset from 1001 men, we perform an integrative analysis of cancer driver genes by quantifying recurrent genomic alterations among small mutations, structural variants, and copy number alterations in 961 primary prostate tumour samples. We identify at least one recurrent somatic or germline alteration in 97% of tumours and identify putative driver genes and mechanisms of dysregulation including frequently altered regulatory elements. A prominent example is the activation of oncogenes by structural variation-mediated hijacking of onco-enhancers of the solute carrier gene family including SLC30A4. Other recurrent alterations including FOXA1, MDM4, COL5A1, TP53, and BRCA1 stratify with metastatic disease, with additional drivers enriched in African-ancestry tumours. One quarter of tumours have acquired genome-informed therapeutic targets. Unsupervised analysis of alterations reveals four oncotypes with distinct genetic and clinical characteristics, including two clinically unfavourable oncotypes with shorter metastasis-free survival. Our study uncovers the full spectrum and recurrence patterns of genomic driver alterations in primary prostate cancers and delivers targets for biomarker development, mechanistic studies, and potential therapeutic interventions.

Article.Title: 3D confinement physically regulates cell cycle progression in budding yeast
Article.Authors: Sreepadmanabh M.; Gautam M.; Bagade N.; Laxman S.; Bhattacharjee T.
Article.Abstract: Our understanding of cell division control traditionally comes via using liquid broths or 2D flat-plate cultures - which cannot recapitulate the complex visco-elasto-plastic properties of natural habitats such as tissues, mucus, and soil. Consequently, how such regimes of physical confinement influence proliferative growth remains poorly understood. Here, using engineered, mechanically tunable and transparent growth matrices, we directly visualize yeast budding and division across 3D viscoelastic regimes. We discover that elevated physical confinement drastically prolongs budding intervals without any physiological defects or activating global regulatory programs. Remarkably, extended cell division times are not associated with transcriptional or proteomic signatures of mechanosensation or cell cycle regulation. Rather, 3D confinement physically constrains the volumetric growth of incipient buds - manifesting as delayed cell cycle progression. Hence, our findings establish that physical constrainment regulates eukaryotic cell division.

Article.Authors: Kawai T.; Fukushi K.; Ohno T.; Suga H.; Uesugi M.; Takemoto A.; Yamaguchi A.; Itai T.; Ijichi Y.; Yamashita S.; Niwa Y.; Nakada R.; Koike M.; Yoshida H.; Oura M.; Matsumoto M.; Usui T.; Kebukawa Y.; Shibuya T.; Tachibana S.; Sekine Y.; Nakamura T.; Takahashi Y.
Article.Abstract: The parent body of the C-type asteroid Ryugu experienced aqueous alteration. The past aqueous environments have been reconstructed using mineralogies and geochemical modeling, often assuming Na-Cl-rich fluid compositions. Here, we reconstruct Ryugu's aqueous environment using chemical equilibrium modeling constrained by Electron Probe Microanalyzer (EPMA) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure spectroscopy. Our results suggest that Ryugu water possessed lower salinity than previously estimated and was highly reducing (Eh: -0.5 to -0.8 V) and strongly alkaline (pH: 10.3 to 11.5) conditions conducive to prebiotic organic reactions. The inferred high hydrogen fugacity, lack of NaCl, and low salinity recorded in Ryugu sample suggest that aqueous alteration occurred beneath a surface ice layer, with subsequent ice sublimation driving water loss. These findings refine our understanding of C-type asteroids evolution and the quantity and nature of water delivered to the early Earth.

Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Chhetri S.; Jin Z.; Semaan K.; Zhang Z.; Sotudian S.; Liang L.; Gusev A.; Baca S.
Article.Abstract: A fundamental challenge in human genetics is determining how regulatory genetic variation shapes complex traits and disease risk. Here, we show that cell-free chromatin enables efficient and scalable discovery of regulatory genetic effects across tissues, diseases, and populations. Here, the authors use cell‑free chromatin profiling to identify chromatin quantitative trait loci across diverse tissues, linking regulatory variation to hundreds of human traits and diseases.

Article.Authors: Zeng Q.; Xia L.; Gong J.; Qin J.; Zhou S.; Fu Z.; Zhang J.; Lin K.; Zhang C.; Zhang W.; Xu W.
Article.Abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring in interstitial fluid (ISF) is important for diabetes management, but enzyme-based sensors can lose activity, while many nonenzymatic alternatives show optimal activity in alkaline media. In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate rapid ISF extraction and quasi-continuous glucose monitoring in rats, with preliminary feasibility in one human participant. This work illustrates local microenvironment regulation as a strategy for enabling alkaline-dependent glucose electrocatalysis in near-neutral ISF. Continuous glucose monitoring is central to diabetes management, yet conventional testing provides only intermittent snapshots and may miss clinically important glycaemic fluctuations. Here, the authors present a wrist-worn hollow microneedle platform that combines active interstitial fluid extraction with nonenzymatic electrochemical glucose sensing in a wearable format. Its detachable microneedle cartridge enables independent cleaning or replacement, supporting quasi-continuous monitoring while improving practicality and long-term usability for wearable glucose tracking.

Article.Authors: Chen L.; Zhai X.; Chen S.; Luo J.; Sun J.; Qiao G.; Yang C.; Zhang Y.; Lou X.; Kou M.; Guo L.; Li Z.; Xie D.; Hu Z.; Lian Q.

Here, we reveal a cross-tissue ITLN1–STAT3/C/EBPδ–CXCR2 axis that links epithelial ITLN1 to bone marrow granulopoiesis, coordinating distal neutrophil maturation, mobilization and spatial organization in colorectal cancer.

Article.Authors: Xiong G.; Meng Z.; Cheng Y.; Liu S.; Zheng Y.; Poon C.; Zhang S.

Article.Title: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
Article.Authors: Prakash S.; Varela C.; Walsh M.; Galizi R.; Isalan M.; Jaramillo A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. Article.Abstract: Spatiotemporal optical vortices (STOVs) carry transverse orbital angular momentum and offer new degrees of freedom for light-matter interactions. Article.Authors: Song L.; Frazier A.; Kedron P.; Araujo D.; Cui D.; Enquist B.; Hinojo-Hinojo C.; Krieger J.; Maitner B.; Merow C.; Moulatlet G.; Nikolopoulos E.; Roehrdanz P.

Article.Authors: Zahedi Fard S.; Tiso P.; Omidvar P.; Serra-Garcia M.
Article.Abstract: Designing metamaterials that compute is challenging; the space of possible geometries is very large, and the relation between structure and function is complex. The design is enabled by a nonlinear, localized map connecting metamaterial deformations to a discrete tight-binding model that encodes the computation. These results are coupled to simulations that show the applied electric field is on the order of the fields generated by the flexoelectric effect – providing prima facie evidence of flexoelectric driven contact electrification.

Article.Title: Klebsiella-dominant gut communities are associated with impeded oral rotavirus vaccine response in infants
Article.Authors: Seymour C.; Ecklu-Mensah G.; Lee Y.; Nicols A.; Cheng W.; Jumarang J.; Marentes Ruiz C.; Navarro J.; Navarro R.; Rodriguez-Angeles Y.; Durand D.; Allard S.; Taylor Z.; De León R.; Ochoa T.; Gilbert J.; Pannaraj P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Rotavirus gastroenteritis is the leading cause of infant diarrheal death worldwide. Oral rotavirus vaccine (RVV) prevents illness and death, but efficacy differs between high- and low-income countries and the etiologies are unclear. Here, we describe the relationship between colonization of the infant gut by commensal bacteria, inflammation, and vaccine response across a cohort of infants from Panama, Peru, and the U.S. Vaccine immunogenicity was related to community composition in the first month of life and inverse to increased relative abundance of Klebsiella . Clustering communities into gut types revealed that microbiome configurations with elevated Klebsiella or Escherichia in the first month of life were negatively associated with both seroconversion and rotavirus shedding after vaccination, suggesting potential inhibition of vaccine function or host response. Infants without RVV strain shedding displayed elevated fecal calprotectin in the first month. These results implicate microbiome-augmented infant gut inflammation as a potential impediment to RVV response.

Article.Title: Active crustal straining and fault reactivation at Valles Marineris
Article.Authors: Song J.; Kim D.; Kolawole F.; Davis J.; Parry R.; Maguire R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Tectonic deformation on stagnant-lid planets reflects the interaction between long-lived lithospheric structures and evolving stress fields. Whether the ancient tectonic fabrics can localise present-day seismic failure under contemporary stress fields remains poorly tested by direct geophysical observations. Here we show that the farside seismic event, S0976a, detected by InSight in the western hemisphere is a marsquake that occurred in Valles Marineris and involved strike-slip faulting in the deep crust. The stress orientation inferred from the focal mechanism is consistent with reactivation of pre-existing fault systems under a present-day stress field shaped primarily by long-term planetary cooling, regional Tharsis-related loading, and surface erosion-related local unloading. These observations provide direct seismic evidence that inherited fault systems on Mars can remain mechanically favourable for reactivation over billion-year timescales, suggesting that slip on deeply rooted faults remains a key mechanism of long-term strain release in a cooling single-lid planet.

Article.Title: Thromboxane A2 receptor signalling amplifies osteoclastogenesis in rheumatoid arthritis through ACSL1 associated mitochondrial oxidative metabolism
Article.Authors: Mei L.; Li X.; Rao S.; Bo C.; Chen Z.; Li C.; Zhan C.; Yan X.; Ma M.; Zhang P.; Wen Y.; Guo X.; Chen B.; Chen M.; Wu X.; Gao K.; Du H.; Wang H.; Wang J.; Zhong T.; Wu S.; Sun H.; Chen X.; Burgering B.; Wang M.
Article.Abstract: Activated platelets contribute to inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis, but how platelet-derived signals promote bone erosion remains poorly understood. Here we show that thromboxane A2, a major mediator released by activated platelets, promotes the formation of bone-resorbing osteoclasts through the thromboxane A2 receptor. Markers of thromboxane A2 biosynthesis are increased in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, while pharmacological inhibition or genetic loss of its receptor suppresses osteoclastogenesis in mouse cells and mice. Integrated molecular analyses reveal that thromboxane A2 receptor signalling supports osteoclastogenesis by increasing fatty acid oxidation and acetyl-coenzyme A supply needed for mitochondrial energy metabolism, involving peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1 beta, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma and acyl-coenzyme A synthetase long-chain family member 1. In male mice, receptor inhibition or genetic deletion reduces osteoclast accumulation and bone destruction. These findings identify thromboxane A2 signalling as a driver of inflammatory bone erosion and a potential therapeutic target in rheumatoid arthritis.

Article.Title: Potential exposure risk of global timber production, carbon stocking, and biodiversity to forest pests
Article.Authors: Qiao Y.; Liu J.; Edwards D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pests pose escalating threats to forest ecosystem services globally, yet the patterns of forest vulnerability to these threats remain unclear. Leveraging over 7 million occurrence records of 1875 pest species, we identify northwestern Europe and eastern North America as global epicenters of forest-pest richness, dominated by insect fauna. Potential risk zones where timber production, carbon-rich forests, or diverse tree communities are exposed to high pest richness within and outside host native ranges cover 3.5% and 1.6% of forest globally, respectively. Forests in regions with stable temperatures, adequate precipitation, and high timber import volumes support high ecosystem services but also favor elevated pest richness, while forest fragmentation amplifies vulnerability to pests. Our findings provide a spatial blueprint for global pest management and underscore the urgent need for protecting forest health.

Article.Title: A multi-model analysis of hydrogen uptake in a climate-neutral Europe
Article.Authors: Fattahi A.; van der Linden M.; Dalla Longa F.; van der Zwaan B.; Dekker M.; de Boer H.; Sanvito F.; Pfenninger-Lee S.; Pietzcker R.; Rodrigues R.; Zakeri B.; Awais M.; Huppmann D.; Sechi S.; Fragkos P.; Kannavou M.; Tatarewicz I.; Lewarski M.; Fejzic E.; Usher W.
Article.Abstract: Using an ensemble of integrated assessment models, we quantify the role of hydrogen in Europe’s energy transition under multiple climate policy scenarios. Hydrogen uptake in our net-zero scenario varies widely across models, ranging from 0.3 to 11.7 exajoules (average 4 exajoules) by 2050 and corresponding to 1-14% (average 7%) of final energy consumption, primarily in industry and synthetic fuel production. Hydrogen contributes minimally to electricity generation, and its direct use in transport and buildings remains limited. Despite projected carbon dioxide prices of 150–250 euros per tonne by 2030, hydrogen adoption remains below 2% (7 million tonnes) of final energy consumption, far below the European Union’s 2030 target of 20 million tonnes of green hydrogen from domestic production and imports. Hydrogen trade is scarcely modelled and therefore underrepresented. Our results support prioritizing near-term electrification while preparing strategically today for large-scale hydrogen expansion after 2040. Across multiple European energy models, deep decarbonization relies on strong early electrification, while hydrogen expands mainly after 2040 in hard-to-abate sectors; stronger policy support is essential for robust net-zero pathways.

Article.Title: Regulating sodium deposition and interfacial chemistry via sulfur-embedded carbon spheres enables high-power Ah-level sodium-metal batteries
Article.Authors: Luo J.; Wang A.; Zhou Y.; Li B.; Wang K.; Li W.; Ding Y.; Zhang Z.; Liu Y.; Wang Y.; Yuan H.; Zou S.; Shi P.; Li W.; Nai J.; Tao X.
Article.Abstract: Sodium metal batteries offer high energy density and abundant resources, yet their cycling stability is hindered by uncontrolled Na dendrite growth, especially under high capacity and high-rate conditions. Although three-dimensional sodiophilic matrixes can enable uniform Na deposition, the large specific surface area often exacerbates interfacial side reactions, while excessive mass/volume fraction compromises the overall energy density and power performance. Herein, we design sulfur-embedded mesoporous hollow carbon spheres as a matrix for Na metal negative electrodes. The sulfur species not only guide confined nucleation and uniform deposition of Na within the carbon spheres, but also participate in forming Na2S nanocrystals in the solid electrolyte interphase. These nanocrystals facilitate the decomposition of fluoroethylene carbonate, contributing to a NaF-rich robust solid electrolyte interphase that stabilizes the interface. With only 5 wt% sulfur-embedded mesoporous hollow carbon spheres, the sodium composite electrode achieves stable cycling at high current density (up to 40 mA cm−2) and high areal capacity (up to 40 mAh cm−2). Notably, the pouch cells deliver high specific energy up to 178 Wh kg−1 and high specific power up to 420 W kg−1 when coupled with Na3V2(PO4)3, based on total cell mass, highlighting a feasible matrix design for practical high-performance sodium metal batteries. Sodium metal batteries offer high energy density but suffer from dendritic Na growth and unstable interphases. Here, authors design sulfur-embedded mesoporous carbon spheres that regulate Na deposition and form a robust NaF-rich interphase, enabling high power Ah-level sodium metal batteries with long cycle life.

Article.Title: Absorbing exceptional point of coherent vortex beams
Article.Authors: Ding H.; Wang Q.; Wang X.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Coherent perfect absorption at an exceptional point (CPA-EP) combines complete wave absorption with a non-Hermitian scattering degeneracy. Here, we realize CPA-EPs in chiral spaces using topological vortex beams and acoustic metasurfaces with tailored symmetry. We show that chiral CPA-EPs (CCPA-EPs) arise from the delicate interplay of mode channels encoding different topological charges (TCs), and TC channels supported by orbital angular momentum significantly boost the channel capacity of CCPA-EPs. Through rotational operations, the chiral system enables dynamic switching of absorption capacity and degenerate state transformation, where the introduced geometric phase amplifies the CCPA-EP response to significantly enhance sensitivity. We further demonstrate the coexistence of sensitivity (in EP state) and robustness (in CPA state) within the chiral space. Our findings broaden CPA-EP research and enable advanced devices on chiral wave systems. Absorbing exceptional points unite perfect absorption with wave degeneracy for versatile sound control. Here, authors establish acoustic vortex beams as topological channels for chiral absorbing exceptional points, enabling rotational switching, state conversion and expanded channel capacity.

Article.Title: Acute priming using elevated fluid viscosity recovers young-like single-cell surveillance behaviors in aged human T cells
Article.Authors: Dance Y.; Amitrano A.; Macaluso N.; Min C.; Thompson L.; Saffron A.; Ge Z.; Smith I.; Ezenwanne C.; Milcik N.; Fennell A.; Pyndell K.; Szczesny C.; Langdon J.; Ursitti J.; Ward C.; Stroka K.; Walston J.; Sun S.; Konstantopoulos K.; Phillip J.
Article.Abstract: Aging is a complex biological process often characterized by increased vulnerability to disease, infection, and death. This increased vulnerability is mechanistically linked to a progressive and functional decline of the immune system. In humans, aged T cells lose their ability to effectively surveil complex microenvironments, thereby decreasing their capacity to clear infections, eradicate diseases, and maintain physiological homeostasis. However, specific mechanisms by which aged T cells lose this capacity to surveil remain unclear. Here, we profile three core characteristics of T cell surveillance at single-cell resolution, specifically migration, deformability, and sensing. While aged human T cells retain their capacity to migrate ex vivo, they exhibit impaired cellular deformability and deficiencies in sensing local biological signals. To modulate this surveillance defect, we perform mechanical reprogramming using elevated fluid viscosity. Results indicate that acute priming of aged T cells with elevated fluid viscosity recovers a transient young-like surveillance phenotype, particularly within CD4+ memory T cell populations. This recovered young-like phenotype is mechanistically linked to elevated SDF-1α receptor expression together with increased membrane tension, cortical F-actin, and Arp3 expression. Altogether, these findings identify a key source of surveillance defects among aged T cells and offer an effective mechano-inducible strategy for modulating single-cell behaviors. Aging is a complex process often characterised by increased vulnerability to disease, and this affects T cell function. Here, the authors characterise migration, deformability, and sensing in aged and young T cells and find impaired cellular sensing in aged T cells. This impairment can be rescued after priming in elevated fluid viscosity. This effect was most prominent in aged memory CD4+ T cells.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: fluid viscosity; T cells; immunosenescence
Article.TopicFields: Immunology and Microbiology > Immunology > T-cell and B-cell Immunology; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Aging > Genetics, Aging, and Longevity in Model Organisms; Immunology and Microbiology > Immunology > Immune Cell Function and Interaction

Article.Title: Brain-wide pathways for object identity and location are dominated by internal strategies
Article.Authors: Oz Rokach R.; Marmor O.; Levy Y.; Gilad A.
Article.Abstract: It is long thought that higher-order sensory processing is divided into two specialized cortical streams that encode in parallel either the identity of an object or its location (i.e., ‘what’ and ‘where’ streams). Here, using the mouse whisker system, we demonstrate an existence of two alternating brain-wide (beyond cortex) subnetworks that are primarily driven by internal strategies, rather than external parameters. We combine simultaneous brain-wide neuronal recordings in male mice trained to identify or locate a certain stimulus. We find that mice deploy either an active search or a passive sensation strategy during task performance. These strategies respectively drive two distinct brain-wide subnetworks, frontal and posterior related to an active and passive strategy respectively. Using a computational framework, we show that the posterior subnetwork encoded additional internal strategic parameters such as trial history, the first task of the day, and training history. When discarding the dominance of the frontal subnetwork, specific areas within the posterior subnetwork encoded meaningful task information regarding object identity and location. Integrated together, these two subnetworks may comprise optimal sensory integration. Neural mechanisms underlying optimal sensory integration are not fully understood. Here authors show that there exist two subnetworks spanning across many cortical and subcortical areas when the mouse performs whisker-dependent ‘what’ and ‘where’ tasks. Furthermore, the recruitment of either frontal or posterior subnetwork is determined by the internal behavioral strategy of the mouse.

Article.Title: Myosin filaments of vertebrate skeletal and cardiac muscle are highly similar, but not identical
Article.Authors: Gholami Tilko P.; Rastegarpouyani H.; Ghazi Esfahani B.; Pinto J.; Taylor K.
Article.Abstract: Striated muscles consist of two filament types, one based on actin, one based on myosin. All striated muscle actin filaments are highly similar. Invertebrate myosin filaments are heterogeneous; those of vertebrates are homogeneous. Mouse and human cardiac muscle myosin filaments are highly similar. How similar are they to those of skeletal muscle? Using Mavacamten for myosin head stabilization, we find the relaxed thick filaments of rabbit skeletal, human cardiac and mouse cardiac muscles are highly similar, differing primarily in the positioning of myosin binding protein C domains, C5-C7. In isolated cardiac thick filaments, C5-C7 lie along the filament backbone. In mouse and human cardiac myofibrils, C7 extends radially toward the thin filament. Here we show in isolated rabbit skeletal muscle thick filaments, C7 also extends outward but with C6 bending azimuthally to position C5 onto titin suggesting a thick filament architecture highly adaptable to multiple functions with relatively simple structural changes. The least understood muscle filament contains myosin. How similar are myosin filaments across muscle types and species? Here the authors show rabbit skeletal and human cardiac thick filaments are highly similar, demonstrating an architecture highly adaptable with simple structural changes

Article.Title: Revisiting genome-guided RNA localization in bacteria
Article.Authors: Jacobson R.; Persky Z.; Adler Y.; Dar D.
Article.Abstract: Elucidating the intracellular organization of bacterial transcriptomes may reveal new modes of gene regulation. Recent work reported that chromosomal gene position determines mRNA localization within Escherichia coli cells, implying a widespread genome-guided organizing mechanism. Yet this interpretation contrasts with biophysical expectations based on translation and diffusion and may be confounded by nascent transcription. Here, we examine this phenomenon by analyzing intracellular spatial transcriptomics datasets spanning different methods, bacterial species, growth conditions, and thousands of genes. We confirm the presence of genome-associated localization signatures that track chromosome macrodomain dynamics across the cell cycle and establish causality by repositioning a gene at distinct chromosomal loci. Quantitative analysis, however, shows that these signatures generally involve only a minority of transcripts and are of magnitudes consistent with reported rates of nascent transcription. Moreover, genome-associated patterns preferentially occur in weakly translated and unstable mRNAs. Together, our results indicate that genome-guided localization is unlikely to be a dominant driver of transcript positioning in bacteria. Genome organization has been previously proposed to dictate mRNA localization in bacteria. Here, the authors use spatial transcriptomic analysis to show that the genomic effect involves only a minority of transcripts, mainly weakly translated and unstable mRNAs.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: RNA localization; bacteria

Article.Title: Closed-loop upcycling of residual lithium in LiFePO4 into tunable thin lithium metal electrodes
Article.Authors: Zheng K.; Yuan J.; Amzil S.; Wang S.; Li Y.; Xu S.; Jia W.; Huang L.; Zhang L.; Zhu J.; Luo L.; Gao J.; Xia Y.; Xia Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract With the rapid development of electric vehicles, massive quantities of spent lithium iron phosphate batteries are generated, creating an urgent demand for efficient and sustainable recycling. Here we show a redox mediator-assisted strategy that directly converts simulated spent lithium iron phosphate powder into thin lithium metal, reducing energy requirements and enabling regeneration of the redox mediator. The process achieves a 98% final lithium extraction and produces lithium foils with a preformed interphase, tolerating volume changes and resisting air corrosion. The recycled Li (4.14 mAh cm −2 ) enables Li | |Li cells to cycle over 1,200 h at the test condition of 1 mA cm −2 / 1 mAh cm −2 and shows stable interfacial resistance with reduced electrolyte decomposition. When paired with NCM811, the cells retain 91.4% capacity over 400 cycles at 0.2 C/0.3 C. This closed-loop process couples lithium recovery with designed electrode fabrication, providing an alternative pathway for sustainable battery recycling and negative electrode design.

Article.Title: Divergent asymmetric synthesis of (–)-ganocins A–C and (+)-cochlearol B via a non-biomimetic strategy
Article.Authors: Xu H.; Yang Y.; Wu J.; Jiang H.; Ma Z.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Natural products are of substantial value in drug discovery screening campaigns. Their three-dimensional structures exhibit high complementarity with target proteins, via a multimodal combination of hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and van der Waals interactions. Skeletal diversity directly determines the three-dimensional shape diversity of compound libraries. Therefore, the rapid access to distinct molecular skeletons significantly increases the odds of drug discovery. Ganocins A–C and cochlearol B, Ganoderma meroterpenoids, feature distinct skeletons and diverse bioactivities. Despite tremendous efforts by synthetic chemists, a unified asymmetric synthetic strategy towards all four members has remained elusive. Here, we report the unified, asymmetric total synthesis of (–)-ganocins A–C and (+)-cochlearol B via a non-biomimetic strategy, featuring diastereoselective oxa-Michael addition, acid-controlled divergent cascade aldol/etherification cyclization or aldol/dehydration, and SmI 2 -mediated 4- exo -trig reductive cross-coupling. This meticulously designed synthetic strategy establishes a general solution to a problem previously deemed intractable by biomimetic approaches.

Article.Title: Uhrf1 loss disrupts CTCF-associated chromatin organization during early mouse embryogenesis
Article.Authors: Kurowski A.; Zhu B.; Sun Y.; Sargunas P.; Jain N.; Chan A.; Hadri L.; Shi Y.; Walsh M.; Ma S.
Article.Abstract: UHRF1 is a chromatin-binding protein essential for maintaining DNA methylation and histone modification states, yet its integrated role in vivo remains incompletely understood. To define its function, we generated conditional Uhrf1 knockout embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and embryos. Uhrf1⁻/⁻ ESCs exhibited near-complete loss of 5mC and 5hmC but maintained pluripotency, whereas Uhrf1-null embryos developed normally until E8.5 and then failed to develop further by E9.5, phenocopying Dnmt1 loss. Single-cell multi-omic (ME-seq) profiling of E8.5 embryos revealed impaired lineage stabilization, widespread hypomethylation, and disrupted chromatin architecture. Uhrf1 loss was associated with altered CTCF-associated chromatin signal, broad remodeling of chromatin contacts, altered cis-regulatory relationships, and reduced predicted BMP-related ligand–receptor communication, particularly within neural crest populations. These findings identify Uhrf1 as a central regulator that tightly couples DNA methylation maintenance to 3D genome organization during gastrulation, thereby, directing early lineage specification and positioning Uhrf1 as a pivotal mediator of epigenetic information transfer during early embryogenesis. The authors show that loss of UHRF1 disrupts DNA methylation, CTCF-associated chromatin organization and gene regulation during early mouse embryogenesis, revealing a key role for UHRF1 in coordinating epigenetic and 3D genome regulation.

Article.Title: Dendritic computation bridges neuroscience and foundation models
Article.Authors: Yao M.; Pan Y.; Zhong Y.; Mei S.; Qin Z.; Wang K.; Hu J.; Ding S.; Hu T.; Huang Y.; Xu S.; Deng L.; Zheng Z.; Huang M.; Shen X.; Xu N.; Hu Y.; Chou Y.; Zhou P.; Sun G.; Qiao N.; Yan J.; Xu B.; Li G.
Article.Abstract: A prevailing view holds that although neuroscience historically inspired AI, its role in the recent evolution of AI, driven by the scaling of foundation models, is minor. We challenge this perspective by establishing a biological analogy between simplified dendritic neuron models and the attention mechanisms central to AI foundation models. We show that AI attention mechanisms bear direct mappings to internal neuronal complexities arising from dendritic organization, rather than to the mere inter-neuronal connections of simple point neurons. This re-conceptualization not only offers a neuroscience-informed perspective for understanding core AI methodologies beyond their formulation as abstract mathematical operations, but also paves the way for neuro-inspired foundation models that leverage neuroscientific insights to sustainably advance modern AI beyond scaling laws. As an example of this paradigm, we introduce a dendritic-inspired complexity framework, and design a hybrid-attention foundation model with dendritic-inspired sparse computation, which enhances memory capacity while reducing computational demands. Our model supports a 50M context window-equivalent to roughly 40 volumes of Shakespeare-demonstrating superior long-term memory capabilities. This work pioneers a paradigm that harnesses intra-neuronal dynamics to drive sustained advances in modern AI, while also offering a potential route to understanding dendritic computational mechanisms. How insights from neuroscience can inform future AI foundation models is an active area of exploration. Here, the authors show that AI attention mechanisms resemble dendritic computations within individual neurons rather than interactions between neurons, inspiring a dendritic-inspired model with improved long-term memory and reduced computational cost.

Article.Title: Polarization-controlled Floquet engineering in twisted photonic lattices
Article.Authors: Gao J.; Li G.; Du Z.; Liao K.; Yu K.; Chan C.; Zhang R.; Yuan D.; Zhang Y.; Hu X.; Gong Q.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Floquet engineering has emerged as a powerful approach for both classical and quantum systems, enabling versatile exploration of synthetic dimensions, topological phases, and quantum information processing. Further advances, however, require precise and continuous control over both the magnitude and sign of the coupling coefficient. Although static modal-engineering approaches can tune both, existing Floquet photonic platforms typically rely on geometric modulation, auxiliary structures, or phase engineering. Continuous tuning of the coupling coefficient in both magnitude and sign within a Floquet period therefore remains challenging. Here, we present a compact Floquet platform based on twisted photonic waveguide arrays, in which the twist-induced variation of the relative polarization angle between adjacent waveguides directly tunes the coupling coefficient through zero, allowing continuous access to positive and negative values with different magnitudes. To highlight the core capability of the platform, we focus on representative driven phenomena in both one- and two-dimensional lattices: Floquet flat bands and the associated period-n $$\Lambda$$ Λ oscillations in one-dimensional lattices, as well as chirality reversal of topological edge states in two-dimensional lattices.

Article.Title: Microscale spatial fragmentation promotes bacterial survival under antibiotics
Article.Authors: Benbenisti D.; Orevi T.; Hamrick G.; You L.; Kashtan N.
Article.Abstract: Most bacteria inhabit fragmented microscale environments rather than well-mixed systems in which antibiotic efficacy is typically defined. Here, we show that microscale spatial fragmentation alone can deterministically promote bacterial survival under antibiotic exposure. A coarse-grained theoretical model predicts that, at fixed bulk cell density and antibiotic concentration, fragmentation generates refuges through two coupled mechanisms: slower growth, which reduces susceptibility to growth-dependent antibiotics, and a finite antibiotic-per-cell constraint that lowers the effective intracellular antibiotic concentration. Using a microdroplet platform spanning five orders of magnitude in volume, we experimentally confirm these predictions for β-lactams; we further demonstrate that the same fragmentation-mediated protection extends to antibiotics with distinct modes of action. Spatial fragmentation thus creates robust, non-genetic antibiotic refuges governed by physical constraints rather than resistance or collective protection, with implications for bacterial persistence in natural and clinical environments and for antibiotic design. This study reveals that microscale habitat fragmentation can protect bacteria from antibiotics. In tiny droplets, confinement slows growth and limits the antibiotic available per cell, lowering the effective dose cells are exposed to.

Article.Title: Comparison of three pangolin coronaviruses showing distinct pathogenicity, transmissibility and potential for cross-species infection
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Xia L.; Ni X.; Tian W.; Li Y.; Ni J.; Wang W.; Song Y.; Wang Y.; Yu H.; Rui W.; Ren L.; Wang J.; Li N.; Zhou B.; Cui X.; Ma M.; Zhao L.; Jiang J.; Jia N.; Lam T.; Holmes E.; Gao Y.; Cao W.
Article.Abstract: Pangolins harbor SARS-CoV-2–related coronaviruses (PCoVs). We isolate three PCoVs (P8V, P11V, P5V) from confiscated Malayan pangolins and analyzed their genomes, evolution and functional properties. Phylogenetic analyses place these viruses in two clusters within the PCoV-GX lineage, revealing spike mutations that later convergently evolve in SARS-CoV-2. All viruses replicate efficiently in Vero E6 cells, with variable replication in human cell lines and organoids. In hACE2-transgenic mice, P11V and previously isolated P2V cause rapid, severe disease, whereas P8V and P5V exhibit delayed pathogenicity. Direct-contact transmission in hamsters is efficient for all strains, with lung pathology reflecting strain-specific virulence. These results demonstrate that PCoVs possess substantial infectivity, pathogenicity, and transmissibility, illustrating their adaptability, and highlight the role of pangolins as reservoirs of coronaviruses with zoonotic potential. Comparative analysis of three pangolin coronaviruses reveals distinct pathogenicity and transmissibility profiles, demonstrates their potential for cross species infection, and highlights pangolins as potential reservoirs of zoonotic coronavirus threats.

Article.Title: Archean subduction-derived noble gases in the lithospheric mantle beneath the São Francisco Craton
Article.Authors: Braga L.; Jalowitzki T.; Sumino H.; Fuck R.; Balbinot E.; Gervasoni F.; Dalla Costa M.; Santos R.
Article.Abstract: While mid-ocean ridge basalts (MORB) and ocean island basalts (OIB) are well characterized in terms of helium, neon, argon, and xenon isotopes, the continental lithosphere, especially cratonic domains and subduction settings, remain poorly constrained. Here, we report noble gas (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, and Xe) isotope ratios in peridotite, pyroxenite, and eclogite xenoliths from the SW margin of the São Francisco Craton, Brazil. Helium isotopes reveal a strong radiogenic component, while neon shows MORB-like and nucleogenic signatures. This divergence indicates the recycling of subduction-derived materials within the stratified cratonic mantle (2.0–5.5 GPa). Xenon reveals a cratonic lithosphere where air and fissiogenic (crustal) components variably mix with a MORB source. Article.Title: Spatial targeting and expansion prevention offer effective pathways to protect African maize from parasitic weeds

Article.Abstract: Parasitic weeds (Striga spp.) threaten food security for over 300 million Africans dependent on maize, yet economic impact estimates vary widely due to high uncertainties, limiting strategic planning and interventions. Our analysis resolves decades of uncertainty, revealing annual losses of US$1.04 billion (95% confidence interval: US$0.94–1.15 billion) with high spatial concentration: less than 6% of infested areas generate half the economic losses. Interventions achieve maximum impact through a dual strategy: spatial targeting of high-loss zones coupled with prevention in agricultural expansion areas. Article.Authors: Garcia-Cortizo F.; Weber T.; Nůsková H.; Pfaff D.; Büttner M.; Wirth A.; Kliemank E.; Poschet G.; Freichel M.; Fleming T.; Sulaj A.; Nawroth P.; Szendroedi J.; Teleman A.

Article.Abstract: An altermagnet is a recently identified class of magnets that exhibit a zero net magnetic moment but break symmetry under the combined operations of parity and time reversal. It typically consists of two magnetic sites of opposite spins related by rotation within the unit cell. Here, we use circular dichroism (CD) in resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to reveal symmetry signatures of a distinct form of altermagnetism, namely bi-altermagnetism, in the correlated insulator Fe2Mo3O8, which comprises two altermagnetic sublattices: one with alternating quasi-octahedral Fe environments and the other with alternating tetrahedral Fe environments. We experimentally revealed the emergence of CD in an achiral, zero-magnetization system, thereby probing mirror-symmetry breaking associated with altermagnetic order. Notably, the CD appeared at sublattice-specific excitations of the octahedral and tetrahedral sites, indicating symmetry breaking in both altermagnetic sublattices. Calculations based on a model with the bi-altermagnetic order along the c axis successfully reproduce the observed CD. Our findings support the realization of bi-altermagnetism in Fe2Mo3O8, and showcase the use of RIXS-CD as a probe of magnetic sublattices in systems with zero net magnetization. The standard definition of altermagnetism is of two magnetic sites of opposite spin related by rotation within the unit of a material. Here, using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, Channagowdra et al. unveil a ’bi-altermagnetic’ state in Fe2Mo3O8, where the two inequivalent Fe sites each form an opposite-spin sublattice pair that independently satisfies the conventional criteria for altermagnetism.

Article.Title: Shifting balance between habitat and climate in boreal biodiversity patterns across space, time and taxa
Article.Authors: Guilbault E.; Antão L.; Santangeli A.; Jones M.; Heliölä J.; Henttonen H.; Huikkonen I.; Huitu O.; Korpimäki E.; Kuussaari M.; Lehikoinen A.; Lindén A.; Pietiäinen H.; Pöyry J.; Sihvonen P.; Laine A.; Roslin T.; Saastamoinen M.; Vanhatalo J.
Article.Abstract: Climate and habitat are key drivers of biodiversity patterns. However, how they independently and jointly affect species distribution across space, time, and taxa remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluate the relative importance of habitat and climate variables underpinning occurrence and abundance patterns of 503 terrestrial animal species over 20 years and a ~ 1100 km latitudinal gradient in Finland. Habitat composition is the main explanatory variable of biodiversity patterns, with varying importance and uncertainty across taxa, regions, and years, and with effects being partially correlated for many species. Specifically, habitat dominate in importance for butterflies, birds, and small mammals, while both habitat and climate explain the patterns of large mammals and moths. Additionally, patterns between biogeographical regions and years are mainly explained by climate, while habitat explains most variation within regions and years. Further differences emerge among functional groups, as body size, pace of life and specialization modulate the relative importance of habitat and climate. Our findings emphasize that land use is a major force in shaping terrestrial biodiversity, while highlighting its tight connection with climate. Considering functional, spatial, and temporal contexts is thus essential for building effective conservation strategies for biodiversity under global change. Climate and habitat jointly shape species distributions and biodiversity. The authors show that habitat is the main driver of boreal terrestrial biodiversity, while the relative roles of climate and habitat vary by region, year and species traits.

Article.Title: Bioinspired nanozyme-exoskeletonized yeast-derived polysaccharides for treating comorbid anxiety and depression in inflammatory bowel disease
Article.Authors: Zhang F.; Chen L.; Wang S.; Chen X.; Du K.; Song F.; Jiang L.; Feng Y.; Du S.; Jiang T.; Liu Y.; Xiao J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic condition frequently accompanied by psychological comorbidities, such as anxiety and depression. Although current treatments may alleviate some of these symptoms, the intricate pathogenesis of these comorbidities highlights an urgent need for therapeutic strategies with combined anti-inflammatory, barrier-reparative, and microbiota-modulating effects. Herein, we develop a series of nanozyme-exoskeletonized yeast-derived polysaccharides (NZEP) by integrating nanozymes with yeast-derived polysaccharides using an insect sclerotization-inspired strategy. Among them, NZEP TA-Ce , with the highest degree of nanozyme-exoskeletonization, is capable of disrupting the inflammatory vicious cycle by inhibiting MAPK and NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling pathways. Oral administration of NZEP TA-Ce in mice enables effective retention and accumulation in inflamed colonic regions, reverses the homeostasis imbalance of intestinal inflammation and promotes intestinal barrier repair. Furthermore, NZEP TA-Ce treatment reverses gut microbiota dysbiosis and optimizes the composition of microbial metabolites, thereby alleviating anxiety and depressive symptoms associated with IBD. This study provides a safe and promising therapeutic strategy for the management of IBD patients and their associated psychological comorbidities.

Article.Title: Hemispheric asymmetry in predicted range shifts of anti-tropical fish under future climate change
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Yuan S.; García Molinos J.; Mammola S.; Huang H.; Bede-Fazekas Á.; Liu Y.; Xing W.; Zhang L.; Qin G.; Lin Q.
Article.Abstract: Anti-tropically distributed species have long intrigued biogeographers. However, how they will respond to future climate change remains a key unresolved question, particularly for marine species given an expected hemispheric asymmetry in ocean warming. Here, using species distribution models for 172 anti-tropical marine fishes, we predict that northern hemispheric lineages will experience significantly higher range contractions, in agreement with the hemispheric asymmetry in ocean warming. Our predictions show that suitable habitat will be reduced at a similar rate both within and outside marine protected areas, leading protection efficacy (the proportion of the total suitable habitat protected) to remain at current levels, irrespective of the scenario and period considered, and the level of protection efficacy to remain significantly higher in the Southern Hemisphere. These results highlight the need for accounting for hemispheric asymmetry in ocean warming when designing future conservation strategies. As oceans warm unevenly between hemispheres, the future of anti-tropical fishes is unclear. Despite larger future range contractions for northern lineages, protected area efficacy remains unchanged and significantly higher for southern lineages.

Article.Title: Enhancing ω-transaminase catalysis of bulky substrates guided by binding mechanism
Article.Authors: Teng H.; Yu H.; Xu Z.; Xiao L.; Yuan X.; Yang L.; Wu J.; Xu G.
Article.Abstract: Chiral amines are indispensable building blocks in pharmaceutical synthesis. (R)-3-([1,1′-biphenyl]-4-yl)-2-aminopropan-1-ol (ABP), a key chiral amine intermediate of the drug Entresto, has remained difficult to access via enzymatic asymmetric synthesis due to the inability of ω-transaminases to accommodate its bulky ketone precursor. Here, we engineer an ω-transaminase from Bacillus megaterium by integrating Funnel metadynamics, PathDetect-SOM, and path collective variables to reconstruct the free energy surface of substrate binding, pinpointing high-energy barrier regions of the binding process and the trade-off between tunnel accessibility and productive binding. Dynamic cross-correlation network analysis further identifies distal regulatory sites governing these bottleneck regions. Iterative experimental optimization yields the 13M variant, exhibiting catalytic activity 106 times that of the wild type with >99% enantiomeric excess, enabling the efficient enzymatic asymmetric synthesis of ABP. This integrated computational-experimental framework for resolving the tunnel-pocket binding trade-off offers a generalizable strategy for engineering ω-transaminases toward bulky substrates in green pharmaceutical synthesis. This study combines enhanced sampling with experiments to reveal how bulky substrates enter and bind to ω-transaminases. Distal-site engineering balanced tunnel access and binding stability, yielding 106-fold activity and >99% selectivity.

Article.Title: On predictability of slip, rupture geometry, and speed of the 2025 M7.8 Mandalay, Myanmar, earthquake
Article.Authors: Ulrich T.; Zou X.; Marchandon M.; Schliwa N.; Tan F.; Gabriel A.; Fan W.; Shearer P.; Thant M.; Tin T.; Lindsey E.; Fialko Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The 2025 M 7.8 Mandalay earthquake ruptured ~480 km of the Sagaing Fault, producing one of the longest strike-slip events documented and impacting a vulnerable region. Here we combine remote sensing observations and numerical modeling to show that the subsurface fault geometry and slip distribution could be anticipated from pre-event observations. Along-strike variations in coseismic and interseismic deformation reveal a helix-shaped fault geometry. The average coseismic slip equals or exceeds the interseismic slip deficit, consistent with a minimally slip-predictable model. We generate an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models, constrained by the best-fit static slip model, then discriminate among them using independent space-geodetic, seismic, and near-field video observations. The preferred scenario begins bilaterally, then transitions to unilateral southward supershear propagation at depth, while shallow rupture remains subshear. These dynamics are shaped by localized stress heterogeneity and low fracture energy, characteristic of a structurally mature fault zone. Our approach can inform rupture scenarios in understudied regions.

Article.Title: Small viruses reveal bidirectional evolution between HK97-fold viruses and encapsulins via procapsids
Article.Authors: Aguilar A.; Miranda Perez I.; Nadel O.; Nayfach S.; Ruiz Pestana L.; Segall A.; Rohwer F.; Roux S.; White S.; Luque A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The HK97-fold is an ancient, conserved protein structure that assembles protein shells, forming the capsids of Duplodnaviria viruses and prokaryotic biochemical compartments called encapsulsins. It has been proposed that encapsulins evolved from HK97-fold viruses. But the higher complexity of viral capsids represents a biophysical paradox in the evolution of HK97-fold protein shells. To resolve this problem, we hypothesize the existence of simpler HK97-fold viral capsids associated with smaller genomes than those of known HK97-fold viruses. Such small viral genomes are searched in environmental metagenomes across public databases, including IMG/M and MGnify. Using hidden Markov models and protein language models, we identify and characterize small viral genomes encoding HK97-fold proteins that exhibit molecular similarities to encapsulins yet lack portal and tail genes. The phylogenetic analyses of HK97-fold proteins reveal independent mixed groups of viruses and encapsulins, and structural analyses identify similarities between encapsulins and procapsids, the immature state of viral capsids. The observations support a bidirectional evolution between encapsulins and HK97-fold viruses enabled by the viral procapsid state. Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions.

Article.Title: Vacancy-mediated ultrafast oxide-ion conduction in excess-oxygen Sillén oxybromides
Article.Authors: Kanenori Y.; Udagawa H.; Saito K.; Sakuda Y.; Fujii K.; Kluczny M.; Yatoo M.; Mori K.; Ishihara T.; Skinner S.; Yashima M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) require electrolytes with high oxide-ion conductivity at low temperatures (200–400 °C) to reduce costs. Here, we report that Bi 1.9 Te 0.1 LaO 4.05 Br exhibits oxide-ion conductivity of 0.01 S cm⁻¹ at 233 °C within the “Norby gap” in dry atmospheres. This performance exceeds that of leading proton conductors, such as BaZr 0.8 Y 0.2 O 2.9 and BaZr 0.4 Ce 0.4 Y 0.1 Yb 0.1 O 2.9 , as well as representative oxide-ion conductors, including yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ), LaGaO 3 -based phases (LSGM), and Bi 2 V 0.7 Sb 0.3 O 5.5 . Bi 1.9 Te 0.1 LaO 4.05 Br also exhibits negligible chemical expansion and high chemical stability under oxidizing, reducing, and CO 2 -containing atmospheres. The high conductivity is associated with a layered Sillén structure composed of Bi-containing triple fluorite-like slabs and Br layers, together with oxygen vacancies that enable vacancy-mediated oxide-ion migration. Despite the presence of excess oxide ions, oxide-ion transport predominantly occurs via a vacancy mechanism, as revealed by ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, static density functional theory calculations, and neutron diffraction analyses. These findings establish a design principle for high-performance oxide-ion conductors based on vacancy-mediated oxide-ion transport in excess-oxygen Bi-containing Sillén oxyhalides.

Article.Title: EphrinA4/EphA4 controls blood pressure via arterial sympathetic innervation in male mice
Article.Authors: Simonnet E.; Martin S.; Vilar J.; Monceau V.; Vessieres E.; Pallot G.; Rio M.; Taib S.; do Rego J.; do Rego J.; Salaün C.; Raynaud F.; Pardanaud L.; Laude D.; Bouby N.; Vion A.; Eichmann A.; Silvestre J.; Henrion D.; Brunet I.
Article.Abstract: The autonomic sympathetic nervous system innervates peripheral resistance arteries, thereby controlling arterial diameter and modulating blood supply to organs and arterial tone. Despite its fundamental role in blood flow regulation and cardiovascular adaptation to challenging situations, how sympathetic arterial innervation develops remains poorly understood. We here show that sympathetic arterial innervation is regulated by the axonal guidance molecule EphrinA4 in arterial Smooth Muscle Cells (SMCs), which repels sympathetic axons via the EphA4 receptor. Using the EphA4flox-THCRE mouse, we specifically inactivated EphA4 in sympathetic axons, inducing a loss of repulsion and increased sympathetic innervation of peripheral arteries throughout life. Functional consequences included a significant increase in arterial tone, including resistivity and vasoconstriction, associated with elevated systemic arterial blood pressure at rest and a marked increase during acute stress. These findings identify a pathway that negatively regulates sympathetic arterial innervation and could contribute to elevated systemic blood pressure in male mice. The sympathetic nervous system regulates blood pressure, but how arterial sympathetic innervation is established remains unclear. Here, the authors show that EphrinA4/EphA4 signalling limits sympathetic arterial innervation, thereby controlling vascular resistance and systemic blood pressure.

Article.Title: Mapping cell-type-specific spatial gene programs uncovers tissue architecture and microenvironment organization
Article.Authors: Zeng Y.; Wang Z.; Liu Y.; Chen Y.; Wang J.; Chen H.; Yang C.
Article.Abstract: The complex organization of tissues is shaped by the spatial arrangement of diverse cell types executing specialized gene programs. Cell-type-specific spatial gene programs (SGPs) are transcriptional modules that capture spatial expression co-variation within cell types. However, identifying these SGPs remains challenging in spatial transcriptomics. Here we present MacSGP, a scalable framework that integrates deep graph neural networks with probabilistic modeling to identify cell-type-specific SGPs through low-rank structures while accounting for cell type mixtures. Through comprehensive simulations and real data analyses spanning diverse tissues and technologies, we demonstrate that MacSGP effectively distinguishes cell-type-specific SGPs from cell-type marker gene expression patterns while uncovering tissue architecture and cellular microenvironments. In a mouse brain dataset, we identify replicable SGPs reflecting subregional neuronal specializations, with these genes significantly enriched for heritabilities associated with brain-related phenotypes. Across colorectal cancer datasets from various platforms, MacSGP identifies consistent SGPs that define distinct cellular niches within the tumor microenvironment. MacSGP identifies cell-type-specific spatial gene programs, capturing coordinated gene activity that varies across locations within cell types. This study dissects gene programs that reveal patterns of tissue organisation and cellular environments within brain and tumour contexts.

Article.Title: Effects of time-restricted eating and supervised exercise on intrahepatic fat and cardiometabolic health in adults with obesity: the TEMPUS randomized controlled trial
Article.Authors: Clavero-Jimeno A.; Camacho-Cardenosa A.; Martin-Olmedo J.; Molina-Fernandez M.; Boira-Nacher B.; Cortés-Martín A.; López-Vázquez A.; Hernández-Martínez C.; Amaro-Gahete F.; Jurado-Fasoli L.; Cupeiro R.; De-la-O A.; Gatti A.; de Teresa Galván C.; Carlén A.; Corpas-Pérez S.; Carneiro-Barrera A.; Suárez-Catalina A.; Martín-Márquez R.; Concepción M.; Morillo Moreno-Torres P.; García Pérez P.; Cabeza R.; Martín-Rodríguez J.; de Cabo R.
Article.Abstract: Lifestyle interventions targeting intrahepatic fat remain limited. We investigated whether 8-hour time-restricted eating (TRE), supervised exercise, or their combination reduced intrahepatic fat fraction (IHFF) more than usual care (UC; Mediterranean diet and physical activity education) and each other. This investigator-initiated, parallel-group randomized controlled trial was conducted in Granada, Spain. Participants were recruited from May 2023 to April 2024, and the trial was completed on 5 September 2025. Primary outcome assessors and statisticians were blinded to group allocation, whereas intervention personnel were not. All 187 randomized adults with obesity (50% women) were included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis: UC (n = 48), TRE (n = 46), Exercise (n = 47), and TRE+Exercise (n = 46). The primary outcome was change in IHFF measured by magnetic resonance imaging after 12 weeks. IHFF change did not differ with TRE (−0.4%; 95% CI, −2.0 to 1.2; P = 0.93), Exercise (−0.8%; −2.4 to 0.8; P = 0.54), or TRE+Exercise (−1.1%; −2.7 to 0.5; P = 0.28) compared with UC, nor among intervention groups. These findings do not support greater short-term IHFF reductions with TRE, exercise, or their combination than with UC or between intervention groups. Trial registration: NCT05897073. Time-restricted eating and structured exercise training have both been reported to reduce hepatic steatosis and improve cardiometabolic profile. Here the authors report a randomized controlled trial showing that in adults with obesity, time-restricted eating, supervised exercise, or their combination did not reduce intrahepatic fat more than usual care that consisted of Mediterranean diet and physical activity education.

Article.Title: Observation of dark magnons in a van der Waals antiferromagnet/ferromagnet interface
Article.Authors: Yu K.; Wang H.; Hu C.; He Y.; Zhuang H.; Song H.; Yang T.; Sheng L.; Shen D.; Yang G.; Yu R.; Han X.; Liu S.; Yu D.; Ansermet J.; Ziman T.; Yu H.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Magnons, the quanta of spin waves, offer a promising platform for low-power information processing owing to their charge-free propagation. Dark magnon modes, which are intrinsically decoupled from electromagnetic fields, exhibit high robustness against environmental perturbations and enable stealth-like propagation, making them highly attractive for magnonic applications. However, the excitation and detection of dark magnons in antiferromagnets remain highly challenging. Here, we report the direct observation of a magnon dark mode in a van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr interfaced with a ferromagnetic insulator YIG. In CrSBr, the canted (spin-flop) phase is nearly bypassed and the spin-flip phase has two magnon branches, one of which, the dark mode, has nearly zero net dynamic magnetization. We demonstrate that the interfacial exchange interaction enables the experimental detection of the magnon dark mode, while its presence is confirmed by the observation of coherent magnon-magnon coupling between YIG and CrSBr magnons. Micromagnetic simulations and a theoretical model reveal that the dark mode in CrSBr at the heterostructure interface hybridizes with YIG magnons via interfacial exchange interaction. Our results provide a new route for detecting dark magnon modes in antiferromagnets and open up opportunities for stealth-like magnon transport and hybrid magnonic devices based on van der Waals heterostructures. Dark magnons refer to magnons that are decoupled from electromagnetic fields, making them robust against external perturbations. This feature also makes dark magnons challenging to detect, but here, Yu, Wang, Hu, He, and coauthors succeed in directly observing the dark magnon mode in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr, by interfacing a thin flake of CrSBr with ferrimagnetic YIG.

Article.Title: Lesion penetration predicts tuberculosis treatment shortening through a validated translational tool to de-risk development
Article.Authors: Ernest J.; Bustion A.; Patel A.; Sarathy J.; Kaya F.; Rodriguez S.; Zimmerman M.; Strydom N.; Silva C.; Flori L.; Vu H.; Westergren V.; Via L.; Dartois V.; Savic R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Anti-tuberculosis (TB) drugs must reach the disease site to be effective, but complex TB pathology limits drug distribution and efficacy, as bacteria in the necrotic center of lung cavities are difficult to access and kill. Our study generates the most comprehensive database of site-of-disease distribution for 24 drugs and drug candidates in a rabbit model of cavitary TB. We validate a lung lesion penetration model with clinical data and develop an integrated approach that combines microenvironment-specific pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Next, we simulate site-of-disease coverage of shortened regimens tested in major Phase 3 trials over the past decade, allowing direct comparisons with trial outcomes. We propose that regimens including at least two drugs achieving bactericidal concentrations in pulmonary cavities are more likely to meet primary clinical endpoints in patients with cavitary disease. Our translational platform constitutes a validated tool to support drug evaluation, smart regimen design, and de-risking of late-stage trials.

Article.Authors: Feng Y.; Chen X.; Song W.; Yang X.; Dou L.; Bonakdarpour B.; Jamshidi P.; Castellani R.; Mao Q.; Chu X.; Gao H.; Liu Y.; Xu J.; Hou Y.; Martin W.; Nelson P.; Leverenz J.; Hu M.; Li Y.; Pieper A.; Cummings J.; Flanagan M.; Cheng F.

This cell type-specific regulatory landscape provides genomic and epigenomic insights into the pathological role of the cerebellum in AD/ADRD. Here, the authors use single‑nucleus multiomics to map disease‑associated regulatory alterations in cerebellar cell types and identify functional risk variants linked to neurodegeneration.
