Article.Title: The basins of attraction of soft-sphere packings are not fractal
Article.Authors: Suryadevara P.; Casiulis M.; Martiniani S.
Article.Abstract: The energy landscape picture is a central tool to study many-body systems. In particular, the energy landscapes of glass-forming liquids, jammed packings, constraint satisfaction problems, or neural networks contain a plethora of minima corresponding to competing states. Due to their complexity, these landscapes resist analytical treatment and must be studied numerically. We focus on jammed soft spheres, a paradigmatic model of glasses and granulars, to expose the limitations of standard numerical methods in resolving the true structure of energy landscapes. We show that the C-language Variable-coefficients ordinary differential equation solver is the one with the best time-for-error trade-off for this problem, outperforming commonly used steepest-descent solvers by several orders of magnitude. Using this numerical approach, we provide unequivocal evidence that optimizers widely used in computational studies destroy all semblance of the true landscape geometry, even in moderately low dimensions. Employing a range of geometric indicators, both low- and high-dimensional, we show that earlier claims on the fractality of basins of attraction of minima originated from the use of inadequate mapping strategies. In reality, the basins of attraction of soft-sphere packings are smooth structures with well-defined length scales, a result that likely extends to a much broader family of problems.

Article.Title: Loss of tRNA uridine thiolation affects mRNA translation, protein production, and metabolite accumulation in Arabidopsis
Article.Authors: Dannfald A.; Cadoudal A.; Carpentier M.; Merret R.; Rigal Q.; Vialaret J.; Attina A.; Kindermans J.; Garcia Llorens S.; Berrissou C.; Tritsch L.; Koprivova A.; Welter B.; Marchand V.; Westhoff P.; David A.; Hirtz C.; Motorin Y.; Favory J.; Kopriva S.; Drouard L.; Deragon J.
Article.Abstract: It is well established in yeast and animal system that the level of uridine thiolation at position 34 of tRNA anticodon loops can impact the decoding potential of the corresponding codons. Using Arabidopsis thaliana , we confirm that the ability of the plant ribosome to decode AAA, GAA, and CAA codons is impaired when this thiol group is lost, leading to a reduction in protein production, especially for genes enriched in these codons. Interestingly, we observed that loss of tRNA thiolation results in variations in the levels of numerous proteins involved in sulfur-compound metabolism and amino acid biosynthesis. These variations, in turn, affect the accumulation of several sulfur-containing metabolites and amino acids, suggesting that the level of tRNA thiolation has a direct and profound impact on plant metabolism. We also demonstrate that U 34 thiolation is essential for adjusting plant growth in response to sulfur limitation and that its absence directly affects the plant’s interaction with bacteria, including both pathogens and beneficial organisms. Our results support the hypothesis that the level of tRNA thiolation can be used in plant to link nutritional status to translation.

Article.Title: Efficient and accurate steering of large language models through attention-guided feature learning
Article.Authors: Davarmanesh P.; Wilson A.; Radhakrishnan A.
Article.Abstract: Activation steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide large language model (LLM) responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly nonsteerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided framework for activation steering that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: 1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; 2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and 3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Topic Modeling; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Domain Adaptation and Few-Shot Learning

Article.Title: AI can persuade people to take political actions
Article.Authors: Hackenburg K.; Hewitt L.; Wagner C.; Summerfield C.; Tappin B.
Article.Abstract: There is substantial concern about the ability of advanced AI to influence people’s behavior. A rapidly growing body of research has found that AI can produce large persuasive effects on people’s attitudes, but whether AI can persuade people to take consequential real-world actions has remained unclear. In two large preregistered experiments ( N = 17 , 950 responses from 14,779 people), we used conversational AI models to persuade participants on a range of attitudinal and behavioral outcomes, including signing real petitions and donating money to charity. We found sizable AI persuasion effects on these behavioral outcomes (e.g. + 19.7 percentage points on petition signing). However, we observed no evidence of a correlation between AI persuasion effects on attitudes and effects on behavior. Moreover, we replicated prior findings that information provision drove effects on attitudes, but found no such evidence for our behavioral outcomes. In a test of eight behavioral persuasion strategies, the strategy focused on information provision produced the smallest behavioral effect, though differences among the eight were small. Taken together, these results suggest that previous findings relying on attitudinal outcomes may generalize poorly to behavior, and therefore risk substantially mischaracterizing the real-world behavioral impact of AI persuasion.

Article.Title: A promoter G-quadruplex recruits Hrb27C to regulate NEMO and immune defense against Lyme disease pathogens in the deer tick
Article.Authors: Lyu B.; Gao X.; Anderson D.; Stanley D.; Song Q.
Article.Abstract: Genomic DNA can adopt noncanonical secondary structures, such as G-quadruplexes (G4s), which serve as critical regulatory elements beyond the traditional double helix. Whether promoter G4s also participate in controlling innate immune signaling and host–pathogen interactions, however, remains unknown in arthropods. In this study, we identify a G4 structure within the promoter of the NEMO (NF-κB essential modulator) gene in the deer tick Ixodes scapularis . Using a combination of circular dichroism, isothermal difference spectra, and fluorescence-based assays, we demonstrate that this sequence forms a stable, parallel G4 topology in vitro and in vivo. Functional characterization via luciferase reporter assays reveals that this G4 scaffold is essential for proper NEMO transcriptional output. Importantly, disruption of the G4 structure significantly reduces NEMO expression and increases the burden of the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi . Genome-wide expression profiling further reveals that perturbation of the NEMO G4 produces transcriptional changes that overlap with those observed following NEMO silencing. These shared transcriptional responses are enriched for immune-associated genes and ribonucleoprotein-related pathways. We further identify the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein Hrb27C as a structural binding protein that specifically recognizes the NEMO G4 through its RNA recognition motif domains and facilitates NEMO expression. Collectively, our findings establish promoter G4 architecture as an important regulatory layer in tick immunity, linking DNA topology to pathogen proliferation and providing a structural framework for understanding host–pathogen dynamics in disease vectors.

Article.Title: Modulation of avian iridescence via melanogenesis
Article.Authors: Barbosa S.; Bittner C.; Arbore R.; Araújo P.; Pereira P.; Andrade P.; Fekete C.; Afonso R.; Afonso S.; Amorim M.; Marques C.; Nicolaï M.; Carita J.; Brejcha J.; Lopes R.; Alves J.; Cruz F.; Gómez-Garrido J.; Zamarreño C.; Gut M.; Alioto T.; Ali M.; Hilpert A.; Hecht A.; Spiecker E.
Article.Abstract: The iridescent colors of birds originate in nanoscale feather structures that interact with light. Although the physical principles governing avian iridescence are well established, the molecular mechanisms assembling these nanostructures into photonic materials remain unknown. Here, we integrated genomic, cellular, and optical approaches to investigate the molecular basis of iridescent color formation in birds. We leveraged mutations that arose in the domesticated Indian peafowl and natural color variation in wild birds. In peafowl, we identified eight genes underlying gains, losses, and shifts of iridescence, whereas in two wild species, we used single-cell transcriptomics to profile asymmetric feathers in which iridescent and noniridescent barbules develop on opposite sides of the same feather. We found that all peafowl mutations mapped to melanogenesis genes, showing that variation in this pathway can modify diverse geometric features of feather photonic nanostructures. Mutations altering melanin composition collapsed multilayered photonic systems and yielded noniridescent tissues, whereas changes in melanosome abundance, elongation, or deposition timing generated multilayer architectures with variable periodicity and color. We further show in peafowl that transitions from noniridescent to iridescent plumage were associated with single-nucleotide mutations in a melanogenesis gene, suggesting that, in species already capable of forming multilayered nanostructures, iridescence can be gained by relatively small genetic changes. Single-cell transcriptomes from wild species also supported extensive melanocyte-centered regulatory rewiring associated with iridescence, including changes in melanosome maturation, trafficking, and intercellular signaling. Together, these results show that the nanoscale order underlying iridescence is developmentally plastic and highly responsive to the melanogenic environment.

Article.Title: Poly(phenolic) deposition is a prerequisite to poly(aliphatic) deposition for functional potato suberin
Article.Authors: Esfandiari M.; Alabi I.; Dhaubhadel S.; Bernards M.
Article.Abstract: Suberin deposition in specialized cells is a critical aspect of plant protection, providing both water retention and pathogen protection functions. Tissue specific suberization during plant development is mirrored by its wound induction in cells that do not normally suberize and provides a robust experimental system to investigate the process. Suberized cells are characterized by a cell wall–associated lignin-like poly(phenolic) domain, and an ester-linked poly(aliphatic) domain, with the latter often laid down in distinct lamellar bands between the cell wall and plasma membrane. Previous work provides evidence that poly(phenolic) deposition precedes, and is necessary for, poly(aliphatic) deposition. To test this further, we generated RNAi knockdown lines of three wound-induced peroxidase genes, PRX19, PRX55, and PRX105 , in potato ( Solanum tuberosum ), the tubers of which produce an abundance of suberin upon wounding. Peroxidases catalyze the oxidative free radical coupling of phenolic monomers to form the suberin poly(phenolic) domain. The wound-induced suberin of PRX19-RNAi tubers had severely reduced poly(phenolics), reduced poly(aliphatics), and no apparent lamella. Functionally, wound-induced PRX19-RNAi tubers were more permeable to water loss and susceptible to bacterial soft rot. Overall, our data support the hypothesis that poly(phenolic) domain assembly is a strict requirement for subsequent deposition of aliphatic lamella within wound-induced suberin.

Article.Title: Physical origins of speed control in swimming fishes
Article.Authors: Seo J.; Zhou J.; Peterson A.; McHenry M.; Di Santo V.; Mittal R.
Article.Abstract: The linear relationship between tail-beat frequency and swimming speed in fish, first described by Bainbridge in 1958, has since been confirmed in species as disparate as eels and tuna. Dimensional scaling has explained why linearity should emerge at high Reynolds numbers, but the frequency–speed relationship itself has remained empirical, with no physical framework describing its behavior across swimming regimes, and no account of what sets the two quantities that define it: the distance covered per tail beat and the frequency below which forward motion supposedly ceases. Here, we derive a relationship from a balance of fin thrust, generated by a leading-edge vortex, and drag due to the boundary layer on the body. This framework yields an explicit expression for speed in terms of midline kinematics and body morphology. This formulation shows that the maximum stride length is set by the undulatory wavelength and the tail-beat phase offset, rather than by the conventional scaling metric of body length, and that no minimum frequency is required for forward motion. The model reproduces kinematic measurements from freely swimming glass catfish, published simulations, and Bainbridge’s original data. Without recalibration, it predicts the results of independent simulations spanning wide variations in wavelength, phase offset, and morphology to within ten percent. Linear scaling is thus one asymptotic limit of a more general propulsive relationship linking morphology and body-wave kinematics to swimming speed in fishes and bioinspired vehicles, where the body waveform, rather than the actuation frequency, emerges as the variable that sets performance.

Article.Title: Omega-3 fatty acids reprogram tumor-associated macrophage cytokine signaling and suppress pancreatic cancer growth
Article.Authors: Sakuma S.; Zhao S.; Hildreth A.; Liu G.; Shah V.; Sun M.; Tan S.; Jacobs E.; LaPorta M.; Furguiele J.; Avina-Ochoa N.; Globig A.; Tripple V.; N/A N/A.; Maier G.; Panda S.; Reyzer M.; Kang J.; Ma D.; Rodeheffer M.; Shaikh S.; Kaech S.; Liu A.; Chervonsky A.; Cassano A.
Article.Abstract: Dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) shape inflammatory signaling within the pancreatic tumor microenvironment (TME), but the cellular mechanisms underlying their effects on tumor progression remain unclear. Using orthotopic models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), we show that omega-3 (n-3) and omega-6 (n-6) PUFAs are differentially incorporated into tumor lipid pools, generating spatially heterogeneous lipid microenvironments. While an n-6–enriched diet accelerated PDAC growth, an n-3–enriched diet suppressed tumor growth in a T cell-independent manner. Examining inflammatory effects in PDAC tumors, the n-3 PUFA–enriched diet reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 family members, and single-cell and spatial analyses identified tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) as the primary diet-responsive population. Indeed, selective conversion of n-6 to n-3 fatty acids within myeloid cells using an inducible fat-1 transgene, which encodes an n-3 desaturase that converts n-6 to n-3 PUFAs in vivo, was sufficient to suppress tumor growth, whereas fibroblast-restricted conversion had no effect. This finding is the first to formally establish that cellular origin of PUFA metabolism within the TME is a key determinant of tumor progression and identifies TAMs as critical mediators of n-3–dependent tumor suppression. Furthermore, the n-3 PUFA–enriched diet reduced Arg1 + immunosuppressive TAMs and promoted C1q + and MHC-II + antigen-presenting TAM populations enriched for antigen processing machinery and T cell–recruiting chemokines, alongside reduced IL-6 family cytokine production. Together, these findings establish macrophages as key mediators of n-3–driven tumor control and define a mechanism by which dietary lipids remodel cytokine signaling in the PDAC microenvironment.

Article.Title: A muscle-enriched mitochondrial protein regulates postnatal heart growth through mitonuclear ubiquinone–PPAR signaling
Article.Authors: Hirose K.; Chen X.; Kalyanaraman C.; Waddingham M.; Nakamura M.; Zhang F.; Chen C.; Yao S.; Chang S.; Yu H.; Wang J.; Barca E.; Nakano H.; Hsu A.; Khyeam S.; Gonzalez Ortega S.; Tajima K.; Yoneshiro T.; Zhang H.; Padmanabhan A.; Kajimura S.; Haldar S.; Nakano A.; Murai M.; Fujihara Y.
Article.Abstract: Increased mitochondrial biogenesis and aerobic respiration in postnatal mammalian organs are essential for adaptation to extrauterine life, yet the functions of many tissue-enriched, developmentally regulated mitochondrial proteins remain poorly defined. By integrating mitochondrial proteome annotations with mouse and human transcriptomic datasets, we identified Coenzyme Q10a (Coq10a), a striated muscle-enriched mitochondrial protein, as a regulator of postnatal cardiac growth. Coq10a, the mammalian homolog of the yeast ubiquinone-binding protein Coq10p, is highly induced in the heart after birth through thyroid hormone-, Nkx2.5-, and Tbx5-dependent regulation. To define its physiological function, we generated three independent Coq10a -deficient mouse models. Both global and cardiomyocyte-specific loss of Coq10a promoted postnatal cardiac hypertrophy without impairing basal cardiac function or mitochondrial respiration. Instead, Coq10a deficiency altered intracellular ubiquinone partitioning, resulting in increased ubiquinone accumulation in a microsomal membrane fraction. Transcriptomic analyses revealed enrichment of PPAR-associated metabolic gene sets and induction of established PPAR-responsive genes in Coq10a -deficient hearts. Pharmacological inhibition of PPARα and PPARγ, but not PPARδ, attenuated the hypertrophic phenotype. Molecular dynamics simulations, docking analyses, and mutagenesis identified PPARα residues that contribute to differential responsiveness to ubiquinone. Although Coq10a -deficient hearts maintained near-normal function under basal conditions, they exhibited increased susceptibility to pressure-overload stress. Together, these findings establish Coq10a as a regulator of intracellular ubiquinone partitioning and support a model linking altered mitochondrial lipid distribution and PPAR-associated signaling to postnatal cardiac growth. More broadly, they demonstrate how tissue-enriched mitochondrial proteins can mediate organ-specific physiological functions beyond energy production.

Article.Title: Nuclear BbAtg8 interacts with BbMac1 as a transcriptional modulator to sustain nuclear copper homeostasis during conidial germination
Article.Authors: Ding J.; Qi G.; Ye D.; Li B.; Lu M.; Feng M.; Cai Q.; Ying S.
Article.Abstract: Pathogenic fungi endure host impose copper starvation by tightly coordinating trace metal homeostasis. However, how pathogens synchronize endogenous metal recycling with exogenous copper uptake to promote infection remains enigmatic. Using the entomopathogenic fungus Beauveria bassiana , we uncovered a synergistic regulatory network that prioritizes nuclear copper enrichment during conidial germination. Under copper deprivation, the fungus deploys a highly coordinated dual-track survival strategy. In the cytoplasm, the core autophagy protein BbAtg8 drives autophagic flux, specifically triggering mitophagy to degrade mitochondria, thereby promoting the turnover and mobilization of endogenous copper stores. Concurrently, a nonlipidated pool of BbAtg8 translocates to the nucleus to coordinate exogenous uptake. Within the nucleus, BbAtg8 directly interacts with the copper-fist transcription factor BbMac1 via a functional Atg8-interacting motif (AIM). This physical interaction serves as a potent transcriptional modulator, significantly enhancing BbMac1’s DNA-binding affinity. Consequently, the Atg8-Mac1 complex hyper-activates the expression of three functionally redundant copper transporters (BbCtr1, BbCtr2, and BbCtr4) to aggressively absorb extracellular copper. Strikingly, severe copper deprivation triggers a dynamic spatial enrichment of these classical copper transporters at the nuclear envelope, which correlates with the sustained maintenance of nuclear copper homeostasis required for essential genomic functions and full fungal virulence. Together, these findings reveal how pathogens synchronize mitophagy-mediated endogenous turnover with Mac1-driven exogenous uptake, fundamentally expanding the role of autophagy proteins BbAtg8 into direct transcriptional coordinators of metal homeostasis. This dual-track regulatory model not only deepens our understanding of fungal adaptation to nutritional immunity but also provides potential targets for disrupting copper homeostasis to control fungal pathogens.

Article.Title: S -adenosyl-L-homocysteine triggers an adaptive response that extends lifespan through the YBT1 ABC transporter
Article.Authors: Masumura K.; Kawasaki S.; Tsutsumi M.; Yamashita H.; Kanai M.; Nakajo H.; Yagi W.; Katsunoi S.; Yoneyama K.; Kawano-Kawada M.; Sekito T.; Ogawa T.; Soga T.; Mizunuma M.
Article.Abstract: S -adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) is a fundamental methyl donor; however, the physiological role of its byproduct and competitive inhibitor, S -adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH), remains unclear. Here, we show that transient reactive oxygen species (ROS) production triggered by SAH during the early logarithmic phase mimics partial SAH hydrolase inhibition, extending the yeast chronological lifespan (CLS) through a hormetic mechanism. This study reveals that the dual nature of ROS in aging is determined by the specific degree of SAH hydrolase activity. We identified the adenosine 5’-triphosphate-binding cassette (ABC) transporter Ybt1 as a key downstream effector of SAH. Ybt1 localizes to the vacuolar membrane and facilitates the sequestration of SAM from the cytosol into the vacuole. Notably, YBT1 overexpression extends CLS, mimicking SAH effects through an integrated pathway involving target of rapamycin complex 1 downregulation, autophagy, and adenosine 5’-monophosphate-activated protein kinase activation. Our findings establish that SAH acts as a metabolic signal coupling nutrient and energy availability to longevity via Ybt1, defining an adaptive/hormetic response for lifespan regulation in yeast.

Article.Title: A conserved Hox9–10 code underlies the early establishment of hind appendage progenitors in zebrafish and the Iberian ribbed newt
Article.Authors: Nakazawa H.; Urakawa K.; Maeno A.; Fujibayashi T.; Ishizaka M.; Ishizu A.; Asano T.; Matsubara H.; Takeuchi T.; Watakabe I.; Higashijima S.; Abe G.; Kawamura A.
Article.Abstract: The acquisition of paired appendages was a key innovation in vertebrate evolution. Although HoxA/D paralog groups (PGs) 9–13 play central roles in patterning paired fins and limbs, the evolutionary origin of this paired appendage-patterning system remains unknown. Here, we show that HoxA/D PG9–10 genes are essential for the early establishment of pelvic fin progenitors in zebrafish, and that Hox9–10 function is similarly required for hindlimb progenitor formation in the Iberian ribbed newt. In zebrafish, combined disruption of five HoxA/D PG9–10 genes abolishes the detectable pelvic fin progenitor population, resulting in complete loss of pelvic fins. A Tg(hoxa10b:EGFP) reporter labeled cells in the presumptive pelvic fin field before pelvic fin bud formation. Importantly, simultaneous CRISPR-mediated disruption of all seven Hox9–10 paralogs in the Iberian ribbed newt similarly impaired the establishment of hindlimb progenitors, suggesting that an early requirement for Hox9–10 function in hind appendage development predates the divergence of ray-finned and lobe-finned vertebrates. Together, these findings identify an evolutionarily conserved role for posterior Hox9–10 genes in the initial establishment of hind appendage progenitors. Because overlapping posterior Hox paralog groups are subsequently deployed during paired appendage patterning, this early Hox9–10 requirement provides a developmental link between the posterior axial Hox code and the paired appendage-patterning system. Our results are therefore consistent with the hypothesis that recruitment of a posterior Hox code into hind appendage progenitor formation contributed to the evolutionary assembly of the vertebrate paired appendage-patterning system.

Article.Title: Dynamic partitioning shapes the in vivo organization of the Escherichia coli RNA degradosome
Article.Authors: Troyer L.; Wang Y.; Wu K.; Kim S.; Kim S.
Article.Abstract: The bacterial RNA degradosome is a central mediator of RNA turnover, yet how its components are organized and regulated in living cells remains unclear. Using live-cell single-molecule imaging, we quantified the spatial distribution and dynamics of the four major Escherichia coli degradosome components: RNase E, RhlB, PNPase, and enolase. These proteins occupied distinct membrane-associated and cytoplasmic pools whose relative abundance varied among proteins and changed with physiological state. In particular, PNPase underwent pronounced redistribution between membrane-associated and cytoplasmic states in response to altered RNA availability and growth conditions, whereas RNase E and RhlB remained largely membrane associated. To determine the functional consequences of this organization, we examined the degradation of lacZ reporter transcripts with different translation initiation strengths. PNPase and RhlB preferentially promoted degradation of weakly translated transcripts, whereas strongly translated transcripts were largely insensitive to their loss. Together, these results reveal that the bacterial RNA degradosome is not a static, uniformly assembled molecular machine. Instead, RNA decay is organized through dynamic intracellular partitioning of degradosome components, linking physiological state and translation status to transcript degradation.

Article.Title: A “knob-in-hole” gate in the antibody C <sub>H</sub> 1 domain underlies subclass-independent IgA hinge cleavage by the commensal metallopeptidase IgAse
Article.Authors: Sebastián Ramírez-Larrota J.; Estivill G.; López-Martín M.; Effantin G.; Gragera M.; Sorzano C.; Marcos E.; Eckhard U.; Gomis-Rüth F.
Article.Abstract: Human immunoglobulin (Ig) A (IgA) protects ≈400 m 2 of mucosae from microbes. Bacterial IgA-peptidases subvert this defense by cleaving the F ab –F c hinge of subclass IgA1 while sparing the hinge-divergent, colon-dominant IgA2 subclass. The exception is IgAse, a ≈140-kDa, seven-domain, membrane-bound metallopeptidase from the colonic commensal Thomasclavelia ramosa that targets both subclasses but no other protein. We previously narrowed the minimal functional assembly down to the IgAse catalytic and wrapping domains (CD and WD) plus the IgA1/2 F ab ′, i.e., the hinge and a F ab of light and heavy chains (LC, HC), each with a variable and a constant Ig domain (V L + C L , V H + C H 1). The transient interaction culminates in cleavage of a proline–valine bond within the first two hinge residues, downstream of a conserved C-terminal C H 1 disulfide (SS2). Here, single-particle cryoelectron microscopy of a disulfide-stabilized minimal IgAse:IgA2 F ab ′ complex yielded high-quality density strongly supporting two states along the cleavage reaction coordinate, a “recognition complex” and a subsequent “precatalytic complex,” in which F ab ′ binds frontally to the IgAse CD via a C H 1 β-sheet and overhang loop LβEβF. This loop binds like a knob to a preformed hole in the active-site cleft. Binding rearranges the knob and rotates SS2 ≈ 180°, enabling access of the hinge into the cleft of the otherwise unaffected precatalytic complex. Together, this work defines a unique, C H 1-mediated hinge-delivering “gate” mechanism, validated by a crystal structure of unbound IgA2 F ab , point mutations disrupting the C H 1:CD interface, and molecular dynamics calculations, which provide the structural framework for subclass-independent IgA cleavage.

Article.Title: Controlled functionalization of cellulose nanocrystals directs polymer-specific protein coronas and immune cell interactions
Article.Authors: Fuku R.; Giuliana P.; Liu Y.; Kumar B.; Malhotra K.; Jiang V.; Sedighi A.; Gunning P.; Edgar L.; Winnik M.
Article.Abstract: Polymer coatings are widely used to suppress nonspecific protein adsorption and modulate nanoparticle–cell interactions. However, the biological outcomes of polymer-functionalized nanoparticles remain difficult to predict in complex biological environments because protein corona formation rapidly alters nanoparticle identity. This challenge is particularly pronounced when hydrophobic moieties are incorporated for imaging or therapeutic applications, as they can promote nonspecific interactions at the nano–bio interface. Herein, we establish a modular grafting-to platform based on cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) that enables systematic comparison of polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based, zwitterionic, and acrylamide-based polymers with controlled grafting density and chain conformation on a common porphyrin-modified surface. We demonstrate that dense polymer brushes reduce nonspecific protein adsorption in single-protein assays. By contrast, all CNC surfaces form dynamic coronas upon exposure to serum proteins, while specific polymer coatings selectively enrich or suppress distinct protein populations. We further demonstrate that polymer-dependent immune cell interactions are substantially reduced following protein corona formation, although differences among polymer chemistries persist. Zwitterionic coatings broadly suppress immune cell interactions, whereas PEG-based coatings preferentially promote interactions with antigen-presenting cells. These findings establish design principles for polymer-functionalized nanoparticles with specific immune cell interaction profiles.

Article.Title: Nitrogen deposition does not alter the temperate forest soil carbon pool: A 14-y experiment on varied nitrogen fertilization
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Hobbie S.; Schlesinger W.; Sun T.
Article.Abstract: Soil carbon (C) pools in nitrogen-limited temperate forests are critical to the global C cycle, but there are no long-term experiments examining soil C, with various nitrogen (N) forms. Here, a 14-y experiment (100 kg N ha −1 y −1 ), with added N simulating atmospheric deposition proportions (~70% inorganic, ~30% organic) did not affect soil C pools, whereas organic N (ON) and inorganic N (IN) individually significantly increased values by 2.7-fold and 1.8-fold, respectively. Although no treatment significantly affected soil pH, treatment effects on pH were negatively associated with soil C pools. In addition, treatments containing ON forms increased mineral-associated organic C fractions, indicating enhanced C stability vs. IN. These findings enhance our understanding of N deposition-soil C pool interactions.

Article.Title: Membrane contact activation of Piezo2 drives lysosome–mitochondrion Ca 2+ transfer and signaling in Trypanosoma cruzi
Article.Authors: Huang G.; Docampo R.
Article.Abstract: Calcium ion (Ca 2+ ) transfer from other organelles is central to mitochondrial metabolism and cell survival, yet how mechanical forces regulate interorganelle communication remains unclear. Here we report a lysosome-to-mitochondrion pathway in Trypanosoma cruzi , the etiologic agent of Chagas disease, mediated by the mechano/osmosensitive channel TcPiezo2. Using ultrastructural, biochemical, and live-cell superresolution imaging, we define lysosome–mitochondrion contact sites (LMCs) that enable direct Ca 2+ transfer. TcPiezo2 triggers Ca 2+ release, which generates perilysosomal nanodomains that drives mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake via the voltage-dependent anion channel and the mitochondrial Ca 2+ uniporter complex. Disruption of TcPiezo2-dependent Ca 2+ transfer impairs mitochondrial metabolism, perturbs redox homeostasis, induces autophagy, and eventually leads to parasite death. These findings establish LMCs as a signaling platform that directly regulates interorganelle Ca 2+ transfer and mitochondrial bioenergetics.

Article.Title: Thermal imbalance drives avian performance and responses to climate warming
Article.Authors: Porter C.; Adams D.; Levy O.; Urinovsky N.; Riddell E.
Article.Abstract: Thermal performance curves are widely used to predict ectothermic responses to climate warming but are less effective for predicting endotherm performance across environmental conditions because thermoregulation often decouples body temperature from ambient temperature. We develop theory and provide empirical evidence for performance curves in endotherms structured by net sensible heat flux (Q), an integrative index of thermoregulatory imbalance. Using biophysical simulations in tree swallows, we show that performance varies predictably with Q (which we term “QPCs”), thereby explaining variation in nestling provisioning performance, reproductive fitness, and geographic limits, while also forecasting responses to climate change. We also demonstrate that thermal imbalance helps shape breeding ranges of birds across North America. Our findings introduce Q as a broadly relevant ecophysiological dimension that constrains performance in endotherms and provides a framework for predicting endotherm responses to climate warming.

Article.Title: Global origins of tuna and billfish fisheries reveal the transition from coastal access to oceanic exploitation
Article.Authors: Rick T.; Andrews A.; Béarez P.; Festa M.; Fossile T.; Hudson M.; Janßen-Kim M.; Juan-Jordá M.; Lambrides A.; LeFebvre M.; Luthra A.; Newsom B.; O’Connor S.; Quintana Morales E.; Spiess A.; Zancan C.; Zimmer C.; Smith E.
Article.Abstract: Ocean ecosystems have played a crucial role in people’s lives around the world for millennia. However, questions persist about when, why, and how people first began removing biomass from offshore habitats and established fisheries in distant, oceanic environments. We explore the antiquity and evolution of tuna (Thunnini) and billfish (Istiophoridae/Xiphiidae) fisheries, two groups of fishes that occur around the world, are economically significant, and are ecologically important open ocean apex predators. The earliest archaeological evidence of fishing for tuna occurs ~44,000 years ago and billfish at ~10,000 years ago, with early fisheries for some tuna species appearing around the world by 3,000 to 1,000 years ago. Most early fisheries are in areas where tunas and billfishes could be accessed relatively close to shore (e.g., submarine canyons) and/or where these fishes may come inshore seasonally or during warm ocean events. Early tuna and billfish fisheries were often linked to ceremony/ritual, alongside advances in maritime technologies. With few exceptions, sustained and intensive commercial exploitation of pelagic predators in offshore and oceanic habitats is a late development in the human past, occurring primarily during the last 200 y. Our findings document a long-term continuum of human interactions with global marine ecosystems spanning thousands of years, including significant differences between the timing and pathways by which people became dominant ecological drivers in nearshore compared to offshore/oceanic ecosystems.

Article.Title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
Article.Authors: Lu Y.; Lu T.; Zhang D.; Ye L.; Li H.
Article.Abstract: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.

Article.Title: Tipping point forecasting in nonstationary dynamics on function spaces
Article.Authors: Liu-Schiaffini M.; Singer C.; Kovachki N.; Leung S.; Bae H.; Azizzadenesheli K.; Anandkumar A.
Article.Abstract: Tipping points are abrupt, drastic, and often irreversible changes in the evolution of nonstationary and chaotic dynamical systems. For instance, increased greenhouse gas concentrations are predicted to lead to drastic decreases in low cloud cover, referred to as a climatological tipping point. In this paper, we learn the evolution of such nonstationary dynamical systems using a recurrent neural operator (RNO), which learns mappings between function spaces. After training RNO on only the pre-tipping dynamics, we employ it to detect future tipping points using an uncertainty-based approach. In particular, we propose a conformal prediction framework to forecast tipping points by monitoring deviations from physics constraints (such as conserved quantities and partial differential equations), enabling forecasting of these abrupt changes along with a rigorous measure of uncertainty. We illustrate our proposed methodology on nonstationary ordinary and partial differential equations, such as the Lorenz-63 and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equations. We also apply our methods to forecast a climate tipping point in stratocumulus cloud cover and airfoil wake and stall transitions using only limited knowledge of the governing equations. For the latter, we show that our proposed method zero-shot generalizes to forecasting multiple future tipping points under varying Reynolds numbers. In our experiments, we demonstrate that even partial or approximate physics constraints can be used to accurately forecast future tipping points.

Article.Title: The historical domestication of a Clostridium botulinum strain used for the industrial production of botulinum neurotoxin
Article.Authors: Keim P.; Nottingham R.; Guevara M.; Miller E.; Vogler A.; Williamson C.; Smith T.; Posner R.; Pellett S.; Lenski R.; Sahl J.
Article.Abstract: Laboratory production of botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) began more than 90 y ago for medical, military, and later pharmaceutical applications, creating one of the longest-running examples of microbial cultivation under sustained human control. A single Clostridium botulinum Group I lineage, Army Hall A (AHA), was established by the US military in 1942 and later gave rise to Hall A-hyper (HAH), the strain widely used for pharmaceutical BoNT production. We analyzed more than 1,000 C. botulinum genomes to identify AHA’s closest relatives and to infer the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) shared with its nearest lineage. Relative to this MRCA, AHA accumulated nearly 100 genetic changes, including 46 single-nucleotide substitutions, 44 small insertions or deletions, and several large deletions and structural variants that led to the loss of more than 80 genes. A nonsense mutation in mutS generated a hypermutator phenotype that accelerated mutation rates and increased genetic diversity. This event is inferred to have occurred early in the lineage’s domestication and appears to have facilitated laboratory-adaptive traits, including the lack of sporulation and increased BoNT yield. Competition experiments under standard growth conditions confirmed substantial laboratory adaptation, with AHA exhibiting a strong fitness advantage over a close relative. Together, these results reconstruct the genomic trajectory of a bacterium evolving under prolonged human-mediated selection and provide a genome-resolved example of microbial domestication. The findings show how laboratory conditions, industrial selection, and changing mutation rates can shape bacterial evolution, and they offer a general framework for understanding domestication and laboratory adaptation across microbial systems.

Article.Title: Multivalent weak contacts shape chaperone–nascent protein interactions
Article.Authors: Rajasekaran N.; Toptygin D.; Liao T.; Hilser V.; Ha T.; Kaiser C.
Article.Abstract: Molecular chaperones interact with non-native proteins, playing crucial roles in preventing misfolding and in enabling efficient folding in the cellular environment. Trigger factor is a bacterial chaperone that binds to ribosomes, interacting with nascent polypeptides emerging from the ribosome and guiding their early folding steps. In contrast to the central role of the chaperone in promoting folding of newly synthesized proteins, its dynamic interactions with nascent chains emerging from the ribosome remain poorly understood. Here, we use single-molecule fluorescence and optical tweezers approaches to directly observe and characterize trigger factor interactions with a ribosome-bound client protein at increasing chain lengths. We find that trigger factor dwell times on ribosome–nascent chain complexes increase non-monotonically with nascent chain length, and that binding to nascent proteins is best described by a combination of multiple weak, dynamic interactions that are established after the chaperone docks onto the ribosome and evolve during polypeptide elongation. Application of mechanical force perturbs trigger factor binding, supporting a multivalent interaction model. This binding mode may help to stabilize nascent proteins against misfolding while allowing them to dynamically sample conformational space in search of their native structures.

Article.Title: Quantum-enhanced sensing of molecular excited-state dynamics with correlated photons
Article.Authors: Fan J.; Liu F.; Lei D.; Mukamel S.; Zhang Z.
Article.Abstract: Squeezed photons, which provide a quantum-correlated light with reduced noise, have emerged as a powerful resource for sensing the structures of matter. Here, we study the pump–probe scheme using squeezed photons whose spectral correlation of amplitudes can be tailored. A microscopic theory reveals a highly time-energy-resolved signal that is not attainable by classical pump–probe scheme. The results show high selectivity of accessing the molecular correlation functions, e.g., suppression of ground-state bleaching signal, and can significantly enhance signal intensity that surpasses the bottleneck by entangled twin photons. An application to a monolayer semiconductor model reveals a real-time monitoring of valley excitons and their dynamics, i.e., conversion between dark and bright excitons. We further show the intermediate squeezing regime–not strong squeezing–where time-resolved spectroscopy is favorable. Our work offers a paradigm for studying nonequilibrium dynamics of matter, in photocatalysis and optoelectronics.

Article.Title: Mechanistic versus descriptive interpretation of brain activity pattern reconstruction
Article.Authors: Jung K.; Eickhoff S.; Patil K.
Article.Abstract: The geometric eigenmodes, derived from the shape of the cortical surface, have been suggested as a better model for explaining brain function due to their high accuracy in reconstructing patterns of both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked brain activity patterns captured by functional MRI, when contrasted with alternative models including structural connectome derived bases. While a descriptive representation offers valuable utility for neuroimaging studies, it is necessary to examine the extent to which it supports a mechanistic explanation for human brain function. Although the observation that geometric eigenmodes accurately fit brain activity is intriguing, we argue that accepting them as a model of brain function risks conflating descriptive and mechanistic interpretations. While a representation that effectively describes the underlying geometry is inherently adept at fitting patterns within that geometric space; it does not necessarily shed light on mechanisms that give rise to the brain’s functional attributes. To this end, we provide two lines of empirical results: a) geometric eigenmodes demonstrate a high flexibility when fit to a range of manipulated patterns, and b) localized parcel-based representations can reconstruct activity patterns as well. Based on those results, theoretical considerations, and previous data, we argue that more consideration is needed regarding the complementary roles of descriptive representation and mechanistic explanation in neuroimaging research. While we recognize the potential role of the brain’s geometry in influencing its dynamics, assertions regarding its efficacy should be weighed against its inherent lack of specificity, biological interpretability, and anatomical evidence.

Article.Title: Global proteolysis during starvation governs proteome remodeling and a survival–regrowth trade-off in bacteria
Article.Authors: Manzanarez G.; Balakrishnan R.; Kannan H.; Abele M.; Okano H.; She F.; Zhang Z.; Wu C.; Freiman L.; Ludwig C.; Mori M.; Hwa T.
Article.Abstract: Starving bacteria must synthesize stress proteins to survive, but how protein synthesis persists in the absence of nutrient influx is unclear. We show that in Escherichia coli , carbon starvation triggers large-scale proteome remodeling, with global proteolysis supplying both the amino acids (AAs) and ATP for protein synthesis. This remodeling occurs in two phases, with a short preparatory phase relying on constitutive proteolytic machinery and fueled by residual carbon waste, and a more extended phase, relying on starvation-induced protein components synthesized during the preparatory phase and fueled by AA catabolism. The starvation-induced protein degradation (SPD) program dominating the extended phase depends on YeaG, a little-known, broadly conserved protein highly expressed in stationary phase under the control of the general stress sigma factor RpoS. SPD fuels the synthesis of stress proteins, including those in the RpoS regulon and AA catabolic enzymes, markedly enhancing survival and accounting for much of the viability benefit conferred by RpoS during carbon starvation. However, in mutants where an energy source can be supplemented without enabling biomass growth, SPD and the accompanying protein synthesis are largely dispensable for survival, indicating that a primary physiological function of the synthesized stress proteins is to conserve or recycle energy during carbon starvation. Because SPD targets biosynthetic enzymes nonspecifically, proteome remodeling via SPD imposes a fundamental trade-off between long-term survival and short-term metabolic activity, manifested as a lag before regrowth upon nutrient replenishment. Together, these findings establish SPD as a general physiological strategy shaping protein synthesis and survival in nongrowing bacteria.

Article.Title: Pollen tube integrity is critical for thermotolerance in tomato and is enhanced by loss of SlRALF1
Article.Authors: Almasaud R.; Yimga Ouonkap S.; Ingram J.; Oseguera Y.; Alosman M.; Travis C.; Hou J.; Henry A.; Medina M.; Oulhen N.; Pryze K.; DaSilva N.; Molina C.; Lisi G.; Pease J.; Palanivelu R.; Wessel G.; DeLong A.; Johnson M.
Article.Abstract: Reproductive success of angiosperms depends on the ability of pollen to build a highly polarized cellular extension (the pollen tube) that delivers sperm to female gametes for fertilization. This process is highly temperature sensitive, but we lack information about how heat stress affects pollen function and the molecular pathways that impart thermotolerance. Here we show that maintaining cellular integrity during pollen tube germination and extension is the pollen performance parameter that distinguishes thermosensitive from thermotolerant tomato cultivars and that loss-of-function of one of four pollen-expressed Rapid Alkalinization Factor (RALF) signaling peptides can enhance thermotolerance. Moreover, we found that heat stress antagonizes RALF signaling required to maintain patterns of pectin distribution in the pollen tube cell wall to ensure integrity. These findings establish a molecular framework for understanding how pollen tube growth is modulated in response to the environment and show that RALF signaling can be altered to achieve thermotolerant pollen tube growth.

Article.Title: Synthetic reconstitution of planar polarity initiation reveals principles of symmetry breaking across scales
Article.Authors: Wallach L.; Thomas C.; Li P.
Article.Abstract: Development often relies on molecular prepatterning over large tissue scales, and how these patterns emerge is an essential question. Planar cell polarity (PCP), manifested as asymmetric distribution of junctional proteins within individual cells and coordinated across entire tissues, is a key module controlling tissue morphogenesis and organization. How tissues break symmetry to initiate PCP remains unknown. By reconstituting polarity initiation ex vivo using engineered epithelial cells, we found that collective migration acts as the symmetry-breaking cue, inducing front–back enrichment of CELSR junctions and establishing aligned multicellular CELSR polarity. Individual cells directly interpret the migration cue and remain sensitive to it. Strikingly, CELSR polarity arises without reciprocal VANGL–FZD interactions, identifying CELSR as the driver for polarity initiation. These findings reveal that collective migration initiates and coordinates PCP across molecular, cellular, and tissue scales, demonstrating that morphogenetic events act as a trigger for spatial pattern emergence.

Article.Title: Microbial niche partitioning explains N <sub>2</sub> O distributions and cycling in marine oxygen minimum zones
Article.Authors: McCoy D.; Sun X.; Buchanan P.; Zakem E.
Article.Abstract: Oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) are marine hotspots for cycling and emission of the powerful greenhouse gas nitrous oxide (N 2 O). Steep redox gradients host diverse microbial communities that produce and consume N 2 O, generating a characteristic vertical distribution, with low concentrations in anoxic cores and supersaturated accumulation in surrounding oxyclines. Although the accumulation is commonly attributed to stronger O 2 inhibition of N 2 O consumption than production, this differential inhibition is not consistently observed, suggesting that interactions among nitrogen-cycling metabolisms may provide additional mechanisms. To evaluate the ecological controls on the N 2 O profile, we embed a trait-based ecosystem model into an eddy-resolving simulation of the Eastern Tropical South Pacific OMZ. In this framework, redox energetics, metabolite exchange, competition, and grazing structure microbial growth, setting emergent niches of microbial functional types, particularly aerobic ammonia oxidizers and diverse anaerobic denitrifiers that mediate N 2 O cycling. In the anoxic core, cross-feeding tightly couples denitrifiers that produce and consume N 2 O, maintaining low concentrations. As O 2 increases in the oxycline, competition with aerobic metabolisms and intensified grazing gradually exclude denitrifiers. However, because they draw on more abundant substrates, N 2 O-producing denitrifiers persist to higher O 2 than N 2 O consumers, reflecting the vulnerability of populations dependent on intermediate metabolites. This ecological decoupling drives N 2 O accumulation and captures the characteristic double-peaked vertical structure without imposing physiological O 2 intolerance thresholds. More broadly, by revealing how niche partitioning and producer–consumer coupling shape other features of OMZ biogeochemistry, these results provide a basis for projecting future shifts in marine nitrogen loss and N 2 O emissions.

Article.Title: Environmental chemical mixtures reprogram mammary epithelial development to epigenetic states associated with breast cancer
Article.Authors: Parrish M.; Seraj M.; Nikoueian H.; Traugh N.; Chen A.; Gupta P.; Monti S.; Kuperwasser C.
Article.Abstract: Environmental exposures occur as complex mixtures, yet the mechanisms by which they alter human tissue development and generate cancer-relevant tissue states remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a physiologically relevant 3D human breast organoid high-content screening platform that relates exposure-induced developmental disruption to cancer-relevant cell states. Screening of structurally diverse environmental chemicals as single agents and mixtures reveals heterogeneous but reproducible developmental responses, indicating that distinct environmental chemicals perturb different aspects of mammary morphogenesis. Focusing on bisphenols, we show that a low-dose mixture (BPA, BPS, and BPF; 3BPX) disrupts organoid development and induces transcriptional programs characterized by extracellular matrix remodeling, epithelial plasticity, and partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition, accompanied by widespread DNA methylation remodeling. A 3BPX exposure signature maps to ER+ luminal breast cancers and is preferentially enriched in invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC), a subtype characterized by epithelial plasticity. The 3BPX-associated methylation signature is detectable in primary tumors and adjacent normal tissue and is enriched in ILC. Together, these findings show that environmentally relevant chemical mixtures induce heterogeneous developmental perturbations that converge on conserved transcriptional and epigenetic programs associated with epithelial plasticity and tissue remodeling. These exposure-associated signatures are represented in defined epithelial and stromal compartments in human breast cancers, supporting a model in which developmental exposures may establish field-like, cancer-relevant tissue states.

Article.Title: An integrative transcriptomic atlas of ALS and aging skeletal muscle defines shared and distinct molecular programs of degeneration
Article.Authors: Grima-Terrén M.; Rommelfanger M.; Campanario S.; Calls-Cobos A.; Cisneros A.; Ramírez-Pardo I.; Chou G.; Zheng Y.; Hah N.; Serrano A.; Perdiguero E.; Isern J.; Muñoz-Cánoves P.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal muscle atrophy and weakness resulting from loss of motor neuron innervation are shared hallmarks of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and age-associated sarcopenia. However, muscle wasting in ALS is rapid and severe, whereas sarcopenia progresses gradually over decades, peaking at an advanced age. The molecular mechanisms underlying muscle wasting in these conditions remain incompletely defined. Here, we used the SOD1 G93A ALS mouse model and wild-type mice across the lifespan to generate an integrated single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of skeletal muscle, mapping changes associated with ALS and aging. This atlas is complemented by structural and functional analyses. Our results identify transcriptionally distinct condition-specific myonuclear states, including disease-responsive programs within synaptic myonuclei at the neuromuscular junction, that are shared or distinct between the two conditions. Notably, at early stages, muscle from ALS mice exhibits molecular hallmarks of aged muscle at the myofiber level, indicating premature aging and reinforcing aging as a risk factor in ALS. At advanced disease stages and in old age, myonuclear subpopulations follow similar degenerative pathways in fast glycolytic fibers, consistent with their loss in both conditions. However, a distinct ALS-enriched myonuclei subpopulation displays uniquely regulated genes not observed in aged muscle, potentially underlying the more rapid and severe pathology observed in ALS. This atlas maps shared and divergent mechanisms of muscle degeneration in ALS and sarcopenia and provides a resource for identifying therapeutic targets tailored to each condition.

Article.Title: Drivers of the likelihood of evolutionary rescue in response to novel infectious diseases
Article.Authors: Balstad L.; Baskett M.
Article.Abstract: The introduction of novel infectious diseases has caused significant declines in many species, and in some cases, local extinction. Simultaneously, hosts might adapt to these novel pathogens, allowing population recovery, an example of evolutionary rescue (ER). Novel infectious diseases differ from sudden, abiotic stressors in that disease only impacts a subset of individuals within the population and individuals might be affected for a finite period. Whether ER occurs in an infectious disease context, and how likely it is relative to abiotic stress, might depend on both host and pathogen characteristics such as the scale of transmission (e.g., local density-dependent transmission only or additional infection through an external reservoir), the degree of fatality or immunity, and the adaptive pathway in terms of whether adaptive alleles reduce mortality, reduce likelihood of infection, or enhance recovery. Here, we use a stochastic mathematical model of host-pathogen dynamics with evolution of a novel allele conferring disease robustness to quantify how population trajectories, including the probability of and time to ER, vary across adaptive pathways and disease characteristics. We find that ER is more likely to occur with dynamical disease transmission compared to a lasting stressor that affects the entire population, indicating that protecting a subset of the population from stress facilitates ER. Among cases with disease transmission, ER is generally more likely to occur with the adaptation of mortality-blocking alleles and sources of transmission that include an external reservoir.

Article.Title: Distinct functional open states of the polymodal nociceptor TRPV1
Article.Authors: Lee B.; Li S.; Vu S.; Yao Z.; Tian Y.; Yarov-Yarovoy V.; Zheng J.
Article.Abstract: The polymodal nociceptor TRPV1 integrates diverse physical and chemical stimuli, yet whether these inputs drive a common activated state remains unresolved. Here, we show that TRPV1 activators stabilize functionally distinct open states that yield discrete single-channel conductance levels. These functional states appear to arise from distinct open-pore conformations, as evidenced by anomalous mole fraction effect measurements. Structurally, stimulus-specific changes in pore conformation were directly observed using site-directed fluorescence recordings, consistent with Rosetta-guided structural models. Notably, coactivation by two stimuli markedly slows channel opening rather than producing synergistic acceleration, suggesting potential conformational incompatibility across subunits. Together, these findings define TRPV1 gating as a stimulus-partitioned, multistate process and highlight opportunities for selective modulation of TRPV1 in pain management.

Article.Title: Restructuring hydrogen-bonding networks via hydroxyl-functionalized covalent organic frameworks for efficient nitrate electroreduction
Article.Authors: Zhang R.; Zhang H.; Duan H.; Han D.; Li X.; Wang Z.; Mao R.; Cai M.; Zhu Y.; Huang H.; Qu W.; Cortes E.; Zhang D.
Article.Abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR) is a promising strategy for nitrate removal and ammonia synthesis, but its efficiency is largely limited by sluggish proton transfer kinetics and poor reaction selectivity. Herein, we rationally design a series of hydroxyl-functionalized copper phthalocyanine-based covalent organic frameworks (Cu-COF-nOH) to regulate interfacial proton transfer via restructuring hydrogen-bonding networks. The hydroxyl functional groups in Cu-COF-nOH enhance water adsorption and dissociation to enrich interfacial proton supply. Optimized hydroxyl loading further induces the formation of continuous hydrogen-bond chains, enabling oriented and accelerated proton shuttling toward Cu active centers instead of stochastic diffusion. Electrocatalytic tests in 0.5 M nitrate electrolyte show that the optimal Cu-COF-4OH catalyst achieves an ammonia Faradaic efficiency of 93.20% and an NH 3 yield rate of 65.84 mg·h −1 , along with excellent long-term stability, outperforming most state-of-the-art NO 3 RR electrocatalysts. Combined with in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations, we clearly clarify that hydroxyl-mediated hydrogen-bonding restructuring plays a critical role in boosting proton transfer kinetics and reaction selectivity. This work provides a versatile interface engineering strategy for efficient multiproton/electron-coupled electrocatalytic reactions, offering insights into the design of high-performance NO 3 RR catalysts.

Article.Title: LEAP2 mediates long-term inhibition of orexigenic neurons of the hypothalamus in mice
Article.Authors: Giovanini L.; Cornejo M.; Gomez I.; Wanionok N.; De Francesco P.; Heredia F.; Castrogiovanni D.; Urrutia L.; Falasco G.; Cantel S.; Fehrentz J.; Schiöth H.; Perello M.
Article.Abstract: Liver-expressed antimicrobial peptide 2 (LEAP2) acts via the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHSR) to reduce food intake, yet the central mechanisms underlying its anorectic effects remain unclear. Here, we show that circulating LEAP2 accesses discrete brain regions, including the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH), where it targets orexigenic AgRP/NPY neurons. Despite the negligible local expression in the hypothalamus, LEAP2 peptide is detectable in this brain region and in the cerebrospinal fluid, suggesting peripheral origin and central retention. Using fluorescent tracers, in vivo, ex vivo, and in vitro approaches indicate that LEAP2 exhibits prolonged binding to GHSR at the plasma membrane without promoting receptor internalization, thereby limiting subsequent ghrelin action. Using male mice, we found that central or systemic LEAP2 pretreatment results in a sustained inhibition of ghrelin-induced feeding that lasts for several hours after pretreatment. Notably, LEAP2 also suppresses food intake and c-Fos induction triggered by pharmacogenetic activation of AgRP neurons, indicating a broader inhibitory control over these circuits. Together, our findings establish that LEAP2 acts as a persistent inhibitor of hypothalamic orexigenic centers, providing a mechanistic framework for its long-lasting anorectic effects. These results highlight LEAP2 as a key regulator of energy balance and support its potential as a therapeutic target for obesity and metabolic disorders.

Article.Title: Interpersonal value regulates infection-risky social contact across 61 societies
Article.Authors: Sun H.; Spadaro G.; Pelica S.; Kamiloğlu R.; Abrahams L.; Ackerman J.; Adams S.; Al-Shawaf L.; Alvergne A.; Amponsah B.; Andersen N.; Antfolk J.; Atamtürk Duyar D.; Bai S.; Barbato M.; Barbosa S.; Barclay P.; Becker D.; de Souza B.; Boggio P.; Böhm R.; Boonyasiriwat W.; Camperio Ciani A.; Can A.; Case T.
Article.Abstract: Interpersonal contact is essential for cooperation and care, but it also provides a route for pathogen transmission between individuals. Hence, a key challenge for social organisms involves maintaining beneficial social contact while also limiting exposure to infection risks. Existing proposals suggest that this trade-off is guided by the interpersonal value of specific social targets. In addition, ecological and cultural factors, including historical pathogen prevalence, individualism-collectivism, tightness–looseness, and relational mobility, might also shape how people avoid pathogens. To test whether and how infection-risky social contact varies with individual-level interpersonal value and these societal-level factors, we collected data from 47,756 participants across 61 societies. Participants were randomly assigned to picture a social target - either a friend, acquaintance, stranger, or enemy. They then rated their comfort with infection-risky contact with that target (e.g., drinking from the same water bottle) and whether they would touch the target when greeting them. In all societies, participants were more comfortable with infection-risky contact and more likely to engage in physical contact during greetings with targets of higher interpersonal value. Such associations varied only modestly across societies. Notably, the associations between infection-risky contact and societal-level factors depended on target interpersonal value and were concentrated among high-value targets—contact was lower where historical pathogen prevalence and tightness were greater and higher where individualism and relational mobility were greater. These findings suggest that infection-risky contact is primarily guided by the value of social targets, with ecological and cultural factors playing a lesser role.

Article.Title: Changing contributions of emotion and reward information to learning through adolescence
Article.Authors: Phaneuf-Hadd C.; Phelps E.; Somerville L.
Article.Abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8 to 22 y completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hampered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially hindered by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

Article.Title: Abiotic conversion of nitrate to ammonium enhances nitrogen use efficiency in paddy soils
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Wang M.; Li H.; Li J.; Xu J.; Zhang N.; Zhu C.; Shan J.; Zhu G.; Zhu Y.
Article.Abstract: Nitrogen (N) use efficiency is critical in ensuring food production while reducing nitrate (NO 3 − -N) to ammonium (NH 4 + -N) is widely recognized as a key for reducing N loss from paddy fields. Microbial involvement has long been regarded as the indispensable step for NO 3 − -N reduction to NH 4 + -N in nature; it remains largely unknown whether abiotic processes can drive this. Here, using laser confocal fluorescence microscopy and thermodynamic laws, we find that Fe(II) ions in the rice rhizosphere exist on iron plaque in a specific manner with strong reducing capability. These specifically adsorbed Fe(II) ions (Fe(II) SA ) could mediate the abiotic reduction of NO 3 − -N to NH 4 + -N, accounting for 57% of the total NO 3 − -N reduction. When cultured in a sterile nutrient solution containing only 15 NO 3 − -N and Fe(II) ions, over 90% of N in the xylem of rice plants exists as 15 NH 4 + -N, directly proving the occurrence of NO 3 − -N reduction to NH 4 + -N and taken up by rice. Theoretical calculations elucidate the Fe(II) SA -induced local electron depolarization enhances interfacial charge transfer which drives this reaction with the conversion of *NO to *NOH/*NHO identified as the rate-limiting step. We then propose a regulatory strategy to establish a stable Fe(II) SA /Fe(III) SA cycle utilizing FeC for controlled-release of Fe(II) ions. Two-year field experiments confirmed this strategy can increase rice yield by 16.1% while cutting half of the N input. Our work enables the design of novel pathways in improving N use efficiency for sustainable rice production.

Article.Title: Two clusters of brain regions with distinct age-related profiles of functional connectivity in autism spectrum disorder
Article.Authors: Li X.; Zuo F.; Cheng Y.; Perkins K.; Cao F.
Article.Abstract: Brain functional connectivity changes throughout development, and individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may follow trajectories that differ from those of typically developing controls. Using large multisite resting-state fMRI cross-sectional datasets, we examined how functional connectivity differences between ASD and typically developing controls change across a broad age range of 5 to 64 y. A data-driven analysis identified two spatially distributed clusters of cortical regions showing distinct age-related profiles of ASD–TD connectivity differences. Cluster 1 was marked by consistent hypoconnectivity across ages, suggesting a stable neural signature of ASD. Cluster 2 was characterized by hypoconnectivity in childhood that gradually diminished with age, suggesting a temporary delay profile. These clusters were systematically organized along the sensory–association axis. Cluster 1 mainly involved lower-rank sensory and sensorimotor cortices, while Cluster 2 mainly involved higher-rank association cortices. Brain–behavior analyses revealed greater and broader ASD symptom associations across ages in the consistent hypoconnectivity profile than the delay profile. Further subtype analyses suggested that social-affect symptoms were associated with greater hypoconnectivity than repetitive behavior symptoms in both clusters. Spatial correlation analyses with neurotransmitter maps revealed associations of Cluster 1 with mGluR5 and of Cluster 2 with GABA A α5, providing insight into the neurobiological basis of the two clusters. In a cross-disorder validation analysis, applying the same analytic framework to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder did not reveal comparable results. Together, these findings suggest that ASD-related functional connectivity alterations are developmentally heterogeneous and organized along the cortical hierarchy, providing a developmental perspective for understanding the neurobiology of ASD.

Article.Title: Suspected distortion of citations in high-impact cancer journals
Article.Authors: Scancar B.; Byrne J.; Causeur D.; Barnett A.
Article.Abstract: Research and scholarship are shaped by article citations, which underpin the communication of ideas, assignment of credit, journal impact factors, and author career progression. Given their key influence on author and journal metrics, citations can be intentionally manipulated to inflate the reputation of journals and researchers. Paper mills, unethical organizations that produce and sell manuscripts and publishing services, may also be manipulating citations, but the extent of this manipulation is unknown. Here, we show that molecular cancer articles sharing features with retracted papers from paper mills display citation patterns that suggest systematic inflation. These articles were published in journals in the top decile of journal rankings. Suspected paper mill articles received 50 to 100% more citations than other papers 1 to 3 y after publication, while paradoxically attracting fewer readers and online accesses. Suspected paper mill articles also cited—and were cited by—other suspected paper mill articles, which frequently appeared in journals previously reported as paper mill targets. Citations from suspected paper mill articles measurably inflated journal citation metrics. These findings suggest that paper mills inflate the citation metrics of supported publications and affected journals at scale. This widespread manipulation of citation metrics may amplify unreliable findings, slowing scientific progress and spurring unreasonable citation benchmarks for research articles, journals, and authors. Our findings point to measurable signatures of citation manipulation that could support article- and journal-level screening.

Article.Title: Superconductivity in the high-pressure tetragonal phase of UTe <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Deng Y.; Mee G.; Wannamaker T.; Feng K.; Xu M.; Xie W.; Maple M.
Article.Abstract: Electrical transport and magnetic measurements have been made on UTe 2 under pressure P up to ~16 GPa to determine the superconducting transition temperature T c vs. P phase diagram in the high-pressure tetragonal phase. Superconductivity emerges near ~5 GPa, coincident with the orthorhombic—tetragonal phase transition; in the tetragonal phase, T c reaches a maximum value of ~4 K at 6 GPa and then decreases with P and appears to vanish near 18 GPa. Tetragonal UTe 2 has a relatively small upper critical field H c2 (0) ≈ 1.2 T at 5.3 GPa, smaller than the Pauli paramagnetic limit, and is orbitally limited with a coherence length ξ tetra ≈ 16.5 nm. This small value of H c2 (0) favors more conventional superconductivity; in contrast, the large values of H c2 ( T ) for orthorhombic UTe 2 exceed the Pauli paramagnetic limit in all three crystallographic directions and have been attributed to unconventional superconductivity, widely believed to involve spin-triplet pairing. The temperature–pressure phase diagram of UTe 2 shows a striking dichotomy: a narrow, fragile, unconventional superconducting region in the orthorhombic phase vs. a broad, robust, and more conventional superconducting dome in the tetragonal phase. This dichotomy is consistent with the proposal that U-dimers, present (absent) in the orthorhombic (tetragonal) phase, may play a role in spin-triplet superconductivity of orthorhombic UTe 2 . In the tetragonal phase, the normal-state electrical resistivity ρ( T ) exhibits metallic behavior with a “knee” at 200 to 240 K that depends weakly on P and most likely marks the onset of a transition to a magnetically ordered phase that coexists with superconductivity.

Article.Title: The impact of modulator therapy on the Pseudomonas aeruginosa cystic fibrosis lung transcriptome
Article.Authors: Letizia M.; Whiteley L.; Diggle F.; Davis A.; Morgan S.; Grogan B.; Baugh J.; McKone E.; Singh P.; Whiteley M.
Article.Abstract: Chronic lung infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major complication of cystic fibrosis (CF), contributing to lung function decline and increased morbidity and mortality. Laboratory models are used to study CF infections, but their relevance depends on how accurately they reproduce microbial physiology during human infection. We previously developed a framework that uses bacterial gene expression in human infections to quantify model accuracy. Here, we applied this framework to determine how a major therapeutic intervention impacts P. aeruginosa physiology in the lungs of people with CF (pwCF) and to develop and evaluate refined preclinical models. We focused on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), a highly effective CFTR modulator therapy that has improved outcomes for pwCF. However, evidence indicates that P. aeruginosa lung infections persist despite ETI therapy. Analysis of P. aeruginosa transcriptomes from human sputum collected before and after ETI initiation revealed minimal changes in gene expression, indicating that the CF airway continues to support a similar bacterial transcriptional state despite therapy. We then evaluated how strain selection, zinc limitation, and polymicrobial coculture influence the ability of laboratory models to recapitulate P. aeruginosa gene expression in human CF sputum. Growth of CF clinical isolates in zinc-limited synthetic CF sputum medium produced the most accurate model, whereas population-based cultures and coculture with Staphylococcus aureus had limited effects. These findings show that ETI therapy has little impact on the conserved P. aeruginosa transcriptional state in human CF sputum and that refined sputum-like models remain useful for studying persistent infection in the postmodulator era.

Article.Title: Structure-based targeting of Atg8 uncovers its essential role in autophagy-mediated detoxification
Article.Authors: Yan J.; Zhu X.; Li L.; Shen Z.; Bao J.; Liang S.; Wu H.; Asif N.; Luo X.; Lv H.; Daskalov A.; Cai Y.; Wei Y.; Lu J.; Liu X.; Naqvi N.; Wilson R.; Lin F.
Article.Abstract: Autophagy degrades and recycles intracellular material, allowing cells to maintain homeostasis and adapt to environmental stress. In the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae , the core autophagy protein MoAtg8 is required for autophagosome formation and host infection. Here, we determined the crystal structure of MoAtg8 and used it for structure-guided virtual screening of a focused compound library enriched for natural products and autophagy-related molecules. This screen identified nordihydroguaiaretic acid (NDGA), a naturally occurring lignan, as a MoAtg8-binding compound. Mechanistically, the 5-lipoxygenase Mo5Lox, a target of NDGA, bound NDGA with lower affinity than MoAtg8. MoAtg8 associated with NDGA through Gln81 and promoted its autophagy-dependent delivery to vacuoles, thereby reducing compound availability to toxicity-associated targets. Disruption of autophagy or mutation of Gln81 in MoAtg8 increased fungal sensitivity to NDGA. These findings identify an autophagy-mediated detoxification route for an exogenous antifungal compound and reveal how MoAtg8-dependent trafficking modulates NDGA efficacy in a plant-pathogenic fungus.
