Article.Title: Spontaneous lytic reactivation drives a persistent B cell-vector pathway for epithelial dissemination of the Epstein-Barr virus
Article.Authors: Vo D.; Chang C.; Ho H.; Huang H.; Poirey R.; Wu L.; Lim Y.; Delecluse H.; Tsai M.
Article.Abstract: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) establishes lifelong B cell infection via oral transmission; however, it paradoxically drives carcinomas in anatomically distant organs with striking geographic disparities. While genomic studies frequently link specific EBV variants to these epithelial cancers, the mechanisms bridging ubiquitous infection to distant, strain-dependent malignancies remain largely unresolved. Using an induction-free primary B cell system, we identify a circulating B cell-vector pathway driving immortalized epithelial dissemination. We demonstrate that B cells infected with carcinoma-associated strains exhibit markedly higher epithelial transmission compared with those carrying lymphoid strains. This contact-dependent process requires spontaneous lytic reactivation, viral DNA replication, and de novo virion production. Crucially, those infected B cells retain their transmission capacity for months, supporting sustained epithelial seeding. Mechanistically, entry requires gH/gL engagement of EphA2/desmocollin-2 (DSC2), with actin- and PI3K-dependent endocytosis. These findings define a lytic-coupled, receptor-dependent pathway by which the EBV exploits B cells to access the epithelium, offering a mechanistic framework for understanding strain tropism and host-virus interactions.

Article.Title: Anticipatory metabolic regulation drives the distinct and improved metabolic state of caloric restriction compared to Fasting-Refeeding cycles
Article.Authors: Velingkaar N.; Astafev A.; Prabahar A.; Maravillas M.; Trokhimenko E.; Rom J.; Asi G.; Piontkivska H.; Jiang P.; Kondratov R.
Article.Abstract: Interest in fasting-based diets to improve metabolic health is growing. Caloric restriction (CR) with one meal per day includes an extended fasting component that contributes to its metabolic and longevity benefits, yet the role of fasting within CR remains unclear. Here, we compare CR with a fasting-refeeding-fasting (FRF) regimen while controlling food intake and fasting duration. Changes in plasma insulin and free fatty acids, hepatic mTOR signaling and ketogenesis, metabolic rhythms, and food digestion kinetics suggest that gastric emptying serves as a primary metabolic trigger in acute fasting. In contrast, CR fasting responses are regulated, suggesting anticipatory mechanisms. CR enhances circadian rhythmicity and metabolic gene coordination, whereas FRF disrupts it. CR improves glucose and fatty acid metabolism, while fasting leads to glucose intolerance and liver fat accumulation. These findings reveal that CR engages clock-aligned, anticipatory metabolic control, while fasting-refeeding cycles rely on direct nutrient cues.

Article.Title: A CsWRKY46-CsPBL9-CsARI1 tripartite regulatory module coordinates H2O2 production and callose deposition in citrus fruit immunity
Article.Authors: Xu C.; Xie D.; Fu Z.; Xiao J.; Yao J.; Kang Z.; Liu F.; Bouzayen M.; Li Z.; Cheng Y.
Article.Abstract: Plant immunity against pathogens involves multiple immune responses and intricate regulatory networks. However, how immune networks are deployed in fruit remains poorly understood. Here, we show that citrus fruit immune responses, including hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) production and callose deposition, are multiply regulated by transcriptional activation, phosphorylation, and ubiquitination. Citrus sinensis genes encoding nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase CsRBOHG and callose synthase CsCalS5, responsible for H2O2 production and callose deposition, respectively, are transcriptionally activated by CsWRKY46. Phosphorylation-enhanced activity of CsRBOHG by CsPBL9 enhances immunity. RING1-IBR-RING2 (RBR)-type E3 ligase CsARI1, acting as an immune brake, ubiquitinates CsRBOHG and CsCalS5 for degradation. Interestingly, CsARI1 also shows a moonlight function wherein it interacts with CsPBL9 in a non-ubiquitination manner, disrupting CsPBL9's interaction with CsRBOHG. This CsARI1-CsPBL9 interaction is stimulated by H2O2 as feedback. Moreover, H2O2 contributes to callose deposition, indicating an interplay between two immune responses. Our study reveals a tripartite regulatory hub orchestrating self-linked immunity in citrus fruit.

Article.Title: The left PBN to aCM pathway mediates pain-related aversion in male mice
Article.Authors: Yan Y.; You H.; Zhang L.; Ha N.; Wang Y.; Deng J.
Article.Abstract: Pain involves both sensory and emotional components, while the circuit mechanisms underlying pain-induced aversion remain poorly understood. Here, using a formalin-induced conditioned place aversion (F-CPA) model, we show a pathway from the left parabrachial nucleus (L-PBN) to the anterior central medial thalamic nucleus (aCM) that modulates F-CPA in male mice. We find that L-PBN neurons exhibit higher F-CPA-induced activity than those in the right PBN (R-PBN). Chemogenetic inhibition of L-PBN-but not R-PBN-attenuates F-CPA, whereas optogenetic activation of F-CPA-tagged L-PBN neurons induces aversion. Furthermore, the aCM-but not posterior CM-is activated by F-CPA, and inhibition of either the L-PBN to aCM pathway or aCM neurons receiving L-PBN inputs significantly reduces F-CPA. In contrast, in female mice, inhibition of neither L-PBN nor R-PBN affects F-CPA. Collectively, these findings identifies a neural circuit underlying pain-related aversion in male mice, advancing our understanding of sexual dimorphism in pain-related affective processing.

Article.Title: Antigenic landscape of rabies and related lyssaviruses revealed by cryo-EM
Article.Authors: Callaway H.; Zyla D.; Hastie K.; Harkins S.; Kothalawalage S.; Samarasinghe N.; Flynn A.; Hariharan C.; Yin J.; Corti D.; Bourhy H.; Dessain S.; Saphire E.
Article.Abstract: Rabies continues to kill over 60,000 people per year despite life-saving vaccines and post-exposure treatments and costs billions of dollars in prevention and treatment. Preventing rabies deaths and reducing the global economic burden of the virus will require both developing a monoclonal antibody cocktail to replace human serum in treatment and improving rabies vaccines to elicit long-lasting protection. Here, we solve nine cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) in complex with the rabies virus glycoprotein (RABV-G). The nine structures span three known antigenic sites plus two additional antigenic sites, not among the five classically identified sites. We find that these antigenic sites, V and VI, are broadly cross-reactive across lyssaviruses, whereas immunodominant sites II/IV and III are rabies specific. Across the mAb panel, fusion inhibition and binding affinity correlate best with neutralization. Together, these results provide a roadmap for structure-guided vaccine and therapeutic antibody design for rabies and related lyssaviruses.

Article.Title: Skin commensals shape the clock-ferroptosis axis to preserve barrier function in psoriasis
Article.Authors: Lin Z.; Li C.; Jin C.; Chen L.; Li Y.; Luo Y.; Han Y.; Wang Y.; Zhu Y.; Zheng Y.; Lin Y.; Zeng D.; Wang P.; Huang X.; Zhang S.; Wu R.; Chen P.; Sweren E.; Alphonse M.; Yang L.; Wang G.
Article.Abstract: Psoriasis ranks among the most prevalent chronic inflammatory dermatoses worldwide and is accompanied by significant alterations in the skin microbiota. In this study, we confirmed microbial dysbiosis in psoriatic lesions and observed a reduction in Lactobacillus. Further functional screening showed that topical administration of Lactobacillus plantarum alleviated psoriatic lesions. Mechanistically, L. plantarum produces indole-3-lactic acid, which restores circadian rhythmicity in keratinocytes, thereby suppressing ferroptosis and promoting epidermal barrier repair. Article.Title: Theta synchronization coordinates ventral temporal and medial temporal coding of human face familiarity
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Zhang J.; Wang Y.; Cho H.; Brunner P.; Thum J.; Willie J.; Cao R.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Recognizing familiar faces is a fundamental social function that depends on interactions between perceptual and memory systems, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we combine single-neuron recordings, intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG), and multi-scale connectivity analyses in the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC) and medial temporal lobe (MTL) to investigate the neural dynamics underlying face familiarity. Theta-frequency phase locking of MTL neurons is associated with face familiarity and familiarization, complementing firing-rate signals. The VTC represents visual features through an axis-based code that disproportionately contributes to familiarity representations. Familiarity is further associated with enhanced theta synchronization between the VTC and MTL, particularly between VTC visual-feature-coding and MTL familiarity-coding channels. Enhanced theta-frequency spike-iEEG coherence for familiar faces suggests that MTL phase locking is coordinated with large-scale VTC activity. Together, these findings identify theta synchronization as a key mechanism coordinating the neural dynamics underlying face familiarity processing in humans.

Article.Title: PADI-dependent mitochondrial adaptation drives resistance to KRAS inhibitors
Article.Authors: Gani M.; Agostini F.; Secco L.; De Pino L.; Picco R.; Licastro D.; Tolotto V.; D’Este F.; Choudhary H.; Ferino A.; Rapozzi V.; Barasa L.; Ohta Y.; Nakagawa H.; Sgarra R.; Thompson P.; Xodo L.; Di Giorgio E.
Article.Abstract: KRAS(ON) and KRAS(OFF) inhibitors have improved the treatment of KRAS-driven tumors, yet resistance remains a major challenge. Here, we identify PADI1 and PADI3 as negative prognostic markers in KRAS-mutant colorectal and pancreatic cancers. KRAS-driven metabolic rewiring sustains their expression through an enhancer within the PADI1 locus. Article.Title: Placental trophoblasts exhibit iron dysregulation and ferroptosis signaling associated with SARS-CoV-2 restriction
Article.Authors: McColl E.; Kumar D.; Jones B.; Marks N.; Diveley E.; Karvas R.; Theunissen T.; Kelly J.; Mysorekar I.

Article.Abstract: Animals rely on neural representations of sensory stimuli to rapidly recognize familiar environments and precisely identify salient cues. Article.Abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, yet dynamic metabolic flux has been difficult to study systematically. Article.Abstract: Breast cancer progression and therapy resistance remain major clinical obstacles. Article.Title: An extramedullary bone model of metastatic dormancy reveals an increased rate of metastatic reactivation upon distant insults
Article.Authors: Di Blasio S.; Rizou T.; Gay L.; Rabas N.; Fan X.; Liu X.; Bridgeman V.; Rodriguez E.; Chakravarty P.; Snoeks T.; Karoutas A.; Rodrigues F.; Montaudon E.; Lo Celso C.; Marangoni E.; Bonnet D.; Qian B.; Abarrategi A.; Malanchi I.
Article.Abstract: Bone metastatic relapse can emerge years after cancer diagnosis, driven by the reactivation of disseminated tumor cells (DTCs) that remain dormant in secondary organs. This behavior is controlled by the tissue microenvironment. We developed a tuneable, skeletal progenitor-based engineered extramedullary (EM) bone model in mice that closely mimics endogenous bone and induces dormancy in metastatic breast cancer cells. Within EM bone, cancer cells remained quiescent, with occasional transient proliferative episodes. Because the model integrates with host vasculature and permits controlled release of specific factors, it enables investigation of systemic influences on dormancy. Systemic inflammation, which increases bone marrow cell production, raised the proliferative fraction of dormant cells in EM bone and increased metastatic incidence in endogenous bone. We also identified high-mobility group box 2 (HMGB2) as a factor that promotes overt metastasis and is present in human bone metastases. Therefore, EM bone represents a powerful platform for studying metastatic dormancy.

Article.Title: A non-canonical redox family protein regulates bacterial interaction machineries
Article.Authors: Barman R.; Baidya A.
Article.Abstract: Flagella and nanotubes are two major bacterial apparatuses involved in driving bacterial interactions. Flagella enable cells to perform exploratory roles, whereas nanotubes physically connect nearby cells, facilitating direct transfer of cytoplasmic materials. The only known regulatory protein in Bacillus subtilis that modulates nanotube biogenesis is metallophosphodiesterase YmdB, a global effector, through a route largely elusive. We report that YmdB recruits YdzF for nanotube production. YdzF is a MarR/DUF24 family transcriptional regulator belonging to MarR superfamily required for oxidative stress adaptation, a phenomenon executed by redox-sensing cysteine switches. However, YdzF behaves non-canonically due to proximally positioned intermolecular cysteine residues, hindering its conformational rearrangement. Independent of redox sensing, YdzF recognizes an unrelated flagellar Pfla/che promoter to modulate fla/che operon expression required for nanotube and flagella biogenesis. This promoter recognition by YdzF is entirely governed by YmdB. Furthermore, YdzF-mediated nanotube formation is widespread in Gram-positive bacteria.

Article.Title: The CUP pilus SMF-1 utilizes a specific antiparallel bundling mechanism to initiate biofilm formation
Article.Authors: Fields J.; Sebastian C.; Zhang H.; Bhaumik R.; Zia A.; Robertson A.; Anderson G.; Mattoo S.; Wu H.; Kiedrowski M.; Wang F.
Article.Abstract: Bacterial biofilms enable microbial communities to withstand environmental stress and antibiotic challenge. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an opportunistic pathogen that frequently colonizes cystic fibrosis airways. Its chaperone-usher pathway (CUP) pilus, SMF-1, is essential for biofilm development, but its molecular architecture has remained unknown. Here, we present a 4.0 Å cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure demonstrating that the classic γ4 CUP pilus SMF-1 assembles into zigzag filaments that pair into antiparallel "pili couples" and higher order bundles. These bundles serve as intercellular tethers that drive rapid cell aggregation during biofilm initiation. Despite belonging to the classic CUP family, SMF-1 lacks the subunit interfaces required for canonical rod-like architectures, providing structural evidence of convergent evolution toward archaic-like biofilm bundling mechanisms. Furthermore, appendage-driven motility acts synergistically with SMF-1 pili to accelerate intercellular encounters and aggregate assembly. Together, these findings reveal a structural mechanism of pilus-mediated crosslinking promoting bacterial colonization.

Article.Authors: Shen S.; Xie X.; Lu L.; Ma W.; Tu H.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Gefitinib improves outcomes in patients with EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer; however, treatment-related gastrointestinal and hepatic toxicity can limit its long-term use. A gut-liver-tumor organ-on-a-chip model further supports these effects. LGG treatment also improves short-chain fatty acid profiles, intestinal barrier markers, and bile acid-related metabolism. Together, these findings suggest that LGG may represent a microbiota-based strategy to enhance gefitinib response while limiting treatment-associated toxicity.

Article.Title: Progressive remodeling of global protein interaction networks in a mouse model of tauopathy
Article.Authors: Lin W.; Phanse S.; van der Spek S.; Lampl N.; Stephens M.; Wang Z.; Nigro J.; Ortiz A.; Hekman R.; Cruz A.; Roberts R.; Jiang L.; Botas J.; Emili A.; Wolozin B.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative disease is marked not just by loss of proteins or cells, but by dynamic rewiring of macromolecular interaction networks that precede and drive pathology. Here, we present a temporally resolved, systems-scale map of multi-protein complex remodeling in a tauopathy model, integrating co-fractionation mass spectrometry, quantitative phosphoproteomics, and machine learning to decode phosphorylation-dependent shifts in protein interactomes across disease progression. This interactomic atlas serves as a resource to investigate functional assemblies, including MAPT-Dpysl2 and Cyfip1-actin, as well as ptk2b-Kars/Dars and ptk2b-Msn-Farsb-complexes, that modulate early disease phenotypes in vivo. Notably, it captures the composition, dynamics, and regulatory state of protein complexes at scale. By revealing how phosphorylation tunes macromolecular complex architecture and function, this work highlights dynamic network instability that develops over the course of tauopathy, and establishes a generalizable framework for mechanistic dissection of functional complexes in neurodegeneration.

Article.Authors: Keck C.; Tachon S.; Sayes F.; Musiani D.; Gianetto Q.; Matondo M.; Vos M.; Brosch R.; Enninga J.
Article.Abstract: Subcellular compartmentalization of metabolic processes is a main feature of prokaryotic and eukaryotic architecture. Environmental bacteria generate intracytoplasmic membranes (ICMs) as a crucial strategy to adapt their metabolism to environmental changes. While pathogenic intracellular bacteria also perceive various stressful stimuli during host interactions, the subsequent re-organization of their internal architecture has not been explored. Single-cell transcriptomics enables investigation of underlying molecular programs of γδ T cell effector functions in health and disease. Article.Title: A Gata4–Loxl2 axis controls ECM remodeling to enable scar-free spinal cord regeneration in zebrafish
Article.Authors: Noel N.; Lima Fernandes V.; Kjar A.; Pfotenhauer P.; Kim H.; Sefogbe M.; Akam-Baxter E.; Lippmann E.; Cigliola V.
Article.Abstract: Spinal cord injury in mammals triggers fibrotic scar formation that impedes axon regrowth, whereas zebrafish regenerate and recover motor function without persistent fibrosis. Loss of Gata4 increases expression of the collagen cross-linking enzyme Loxl2b, resulting in excessive collagen cross-linking, matrix stiffening, and a regeneration-inhibitory ECM environment. Article.Authors: Gao Y.; Cai T.; Wang X.; Nadal-Jimenez P.; Li C.; Su C.; He S.; Li J.; Wan H.

Article.Authors: Cai M.; Luo L.; Liu Y.; Wang X.; Wu X.; Liang Q.; Zhuo C.; Li Y.; Liu C.; Zhou Z.; Zhu B.

This workflow provides a practical, interpretable, and capillary electrophoresis-compatible solution for forensic biogeographical ancestry inference and micro-genetic structure mapping.

Article.Abstract: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) are a class of lymphocytes whose activation is independent of antigen receptors. Article.Title: Quantifying the energetic costs and growth benefits of phagocytosis
Article.Authors: Schavemaker P.; Tam K.; Lynch M.
Article.Abstract: Phagocytosis, the ingestion of cells by other cells, is ubiquitous among eukaryotic life. It is utilized for food uptake and in the immune response in many species. Drawing on a wealth of empirical data, we integrate prey capture, engulfment, and internal and external digestion into a mathematical model that quantifies the cellular performance of a primitive phagocytoser relative to a non-phagocytosing ancestor. The primitive phagocytoser can outperform the ancestor in a range of situations. The rate of engulfment delineates when phagocytosis is advantageous, providing clear benchmarks for interpreting the importance of results in genetic knockout studies and mechanical models. Article.Title: Rotational settings quantize nucleosome movement by chromatin regulators
Article.Authors: La V.; Trouth A.; Ramani V.; Ramachandran S.
Article.Abstract: Proper nucleosome positioning is essential for gene regulation and genomic integrity. These presynaptic roles were synapse specific: STIM1 predominantly supported excitatory synapses, whereas STIM2 was critical for the inhibitory counterparts. Postsynaptically, STIM1 and STIM2 exerted opposing effects on glutamate and GABA receptor levels, such that simultaneous loss of both isoforms rescued postsynaptic function. Together, the findings show that STIM1 and STIM2 differentially tune synaptic efficacy according to synapse type and subcellular compartment.

Article.Title: Cross-species atlas of bacterial RNA 3′ ends reveals termination mechanistic signatures and evolutionary patterns

Article.Abstract: Deciphering the generation mechanisms and regulatory roles of bacterial transcript 3' termini requires large-scale 3' terminus data. Intriguingly, orthologous genes with corresponding 3' termini show different termination mechanisms in different bacteria, often matching the dominant mechanism of the respective bacterial species. Analysis of condition-dependent 3' termini revealed some conservation across species, supporting the conjecture that alternative 3' termini can play a role in gene expression regulation. Article.Title: Molecular triage and isoform protection safeguard ubiquitin chain editing on DNA
Article.Authors: Zhou X.; Attwood M.; McStea A.; Foster B.; Gibbs-Seymour I.
Article.Abstract: In an accompanying study, we identify the RPA-ZUP1 complex as a ubiquitin chain-editing machine that promotes removal of RPA from ssDNA. ZUP1 ubiquitination promotes recruitment of p97/VCP and ATXN3, defining a molecular triage pathway that protects ZUP1 from premature proteasomal degradation. Opposing this, the E3 ligases UBR5 and HUWE1 define a degradative branch that limits ZUP1 abundance, with HUWE1 restricting its accumulation on damaged chromatin. We further show that cells express a naturally occurring ZUP1 isoform resistant to efficient ubiquitination and turnover, suggesting that isoform diversity provides a protected pool of chain-editing activity. Together, these findings define a homeostatic system that preserves ZUP1 while limiting its persistence on damaged chromatin.

Article.Title: RAD54L counteracts topoisomerase I cleavage complexes by stabilizing E3 ligase TRIM21 to maintain genome stability
Article.Authors: Li C.; Wang S.; Xu W.; Kong Z.; Wen C.; Zhao S.; Cao L.; Chen Z.; Zhao S.; Qin Y.; Yang Y.

Article.Title: Pain education in Brazilian medical schools: a national curriculum analysis
Article.Authors: Silva T.; Domingues F.; Medeiros D.; Gandolfi A.; Reis F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide, yet undergraduate medical education remains insufficient to prepare future physicians for its assessment and management. The International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) has proposed a competency-based curriculum framework; however, its implementation in Brazilian medical education is unclear. The aim of this study was to evaluate the availability of pain education in Brazilian medical schools and assess its alignment with the IASP Curriculum Outline on Pain for Medicine. We conducted a national cross-sectional documentary analysis of all medical schools registered in the Brazilian Ministry of Education database between May 2024 and December 2025. Institutional websites were systematically screened for publicly available curricular documentation, and data were independently extracted by 2 reviewers. Variables included the presence of pain-related content, existence of a dedicated pain course, course workload, timing within the curriculum, and type of offering. Among 447 identified schools, 277 (62.0%) provided accessible curricular information. Only 47 institutions (16.9%) offered a stand-alone pain course, and 29 had detailed syllabi for item-level analysis. Most analyzed courses were mandatory and delivered in the early years of training. Alignment with IASP competencies was incomplete across all domains, with greater coverage of neurobiological and pharmacological content and limited inclusion of pain assessment and measurement, psychosocial and behavioral management, public health, ethics, and care for special populations. Pain education in Brazil is inconsistently structured and only partially aligned with international recommendations, indicating the need of comprehensive, competency-based curricular reform.

Article.Title: The analgesic efficacy of opioids in different application modalities for the treatment of breakthrough cancer pain—a systematic review with network meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Dinges H.; Thiedmann S.; Weyland J.; Volberg C.; Schmitt F.; Wulf H.; Schubert A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Breakthrough cancer pain episodes often require oral immediate release opioids or parenteral opioid treatment. Different formulations and application modalities have been approved for this condition. This study aimed to identify the most effective of the available substances and applications to treat breakthrough cancer pain. We conducted a comprehensive systematic review with network meta-analysis. The database search included MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible were randomized controlled trials comparing opioids and application modalities for the treatment of breakthrough cancer pain episodes. Primary end points were the pain intensity difference (PID) at 15 and 30 minutes. Secondary end points were side effects and adverse events, as well as dichotomous outcomes of treatment success. Frequentist network meta-analysis was conducted using the package netmeta in R. From 5133 records initially identified by the literature review, 23 studies were eligible for quantitative analysis. Compared with placebo, the most effective interventions at 15 minutes (PID) were intravenous or subcutaneous applications of morphine, and intranasal fentanyl or sublingual fentanyl tablets. After 30 minutes (PID), the most effective interventions were still subcutaneous and intravenous morphine, but also sublingual fentanyl tablets. Intranasal fentanyl spray was equally effective as buccal and other transmucosal applications by 30 minutes. The quality of evidence on the topic is poor as most studies are phase III trials for drug approval. The risk of publication bias is therefore high. Sublingual fentanyl tablets were as effective as intravenous or subcutaneous morphine and are a practical modality for self-administration.

Article.Title: Evoked alpha oscillatory activity is suppressed by prolonged elbow pain and modulated by repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
Article.Authors: Chowdhury N.; Hoddinott J.; Chang W.; Cheng D.; Manivasagan N.; Schabrun S.; Seminowicz D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Alpha-band oscillatory activity, assessed using electroencephalography (EEG), is among the most widely studied neurophysiological markers of pain. However, the literature has focused predominantly on resting-state measures, leaving unclear whether pain also alters evoked alpha-band dynamics, measured via cortical perturbation using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Here, we examined whether prolonged pain alters TMS-evoked alpha event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) and intertrial coherence (ITC), reflecting cortical reactivity and phase consistency, and whether 10-Hz repetitive TMS (rTMS) modulates these responses. We performed a secondary analysis on 2 previous experiments, which used nerve growth factor (NGF) injection to induce prolonged elbow muscle pain. In experiment 1, participants underwent primary motor cortex (M1) TMS-EEG at baseline (day 0) pre-NGF injection and day 2 (peak pain) and day 7 (pain resolution) post-injection. In experiment 2, M1-TMS-EEG was assessed on day 0 before NGF injection and again on day 4 after injection, with active or sham 10-Hz rTMS delivered to M1 between these assessments. In experiment 1, M1 TMS-EEG showed reductions in alpha ERSP ( P = 0.014) and alpha ITC ( P = 0.041) from day 0 to day 2. In experiment 2, active rTMS produced a more positive pre-to-post change in alpha ERSP ( P = 0.006) relative to sham but did not alter alpha ITC ( P = 0.804). Our findings suggest that prolonged experimental pain is associated with diminished evoked alpha oscillatory activity, whereas high-frequency rTMS modulates this activity in the positive direction. These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked alpha metrics warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of pain state and response to neuromodulation.

Article.Title: Beyond intensity: pain distribution shapes healthcare- and treatment-seeking beliefs in individuals with and without clinical pain
Article.Authors: Frankenstein T.; Intert S.; Szikszay T.; Katra M.; Elsner B.; Coghill R.; Luedtke K.; Adamczyk W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain is commonly described in sensory terms, yet its spatial characteristics are rarely quantified. We investigated whether lay beliefs about pain distribution influence theoretical decisions to seek care and treatment preferences. In a cross-sectional survey (N = 503; 49% reporting pain), participants completed thought experiments in which both visually presented pain distribution patterns (small, moderate, or large) and pain intensity (Numerical Rating Scale scores: 2, 5, 8/10) were systematically varied. For each scenario, they rated the likelihood of (1) seeking professional help (LoSH) and (2) taking analgesic medication (LoTM) on 0 to 100 scale. Participants also completed a spatial–intensity trade-off task, in which they chose between a fixed 20% reduction in intensity and variable reductions in pain distribution (20%-80%). A reversed version contrasted a fixed 80% reduction in pain distribution with variable reductions in pain intensity. LoSH and LoTM increased significantly with greater pain distribution ( P < 0.001), mirroring the gradient observed for pain intensity. In the spatial–intensity trade-off task, participants' choice followed a sigmoid-like function ( P < 0.001): 1% reduction in intensity was treated as equivalent to approximately a 3% reduction in distribution, indicating a systematic valuation of pain distribution. This ratio was lower in individuals experiencing pain compared with pain-free individuals. Moreover, 61% reported that pain distribution should be routinely considered in pain management alongside intensity. Results suggest that pain distribution is not merely a trivial descriptor, but a meaningful determinant of healthcare-related decision-making beliefs. Incorporating spatial metrics into clinical assessment and research may better capture how individuals implicitly evaluate pain severity.

Article.Title: Brain gray matter changes across chronic pain trajectories: MRI evidence from 35,000 individuals
Article.Authors: Zorina-Lichtenwalter K.; Bango C.; Petre B.; Rader L.; Čeko M.; Lindquist M.; Friedman N.; Wager T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic pain affects brain gray matter structure, but the magnitude, pattern, and reversibility of brain changes upon pain recovery remain unclear because of inconsistent findings from small-scale studies. Brain magnetic resonance imaging data were available from the second time point. Resolved pain demonstrated reversibility of most brain changes, except sustained surface area reductions in the primary somatosensory cortex. No areas showed effects consistent with a predisposition to pain. Most changes appear reversible with pain resolution, underscoring the importance of effective pain treatment to alleviate symptoms and support recovery of brain structure and function.

Article.Title: Pain as a predictive process in the brain: how the Bayesian brain generates, amplifies, and relieves pain
Article.Authors: Lyndon S.; Nedeljkovic S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain is not a passive readout of nociceptor traffic; it reflects the brain's inference about bodily threat under uncertainty. Building on predictive processing, active inference, and the free energy principle, we frame acute, chronic, and phantom pain as regimes of hierarchical inference in which memory, affect, and context shift the relative influence of prior beliefs vs incoming nociceptive evidence. Prior work links expectations to pain, but translating these ideas into a clinically usable account that links expectation mechanisms to measurable proxies of belief updating and to principled routes for personalized intervention remains challenging. We propose a generative model that links inferred threat to action policies, so that pain intensity and pain behavior can be studied within the same inferential loop. Within this framework, chronic pain can persist when threat beliefs remain overly influential despite corrective evidence. Placebo/nocebo effects illustrate how shifting expectations can amplify or relieve pain. Phantom pain illustrates how stable body-related beliefs can sustain pain-like perception even with minimal or absent afferent input. We outline candidate measurements and falsifiable predictions by linking expectation- and precision-related effects to a cingulate–insula-centered hub and associated descending control circuitry (periaqueductal gray to spinal dorsal horn). This account suggests principles for selecting and sequencing treatments to target belief content (expectations), evidence (corrective sampling), and gain control (context and neuromodulation), for matching mechanisms to patient-specific phenotypes, and for stratifying patients by dominant mechanism (overly threat-biased beliefs, reduced corrective sampling, or biased precision/gain control) to enable more testable trials and clearer interpretation of treatment response.

Article.Title: Unraveling the profile of cognitive deficits associated with chronic pain: a meta-analysis and cross-sectional study
Article.Authors: Gentile E.; Guglietti G.; Haward B.; Borokhovski E.; Plante I.; Fitzcharles M.; Vachon-Presseau E.; Roy M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Self-reported cognitive difficulties are a common, yet underexplored, complaint of patients with chronic pain (CP). These deficits hinder daily functioning and reduce quality of life, contributing to disability. However, the extent and profile of these impairments remain unclear. Our study synthesized findings from a meta-analysis (Study 1; n = 67 studies, 6,899 patients and controls) with data from the UK Biobank (Study 2; n = 37,139 participants with CP and controls) to ascertain the magnitude and profile of cognitive deficits on performance-based measures in CP sufferers relative to healthy controls. Study 2 replicated these findings, though to a lesser magnitude ( d = 0.04-0.30). Furthermore, participants with higher pain severity (4+ pain sites) showed an advanced cognitive age pattern. The cognitive difficulties observed among CP participants may be indicative of stress-related advanced cognitive age, resulting from persistent and uncontrollable pain. However, it is important to note that these deficits are small to moderate in severity, and, therefore, the observation of more pronounced impairment in CP warrants further clinical evaluation, particularly if their extent appears disproportionate to pain severity.

Article.Title: Clinical and preclinical investigation of the mechanism promoting aura in post-traumatic headache and inhibition of pain-related behavior in mice by onabotulinumtoxinA
Article.Authors: Bader C.; Haskie K.; Li G.; Vizin R.; Chong C.; Dumkrieger G.; Koprusinski C.; Dodick D.; Navratilova E.; Porreca F.; Schwedt T.; Anderson T.

After closed-head mTBI, injured mice exhibited a 160% increase in CSD induction probability (ie, lowered threshold) and became sensitized to CSD induction by brief exposure to stress, a common headache trigger. When evoked optogenetically, CSD produced prolonged periorbital and hind paw allodynia, consistent with headache-like pain. Subcutaneous onabotulinumtoxinA administered to the scalp after mTBI did not alter CSD susceptibility but completely abolished optogenetic CSD-induced allodynia. These findings suggest that mTBI elicits sensitization to CSD induction and promotes the emergence of aura in humans, likely contributing to PTH. It is important that, even after mTBI-induced sensitization, onabotulinumtoxinA decoupled CSD from pain behaviors, suggesting efficacy in treating PTH associated with aura.

Article.Title: Organelle associations and metabolic rewiring of size-defined hepatic lipid droplets
Article.Authors: Liao Q.; Fu X.; Wang Y.; Xu Y.; Cao Z.; Wang Y.; Pan B.; Wang J.; Liu P.; Yang Z.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Lipid droplet (LD) size is a key determinant of hepatic lipid metabolism, yet the molecular programming routing size-defined subpopulations to distinct fates remains unclear. Here we show that a fractionation workflow resolves hepatic LDs by size and organelle association, defining a high-confidence intrinsic LD proteome. Moreover, comparative proteomics of fasted livers reveals a clear ‘division of labor’: Large LDs (L-LDs) function as specialized mitochondrion-coupled ‘putative fueling hubs’, whereas small LDs (S-LDs) serve as lysosome-coupled ‘putative trafficking and turnover hubs’. This interaction map is highly plastic; metabolic stress (fasting or steatosis) triggers a programmatic remodeling where lysosomal machinery is inducibly recruited to S-LDs. Crucially, in vivo stress recruits mitochondria to both pools, supporting a ‘parallel programs’ model where S-LD-associated mitochondria are hypothesized to power the energy-intensive degradative machinery. These findings establish that metabolic state leverages LD size to direct organelle partnerships, nominating the small-LD lysosomal axis as a critical regulatory node in metabolic-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD).

Article.Abstract: Tissue phantoms mimicking microvasculature and perfusion are essential for vasculature modelling and calibrating imaging systems, which require faithful replication of vascular geometry and flow. Conventional fabrication methods, including lithographic micromachining and additive manufacturing remain constrained by predefined designs, rectangular channel cross-sections, limited scalability, and high production costs. Here we present a lithography-free approach based on a modified lifted Hele-Shaw cell method where, unlike above-mentioned methods, random fractal-like vascular structures emerge naturally. This results in channels of widths 100-1000 μ m with smooth Gaussian cross-section and natural diameter tapering. We demonstrate this with four phantom designs: a planar vascular tree, a cerebral vasculature-mimicking guided tree network, a conformable curved substrate and a retinal vasculature-mimicking network. Flow visualisation with laser speckle contrast imaging shows close agreement with in vivo observations and consistency with the generalized Murray’s law. This approach uniquely combines fractal-like network formation leading towards realistic vascular geometry and flow characteristics, offering an in vitro alternative to small animal vascular models.

Article.Title: FOXO3 induces chromatin changes in a model of DNA damage-induced senescence
Article.Authors: Brown A.; Arevalo J.; Holcom A.; Finch A.; Maybury-Lewis S.; McNamara A.; Webb A.
Article.Abstract: FOXO transcription factors are critical for cellular homeostasis and the stress response and have been implicated in longevity in several species. Yet, how these factors function at the chromatin level in differing conditions in human cells is poorly understood. Here, we take an integrated multi-omics approach to identify the chromatin-level mechanisms by which FOXO3 coordinates transcriptional programs in replicating cells and in a model of cellular senescence. In a DNA-damage induced senescence, FOXO3 levels are elevated early in senescence entry. Increased FOXO3 expression induces expression of chromatin remodeling factors, and impacts chromatin accessibility across the genome together with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers. As cells enter DNA-damage induced senescence, FOXO3 is essential for chromatin remodeling and reprogramming of a genomic network that functions to modulate cell stress and lineage-specific cellular functions. Altogether, we identify a FOXO3-SWI/SNF network that regulates key cellular processes including metabolism, proteostasis, epigenetics, and cell lineage, and is dynamically controlled under DNA damaging conditions.

Article.Title: Large-scale functional overlap between dorsal and ventral object-responsive networks
Article.Authors: Simmons C.; Behrmann M.; Ayzenberg V.
Article.Abstract: The processes of acting on and recognizing objects have traditionally been attributed to dorsal and ventral visual pathways, respectively. Although extensive evidence suggests that the two pathways interact, the extent and the strength of these interactions across whole-brain networks remain unclear. In two experiments, we characterized the whole-brain network connections of object-selective regions in each pathway using functional magnetic resonance imaging data acquired while participants viewed objects. Here, we show substantial spatial overlap in connectivity networks generated from the dorsal and the ventral seed region—with greater similarity between object networks within an individual than each network shows across individuals. This overlap persists across viewing of tools and non-tools and even after controlling for the shared variance between pathways. Together, these findings reveal that dorsal and ventral pathways form highly overlapping and distributed networks in the service of object perception.

Article.Title: Estradiol deficiency aggravates AngII-induced vascular remodeling by failing to inhibit GRK2 through ERα-mediated autophagy
Article.Authors: Ji M.; Song N.; Adu-Amankwaah J.; Liu C.; Wang G.; Zhou W.; Hao Y.; Shi Y.; Wu J.; Li K.
Article.Abstract: Hypertension acts as a critical cardiovascular risk factor that drives vascular remodeling, which manifests as vascular media thickening triggered by excessive proliferation and migration of vascular smooth muscle cells. Angiotensin II promotes vascular remodeling by upregulating G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2. Estradiol deficiency, particularly among postmenopausal individuals, increases susceptibility to hypertension by overactivating the renin-angiotensin system, while the precise mechanism remains unkown. Here we show that estradiol inhibits G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 to ameliorate hypertensive vascular remodeling. Ovariectomy in spontaneously hypertensive rats exacerbate hypertension, while estradiol supplementation significantly reduced blood pressure and attenuated vascular remodeling. Mechanistically, Estradiol downregulated G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 expression, leading to decreased β-arrestin2 recruitment and ERK signaling, thereby reducing vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and migration. Additionally, Autophagy or estrogen receptor α blockade abolishes the effects of estradiol on G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 degradation. This study provides a potential therapeutic strategy for hypertensive vascular remodeling. Ji and colleagues show that estradiol (E2) enhances autophagy and ERalpha-AMPK signaling in a mouse model of hypertension and vascular remodeling.

Article.Title: A Colletotrichum orbiculare-based fungal model recapitulates conserved cellular defects of Niemann–Pick type C disease and enables therapeutic evaluation
Article.Authors: Sano H.; Takezawa S.; Saomoto N.; Chiba A.; Tanaka C.; Kato N.; Nishiuchi T.; Nishisaka H.; Kitatani K.; Kodama S.; Kubo Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Niemann–Pick type C disease is a fatal lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in NPC1 or NPC2 , leading to lipid accumulation and progressive neurodegeneration. Current mammalian models recapitulate major pathological features but are limited by long disease courses and low throughput. Here, we establish the plant-pathogenic fungus Colletotrichum orbiculare as a scalable eukaryotic model of Niemann–Pick type C disease. Introduction of disease-associated mutations into fungal NPC1 or NPC2 homologs abolishes pathogenicity, showing that NPC dysfunction compromises lipid-dependent morphogenesis required for host penetration. Conversely, human NPC1 partially restores fungal infection. Together, these findings support functional conservation of NPC-dependent cellular processes across kingdoms. Miglustat and 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin restore pathogenicity through distinct lipid pathways. These complementary modes of rescue indicate that NPC1 and NPC2 dysfunction converges on lipid-dependent morphogenesis closely linked to actin organization. By connecting lipid metabolism, actin organization, and pharmacological rescue to a measurable infection outcome, this fungal model provides a tractable and scalable platform for mechanistic and therapeutic exploration.

Article.Title: Flippability of Escherichia coli membrane proteins under lipid stress reveals a new job for old genes
Article.Authors: Sawasato K.; Bogdanov M.
Article.Abstract: Normally, the “flip-flop” motion is reserved for small lipid molecules which move from one leaflet of the membrane to the other, and even that process is very slow without the aid of specific enzymes. Unexpectedly, we recently found that despite a prohibitively high energy barrier, Escherichia coli cardiolipin (CL) synthase A (ClsA) flips its large catalytic domain across the inner (cytoplasmic) membrane (IM) when cells were fully or partially depleted of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and that this was necessary to support cell viability. Here, we demonstrated that production of the non-native phospholipid phosphatidylcholine (PC) in PE-depleted cells prevents ClsA flipping and halts cell growth, a phenotype rescued by constitutively inverted ClsA. Surprisingly, properly oriented lactose permease (LacY) acts as a multicopy suppressor, rescuing the growth defect in the -PE+PC cells. These data indicate that neutral PC regulates the membrane topology of ClsA and LacY, and subsequently the appearance of CL to the periplasmic leaflet required for viability. Therefore, ClsA and potentially LacY may achieve varied roles from the same amino acid sequence through an unusual flip-flopping mechanism. This fruitful “repurposing” of genetic material highlights the remarkable adaptability of living organisms and their membranes. Altering E. coli lipids disrupts growth, but controlled membrane protein flipping simulates natural selection and resemonstrates that membrane proteins can re-evolve under the selective pressure of an altered lipid bilayer.

Article.Title: The representation of order and randomness in the auditory cortex
Article.Authors: Bashari S.; Jankowski M.; Nelken I.
Article.Abstract: Perception fundamentally relies on the brain’s ability to extract structure from its sensory environment. The auditory cortex possesses significant sensitivity to statistical regularities in tone sequences. To examine this phenomenon at the single-neuron level, we used multitone sequences and recorded responses from the auditory cortex of awake adult female Sprague Dawley rats. Tones were presented in periodic sequences with a fixed, repeated cycle; in a fully random condition; or in an intermediate condition in which cycles were maintained, but tones were randomly permuted within each cycle (random cycle condition). Units showed a continuum of preferences between order-preferring neurons and randomness-preferring neurons. Unexpectedly, we found sensitivity to the position of sounds in the cycle (‘phase modulation’). The strongest and most consistent phase modulations were in the responses to the random cycle condition. Finally, we show how such phase sensitivity may emerge from a simple, biologically plausible computation. Neurons in the auditory cortex exhibit a continuum of preferences from order to randomness, and show sensitivity to the position of tones in abstract repeating patterns.

Article.Title: VASP cooperates with zyxin to organize mechanically competent adhesions
Article.Authors: Chung W.; Boujemaa-Paterski R.; Winograd-Katz S.; Eibauer M.; Geiger B.; Medalia O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Focal adhesions (FAs) are dynamic macromolecular assemblies that anchor the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix via integrin receptors, thereby regulating cell morphology and migration. Here, we show that the vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein (VASP) cooperates with the mechanosensitive scaffold protein zyxin to maintain FA during maturation under actomyosin-generated tension. Using sequential CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing and cryo-electron tomography, we resolved the in situ nanoarchitecture of the FA-stress fiber interface. We establish that tropomyosin decorates the dorsal aspect of adhesion-associated stress fibers independently of VASP and zyxin. VASP and zyxin are required for the assembly of dense, aligned actin bundles with uniform polarity, oriented with their barbed ends toward the cell edge. Live-cell imaging and quantitative analyses of cells confined on micropatterns reveal that VASP and zyxin cooperate to preserve the mechanical coupling between FAs and the actin cytoskeleton under contractile load. Our findings establish that VASP and zyxin perform distinct yet complementary functions to organize FA-associated actin into mechanically competent force-transmitting units.

Article.Title: BUB signaling in cancer and molecular insights into targeted therapies
Article.Authors: Baweja B.; Saini C.; Vats P.; Soni R.; Jangir K.; Patidar P.; Kumar A.; Nema R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) is vital for proper chromosome segregation during cell division and for maintaining genomic integrity; its disruption can cause aneuploidy and tumors. The BUB gene family ensures SAC fidelity by regulating kinetochore–microtubule attachments and mitotic progression. Dysregulation leads to chromosomal instability (CIN), contributing to cancer progression, heterogeneity, metastasis, and therapy resistance. Beyond mitosis, BUB proteins influence DNA repair, chromatin remodeling, transcription, and immune responses. They interact with cell cycle and genome stability pathways, impacting cancer prognosis and therapy response. Research is ongoing to validate BUB proteins as biomarkers and develop inhibitors, possibly combined with immunotherapies or DNA-damaging agents for resistant tumors. This review summarizes their functions, highlighting their potential in personalized cancer treatment.

Article.Title: A circRNA-microRNA-Pdcd1 axis drives microglial activation and retinal ganglion cell degeneration
Article.Authors: Sun L.; Ke X.; Yu J.; Wei J.; Gu J.; Zhou W.; Cen Y.; Huang J.; Zhang X.; Zhang J.; Zhang S.; Liu X.; Ji Y.; Yan W.; Pan S.; Zhou M.; Wu W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration is the primary cause of vision loss, driven by the complicated effects of intrinsic neuronal damage and neuroinflammation. However, current single-target therapies fail to address these dual pathological challenges. CircRNAs, functioning through ceRNA networks, represent a multi-target intervention due to their stability. Here we show that, using whole‑transcriptome sequencing of optic nerve crush (ONC), we bioinformatically predicted nine candidate ceRNA networks. Among these, the network centered on circAgtpbp1 was significantly up-regulated post-injury, independent of its host gene. Mechanistically, circAgtpbp1 functions as a ceRNA by sequestering miR-3098-3p, thereby de-repressing the translation of PD-1 ( Pdcd1 ). In the ONC model, this upregulation of PD-1 protein amplifies microglial activation, creating a pathogenic non-cell-autonomous inflammatory amplification loop that drives RGC degeneration. Our findings not only uncover a novel circRNA-mediated mechanism in neurodegeneration but also identify the circAgtpbp1-miR-3098-3p-Pdcd1-microglia axis as a promising therapeutic target for neuroprotective interventions.

Article.Title: Towards a comprehensive landscape and mechanism understanding of virus-disease associations
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; You R.; Feng Y.; Lu S.; Chen S.; Fu P.; Zhu Z.; Lu C.; Zhang Z.; Xu L.; Li H.; Wang X.; Wang X.; Huang Q.; Liu X.; Xu Z.; Dong G.; Li S.; Hu X.; Xiang Z.; Hu Y.; Mao L.; Miao Z.; Meng X.; Peng Y.
Article.Abstract: Viruses are linked to human diseases through complex molecular mechanisms, yet a comprehensive investigation of virus-disease associations and their molecular basis remains lacking. We curated 3,555 high-confidence virus-disease associations involving 267 viruses and 954 diseases through text-mining over 28 million PubMed abstracts followed by rigorous manual verification, establishing the most comprehensive resource in this field to date. We then developed AVD, a user-friendly online database to store, visualize, and analyze these associations and their molecular mechanisms. Our analysis revealed that virus-disease association patterns are significantly influenced by viral taxonomy, phenotype, and key biological traits such as transmissibility, transmission routes, and tissue tropism. Molecular analysis identified a core set of bridging genes involved in the majority of virus-disease associations. Notably, these bridging genes were extensively involved in viral infections and diseases, and exhibit distinct characteristics, including a high proportion of secreted proteins, elevated expression across human tissues, and high centrality in the human protein-protein interaction network. Furthermore, we developed a machine-learning model capable of accurately predicting virus-disease associations. Collectively, this study provides a valuable data resource and analytical framework for studying virus-disease relationships and offers novel insights into their molecular mechanisms. In this manuscript the authors analyze viral-disease associations and identified that virus-disease associations are significantly influenced by viral taxonomic, phenotype, and their biological traits. Genes that may mediate the viral-disease associations are also discovered. A database called AVD (Association of Virus and human Diseases) is also constructed to facilitate the storage and convenient analysis of the associations.

Article.Title: Metabolic characteristics and evolutionary history of the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts of pennate diatoms
Article.Authors: Cheung S.; Cornejo-Castillo F.; Bianchini G.; Coale T.; Vieyra-Mexicano C.; Sánchez-Baracaldo P.; Zehr J.; Turk-Kubo K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are important sources of bioavailable nitrogen on Earth. Some nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are endosymbionts of algae, and recently one of them, UCYN-A2, was shown to be an early-stage organelle (nitroplast) of haptophytes. These biological associations are important models for studying co-evolution and organellogenesis. Endosymbioses between Rhopalodiaceae diatoms and nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria (spheroid bodies, SBs) are widespread in marine and freshwater ecosystems, but their adaptation and evolution remain unclear. We found that the genomes and metabolic characteristics of marine and freshwater SBs are remarkably similar. Purifying selection pressures dominated SB diversification both within marine and freshwater habitats and across habitat boundaries. The metabolic characteristics and genome reduction of SBs are substantially different from UCYN-A, suggesting different evolutionary journeys for the endosymbionts influenced by different hosts. We estimated that the marine SBs diversified ~185 Mya (95% highest posterior density (HPD): 340-88 Mya), which was within a prolonged oligotrophic period in the ocean, during which UCYN-A also diversified. The freshwater SBs diversified from the marine SBs ~137 Mya (95% HPD: 258-66 Mya) and further diversified ~80 Mya (95% HPD: 157-31 Mya), when sea level was increasing. Our study reveals the genetic and metabolic underpinnings characterizing the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts of Rhopalodiaceae diatoms.

Article.Title: Conserved Core but Divergent Biochemical Features of RAS-MAPK Signalling in C. elegans
Article.Authors: Bernal Astrain G.; Strakhova R.; Amro J.; Banerjee R.; Teszner E.; Decorso I.; Reiner D.; Smith M.
Article.Abstract: Genetic studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have established core principles of RAS-MAPK signalling. These nematodes encode three RAS proteins: LET-60/KRAS is essential for vulval induction, while RAS-1 and RAS-2 are orthologs of RRAS/RRAS2 and MRAS, respectively, but remain biologically and biochemically uncharacterized. We here present a comprehensive biochemical analysis of all three C. elegans RAS proteins, defining nucleotide cycling and effector interactions. We show that conserved RAS scaffolds are tuned by sequence variation to balance signalling with developmental fidelity. LET-60 has significantly impaired nucleotide exchange and changing its sequence to match human KRAS induces a protruding vulva phenotype in vivo. RAS-1 rapidly exchanges GDP-to-GTP, whereas RAS-2 remains consistently GDP-bound. LET-60 engages the RAF ortholog LIN-45 through a divergent interface, and RAS-1 unexpectedly drives SOC-2:RAS:PP1C holophosphatase assembly in a nucleotide-independent manner. Our findings reveal both conserved and distinctive biochemical features underlying RAS signalling and suggest species-specific tuning of this key proliferation pathway.

Article.Title: Age-related shift towards feedforward motor control under uncertainty
Article.Authors: Kreter N.; Sager C.; Barany D.; Dundon N.; Marneweck M.
Article.Abstract: Humans perform movements in the face of uncertainty on a daily basis. To accomplish these tasks without error, young adults frequently rely on feedback-mediated motor strategies that allow them to update their movement as uncertainty evolves. However, it remains unclear how aging impacts the ability to plan and execute movement under uncertain conditions. Here we use a “go-before-you-know” pointing task completed during functional neuroimaging to examine how aging influences movement planning under uncertainty. Behaviorally, young adults employed a strategy consistent with feedback-mediated control, biasing their trajectories toward the more likely target when uncertainty was low, and intermediate to potential targets when uncertainty was high. Older adults employed a different approach, shifting away from an intermediate reaching strategy, particularly under high uncertainty, suggesting a shift toward feedforward control. Neuroimaging mirrored these behavioral patterns, revealing that young adults encoded task uncertainty and movement direction in sensorimotor regions more strongly than older adults. Overall, these findings suggest that aging diminishes the ability to flexibly encode task-related uncertainty, leading to a shift towards feedforward control strategies.

Article.Title: Distinct genetic perturbations at the endogenous Atf4 locus uncouple polyadenylation loss from transcriptional readthrough
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Wu T.; Chen Z.; Chen D.; Ye M.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transcription termination by RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is coupled to co-transcriptional cleavage and polyadenylation directed by the canonical AAUAAA polyadenylation signal (PAS). However, the in vivo requirement of the canonical PAS for termination fidelity remains unclear. Here, we dissect PAS-dependent termination at the endogenous Atf4 locus using complementary mouse models. A previously characterized Atf4 ΔCDS + ΔPAS allele deleting exons 2-3 induces strong transcriptional readthrough, producing an Atf4 – Cacna1i fusion transcript that suppresses Rps19bp1 and causes severe cardiac defects. To isolate PAS function, we generated an Atf4 ΔCDS allele retaining the PAS and an Atf4 ΔPAS allele preserving the coding sequence but deleting the PAS. The ΔCDS allele produces modest readthrough, whereas ΔPAS does not produce detectable downstream readthrough. Instead, PAS loss permits utilization of a cryptic intragenic polyadenylation site within exon 3, generating a prematurely terminated transcript. These findings demonstrate that PAS loss does not necessarily cause transcriptional readthrough in vivo and can instead promote alternative polyadenylation at an endogenous mammalian locus.

Article.Title: Towards a unified biology of vertebrate number sense
Article.Authors: Zanon M.; Messina A.; Butterworth B.; Vallortigara G.; Brennan C.; Torres-Pérez J.; Miletto-Petrazzini M.
Article.Abstract: Number sense, the ability to estimate and compare numerical quantities, emerges early in development and is widespread across species. Despite decades of work on behavioural and neural correlates of numerosity, the genetic and mechanistic foundations remain poorly integrated. We propose a review and perspective that brings together evidence from vertebrates. Our unique focus relies on how genetic variation, brain lateralisation, and neural circuit organisation across development shape number cognition. We highlight zebrafish (Danio rerio) and chicks (Gallus gallus) as complementary comparative models that can uncover conserved principles and novel mechanisms, opening new avenues for studying the biological bases of numerical cognition and its disorders from the very early developmental stages.

Article.Title: Spi1 and Usp7 aggravate diabetic encephalopathy through regulating Ddx3x
Article.Authors: Zhao N.; Chen L.; Qin L.; Liu T.; Han G.
Article.Abstract: DEAD-box helicase 3 X-linked (DDX3X) can interact with NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) to drive inflammasome activation. Nonetheless, the role of DDX3X on NLRP3 inflammasome activation in diabetic encephalopathy remains unidentified. Here, Ddx3x knockdown alleviates microglial NLRP3 activation, which reverses the increased permeability and decreased tight junction proteins induced by conditioned medium of lipopolysaccharide-stimulated microglia (LPS-CM) in bEnd.3 endothelial cells, and overturns LPS-CM-elicited apoptosis promotion in HT22 neurons. In male type 2 diabetes db/db mice, Ddx3x silencing mitigates microglial activation, blood-brain barrier disruption, neuronal apoptosis and cognitive impairment. Spi-1 proto-oncogene (SPI1) transcriptionally activates Ddx3x ; Additionally, ubiquitin-specific protease (USP)7 reduces DDX3X ubiquitination to increase its protein stability. Silencing Spi1 / Usp7 exerts beneficial effects in vitro and in vivo, which are neutralized when overexpressing Ddx3x . In conclusion, Spi1 / Usp7 knockdown downregulates DDX3X to inhibit microglial NLRP3 activation, alleviating BBB dysfunction and neuronal loss to ameliorate diabetic encephalopathy, which suggests prospective targets for diabetic encephalopathy.

Article.Title: Evolutionary transitions in social organization and the relationship between climate and queen number in ant societies
Article.Authors: De Gasperin O.; Silvestro D.; Helanterä H.; LeBoeuf A.; Downing P.; Chapuisat M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In about one fourth of ant species, multiple queens reproduce within the same colony (‘polygyny’), reducing relatedness and potentially fuelling evolutionary conflicts among colony members. Polygyny is more common at higher altitudes / latitudes in several species, suggesting that cold climates favour multiple queens. We tested this prediction with phylogenetic analyses comparing 263 ant species and modelled the evolutionary pathways between alternative social structures. Queen number was phylogenetically labile, with bidirectional transitions between single and multi-queen species passing through socially polymorphic species (with both types of colonies). Contrary to our predictions, polygyny was not more common at higher latitudes or altitudes. Socially polymorphic species tended to occur in environments with more uniform precipitation throughout the year, and queen number increased towards the tropics. We discuss how multiple queening may be favoured in warm climates due to competitive advantages of faster colony growth and higher genetic diversity. We also call for more studies in tropical regions, as most studies were performed in the northern hemisphere.

Article.Title: CircAbcc1-encoded ABCC1-677aa modulates DLX1 to suppress ferroptosis in chronic cerebral ischemia
Article.Authors: Yang J.; Yu Y.; Fan J.; Hong K.; Zhang N.; Zheng J.
Article.Abstract: Cerebral ischemia leads to progressive neurological dysfunction due to restricted blood perfusion in the brain. While circular RNAs are known to regulate pathological processes, their ability to encode functional proteins during ischemic injury remains unclear. Here, we show that the circular RNA circAbcc1 suppresses ferroptosis in mouse and cellular models of chronic cerebral ischemia‘. We found that circAbcc1 translates into a functional protein, ABCC1-677aa. This protein actively interacts with and phosphorylates the transcription factor DLX1, triggering its export from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. This translocation prevents DLX1 from transcriptionally repressing the crucial anti-ferroptotic genes, Gpx4 and Fsp1. The subsequent upregulation of Gpx4 and Fsp1 limits lipid peroxidation and iron accumulation, successfully protecting brain neurons from ferroptosis. These findings elucidate a regulatory mechanism driven by a circular RNA-encoded protein and identify the circAbcc1-DLX1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for cerebral ischemic injury. A circular RNA, circAbcc1, protects neurons from ferroptosis during chronic cerebral ischemia by encoding the protein ABCC1-677aa. This protein relieves repression of anti-ferroptotic genes, reducing neuronal damage and highlighting the circAbcc1-DLX1 pathway as a therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Uncoupling of seagrass host selection and succession for microbial guilds in meadow chronosequence
Article.Authors: Maithani P.; Sim C.; Srinivas S.; Kwek Z.; Case R.
Article.Abstract: Succession describes the predictable assembly of communities and habitats towards increasingly complex ecosystems. In marine meadows, the relative roles of succession and host selection in structuring microbial communities and functions remain unclear. Using chronosequences of the pioneering seagrass Halophila ovalis , we examined bacterial community succession (16S rRNA gene) and functional genes linked to nitrogen fixation and sulfur cycling ( nifH , soxB , aprA , dsrA ) across meadow sediments and seagrass microbiomes (rhizoplane and phylloplane). Sediment communities diversified progressively with distance from the patch edge, whereas host-associated microbiomes were differentially impacted from the meadow sediments, indicating strong host selection. For sulfur-cycling genes, taxonomic succession was decoupled from gene-sequence diversity, while only nifH exhibited successional patterns. Nevertheless, all communities displayed directional assembly trajectories despite being shaped by contrasting ecological processes. Our findings show that both succession and host selection predictably drive microbial community assembly in developing seagrass meadows, while functional gene potential responded in a niche-dependent manner.

Article.Title: Selective inhibition of IL-6 trans-signalling reveals distinct mechanisms of human classic and trans-signalling receptor-complex formation
Article.Authors: Rieneck E.; Haak J.; Asgarov K.; Pallandre J.; Wundrack N.; Ettich J.; Miri N.; Floss D.; Scheller J.; Garbers C.; Clark A.; Wijdenes J.; Schaper F.; Dittrich A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The cytokine interleukin-6 orchestrates inflammation through two distinct pathways of receptor activation: anti-inflammatory classic signalling via membrane-bound interleukin-6 receptor and pro-inflammatory trans-signalling via soluble interleukin-6 receptor. Current interleukin-6-targeted therapies block both pathways, thereby disrupting essential homeostatic functions initiated by classic signalling. We here show a high-affinity, human-specific antibody that selectively inhibits interleukin-6 trans-signalling. This antibody maintains classic signalling-induced expression of hepatic acute phase genes while completely blocking trans-signalling-induced activation of endothelial cells. By targeting the domain D2 of membrane-bound and soluble human interleukin-6 receptor, the antibody selectively prevents formation of the trans-signalling receptor complex without interfering with ligand binding. This selective blockade demonstrates that human interleukin-6 classic and trans-signalling proceed through distinct receptor assemblies. Our findings describe mechanistic insight into interleukin-6 receptor assembly and provide a strategy to suppress inflammatory interleukin-6 activity while preserving regenerative and anti-inflammatory signalling, thus offering both conceptual and potential therapeutic advances in the targeted modulation of cytokine signalling networks.

Article.Title: NEDD1 stabilization regulated by hUTP14a and FBW7γ axis safeguards mitotic cell fate homeostasis
Article.Authors: Su Y.; Jiang Y.; Sun X.; Zhang C.; Zhao Z.; Li L.; Du X.
Article.Abstract: Accurate spindle formation is vital for mitotic progression and genomic DNA segregation, with γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) mediating microtubule nucleation, and NEDD1 serving as its essential recruitment/anchoring adaptor. Here, we identify a pathway that controls NEDD1 stability during mitosis. hUTP14a relocates to the perichromosomal region at mitotic onset; its depletion causes mitotic catastrophe, impaired chromosomal congression, and reduced γ-tubulin recruitment around chromosomes. Mass spectrometry identifies NEDD1 as a critical hUTP14a-interacting partner during mitosis. hUTP14a protects NEDD1 from ubiquitin-mediated degradation. UbiBrowser 2.0 database prediction and validation experiments identify FBW7γ as an E3 ligase to promote NEDD1 K323 ubiquitination-mediated degradation, while hUTP14a facilitates FBW7γ degradation in a leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-dependent manner. The hUTP14a depletion-induced mitotic catastrophe is reversed by ectopic Flag-NEDD1-K323R but not wild-type Flag-NEDD1. Article.Title: Engineering T cell-selective chemokine inhibitors through network-level directed evolution
Article.Authors: Payne M.; Durães F.; Clark C.; Wilde E.; Karuppanan K.; Chandra S.; Brennan P.; Hodson D.; Smagurauskaite G.; Bhattacharya S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) are sustained by chemokine-driven recruitment of effector T cells. Although direct suppression of T cell function can be effective, systemic immunosuppression and infection risk limit clinical utility. Targeting chemokine networks offers an alternative strategy, yet chemokine redundancy has hindered the development of clinically effective inhibitors. Tick evasins overcome chemokine redundancy by binding multiple chemokines. Here we show that network-level directed evolution of class B evasin-derived peptides generates T cell-selective chemokine inhibitors. In contrast to analogous class A-derived peptides, these preferentially bind and inhibit chemokines that drive T cell migration. Structural modelling of chemokine:peptide complexes and structure-guided mutagenesis suggest that evasin-derived peptides sterically occlude receptor-binding surfaces and that class B-derived peptides exhibit a more compact organisation of key interaction hotspots than a previously characterised class A-derived peptide. Article.Title: Divergent processing strategies for auditory sequence recognition in humans and zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata)
Article.Authors: Ning Z.; Li J.; ten Cate C.; Honing H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deriving sequential information from complex sounds is a challenge for auditory systems, yet it remains unclear whether humans and nonhuman species integrate multidimensional cues or prioritize a single dimension when processing multidimensional input. By presenting probe stimuli that selectively preserved or disrupted either pitch or formant trajectory, we quantified these processing strategies. We show that zebra finches employ an additive integration strategy, treating pitch and formant trajectories as complementary components of a unified auditory pattern. In contrast, humans exhibit a dominant reliance on pitch. Experience further modulates this bias, with trained human listeners recruiting secondary cues to preserve learned relational structure when pitch is unreliable. These findings imply a cross-species divergence in auditory representation, suggesting that auditory processing is shaped by an interplay of species-specific priorities and experience-dependent functional substitution.

Article.Title: Functional specialization and dynamical interaction in human amygdala subregions support fearful-expression processing
Article.Authors: Cao D.; Cui J.; Yan X.; Zhang X.; Dang Y.; Zhao H.; Li J.; Zhang J.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Fearful-expression processing supports adaptive responses to potential threats, requiring both rapid threat evaluation and face-related information processing. Control analyses preserve the main neural effects. In a separate cohort of seven patients, intracranial stimulation produces dissociable behavioral effects, with lateral stimulation impairing fear matching and medial stimulation facilitating neutral-face matching. Together, these findings reveal a condition-dependent functional differentiation within the human amygdala during fearful-expression processing.

Article.Authors: Fu Y.; Xu Z.; Yao Q.; Mu Y.; Jiang Y.
Article.Abstract: The ability to perceive linguistic features is essential for language comprehension, yet how our brains dynamically recognize, integrate and process distinct linguistic features is still controversial. By linking behavior to neural responses, we uncover the frontal-parietal network associated with individual differences in response to dual-feature violations. Article.Title: Time-locked activities of resting-state networks that transiently occur in human resting-state brain activities
Article.Authors: Takeda Y.; Hiroe N.; Yamashita O.
Article.Abstract: Spontaneous brain activities at rest are organized into resting-state networks, such as the default mode network. While the default mode network is assumed to interact with other networks to integrate distributed information, its fine-scale temporal dynamics remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate how the default mode network interacts with other networks at millisecond-scale temporal resolution. Using a large dataset of resting-state magnetoencephalography and our recently proposed method, we estimated the spatiotemporal patterns that recur in resting-state brain activity and then examined the interactions across the resting-state networks in these patterns. In the alpha/beta band component of the spatiotemporal patterns, the default mode network and the visual/sensorimotor network alternately appear with a lag of about 24/13 ms, corresponding to about π /2 rad in the alpha/beta oscillation. These alternating and orthogonal activities of the resting-state networks may reflect the brain’s strategy to achieve both the integration and separation of visual and sensorimotor information via the default mode network. Furthermore, we reveal how these activities consecutively move between the default mode network and the visual/sensorimotor network in tens of milliseconds. Article.Title: MUFASA: a continuous-time stochastic framework for realistic fluorescence microscopy simulation
Article.Authors: Omezzine W.; Schaub S.; Blanc-Féraud L.; Calatroni L.
Article.Abstract: We present MUFASA ( M ulti-Protocol U nified F luorescence-based A dvanced S imulation A lgorithm), a physically grounded, continuous-time simulator of several super-resolution fluorescence microscopy protocols. By modeling fluorophore dynamics using continuous-time Markov chains, MUFASA’s simulation features yield realistic photon emission behavior across both Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM) and fluorescence fluctuation-based (FF-SRM) settings–independently of frame duration and sampling. The framework supports both individual emitters and structure-level simulations, incorporating photophysical transitions, photobleaching, and camera properties.To quantitatively compare simulations with real data, we introduce a novel validation metric based on the 1-Wasserstein distance between simulated and experimental photon-count distributions. Another functionality of MUFASA is the estimation of key photophysical parameters (e.g., molar extinction coefficient) and the suggestion of optimal light-source power ranges from fluctuation data.An intuitive Python-based graphical interface for real-time parameter tuning, visualization, and TIFF export is provided.Designed for biologists, physicists, microscopists, and computational imaging engineers, MUFASA offers a practical platform for microscopy experiment design, hypothesis testing and holds the potential of being used for the generation of realistic training data for data-driven methods across modalities.

Article.Title: Machine learning analysis of cilia driven particle transport distinguishes primary ciliary dyskinesia from normal cilia
Article.Authors: Hadas N.; Xu H.; Neupane S.; Twan W.; Elgamal A.; Lunel A.; Mahjoub M.; Horani A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic condition causing dysmotile cilia and abnormal mucociliary clearance. Using high-speed video microscopy, we captured fluorescent microsphere movement on cultured multiciliated cells from 14 individuals with primary ciliary dyskinesia and 10 healthy donors (602 videos). Quantitative and visual analyses reveal distinct motility profiles between PCD and non-primary ciliary dyskinesia and normal recordings. Classical machine learning models and a convolutional neural network classify recordings with 95-97% accuracy and differentiate affected from normal samples. Machine learning provides an objective, accurate framework for characterizing ciliary dysfunction, offering potential as a diagnostic tool for primary ciliary dyskinesia.
