Article.Title: IFN ‐ γ ‐Responsive Microglia‐Derived Extracellular Vesicles Impair White Matter Repair After Stroke Through a miR ‐9‐5p/ NEDD4 ‐Dependent Mechanism
Article.Authors: Qian D.; Xu T.; Guo Y.; Deng S.; Geng Y.; Li H.; Gan L.; Lian Q.; Xu J.; Yao H.; Ye J.; Myagmartsend E.; Yang G.; Wang J.; Tang Y.; An Q.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Promoting white matter repair is crucial for functional recovery after ischemic stroke. Our previous study has identified an IFN‐ γ ‐responsive microglia phenotype in the brain after stroke. However, its role in white matter repair remains poorly understood. Herein, we find that extracellular vesicles derived from IFN‐ γ ‐responsive microglia (IFN‐ γ EVs) are internalized by oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), leading to impaired OPCs proliferation, survival, and differentiation and reduced white matter repair in a murine transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model. Mechanistically, miR‐9‐5p enrichment in IFN‐ γ EVs suppresses NEDD4 expression, a key regulator of myelination, leading to reduced OPCs maturation and white matter repair. Genetic interventions including miR‐9‐5p knockdown in IFN‐ γ EVs or NEDD4 overexpression in OPCs restore remyelination and functional recovery. Our findings demonstrate that IFN‐ γ EVs act as negative regulators of OPCs differentiation and remyelination following ischemic stroke via miR‐9‐5p/NEDD4 pathway. Targeting this signaling axis may represent a novel therapeutic strategy to enhance remyelination and functional recovery after stroke.

Article.Title: Potential Roles of Flavonoids from Chrysanthemi Flos and Chrysanthemi Indici Flos in Modulating Bile Acid Metabolism: Mechanistic Insights and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zhao S.; Zeng L.; Tang H.; Cui Y.; Zeng R.; Xie J.
Article.Abstract: Changes in bile acid metabolism are associated with metabolic liver disease, inflammation, and immune dysfunction. Therefore, regulating bile acid homeostasis may help in preventing and treating liver injury and metabolic disorders. Chrysanthemi Flos and Chrysanthemi Indici Flos contain many bioactive flavonoids and have several reported pharmacological effects. However, how their flavonoids regulate bile acid metabolism has not been reviewed in detail. This review summarizes 52 flavonoids identified in Chrysanthemi Flos and Chrysanthemi Indici Flos. We review their reported effects on bile acid conjugation and synthesis, secretion and excretion, enterohepatic circulation, and main receptors, including FXR (farnesoid X receptor, nuclear bile acid receptor; regulates synthesis/transport), TGR5 (Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5, GPCR (G protein-coupled receptor) bile acid receptor; GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) secretion, energy/anti-inflammation, incretin; glucose/lipid homeostasis), and LXRα (liver X receptor α, nuclear receptor; cholesterol efflux and CYP7A1 (cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase, rate-limiting enzyme of classical bile acid synthesis; cholesterol → 7α-hydroxycholesterol) regulation). We also consider how these pathways may affect inflammation and metabolic disorders. This review relates the reported mechanisms to the traditional use of these medicinal plants for “clearing the liver and promoting bile flow.” It also outlines research needs for assessing natural hepatoprotective and metabolic disease interventions that target bile acid metabolism.

Article.Title: Limited Gut Microbiome Differences Between Relapsing–Remitting and Secondary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis: A Shotgun Metagenomic Study
Article.Authors: Vacaras C.; Vacaras V.; Nistor C.; Vesa S.; Jucan C.; Furdui I.; Strilciuc S.; Stefanescu E.; Chira D.; Rafila A.; Muresanu D.
Article.Abstract: The gut microbiome may contribute to multiple sclerosis (MS) pathophysiology, but its relationship with disease phenotype and progression remains unclear. To characterize taxonomic and functional gut microbiome differences between relapsing–remitting MS (RRMS) and secondary progressive MS (SPMS) and their associations with neurological disability and circulating biomarkers. This cross-sectional study included 89 participants (30 healthy controls, 29 RRMS, and 30 SPMS). Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was used to assess microbial diversity, taxonomic profiles, and predefined short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-related pathways, integrated with disability measures and serum GFAP, NfL, and S100B. SPMS participants were substantially older than those with RRMS (median 49.0 vs. 31.0 years), prompting age-adjusted analyses and an age-overlap sensitivity analysis. Alpha diversity and overall microbial community composition were similar across groups. SPMS showed greater interindividual microbial community dispersion than RRMS in the full cohort, with a similar direction and magnitude but attenuated statistical significance in the age-overlap sensitivity analysis. Exploratory taxonomic signals were not confirmed by FDR-controlled analyses. No robust phenotype-specific differences in predicted SCFA-related pathways or associations of taxonomic or functional features with disability or circulating biomarkers were identified. Greater microbial community dispersion in SPMS was observed in the full cohort, but this finding was attenuated in the age-overlap sensitivity analysis and should be considered preliminary. Overall, these findings do not support a distinct SPMS-associated gut microbiome signature, although potential phenotype-related differences cannot be excluded.

Article.Title: RNA Interference-Mediated Suppression of RAGE
Article.Authors: Muzaffarova T.; Malinovskaya E.; Moskalev A.
Article.Abstract: The receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE/AGER) is an important mediator of inflammatory signaling and has been implicated in chronic low-grade inflammation associated with aging. Chronic low-grade inflammation (“inflammaging”) is a characteristic feature of biological aging, providing a rationale for investigating molecular regulators of inflammatory signaling such as RAGE. This study aimed to develop and validate short hairpin RNA (shRNA) constructs suppressing AGER/RAGE in human cell models. Five shRNA constructs targeting human AGER were designed, cloned into pLSL-puro, and verified by Sanger sequencing. Lentiviral vectors were produced in HEK293T cells and used to establish stable HEK293T, 786-O, and human umbilical vein endothelial cell (HUVEC) populations with AGER knockdown. AGER/RAGE expression was assessed by RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and flow cytometry. Silencing efficiency varied with the construct and the cellular model. sh1 produced the strongest suppression of AGER, exceeding 70% in selected models, whereas sh2 was effective in HEK293T and 786-O cells. Reduced RAGE expression was confirmed at the mRNA, protein, and cell-surface levels, identifying sh1 and sh2 as lead candidates. An AGER-focused workflow for lentiviral shRNA construct screening and experimental validation was established, providing a reproducible approach for generating stable cell models with reduced AGER/RAGE expression. Further work is required to confirm isoform specificity, assess off-target effects, and define the functional consequences of RAGE suppression.

Article.Title: Exploring Pathophysiological Processes Shared Between Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Osteoarthritis
Article.Authors: Majeed Y.; Schulze-Tanzil G.; Kokozidou M.
Article.Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and osteoarthritis (OA) are highly prevalent chronic disorders with increasing global burdens that frequently coexist and share common risk factors, including obesity, aging and chronic low-grade inflammation. This narrative review aims to summarize current evidence regarding the epidemiological, clinical and molecular links between T2DM and OA and to highlight potential therapeutic implications. Growing evidence suggests that T2DM contributes to OA development and progression through multiple interconnected mechanisms. These include advanced glycation end-product (AGE) accumulation, oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix degradation, impaired autophagy, ferroptosis, mesenchymal stem cell dysfunction and microvascular impairment within joint tissues. In addition, shared genetic and molecular pathways, including AGE–RAGE, IL-17, PI3K/Akt/mTOR and LGR6/Wnt/β-catenin/NRF2 signaling, further support a biological connection between the two diseases. Clinically, T2DM is associated with increased OA severity, enhanced pain sensitization, accelerated disease progression and higher rates of joint arthroplasty. Emerging evidence also suggests that antidiabetic agents, particularly metformin and glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, may exert disease-modifying effects through anti-inflammatory, metabolic and chondroprotective mechanisms. Overall, T2DM and OA should be regarded as interconnected metabolic-inflammatory disorders. Improved understanding of their shared mechanisms may facilitate earlier intervention, therapeutic repurposing and integrated multidisciplinary management strategies to reduce disease burden and improve patient outcomes.

Article.Title: From Chronic Infection to Microbial Imbalance: Rethinking Chronic Rhinosinusitis
Article.Authors: Łabaz J.; Guth M.; Kaleta J.; Kaczmarek J.; Kinczel M.; Kornak K.; Kaczor M.; Leszczyszyn A.; Dorobisz K.; Pazdro-Zastawny K.
Article.Abstract: Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) has traditionally been viewed as a chronic inflammatory disease in which microbial factors are implicated. However, increasing evidence suggests that CRS may be better understood as a disruption of sinonasal microbial homeostasis rather than as a chronic infection caused by a single pathogen. This review summarizes current knowledge on healthy sinonasal microbiome composition and function as well as microbial alterations in CRS. Particular attention is given to dysbiosis involving potentially pathogenic microorganisms, including Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, as well as biofilm formation and its interactions with the epithelial barrier and host immune response. We also discuss host-related, therapeutic, hormonal, and environmental factors that may contribute to microbial imbalance. Current evidence does not clearly establish whether dysbiosis is a cause or consequence of chronic inflammation. Based on the evidence synthesized here, we propose that CRS may be understood as a dynamic, bidirectional interaction between microbial imbalance and chronic inflammation, whereby microbial alterations may contribute to epithelial and immune dysregulation, while changes in the host environment influence the sinonasal ecosystem. By integrating these microbiological and host-related perspectives, this review provides a boarder framework for understanding CRS pathophysiology and guiding future research into individual patterns of sinonasal microbial homeostasis.

Article.Title: Changes in Connexin-43 Expression and Neuropil Ultrastructure in the Cerebral Cortex of Bats During the Sleep–Wake Cycle
Article.Authors: Rodkin S.; Bachurin S.; Nabiullina R.; Shebeko S.; Logvinov A.; Nwosu C.; Kirichenko E.
Article.Abstract: Sleep maintains central nervous system homeostasis, but many molecular mechanisms of sleep–wake regulation remain poorly understood. Connexin-43 (Cx43), the astrocytic gap junction protein, supports neuroglial communication, yet its role in physiological sleep is little studied. Here, we analyzed Cx43 expression, gap junction organization and neuropil ultrastructure in the motor cortex of common noctule bats (Nyctalus noctula) during sleep and wakefulness using confocal microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, semi-automated image analysis, and molecular dynamics. Sleep was associated with higher Cx43 immunoreactivity and with more and larger astrocytic gap-junction plaques than wakefulness. Across neuropil fields, synaptic, process and mitochondrial counts and total active-zone length were higher during wakefulness, and mean mitochondrial profiles were larger during sleep; after averaging within animals, only total active-zone length remained significantly greater during wakefulness. More perisynaptic astrocytic process (PAP) profiles contacted synapses during wakefulness, whereas individual PAPs were larger during sleep; both contrasts remained significant after animal-level averaging. As a secondary, hypothesis-generating analysis, we simulated histidine protonation of the Cx43 hemichannel as a simplified model of acidic conditions. Cerebral pH was not measured, and the simulations do not explain the sleep-associated Cx43 increase. In silico, protonation reduced conformational flexibility and narrowed the central and extracellular pore regions.

Article.Title: Rapidly Progressive Dedifferentiated Liposarcoma of the Spermatic Cord: A Case Report
Article.Authors: Rocha F.; Figueroa-Emiliani J.; Vargas-Castellanos E.
Article.Abstract: Dedifferentiated liposarcoma (DDLPS) of the spermatic cord is an exceptionally rare and aggressive malignancy for which diagnostic and therapeutic guidelines remain limited. We report the case of a 73-year-old man who presented with a rapidly enlarging left inguinal/paratesticular mass. Initial ultrasonography showed a 4.3 × 3.0 × 3.7 cm hypoechoic lesion interpreted as suggestive of leiomyoma. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging subsequently demonstrated a 10 × 5 × 5 cm neoplastic mass arising from the spermatic cord. The patient underwent radical left orchiectomy. Histopathological examination revealed a high-grade spindle-cell neoplasm with marked pleomorphism and up to 30 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for p16, MDM2, and CDK4, with a Ki-67 proliferative index of 95%, supporting the diagnosis of high-grade DDLPS. Although surgical margins were negative, the disease progressed rapidly. Nineteen days after surgery, the patient developed bilateral pleural effusion, pleural infiltration, pulmonary metastases, and a probable pathological T11 fracture. Because of extensive metastatic disease and clinical deterioration, systemic antineoplastic therapy was not initiated in this advanced setting. The patient died 27 days after hospitalization due to progressive metastatic disease. This case highlights the diagnostic difficulty, aggressive biological behavior, and need for early multidisciplinary management of spermatic cord DDLPS.

Article.Title: Integrative Genetic and Transcriptomic Analysis Reveals Candidate Molecular Differences Among Dementia with Lewy Bodies, Alzheimer’s Disease, and Parkinson’s Disease Dementia
Article.Authors: Öztan G.; İşsever T.; İşsever H.
Article.Abstract: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) shares substantial clinical and molecular features with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD), complicating the identification of disease-specific molecular alterations. This study aimed to characterize transcriptomic differences among these disorders and to integrate expression findings with published Lewy body dementia (LBD) genetic evidence. Gene-level expression profiles from 42 postmortem prefrontal cortex samples in GSE150696, including controls, AD, DLB, and PDD, were analyzed using age- and sex-adjusted empirical-Bayes models with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, followed by sensitivity analyses, post hoc exploratory candidate selection, and integration with an external LBD multi-omics gene-prioritization dataset. No gene reached FDR < 0.05 in the DLB-versus-AD comparison. In contrast, SLC19A2, VAMP1, and COX5B were lower in DLB than in PDD and were FDR-supported in the primary age- and sex-adjusted model, although their statistical significance was partly model-dependent. A post hoc cross-disease analysis identified 60 exploratory candidates, of which SYT11 was the only gene overlapping with the published LBD-prioritized gene set. The overall 60-gene set was not significantly enriched for LBD-associated genes. These findings did not demonstrate broad robust disease–disease differences and are consistent with substantial molecular overlap, while remaining compatible with limited statistical power. A limited number of transcriptomic candidates, including the exploratory SYT11 overlap, warrant independent validation.

Article.Title: Stem Cell and Exosome Treatment for Organ Health and Longevity
Article.Authors: Prodromos C.; Del Villar R.; Striegel A.; Pena G.; Dixit R.; Xu A.
Article.Abstract: Aging is associated with inflammation and is the greatest risk factor for chronic disease. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and exosomes have anti-inflammatory, pro-healing, and immunomodulatory effects that make them appealing candidates to reverse tissue and organ aging, improve overall organ function, and promote longevity. We hypothesized that treatment with MSCs and/or exosomes would improve the function of healthy mammalian organ systems and tissues, extend lifespan, and that treatment with stem cells from younger animals would have a greater rejuvenative effect than those from older animals. Through a review of the PubMed-indexed scientific literature, we sought to determine whether there is sound preclinical and/or clinical evidence to support these hypotheses. 34 preclinical studies were chosen as they demonstrated that stem cells and/or exosomes can restore bone density, improve muscle strength, significantly rejuvenate multiple organ systems, and increase longevity. Stem cell treatment appears to increase longevity, and both stem cell and exosome treatments are effective in rejuvenating and improving tissue and organ function in mammalian systems. Stem cells can extend overall mammalian lifespan. Transplantation of bone-marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells can restore bone density in mice. MSCs have a regenerative effect on aging muscles in mice. Both stem cells and exosomes have a rejuvenative effect on animal organ systems. Stem cells and exosomes improve organ function in the absence of pathological states.

Article.Title: Nanopore Sequencing for Epigenetic Decoding: Applications, Analytical Constraints, and Translational Prospects
Article.Authors: Xin J.; Liu J.; Liu Y.; Liu X.; Ma M.; Huang A.; Ye Z.; Zhang P.; Wang X.; Zeng T.; Lin X.; Liu C.; Lu L.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Epigenetic regulation involves multiple molecular layers, including DNA and RNA modifications, histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), and chromatin accessibility. These processes contribute to cell identity, development, and disease, but their measurement remains technically challenging because sequence context, molecular modification, chromatin state, and transcript structure are often assayed separately. As a representative third-generation sequencing technology, nanopore sequencing is profoundly reshaping the interpretation of the epigenetic code through its distinctive capabilities, including long-read sequencing, direct single-molecule signal detection, and the identification of nucleic acid modifications without bisulfite conversion or PCR in appropriate workflows. This review summarizes applications of nanopore sequencing in epigenomics and epitranscriptomics and evaluates emerging nanopore-based approaches for protein and histone sensing. We focus on what can currently be measured, the experimental and computational requirements for reliable decoding, and the limitations that must be addressed before broader multi-omic and clinical use.

Article.Title: The NLRP3 Inflammasome Across the AKI–AKD–CKD Continuum: Mitochondrial, Epigenetic and Endocrine–Metabolic Regulation
Article.Authors: La Russa D.; Bossio S.; La Russa A.; Di Dio M.; Pellegrino D.; Perri A.
Article.Abstract: The NLRP3 inflammasome has emerged as a potential molecular link between cellular stress, sterile inflammation, and progressive kidney damage. This review critically examines canonical, non-canonical, and mitochondrial mechanisms of NLRP3 regulation across the acute kidney injury (AKI)–acute kidney disease (AKD)–chronic kidney disease (CKD) continuum, integrating their relationships with pyroptosis, maladaptive repair, fibrosis, and epigenetic regulation. Particular attention is given to endocrine–metabolic signals that may shape renal inflammasome activity. Hyperglycemia, advanced glycation end products, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, TXNIP signaling, lipotoxicity, impaired tubular fatty-acid oxidation, podocyte insulin resistance, obesity-related adipokine imbalance, and aldosterone-mineralocorticoid receptor activation may converge on NLRP3. Conversely, inflammasome-dependent cytokine release and pyroptosis may amplify insulin resistance, metabolic dysfunction, and cardiorenal injury, establishing a bidirectional endocrine-renal inflammatory loop. Importantly, increased NLRP3 mRNA or protein abundance is distinguished from functional inflammasome activation, which is more strongly supported by downstream evidence such as ASC recruitment/oligomerization, caspase-1 activation, mature IL-1β/IL-18 production, GSDMD cleavage, or pyroptotic cell death. A central issue is whether NLRP3 is a causal driver of kidney disease or a marker of ongoing tissue injury. Although genetic and pharmacological studies support a pathogenic role in experimental models, clinical evidence remains largely associative and disease-dependent. NLRP3-related signals should therefore be regarded as candidate, rather than validated, biomarkers. SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists and finerenone may indirectly attenuate NLRP3 signaling, but mechanistic mediation of their clinical benefits remains unproven. Defining cell-specific activation and clinical target engagement will be essential to establish NLRP3 as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Expression Analysis of the HDAC Gene Family in Stevia rebaudiana
Article.Authors: Zhao C.; Fu Y.; Wang D.; Lin K.; Yun L.; Xie F.; Bai G.
Article.Abstract: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are crucial epigenetic regulators that modulate chromatin structure and gene expression through histone deacetylation. Stevia rebaudiana, a natural source of high-intensity sweeteners, faces significant cultivation challenges due to environmental stresses such as osmotic stress and salinity. However, the HDAC gene family in S. rebaudiana remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we present the first genome-wide analysis of the HDAC family in S. rebaudiana, identifying 22 SrHDAC transcripts derived from 18 gene loci, which were classified into three subfamilies (RPD3/HDA1, SIR2, and HD2). Systematic characterization of gene structure, conserved domains, and promoter cis elements indicated their potential involvement in hormone signaling and abiotic stress regulation. Expression profiling revealed tissue-specific expression patterns and differential responses to methyl jasmonate (MeJA) treatment and PEG-induced osmotic stress. Subcellular localization of representative proteins in Nicotiana benthamiana leaf cells supported nucleolar-associated functions. These findings provide a foundation for understanding HDAC-mediated epigenetic regulation in S. rebaudiana growth, development, and stress adaptation, and identify candidate genes for future functional studies toward stress-tolerant cultivar improvement.

Article.Title: Analysis of Melatonin Secretion Patterns in Buffalo Milk and Its Association with AANAT Polymorphisms
Article.Authors: You S.; Fu Y.; Li Y.; Jiang J.; Hau E.; Wei X.; Long Z.; Zeng Q.; Liu Q.; Li L.
Article.Abstract: Melatonin (MT) is an important bioactive functional component of milk, where its content and biosynthetic mechanism are of considerable relevance to the quality regulation of dairy buffalo milk. This study aimed to investigate the variation patterns and biosynthetic mechanisms of melatonin in milk from dairy buffaloes. A total of 125 buffalo milk samples were collected, and MT content was determined using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). MT secretion patterns were evaluated according to breed, lactation, parity, and milking time (light exposure). In addition, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data were used to screen for single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), which are significantly associated with melatonin biosynthetic enzyme genes. The results showed that breed, milking time, and lactation were the major factors affecting MT content in buffalo milk. Based on the WGS data, two SNPs significantly associated with MT secretion and synthesis were identified within the aralkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT) region, among which the GG genotype at 3-8019407 and the CC genotype at 3-8019446 were associated with higher MT content. The MT content for both wild-type homozygotes was 59.54 pg/mL, which was higher than that of heterozygotes (39.12 pg/mL) (p < 0.05). With the exception of SNP2 and SNP8, all other SNPs were in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. These findings will serve as a reference for the subsequent selection and identification of breeding materials for high MT dairy buffalo, as well as for the development of high MT buffalo milk products.

Article.Title: Receptor-Side Neuroimmune Remodeling in IBD: Participant-Level Associations with Metabolite-Sensing Programs and Colorectal Neoplasia Context
Article.Authors: Hu H.; Xu K.; Yuan X.; Lei Z.; Lu Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Microbial metabolite sensing and neuroimmune signaling are increasingly recognized as interacting components of the mucosal response in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). However, their organization across individuals and the cellular compartments carrying the relevant receptor machinery remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether metabolite-sensing host programs covary with neuroimmune receptor-side mucosal states at the participant level and whether the corresponding receptor transcripts map to defined mucosal compartments. Methods: HMP2 mucosal transcriptomes were analyzed at the participant level to evaluate prespecified relationships between metabolite-sensing and neuroimmune receptor-side host programs. Receptor-side neuroimmune remodeling was operationalized as cross-sectional participant-level host-program organization together with compartmental localization of the corresponding receptor transcripts, rather than longitudinal change or receptor activation. The stability and interpretation of these relationships were examined through diagnosis/inflammation adjustment, participant-grouped explanatory modeling, and tissue-composition sensitivity analyses. Complementary metabolomic, single-cell, UC, and colorectal-neoplasia datasets were used to examine synchronized metabolic associations, receptor-transcript localization, and the broader disease context of the identified mucosal programs. The microbiome, metabolomic, and transcriptomic datasets were obtained from multiple independent public cohorts. Results: Among 251 HMP2 biopsies from 90 participants, 13 of 20 prespecified host–program associations passed FDR correction in participant-mean analyses, and 13 of 20 remained supported after diagnosis/inflammation adjustment, with 12 associations shared between the two analyses. The strongest relationships connected the SCFA receptor/barrier-response program with the inflammation-associated reactive/glial-adjacent state (ρ = 0.727) and the CGRP/adrenomedullin-family receptor-side score (ρ = 0.552), and connected the AHR-response context with the same receptor-side score (ρ = 0.531). Single-cell analyses localized CALCRL, RAMP2, and RAMP3 mainly to endothelial cells, VIPR1 to epithelial cells, and VIPR2 to stromal cells. The attenuation of incremental model fit after composition-proxy conditioning further indicated that this organization is closely embedded in mucosal tissue ecology. Matched metabolomic and premalignant-cohort analyses provided complementary evidence on the scope of this framework but did not extend it to synchronized metabolite coupling or neoplastic progression. Conclusions: Participant-level associations and compartment-resolved receptor localization support a cross-sectional receptor-side neuroimmune remodeling framework in IBD. The convergence of host-program organization and cellular localization prioritizes specific receptor–compartment relationships for spatial validation, functional receptor perturbation, and prospectively matched stool–mucosal studies.

Article.Title: Tenascin X and Tenascin C Serum Levels in Relation to Age and Cardiometabolic Risk Parameters
Article.Authors: Baumgartner-Parzer S.; Fuhrberg K.; Wagenlechner C.; Schnait F.; Schmid N.; Bayerle-Eder M.; Grimm G.; Vila G.; Schernthaner-Reiter M.
Article.Abstract: Tenascin C (TNC) and tenascin X (TNX) are extracellular matrix glycoproteins in the same family but with reportedly distinct functions: TNC is acutely up-regulated during tissue damage, whereas TNX maintains structural connective tissue stability. Recently, recurring pathogenic variants in the TNX gene (TNXB) were linked to Ehlers–Danlos syndrome in patients with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, yet the regulation and clinical function of TNX remain poorly understood. In this retrospective cohort study, serum TNX and TNC were measured by ELISA in 274 patients with prevalent cardiovascular risk factors. In bivariate analyses, TNX levels correlated negatively with age and cardiometabolic risk parameters (blood pressure, glucose) and positively with kidney function; in multivariable regression, TNX was independently associated with age, sex, and height, whereas the associations with cardiometabolic parameters were no longer significant. TNX levels remained unchanged following acute glucocorticoid administration. TNC levels correlated negatively with age and glycated hemoglobin and positively with kidney function in bivariate analyses. These findings support distinct but overlapping roles for TNX and TNC in connective tissue function and extend current knowledge, suggesting both proteins as candidate systemic biomarkers for aging. A further investigation of TNX and TNC in a clinical context could reveal new mechanisms for the detection or prevention of cardiometabolic disease.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal Analysis of Intranuclear Inclusion Body and Virus Formation in Human Adenovirus Type 5-Infected Cells
Article.Authors: Wu H.; Fujioka Y.; Sakaguchi S.; Odake C.; Suzuki Y.; Nakano T.
Article.Abstract: Human adenovirus type 5 (HAdV-5) forms a characteristic intranuclear inclusion body in infected cells. However, the relationship between the intranuclear inclusion body and virus formation in HAdV-5-infected cells remains unclear. This study conducted a detailed investigation of the relationship between the structure of the inclusion body and the localization of the virus in HAdV-5-infected cells using electron microscopy and three-dimensional (3D) tomography analytical techniques. Immunostaining for viral proteins was also performed to determine their colocalization with the intranuclear inclusion body. 3D analysis revealed the intranuclear inclusion body as the major site of viral particle accumulation in the cells. Viral particles were identified within the intranuclear inclusion body and arranged in a crystalline structure parallel to the fibrous structures of this body. Moreover, mature viral particles were predominantly distributed around the intranuclear inclusion body. Certain viral proteins were also detected in the intranuclear inclusion body by immunoelectron microscopy. We propose that intranuclear inclusion bodies serve as sites of viral replication in HAdV-5-infected cells. Through the 3D analysis, we clarified the relationship between the distribution and localization of intranuclear inclusion bodies and viral particles in HAdV-5-infected cells. These findings can improve our understanding of adenoviral infection mechanisms and may contribute toward developing novel antiviral strategies.

Article.Title: AIRE Deficiency Impairs Thymic Epithelial Progenitor Differentiation from Mouse Embryonic Stem Cells and Accelerates Type 1 Diabetes in NOD/Ltj Mice
Article.Authors: Li Y.; He K.; Qu X.; Gao J.; Hu R.; Su M.
Article.Abstract: The autoimmune regulator (AIRE) is essential for central immune tolerance, but its role in thymic epithelial cell (TEC) differentiation and development remains incompletely understood. To address this, we knocked down AIRE in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) and analyzed thymic epithelial progenitor (TEP) differentiation using RNA-sequencing and also performed thymic AIRE knockdown in NOD/Ltj mice to evaluate type 1 diabetes (T1D) pathogenesis. AIRE knockdown significantly reduced the proportion of K5+/K8+ TEPs among EpCAM1+ cells and altered the ECM–receptor interaction pathway, with downregulation of SPP1 and upregulation of Fn1 and CD44. Importantly, re-expression of AIRE using an shRNA-resistant rescue vector partially reversed these molecular changes and partially restored TEP differentiation. In vivo, thymic AIRE knockdown accelerated blood glucose elevation, aggravated insulitis, and reduced expression of T1D-associated TSAs (INS2, GAD67) and maturation markers (CD80, MHC-II). Importantly, the changes in SPP1, Fn1, and CD44 were consistent between in vitro and in vivo models. Furthermore, AIRE deficiency increased CD4+ single-positive thymocytes, reduced splenic Treg frequency, and enhanced antigen-specific T cell proliferation and activation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AIRE deficiency impairs TEP differentiation and alters the ECM-receptor pathway, while thymic AIRE deficiency compromises immune tolerance and accelerates T1D progression in NOD/Ltj mice.

Article.Title: PM2.5 Exposure Disrupts Sympathetic Neurotransmission by Impairing Voltage-Gated Ca2+ Channels and Remodeling Satellite Glia in the Superior Cervical Ganglion
Article.Authors: Do P.; Nguyen H.; Cha S.
Article.Abstract: Airborne fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure is associated with central neuroinflammation and autonomic dysfunction, but its effects on peripheral sympathetic ganglia remain poorly defined. Here, we examined the effects of central PM2.5 administration and direct PM2.5 exposure on the superior cervical ganglion (SCG), a primary sympathetic relay governing cephalic noradrenergic outflow. Intracerebroventricular (ICV) administration of PM2.5 increased hypothalamic TNF-α and IL-6 levels and reduced presynaptic synaptophysin expression, while SCG tyrosine hydroxylase expression remained unchanged. Mechanistically, live-cell Ca2+ imaging revealed attenuated depolarization-evoked Ca2+ responses in SCG neurons following either 24-h direct exposure or in vivo ICV administration. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings further demonstrated reduced voltage-gated Ca2+ channel (VGCC) current density in neurons isolated from ICV PM2.5-treated rats. This functional reduction was not accompanied by significant changes in the SCG mRNA levels of the examined pore-forming Cavα1 subunits. In parallel, ICV PM2.5 administration increased GFAP and Kir4.1 protein levels and enhanced perineuronal GFAP immunoreactivity, consistent with satellite glial cell reactivity. Together, these findings identify impaired neuronal Ca2+ signaling and accompanying glial alterations in the SCG following PM2.5 exposure. The reductions in extracellular NE accumulation and VGCC function across complementary exposure models support a potential contribution of impaired Ca2+-dependent secretion to PM2.5-associated sympathetic dysfunction.

Article.Title: Targeting of Immune Cells by Human Adenoviruses: CD46 Receptor Density Influences Entry of Chimaeric Ad5F35 into Natural Killer Cells
Article.Authors: Barr T.; Aktar E.; Drake S.; Karwatka M.; Wilson E.; Hughes R.; Blair G.; Cook G.
Article.Abstract: Most adenovirus (Ad) vectors are based on the genome of human Ad type 5 (Ad5), which targets their entry to cells that express the Coxsackie and adenovirus receptor (CAR or CXADR). However, certain human Ads do not use CAR; for example, Ad35 interacts with cell surface CD46 and Ad3 uses desmoglein 2 (DSG2) for cell entry. In this study, a comparison of different Ad receptors using transcriptomic and proteomic databases showed that CD46 is widely expressed across human cells and tissues whereas CAR and DSG2 are more restricted to epithelial cells. We have used a hybrid virus, Ad5F35, that comprises an Ad5 genome in which the Ad5 fibre was replaced with that of Ad35, thus retargeting the virus from CAR- to CD46-expressing cells and enabling transduction of primary human NK and T cells. However, lymphocytes required approximately 10-to-20-fold-more Ad5F35 particles per cell (ppc) compared to A549 epithelial cells to achieve a similar level of transduction. Consistent with this, quantitation of the cell-surface density of CD46 molecules revealed approximately 100 CD46 molecules per µm2 in primary NK cells compared with approximately 2000 CD46 per µm2 in HeLa cells, a 20-fold difference. Cell surface CD46 density was reduced by approximately 95% by RNA interference in HeLa cells to levels that approximate those found on NK cells. Lower CD46 density reduced transduction by Ad5F35 but this could be compensated for with increased MOI. Our results identify the density of cell surface CD46 as a critical determinant of Ad5F35 transduction and demonstrate that Ad5F35 is an efficient vector for gene delivery in primary human NK cells.

Article.Title: Disentangling the Effects of Craniotomy and Traumatic Brain Injury in Experimental Models: A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Gribovskaya V.; Adzhemian D.; Rogozin P.; Nesterova V.; Gureev A.; Silachev D.
Article.Abstract: Many widely used open-head models of traumatic brain injury (TBI) require craniotomy before injury, while sham-operated animals undergo surgery without impact and serve as controls. However, sham surgery itself may alter physiological, molecular, and behavioral parameters, complicating interpretation of TBI-specific effects. This narrative review, based on a structured PubMed search, synthesizes studies employing a three-group design to distinguish injury-related changes from those associated with craniotomy and other perioperative procedures. Evidence indicates that sham surgery produces outcome-, region-, and time-dependent effects that are generally milder, more localized, and more transient than TBI. These include neuroinflammatory responses, localized neuronal alterations, temporary sensorimotor and cognitive deficits, nociceptive changes, and shifts in gut microbiota. In contrast, TBI causes more severe abnormalities, including extensive neuronal damage, sustained astrogliosis, microglial activation, neutrophilic infiltration, mitochondrial dysfunction, and long-term dysbiosis. Most electrophysiological parameters are relatively unaffected by sham surgery, although selected changes have been reported. Importantly, differences between naïve and sham animals cannot be attributed exclusively to craniotomy, as anesthesia, analgesia, and surgical technique may contribute. Thus, sham surgery should not be considered a biologically neutral control. Inclusion of both naïve and sham groups is particularly important when distinguishing surgery-associated from injury-specific effects in preclinical studies.

Article.Title: Protein Self-Assembly as a Design Principle for Enzyme Immobilisation in Biocatalysis
Article.Authors: Vijayakumar S.; Sunna A.
Article.Abstract: Enzyme immobilisation is essential for translating biocatalytic processes from the laboratory to industrial applications by improving enzyme stability, recovery, and reuse. It underpins sustainable processes in pharmaceuticals, biofuels, and food production, but conventional immobilisation strategies involve inherent trade-offs. Covalent attachment prevents enzyme leaching but may distort the active site, whereas physical adsorption better preserves enzyme conformation but allows enzyme leaching. Furthermore, carrier-based methods frequently encounter mass-transfer limitations and may require external cross-linkers, hindering broader industrial application. Recent advances in synthetic biology and materials science have accelerated the development of protein-based materials for biocatalysis. This review examines protein self-assembly as a unifying design principle for enzyme immobilisation, enabling programmable assembly under relatively mild conditions to overcome key limitations of conventional strategies. We discuss naturally derived structures such as bacterial microcompartments and engineered systems including virus-like particles, elastin-like polypeptides, and SpyTag/SpyCatcher, which support programmable enzyme organisation and enable compartmentalised multi-enzyme cascade reactions. Building on this, a major focus is placed on catalytically active inclusion bodies (CatIBs). As robust, intrinsically self-immobilised protein aggregates, CatIBs represent a simplified, carrier-free platform offering potential process and cost advantages for industrial biocatalysis.

Article.Title: Deep Genomic Characterization of Bacillus subtilis SNUY1 & 168 Using MAYA (Multistage Analysis of Prokaryotic Annotations): An Integrated Snakemake-Based Bioinformatics Pipeline
Article.Authors: Kumar Narendran S.; Presannan A.; Indulekha L.; Shibu A.; Rajeev A.; Krishna Chakkadath S.; Vijay V.; Babu P.; Kumar G.; Nair B.; Subramaniam S.; Melethadathil N.
Article.Abstract: Bacillus subtilis is an extensively characterized Gram-positive bacterium with broad applications in agriculture, biotechnology, and biocontrol. Strain SNUY1, known for its antifungal properties and use as an edible coating, has been completely sequenced and deposited in NCBI (accession: CP199918), making it an important model for genomic and functional characterization. Here, we present the MAYA pipeline, a fully automated, rule-based Snakemake workflow that integrates eighteen bioinformatic tools into a single end-to-end framework. MAYA accepts either raw Illumina paired-end FASTQ reads or pre-assembled FASTA sequences, utilizing per-rule Conda environment isolation to ensure strict version control and reproducibility across all constituent tools from quality control and assembly through functional annotation, plasmid typing, and detection of biosynthetic and antimicrobial resistance gene clusters. To benchmark pipeline accuracy across both input modes, MAYA was evaluated using Bacillus subtilis subsp. subtilis str. 168(AL009126 OZ025638). The FASTA assembly yielded a circularized 4,215,606 bp chromosome (N50: 4.21 Mb, 43.51% GC) with 98.28% CheckM completeness and 100.0% BUSCO ortholog recovery. Prokka annotation predicted 4214 CDSs (86 tRNAs, 30 rRNAs) in FASTA mode compared to 4313 CDSs (106 tRNAs, 25 rRNAs) in FASTQ mode, reflecting expected read fragmentation in unassembled data. DIAMOND mapping against SwissProt yielded 4135 hits (99.90% mean identity) in FASTA mode and 4170 hits (99.75% mean identity) in FASTQ mode. Both modes identified identical ST1 Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST) profiles and six core AMR determinants (mphK, vmlR, rphC, aadK, satA_Bsub, and tet(L)), while antiSMASH detected 15 biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) regions (22 protoclusters) in FASTA mode versus 16 regions (23 protoclusters) in FASTQ mode. MOB-suite resolved two non-mobilizable plasmids in the FASTQ assembly (bioproject: PRJNA76): pAC670 and a novel 1666 bp plasmid. Furthermore, nucleotide BLASTN analysis resolved a 76-CDS discrepancy between published NCBI annotations and MAYA/Prokka, demonstrating 95.5% (4081/4272) stringent sequence match and confirming that differences stem from gene-model predictions rather than omitted loci. To demonstrate the FASTA-mode application workflow, the complete SNUY1 (NZ_CP199918) genome assembly was processed through MAYA, yielding a single, contiguous chromosome of 4,196,931 base pairs with a GC content of 43.69% (98.28% CheckM, 100% BUSCO completeness). Annotation identified 4196 coding sequences, while antiSMASH profiling revealed 13 candidate biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) regions comprising 20 protoclusters (including NRPS, lanthipeptides, terpenes, and sactipeptides), aligning with the strain’s biocontrol capabilities. AMR profiling identified six chromosomally encoded resistance genes (mphK, vmlR, rphC, aadK, satA_Bsub, and tet(L)). In silico mobility analysis via MOB-suite demonstrated that these sequences lack functional conjugation machinery and are classified as non-mobilizable. Executing in 3–4 h on an Intel Xeon server (128 GB RAM, 29 CPU cores), MAYA delivers an efficient, audit-ready framework for end-to-end bacterial genomic profiling.

Article.Title: Sleep Disturbances and Circadian Phase Delay in People Living with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV): A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Gomila-Cardona A.; Ferrández-Sempere S.; Cañellas F.; Gamundí A.; Akaârir M.; Nicolau C.; Rubiño-Díaz J.
Article.Abstract: Advances in HIV research and antiretroviral therapy (ART) have substantially increased life expectancy among people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, challenges affecting quality of life and alterations in daily physiological processes persist. Among the health dimensions most affected are sleep quality and circadian rhythms, resulting in significant biological alterations. The main objective of this study is to analyze the existing scientific evidence regarding the effects of HIV on sleep quality and on the alignment and synchronization of circadian rhythms. The bidirectional interaction between these physiological alterations and associated clinical, immunological, and metabolic factors in people living with HIV (PLHIV) was evaluated, emphasizing their integration. For this review, searches were conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases. Eligibility criteria were applied, resulting in a final selection of 15 studies based on search strategies. The findings demonstrated a high prevalence of poor sleep quality as well as delayed circadian phase. These chronobiological alterations were closely associated with systemic inflammation, altered melatonin levels, impaired cognitive performance, and an altered metabolic profile involving leptin, ghrelin, adiponectin, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling. Despite the consistency of the results, the methodologies of individual studies varied, and a notable absence of clinical trials aimed at addressing poor sleep quality and chronodisruption was observed. A promising clinical approach involves complementing antiretroviral therapy (ART) with chronotherapeutic interventions and sleep hygiene. In conclusion, HIV can disrupt personal temporal organization at a systemic level; consequently, incorporating assessments of sleep and circadian rhythms into clinical care may be warranted, while chronotherapeutic interventions should be further investigated.

Article.Title: EP2 and EP4 in Alzheimer’s Disease: Cell-Dependent Signalling and Implications for Selective Targeting
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Zeng Y.; Song Z.; He J.; He Q.; Lin H.; Liu L.; Yu W.; Cheng S.
Article.Abstract: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) signalling influences amyloid-β (Aβ) processing, myeloid function, and neuronal injury in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Although EP2 and EP4 share Gs–cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signalling, their cellular effects differ. This review integrates genetic, pharmacological, ageing, and AD-model evidence to assess receptor-selective targeting. EP2 deletion enhances myeloid Aβ handling and reduces microglia-mediated neuronal injury in experimental systems, providing a rationale for selective EP2 inhibition. In aged mice, PGE2–EP2 signalling redirects glucose towards glycogen storage and restricts myeloid mitochondrial respiration; benefits from a predominantly peripheral antagonist suggest that some age-related outcomes may improve without high brain exposure. Chronic antagonist studies in AD models, however, show variable effects on inflammation, amyloid burden, and behaviour. EP4 exhibits contrasting cell-dependent actions: activation supports microglial Aβ uptake and inflammatory control, whereas signalling in some amyloid precursor protein (APP)-expressing cells promotes APP internalisation and Aβ production. Human AD evidence remains mainly tissue-based; EP2 antagonist testing has involved healthy volunteers, not patients with AD. These findings indicate that receptor selectivity alone is insufficient to predict therapeutic outcomes. Further studies should combine cell-specific receptor manipulation, measurements of central and peripheral exposure, and separate assessments of Aβ production, clearance, tissue injury, and functional outcomes.

Article.Title: N1-Methylpseudouridine-Modified mRNA-Transfected Dendritic Cells Enable Efficient Generation of Functional Tumor Antigen-Specific Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes
Article.Authors: Ngan T.; Sioud M.
Article.Abstract: Efficient generation of tumor-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) remains challenging. Although mRNA-based approaches enable the delivery and expression of diverse tumor-specific antigens, unmodified mRNA can trigger innate immune responses that suppress translation. Here, we investigated whether 1-methyl-pseudouridine (m1Ψ)-modified mRNA enhances antigen expression in human dendritic cells (DCs) and promotes the induction of antigen-specific CTLs, using survivin and MART-1 as model tumor-associated antigens. Remarkably, m1Ψ modification increased protein production in DCs by up to 20-fold compared with unmodified mRNA. DCs transfected with m1Ψ-modified mRNAs efficiently primed survivin- and MART-1-specific CD8+ T cells from autologous peripheral blood mononuclear cells of healthy donors, as demonstrated by HLA class I peptide–MHC dextramer staining. Expanded CTL lines exhibited potent effector functions, including IFN-γ production, CD107a mobilization, and robust cytotoxicity against peptide-pulsed T2 cells and tumor cell lines expressing survivin or MART-1. Translation of the engineered mRNA variants in human HeLa cells and DCs is strongly dependent on the poly(A) tail. Together, these findings demonstrate that m1Ψ modification substantially enhances antigen expression and supports the efficient generation of functional, antigen-specific CTLs, providing a promising platform for next-generation mRNA-based cancer vaccines and adoptive T-cell therapies.

Article.Title: Identification and Dynamic Remodeling of Bivalent Chromatin Regions in Sheep Early Embryos and ESCs
Article.Authors: Song L.; Yang H.; Gan L.; Chen H.; Liao Z.; Kuang E.; Deng M.
Article.Abstract: Bivalent chromatin, marked by H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, contributes to maintaining developmental genes in a poised state. However, it remains unclear whether sheep embryonic stem cells (ESCs) establish bivalent domains. In this study, we identified bivalent chromatin regions and characterized the dynamics of H3K4me3, chromatin accessibility, and expression of bivalent chromatin-associated genes in sheep early embryos and ESCs. Using an overlap threshold of >200 bp between H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 peaks, we identified 40,543 bivalent regions in sheep ESCs. These regions preferentially occurred at promoters and were enriched in RNA processing, translation, and ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis. By integrating Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag), Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq), and RNA-seq data across preimplantation development from MII oocytes to hatching blastocysts, we found that ESC-defined bivalent regions underwent dynamic changes in H3K4me3 enrichment and chromatin accessibility, with distinct patterns across developmental stages. Bivalent-associated genes also exhibited stage-specific expression patterns, and key pluripotency- and lineage-associated transcription factors, including SOX2, SOX17, POU5F1, and ZFP42, showed distinct developmental expression profiles. Moreover, formative ESCs displayed higher transcriptional activity and chromatin accessibility at bivalent regions than that of primed ESCs. Together, these results characterize the genomic distribution of bivalent chromatin in sheep ESCs and its stage-specific remodeling during preimplantation development, providing a resource for further investigation of epigenetic regulation during early embryonic development in sheep.

Article.Title: Exosomal CircRNA_102619–miR-330-3p Interaction Regulates Osteosarcoma Progression and Metastasis by Forming the Lung Pre-Metastatic Niche
Article.Authors: Lien M.; Chang Y.; Tsai H.; Hsu C.; Liu C.; Guo J.; Ho T.; Lin L.; Fong Y.; Tang C.
Article.Abstract: Osteosarcoma, the most prevalent primary bone tumor, predominantly influences children and adolescents. The pre-metastatic niche (PMN) is a specialized microenvironment that forms before clinically detectable metastatic lesions. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) play a crucial function in triggering lung metastasis by coordinating PMN formation in the lung. We found that circRNA_102619, delivered by osteosarcoma-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs), promotes the reprogramming of lung fibroblasts (LFs) into CAFs and PMN formation both in vitro and in vivo. High-throughput protein array analysis revealed that CXCL10, a critical factor secreted by CAFs, drives osteosarcoma proliferation, migration, and resistance to natural killer (NK) cell cytotoxicity. Additionally, circRNA_102619 acts as a sponge for miR-330-3p, thereby controlling CXCL10 production. Importantly, in vivo studies confirmed that osteosarcoma-derived EVs enhance lung PMN formation, promoting osteosarcoma progression and metastasis. Inhibiting osteosarcoma-derived EVs represents a novel strategy to block osteosarcoma progression and metastasis.

Article.Title: ZEB1 Defines the Interaction Between Breast Cancer Cells and Macrophages by Upregulating the Expression of CCL2 Cytokine
Article.Authors: Semenov O.; Nevzorov I.; Silonov S.; Daks A.; Kabasheva A.; Nazarov A.; Kriger D.; Kuneev I.; Petukhov A.; Gnennaya Y.; Tulchinsky E.; Shuvalov O.; Barlev N.
Article.Abstract: The survival of disseminating tumor cells at the invasive edge and in metastatic foci depends on their ability to counteract anti-tumor immunity. The epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) process is associated with the recruitment of immune-suppressive myeloid cells. The onset of the EMT gene expression program is controlled by several transcriptional master-regulators, including ZEB1. Using engineered breast cancer cell lines with different statuses of ZEB1, we examined the effects of ZEB1 on the expression of different pro-inflammatory cytokines. Our results suggest that ZEB1 plays an important role in regulating the expression of CCL2 (C-C motif ligand 2, a.k.a. MCP-1), the main chemoattractant of monocytes. Forced expression of ZEB1 in epithelial MCF-7 cells significantly increased the expression level of CCL2, which was further enhanced by TNF-α. On the contrary, knock-out of ZEB1 in pseudo-mesenchymal MDA-MB-231 cells led to a complete loss of CCL2 expression. Moreover, this effect was not restored by TNF-α induction. Also, positive ZEB1 status in breast cancer cells promoted the chemoattraction of THP-1 macrophages in co-culture experiments. Analysis of publicly available ChIP-seq data implicated ZEB1 in the regulation of CCL2 gene transcription. Taken together, these data suggest that ZEB1 is involved in the formation of the EMT-associated pro-tumor immune microenvironment.

Article.Title: Modulation of Osteogenesis by Conditioned Media of Differently Activated Macrophages: A Comparative In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Najman S.; Živković J.; Stojanović S.
Article.Abstract: Macrophages play an important role in bone regeneration by releasing bioactive factors that regulate the behavior of osteoprogenitor cells. In this in vitro study, we investigated how conditioned media (CM) derived from RAW 264.7 macrophages treated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS; 1 or 100 ng/mL), dexamethasone (DEX; 10−6 M), or left untreated, modulate the proliferation and osteogenic differentiation of MC3T3-E1 preosteoblasts. Exposure to LPS and DEX produced different patterns of macrophage activation, assessed by microscopic morphology, nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) reduction, and measurement of TNF-α secretion from macrophages. In the L929 bioassay, no CM was cytotoxic, while effects on MC3T3-E1 proliferation and differentiation varied with macrophage treatment and CM dilution. CM obtained from DEX-treated macrophages elicited the most pronounced pattern of osteogenic activity that included reduced cell proliferation, acquisition of osteoblast-like morphology, enhanced von Kossa staining, and pronounced osteocalcin and osteopontin immunoexpression. CM from untreated macrophages also supported osteogenesis, although to a lesser extent. At 100%, CMs from LPS-treated macrophages supported greater preosteoblast proliferation than other CMs, while their effects on differentiation depended on LPS dose and CM dilution. These findings indicate that macrophage-derived signals differentially modulate preosteoblast proliferation and differentiation depending on their functional state. This study provides a valuable in vitro cell model for the development of immunomodulatory and regenerative strategies in bone tissue engineering and broader applications in wound healing.

Article.Title: Autophagy in Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumors (PitNETs): Molecular Mechanisms, Secretory Homeostasis, Therapeutic Resistance, and Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: Rizzuto I.; Pepe L.; Broggi G.; Caltabiano R.; Fiorentino V.; Ieni A.
Article.Abstract: Pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs) are usually indolent but may show invasive growth, recurrence, hormonal hypersecretion, and treatment resistance. Autophagy intersects with nutrient sensing, lysosomal homeostasis, mitochondrial quality control, and secretory-granule turnover, but its biological effects in PitNETs are context-dependent. This narrative review synthesizes PitNET-specific and mechanistically relevant evidence on macroautophagy, mitophagy, crinophagy, non-coding RNA and epigenetic regulation, treatment resistance, and pharmacological modulation, emphasizing the distinction between static autophagy markers and dynamic autophagic flux. Evidence is interpreted across human tissue, primary human cells, pituitary tumor cell lines, animal models, and clinical observations, while preserving clear separation between human observations and mechanistic evidence derived from experimental models. Across experimental systems, autophagy activation is associated with antitumor effects in selected settings, whereas completed basal flux may support stress adaptation and late-stage or selective-autophagy inhibition may enhance cytotoxicity. Biological outcome therefore depends on tumor lineage, treatment, the pathway stage affected, and whether flux is completed. Recent studies extend this framework to selective mitophagy, ncRNA/exosomal resistance networks, epitranscriptomic regulation, somatostatin-analogue resistance, and tumor-microenvironmental signaling. Clinical translation remains limited, and no autophagy-modulating strategy is validated for routine PitNET management. Future studies should integrate dynamic flux measurements, lineage-specific biomarkers, pharmacodynamic target engagement, and prospective clinical endpoints.

Article.Title: Mapping and Evaluation of Quantitative Trait Loci for Adult-Plant Stripe Rust Resistance in the Sichuan Wheat Cultivar Chuanmai 62
Article.Authors: Yao F.; Yang E.; Li J.; Yang W.; Yang M.
Article.Abstract: Stripe rust, caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst), poses a persistent threat to wheat production in China. The Sichuan cultivar Chuanmai 62 (CM62) has exhibited stable adult-plant resistance (APR) for over a decade. To elucidate its genetic basis, we evaluated a recombinant inbred line population (CM62 × Avocet S) across 13 environments and genotyped it using the 55K SNP array. QTL mapping identified six QTL distributed on chromosomes 1BL, 2AS, 2BL, 5AL (two loci), and 5BL. Among these, three major QTL (QYr.CM62-1BL, QYr.CM62-2AS, and QYr.CM62-2BL) were detected. Notably, QYr.CM62-2BL was the preeminent locus, explaining 8.97–50.59% of phenotypic variance and exhibiting high stability across 11 of the 13 environments; this locus is closely linked to the previously reported QYR1 region, although whether it is allelic to QYR1 remains unclear. QYr.CM62-2AS corresponded to Yr17/YrM1225, while QYr.CM62-1BL aligned with Yr29. A significant finding was the identification of QYr.CM62-5BL, a novel minor-effect QTL mapped to the rearranged 5BL·7BL segment resulting from a 5B/7B reciprocal translocation present in both parents. Furthermore, two Kompetitive Allele-Specific PCR (KASP) markers (KASP-AX-109507945 and KASP-AX-109844182) were developed for QYr.CM62-2BL. Polymorphism screening of 328 cultivars confirmed their utility for marker-assisted selection. Collectively, our results demonstrate that the durable APR in CM62 is governed by multiple additive QTL. The newly developed KASP markers, together with the novel QYr.CM62-5BL locus and prioritized candidate genes from in silico annotation of the QYr.CM62-2BL interval, provide valuable genetic resources for pyramiding resistance alleles and future map-based cloning in wheat breeding programs.

Article.Title: Development and Genomic Validation of a Population-Specific SNP Panel for Parentage Verification in Chinese Holstein Cattle
Article.Authors: Dou J.; Gu J.; Wang A.; Luo Z.; Huang H.; Sheng X.; Wang Y.; Yu Y.
Article.Abstract: Accurate pedigree information is essential for genetic evaluation and genomic selection in dairy cattle. However, the performance of SNP-based parentage verification depends on marker informativeness, genomic distribution, and compatibility with the target population. In this study, we developed and validated a population-specific 260-SNP panel for parentage verification in Chinese Holstein cattle. The panel was selected from BovineSNP150K genotype data of 2954 Chinese Holsteins based on high marker informativeness, genotyping quality, LD-based control of marker redundancy, and genome-wide distribution. The selected SNPs had a mean minor allele frequency of 0.4981, expected heterozygosity of 0.5000, and polymorphism information content of 0.3750, with a combined probability of exclusion >0.999. Parentage verification of 867 recorded candidate parent–offspring pairs using likelihood-based and Mendelian exclusion-based approaches showed 99.54% agreement, with a Cohen’s κ of 0.981. Random SNP-subset analyses showed greater variation in pedigree concordance estimates with smaller marker sets, whereas larger subsets produced more stable estimates across replicate subsets. Independent validation using targeted-capture sequencing showed a mean SNP detection rate of 99.96% and complete genotype concordance in duplicate tests. Independent validation across six commercial dairy farms identified an overall inconsistency rate of 12.97% between recorded pedigree relationships and genotype-based parentage evidence. These results demonstrate that the population-specific 260-SNP panel provides informative and reproducible genotyping for parentage verification in Chinese Holstein cattle and offers a practical tool for pedigree quality control in dairy cattle breeding programs.

Article.Title: Circulating suPAR in Relation to Renal and Cardiovascular Involvement in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Pilot Study
Article.Authors: Napolitano F.; Mormile I.; Cevini F.; de Paulis A.; Rossi F.; Montuori N.
Article.Abstract: Soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) is an inflammatory biomarker associated with immune activation, endothelial dysfunction, and chronic inflammation. Increasing evidence suggests that suPAR may be involved in renal and cardiovascular injury and may reflect cumulative organ damage in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Serum suPAR levels were measured in patients with SLE and healthy controls. Within the SLE cohort, suPAR levels were further evaluated according to the presence or absence of organ involvement. In this pilot study, serum suPAR levels were significantly higher in patients with SLE than in healthy controls. Within the SLE cohort, patients with renal involvement and those with reduced renal function had higher suPAR levels than their respective comparison groups. Similarly, patients with cardiovascular involvement showed significantly higher suPAR levels than SLE patients without cardiovascular involvement and healthy controls. However, serum suPAR levels were not significantly correlated with estimated glomerular filtration rate. Circulating suPAR levels are elevated in SLE and may be particularly associated with renal and cardiovascular involvement. These findings support the potential role of suPAR as a biomarker of cardiorenal involvement in SLE, although its relationship with renal function and clinical outcomes requires validation in larger prospective cohorts.

Article.Title: HDL Functionality, Cholesterol-Related Biomarkers and Incidence of Dementia: A Case–Cohort Study in Older Adults at High Cardiovascular Risk
Article.Authors: Malcampo M.; Hernáez Á.; Hernando-Redondo J.; Ros E.; Corella D.; Martínez-González M.; Salas-Salvadó J.; Estruch R.; Timiraos J.; Gómez-Gracia E.; Fiol M.; Lapetra J.; Serra-Majem L.; Riera-Mestre A.; Pintó X.; Puig-Pijoan A.; Ruiz-Canela M.; Sorlí J.; Babio N.; Lamuela-Raventós R.; Khymenets O.; Sala-Vila A.; Castañer O.; Fitó M.
Article.Abstract: Associations of lipid profiles, including qualitative and functional high-density lipoprotein (HDL) traits, and cholesterol-related biomarkers with incident dementia and Alzheimer’s disease (AD), remain unclear. In this regard, older adults at high cardiovascular risk are at particularly high risk of developing dementia. The aim is to evaluate whether these biomarkers are associated with the incidence of dementia and AD in older adults at high cardiovascular (CV) risk. In a case–cohort study, we selected 106 incident dementia cases (82 AD) and a random subcohort of 201 non-cases. We quantified (baseline and at one-year), lipid profile; HDL-mediate cholesterol efflux capacity in a model of human neurons; HDL-mediated anti-inflammatory protection in a model of brain endothelial cells; 24S-hydroxycholesterol and apolipoprotein E. Multivariable-adjusted Cox models were addressed. HDL cholesterol was inversely associated, whereas triglycerides directly associated, with dementia and AD incidence. Higher HDL-mediated cholesterol efflux was inversely associated with dementia (HR 0.64, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.45–0.91) and AD (HR 0.52, 0.35–0.76). Greater HDL-mediated endothelial protection was associated with lower dementia and AD incidence (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.99 and HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.91, respectively). A one-year increase in 24S-hydroxycholesterol was associated with a higher incidence of any dementia (HR 2.38, 1.33–4.27) and AD (HR 2.24, 1.11–4.53). Enhanced HDL functional properties ex vivo, in preclinical models using human brain cells, together with lower levels of 24S-hydroxycholesterol, are inversely associated with the incidence of dementia and AD, highlighting these factors as promising prognostic targets in older adults at high CV risk.

Article.Title: RNA–Protein Dynamics of the Segmentation Clock and Its Implications in Developmental Disorders
Article.Authors: Tan W.; Kobayashi A.; Niizuma K.
Article.Abstract: Somitogenesis is orchestrated by the segmentation clock, a highly conserved developmental oscillator that generates periodic gene expression waves to establish precise somite boundaries along the vertebrate body axis. While transcriptional feedback circuits and signaling gradients are recognized as central determinants of clock dynamics, accumulating evidence indicates that RNA-centered regulation provides an important layer of temporal control. We therefore focus primarily on established RNA-regulatory processes, including nascent RNA synthesis, pre-mRNA processing, transcript stability and degradation, and translational control, and examine how these processes interact with protein turnover and intercellular signaling to shape oscillation period, amplitude, and synchronization. Because the molecular implementation of the clock differs among vertebrates, we distinguish species-specific systems throughout: mouse studies primarily define hairy and enhancer of split 1 (Hes) 7/lunatic fringe (Lfng)/Delta-like canonical Notch ligand (Dll) 1 dynamics, zebrafish studies define Hes-related bHLH transcriptional repressor (her) 1/her7/deltaC/deltaD dynamics, chick studies established cyclic c-hairy1/lfng expression, and human HES7/LFNG dynamics are examined mainly in stem-cell-derived presomitic mesoderm (PSM) models. These mechanisms are used to formulate experimentally testable hypotheses about phase-dependent RNA stability, translation, and developmental state transitions. Together, the segmentation clock provides a quantitative framework for distinguishing established RNA–protein mechanisms from emerging RNA-regulatory hypotheses and for understanding how their disruption may contribute to congenital vertebral disorders.

Article.Title: Fenvalerate Induces Airway Epithelial Injury Through CHRM3-Associated NF-κB Activation
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Li J.; Liu T.; Sheng M.; Liu J.; Yang Z.; Chu H.; Jia A.; Xu W.
Article.Abstract: Fenvalerate (FEN) is a widely used pyrethroid insecticide with potential respiratory toxicity; however, its contribution to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-related pathological processes remains unclear. We investigated molecular mechanisms linking FEN exposure to airway epithelial injury. COPD transcriptomic datasets were integrated with predicted FEN targets, and candidate genes were prioritized using machine-learning algorithms. Immune infiltration and single-cell transcriptomic analyses were used to examine immune associations and cell-type-specific expression. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations assessed potential FEN-target interactions, followed by validation in BEAS-2B human bronchial epithelial cells. Intersecting FEN-COPD genes were enriched in inflammatory, immune-regulatory, neuroactive ligand-receptor, and epithelial injury-related pathways. Eight candidate genes showed distinct expression patterns across airway epithelial and immune cell populations. Computational analyses supported a potentially stable FEN-CHRM3 interaction. In BEAS-2B cells, FEN reduced viability, increased IL-6 and IL-8 secretion, promoted apoptosis, upregulated CHRM3, and enhanced IκBα and p65 phosphorylation. Pharmacological inhibition of CHRM3 or NF-κB partially attenuated these responses. Thus, FEN-induced epithelial inflammation and apoptosis may involve CHRM3-associated NF-κB activation, providing mechanistic insight into pesticide-related respiratory toxicity.

Article.Title: Identification of Calcium-Sensing Receptor (CAS) as a Phytaspase Interactor: Implications for the CAS Trafficking Pathway
Article.Authors: Litvinova A.; Pigidanov A.; Torosian T.; Zgoda V.; Serebryakova M.; Kovaleva I.; Mamedov M.; Golyshev S.; Safronov G.; Chichkova N.; Vartapetian A.
Article.Abstract: Proteolytic enzymes play important and diverse roles in regulating protein homeostasis in living cells. Phytaspase, a member of the plant subtilisin-like protease family possessing a ‘caspase-like’ selectivity and specificity of hydrolysis of its targets, is a cell death-related protease. Phytaspase displays a peculiar trafficking pattern and is involved in the execution of plant cell death induced by biotic and abiotic stresses. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms of phytaspase functioning, a search for Nicotiana tabacum phytaspase (NtPhyt)-interacting proteins was performed using the BioID approach. This search identified the calcium-sensing receptor (CAS) protein as a candidate NtPhyt interactor. Direct interaction of NtPhyt with N. tabacum CAS (NtCAS) was corroborated by an in vitro analysis utilizing the purified proteins. Furthermore, NtPhyt was shown to introduce five cleavages in the CAS molecule in vitro. For NtCAS-EGFP produced in N. benthamiana leaves, dual localization to chloroplasts and the cell periphery, including the plasma membrane, was observed, whereas NtPhyt proteolytic activity was undetectable in the chloroplasts. A CAS precursor protein apparently preserving the chloroplast transit peptide was found to accumulate upon a light-to-dark transition and to disappear in the presence of elevated levels of NtPhyt. A requirement for CAS for stress-induced retrograde transport of NtPhyt was uncovered, and partial co-localization of CAS with NtPhyt was observed in cells subjected to oxidative stress. Our results are consistent with the model according to which CAS transiently localizes to the plasma membrane as an intermediate location on its way to its final destination, the chloroplasts, and interacts with NtPhyt at this stage.

Article.Title: Evolution of (S)-2-Aminobutanol Synthesis from Chemical Resolution to Biomanufacturing
Article.Authors: Wang B.; Chen C.; Han Y.; Tong W.; Gao H.; Ma W.; Liu J.; Xu J.
Article.Abstract: As a pivotal chiral precursor for the synthesis of the antituberculosis drug ethambutol and antiepileptic drugs such as levetiracetam, Chiral (S)-2-aminobutanol requires high optical purity for clinical safety. This review systematically summarizes the evolution and recent advances in its synthetic routes. Traditional chemical methods, including the 1-nitropropane and 1-butene epoxidation routes, suffer from severe safety hazards and heavily rely on downstream chiral resolution. However, both chemical crystallization and enzymatic kinetic resolution are constrained by a 50% theoretical yield ceiling and incur heavy environmental burdens. To break this bottleneck, in vitro multienzyme cascades utilizing amine dehydrogenases (AmDHs) and ω-transaminases (ω-TAs) have emerged, achieving 100% theoretical yield from prochiral precursors and >99% enantiomeric excess (ee) driven by a distinct dual-pocket active site model. Furthermore, synthetic biology has enabled de novo biosynthesis via whole-cell cell factories. It should be noted that the recently reported 45.3 g·L−1 titer refers to the upstream amino acid precursor L-2-aminobutyric acid (L-2-ABA), not to the final (S)-2-aminobutanol product. To overcome bottlenecks like the intracellular toxicity of the intermediate 2-ketobutyrate (2-OBA), strategies including efflux pump engineering (e.g., rhtA) and quorum sensing-based dynamic regulation have successfully boosted the fermentation titer to 45.3 g·L−1. Finally, the industrialization potential of these generations of technologies is evaluated, highlighting that the transition toward in vitro continuous-flow microreactors and a hybrid whole-cell + cell-free architecture, combined with the integration of AI into whole-cell factories, represents a future trend for green and low-carbon manufacturing.

Article.Title: QSAR-Guided In Silico Design of Piperazinylanthranilamide Factor Xa Inhibitors: Applicability-Domain Assessment, ADMET Profiling, Molecular Docking, Molecular Dynamics, and MM/GBSA
Article.Authors: Gordon P.; Janiak M.; Gackowski M.; Zielińska-Pisklak M.; Szeleszczuk Ł.
Article.Abstract: An integrated computational workflow was developed to prioritize piperazinylanthranilamide factor Xa (FXa) inhibitor candidates. Twenty literature compounds were geometry-optimized and described using alvaDesc to construct a constrained additive multivariate adaptive regression splines model. Internal validation and an assessment of the applicability domain guided the evaluation of 20 prospective analogs. Ten selected analogs and two same-series references were docked to FXa, with apixaban as the crystallographic comparator. Thirteen initial 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations were supplemented by two independent runs for each of PAX-M09, PAX-M15, and PAX-M18. Binding energetics were assessed using molecular mechanics/generalized Born surface area (MM/GBSA), alongside in silico developability profiling. The model achieved R2 = 0.904 and an internal leave-one-out Q2 of 0.846. PAX-M09 was the strongest strict in-domain prediction, whereas PAX-M15 was borderline. Apixaban redocking yielded a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.953 Å. Although PAX-M17 and PAX-M19 ranked highest in docking, subsequent analyses prioritized PAX-M15, PAX-M09, and PAX-M18. PAX-M15 showed the most consistent positional behavior across replicates and consistently favorable run-specific MM/GBSA estimates (−68.76, −70.11, and −69.42 kcal/mol). PAX-M09 and PAX-M18 showed greater between-run heterogeneity. Solubility, metabolic, and toxicity liabilities remained important. The results support experimental investigation of the three candidates without changing their applicability-domain classifications or establishing superior experimental potency.
