Article.Title: Molecular Targeting of the Peripheral Nerve–Tumor Axis in Extracranial Solid Cancers: Eight Signaling Systems, One Effect—Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Tudorașcu D.; Vere C.; Petrescu M.; Ciurea A.; Pană R.; Dan A.; Târtea E.; Greșiță A.; Hădăreanu D.; Obleagă C.; Târtea G.
Article.Abstract: The peripheral nerves that innervate solid tumors communicate with the malignant cells through a restricted set of molecular signaling systems: adrenergic and muscarinic receptors, sensory neuropeptides, neurotrophins and their tyrosine kinase receptors, axon guidance molecules, and nociceptor ion channels. Each has been proposed separately as a therapeutic target but never quantitatively compared with the others. The question is whether one of them dominates—or whether the real target is the axis as a system. We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, with four query modules per database, without year or language restriction. We included in vivo studies in mammals, on extracranial solid cancers, with an intervention that modulated tumor innervation, peripheral nerve activity, or neural signaling, and with at least one tumor burden outcome. Of 16,649 unique records, 362 were included, with 1291 experiments and 1437 effects. Blockade of the peripheral nerve–tumor axis reduced tumor burden by −44.8%. In the prespecified primary analysis, on established tumors, the reduction was −52.0% with no significant difference from preventive interventions (p = 0.17). All eight molecular signaling systems responded to blockade, with estimates ranging from −34.3% for TRP channels to −70.2% for glutamatergic signaling. Interventions that activate the axis produced the opposite effect, with a 52.1% increase (95% CI: 32.1 to 75.1) across 253 effects, and bidirectionality was demonstrated within the same molecular system for the adrenergic compartment (−42.8% for blockade vs. 58.1% for activation), axon guidance molecules, and TRP channels. Egger’s test indicated marked small-study effects (slope −1.12; p < 0.001); the estimate remained stable when low-confidence digitized values were excluded (−42.6%). Eight distinct molecular signaling systems, disrupted by methods with nothing in common, produce reductions of a similar magnitude in tumor burden, and stimulation of three of them produces the opposite effect.

Article.Title: HDAC Inhibitors Potentiate Doxorubicin Cytotoxicity in HepG2 Cells and Alter DNA-Repair- and p53-Associated Transcriptional Programs
Article.Authors: Guo K.; van Herwijnen M.; Caiment F.; van den Beucken T.
Article.Abstract: Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACis) can enhance responses to DNA-damaging chemotherapy, but how they alter doxorubicin (DOX)-induced transcriptional programs remains incompletely understood. We investigated the effects of valproic acid (VPA) and vorinostat (SAHA) on DOX cytotoxicity and associated molecular responses in HepG2 cells. HDAC inhibition, cell viability, apoptosis, and DOX IC50 values were assessed using histone H3 acetylation, cell counting, Alamar Blue assays, and cleaved caspase-3 immunofluorescence. Transcriptomic responses were analyzed by RNA sequencing, differential expression analysis, and Hallmark gene set enrichment analysis, with selected findings evaluated by RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and comparison with published CRISPR/Cas9 DOX-response data. Both HDAC inhibitors increased histone H3 acetylation and enhanced DOX cytotoxicity, markedly reducing DOX IC50 values. VPA co-treatment also increased DOX-induced cleaved caspase-3 signaling. RNA-seq showed broad transcriptional remodeling, including depletion of the DNA-repair gene set following VPA treatment and attenuation of canonical p53-responsive genes during HDACi–DOX co-treatment. Several HDACi-repressed DNA-repair genes overlapped with genes whose loss sensitized cells to DOX in a published CRISPR screen. HDAC inhibition therefore enhances DOX cytotoxicity and is accompanied by alterations in DNA-repair-associated and p53-responsive transcriptional programs.

Article.Title: Chronic Ultrasound (‘Emotional’) Stress in Mice Exacerbates Colitis Through GSK3β-Mediated Neuroimmune Dysregulation and Is Ameliorated by Probiotic Intervention
Article.Authors: Gorlova A.; Haque A.; Reid N.; Inozemtsev A.; Askarova S.; Umriukhin A.; Obleukhova A.; Zakharova E.; de Munter J.; Dudchenko A.; Kushugulova A.; Deykin A.; Cherdyntseva T.; Pavlov D.; Strekalova T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Growing evidence supports a bidirectional relationship between ‘emotional’ (psychological) stress and intestinal inflammation. ‘Emotional stress’, a form of stress that is triggered by negative information and experiences of non-physical nature, is an established risk factor for the development of subclinical intestinal inflammation, called irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). However, the underlying mechanisms of this transition remain unclear, owing to the limited availability of appropriate animal models. Glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a molecular hub of ‘emotional stress’ response, as shown particularly in the ultrasound stress (US) model, and an important player in gut inflammation, may underlie this transition. Here, we propose a mouse paradigm for the progression from IBS to IBD-like syndrome by combining the US with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis paradigm in mice and investigate the role of GSK3β signaling under these conditions. Methods: C57BL/6 mice were subjected to a 21-day US consisting of irradiation of alternating ‘negative’ and ‘neutral’ frequencies, followed by 5 days of 0.5% DSS exposure via drinking water. A standardized anti-inflammatory probiotic VSL#3 whose efficacy was shown in DSS-based models was administered to a subgroup of mice. Behavioral, histological, and molecular outcomes previously established in US and IBS models were evaluated. This included parameters of anxiety, anhedonia, time of intestinal transit, fecal water content, and brain and gut neutrophil infiltration, as well as gene expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and of GSK3β, and serum levels of pro-inflammatory molecules. Given the important role of the nervus vagus in brain–gut interactions, molecular changes were studied in the nervus vagus as well. Results: Mice exposed to the combined US and DSS challenge had impaired intestinal transit and increased fecal water content, neutrophil infiltration, the upregulation of pro-inflammatory mediators and GSK3β in the gut that together manifested the IBD-like state. In this group, upregulated gene expression of these markers was found in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus, as well as in the vagus. The combined US and DSS challenge exacerbated anxiety- and anhedonia-like behaviors and elevated blood cytokine and chemokine levels. In comparison to these changes, solitary exposures to US or DSS exerted smaller effects on the majority of measured parameters. Probiotic treatment attenuated most of the physiological, inflammatory, and behavioral abnormalities induced by the combined US and DSS intervention. Conclusions: The mouse model employed here using both US and DSS recapitulated the progression of IBS to the IBD associated with ‘emotional stress’ and demonstrated upregulated gut and brain Gsk3β expression accompanying this transition. The described model provides a useful paradigm for investigating the mechanisms underlying the disease development from IBS- to IBD-like pathology.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide DNA Methylation Sequencing Identifies Methylation-Associated Genes Related to Porcine Skeletal Muscle Fiber Diversity
Article.Authors: Zha C.; Li B.; Yang W.; Hou L.; Chao Z.; Wu W.
Article.Abstract: Alterations in skeletal muscle fibers are closely linked to human diseases, yet the mechanisms by which DNA methylation drives muscle fiber diversity remain unclear. Here, we performed whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) to generate single-base-resolution DNA methylomes of fast-twitch Biceps Femoris (Bf) and slow-twitch Soleus (Sol) muscles and integrated transcriptomes to reveal associations between DNA methylation and gene expression. The global methylation level in skeletal muscle averaged 4.22%, with context-specific rates of 70.0% (CG), 1.16% (CHG), and 1.12% (CHH). The distribution of methylation levels of the mCs in CG and CHG contexts was similar but distinct from that in the CHH context. Furthermore, 152,286 DMCs and 51,079 DMRs were identified between Bf and Sol muscles. Bf showed higher global methylation (4.54%) than Sol (3.90%), and distinct differences in DNA methylation occurred throughout the genomic regions and gene functional element regions. CG-context DMCs and DMRs were mainly located in CpG islands and introns, while CHG and CHH DMCs and DMRs were exon-enriched. DMR-associated genes were significantly enriched in pathways related to muscle growth and remodeling and disease-related pathways. Moreover, five DMR-linked differentially expressed genes—HSPB6, ATP2A2, TNNI1, HOXA11, and PTPN3—were identified as critical candidate regulators of muscle fiber diversity. In addition, a context-dependent (CG, CHG, CHH) relationship between DNA methylation patterns and gene expression was observed across different genomic regions in the two muscle types. Our findings highlight the essential role of DNA methylation in skeletal muscle fiber diversity and identify potential epigenetic targets and pathways.

Article.Authors: Fernández Armúa E.; Serrano M.; Santana D.; Carrasco M.; Molina M.; Aznar I.; Acosta M.; Villar B.; Ferrari J.; Touya D.; Osinaga E.; Berois N.
Article.Abstract: Reliable circulating biomarkers for prognosis and treatment monitoring in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain limited. GALNT13 expression in CTCs emerges as a promising biomarker for prognosis and treatment monitoring in NSCLC. Prospective studies in larger cohorts are warranted to validate its clinical utility.

Article.Title: Endothelial Redox Dysregulation in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: Compartmentalized Mechanisms and Therapeutic Implications
Article.Authors: Moreno-Caceres S.; Marciano D.
Article.Abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive pulmonary vasculopathy in which endothelial dysfunction drives increased pulmonary vascular resistance and arterial remodeling. Redox signaling is central to endothelial homeostasis, and its disruption in PAH reflects changes in the magnitude, source, and subcellular location of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, as well as the molecular targets they engage. In healthy endothelium, compartmentalized redox signaling supports adaptive responses while preserving nitric oxide bioavailability. Loss of this spatial control in PAH can convert normally transient redox signals into persistent endothelial dysfunction, although the strength of evidence for this conversion differs substantially between pathways. This review examines how disease-associated stressors reshape endothelial redox signaling through NADPH oxidases, mitochondria, eNOS, iron-dependent chemistry, and nuclear pathways and how these compartments communicate. We also examine emerging circulating markers of redox and endothelial dysfunction and evaluate redox-directed therapies across experimental pulmonary hypertension and PAH. Throughout, we grade each mechanism according to whether it is supported by evidence from human PAH vascular tissue, patient-derived pulmonary arterial endothelial cells, experimental pulmonary hypertension models, and pulmonary endothelial models or by extrapolation from other relevant disease systems, and we identify where compartment-specific evidence is inferred from enzyme localization rather than measured directly. Current evidence supports moving beyond broad antioxidant approaches toward strategies that selectively target pathogenic redox signaling within the relevant endothelial compartment.

Article.Abstract: We characterized the intestinal microbiota of Misgurnus anguillicaudatus using 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V4 region). Microbial diversity analysis revealed that the intestinal microbiota of M. anguillicaudatus was dominated by the genera Vibrio, Pseudoalteromonas, and Aeromonas as core predominant taxa. Article.Title: Effects of Losartan on Renal Dopaminergic and Renin–Angiotensin System Alterations Induced by a High-Fat Diet in Sprague-Dawley Rats
Article.Authors: Cantú S.; Lee H.; Höcht C.; Donoso A.; Valtuille R.; Puyó A.; Choi M.

(Mean ± SD; p < 0.05). L prevented the following: HFD-induced increases in systolic blood pressure (SBP) and L-Dopa/dopamine urinary index (HFD vs. C, p < 0.01; HFDL vs. HFD, p < 0.01); lower expression of OCTN-1/2/3 (HFD vs. C, p < 0.01; HFDL vs. HFD, p < 0.05); overexpression of D1DR and Na+/K+-ATPase (HFD vs. C, p < 0.01; HFDL vs. HFD: D1DR p < 0.01; Na+/K+-ATPase p < 0.05), NF-κB1 and TGF-β1 (HFDL vs. HFD, p < 0.01). L mitigated proximal tubular alterations and interstitial fibrosis (HFDL vs. HFD, p < 0.01). Article.Title: G Protein-Coupled Receptors in Prostate Cancer: Pathophysiological Implications and Potential for Innovative Therapeutics
Article.Authors: Sarmento-Cabral A.; Herrero-Aguayo V.; Sáez-Martínez P.; Alors-Pérez E.; León-González A.; López-Cánovas J.; Montero-Hidalgo A.; Gahete M.; Jiménez-Vacas J.; Luque R.
Article.Abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) is one of the leading causes of cancer-related death among men worldwide. Considerable efforts have been devoted to developing more effective therapeutic strategies for PCa, particularly for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), wherein resistance to androgen-receptor pathway inhibition remains a major clinical challenge. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest family of cell surface signaling receptors, regulate numerous physiological and pathological processes and represent major therapeutic targets across multiple diseases, including cancer. In PCa, hormone- and inflammation-related GPCRs have emerged as key regulators of tumor initiation, progression, therapeutic resistance, and metastasis. Accordingly, understanding the contribution of GPCR signaling to PCa biology may reveal novel opportunities for therapeutic intervention, particularly in mCRPC. In this review, we summarize the current knowledge on the expression and function of GPCRs in PCa development, progression, and metastasis, highlighting their potential as therapeutic targets and discussing opportunities for drug development, combination therapies, and drug repurposing.

Article.Title: Genomic Amplification and Ovary-Specific Expression of Zona Pellucida Genes in Channel Catfish and Blue Catfish
Article.Authors: Chen T.; Gao D.; Su B.; Dunham R.; Liu Z.
Article.Abstract: Channel catfish (Ictalurus punctatus) is the most important aquaculture species in the United States, with the interspecific hybrid made from mating female channel catfish with male blue catfish (I. furcatus) being the predominant genotype for the catfish industry. While studying the mechanisms of their reproductive isolation, we determined zona pellucida (ZP) genes in both species. While ZP genes are well known for their ovary-specific expression in higher vertebrates such as mammals, the site of their expression in fish varies depending on species. In this study, we annotated the ZP genes in channel catfish and blue catfish and conducted phylogenetic analysis. We found that ZP genes are highly amplified in the catfish genomes, with ZP3- and ZP4-like genes being the most abundant in the genomes, derived from tandem and segmental duplications. A total of 39 and 49 ZP genes (including 4 and 5 pseudogenes) in the blue catfish genome and channel catfish genome were identified, respectively. Expression analysis using RNA-Seq revealed ovary-specific expression in females, with no expression in the gonadal tissues of males, nor in any other tissues of either males or females. RT-PCR analysis indicated that the ZP genes were not expressed until 90 days post fertilization, consistent with the timing of oogenesis of the developing gonad. Single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-Seq) confirmed expression of ZP genes only in oocytes. Future studies are warranted to determine the molecular mechanisms of sex-, tissue-, and time-specific expression of ZP genes, especially in relation to various taxa within teleost fish.

Article.Title: Effect of Leucovorin on Mitochondrial Respiration and One-Carbon Metabolism in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Substudy
Article.Authors: Rose S.; Melnyk S.; James S.; Frye R.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired methylation are implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Leucovorin, a reduced folate that bypasses both dihydrofolate reductase and folate receptor alpha, has shown clinical benefit in small trials in children with ASD, but the underlying biology is incompletely understood. In this pre-specified biomarker substudy of a completed double-blind placebo-controlled trial (NCT02000284; NCT01602016), children with ASD received leucovorin (2 mg/kg/day, maximum 50 mg/day) or a matched placebo for 12 weeks. Peripheral blood mononuclear cell respiration was measured by extracellular flux with a graded 2,3-dimethoxy-1,4-naphthoquinone (DMNQ) challenge (38 participants; 17 leucovorin, 21 placebo) and plasma thiol-methylation metabolites were measured pre- and post-treatment (42 participants; 18 leucovorin, 24 placebo). Leucovorin increased basal, ATP-linked, proton-leak, maximal, and reserve respiration relative to the placebo (Group × Visit p ≤ 0.012, all q ≤ 0.012; Cohen’s d 0.48–0.92); there was no evidence that the treatment effect varied across the tested DMNQ concentrations. In exploratory moderator analyses, folate receptor alpha autoantibody (FRAA) status modified the effect on maximal respiratory capacity and reserve capacity (both p < 0.001), with the largest gains in FRAA-positive children receiving leucovorin, and a history of neurodevelopmental regression modified the effect on basal, proton-leak and reserve respiration. The plasma SAM/SAH ratio increased (d = 0.77) and S-adenosylhomocysteine decreased (d = −0.67) on leucovorin; both were nominally significant (p = 0.020 and 0.050) but neither survived false-discovery-rate correction within the thiol family. The findings support the folate–mitochondrial–redox axis as a candidate therapeutic target in ASD and warrant replication in larger independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Peptides and Peptide Analogues Targeting Acetylcholinesterase-Associated Mechanisms in Alzheimer’s Disease and Dementias: Evidence Gaps, Design Strategies, and Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zdunek J.; Grodner B.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias involve interacting disturbances in amyloid-β, tau, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, synaptic integrity, and cholinergic neurotransmission. Acetylcholinesterase, in addition to terminating cholinergic signalling through acetylcholine hydrolysis, participates in non-catalytic interactions associated with amyloid-β, providing a mechanistic rationale for multi-target therapeutic strategies. This critical narrative review evaluates natural acetylcholinesterase-inhibitory peptides, amyloid-targeting sequences, D-enantiomeric and retro-inverso analogues, endogenous and neuroprotective peptides, and selected peptidomimetic and multifunctional designs. The literature is considered according to an evidence hierarchy that distinguishes direct acetylcholinesterase/peripheral anionic site target engagement from independently demonstrated secondary mechanisms, cellular activity, central nervous system exposure, in vivo pharmacodynamics, and clinical efficacy. The reviewed evidence indicates that peptides and peptide-derived compounds offer substantial molecular recognition and structural adaptability and may, in principle, be engineered to combine selected cholinergic and disease-relevant functions. Importantly, no single candidate reviewed here has experimentally demonstrated all of the proposed cholinergic, anti-amyloid, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, mitochondrial, and synaptoprotective activities simultaneously. However, neuroprotective, anti-amyloid, or cognitive effects alone do not establish direct acetylcholinesterase modulation, and many proposed multifunctional candidates lack experimental evidence of acetylcholinesterase/peripheral anionic site engagement. Overall, the available literature supports the feasibility of designing multifunctional peptide-based acetylcholinesterase-directed agents, but the evidence remains insufficient to establish a clinically validated class of multifunctional acetylcholinesterase modulators.

Article.Title: Directional Muscle-to-Bone Crosstalk via the Muscle Secretome: A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Rus Ž.; Mlakar S.; Ostanek B.; Marc J.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal muscle communicates biochemically with bone via a secretome consisting of soluble factors and extracellular vesicles (EVs). This secretory activity is regulated by mechanical stimuli and the muscle’s metabolic state. The aim of this systematic review was to evaluate the effects of the muscle secretome, specifically muscle-derived conditioned media and EVs, on bone mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs), osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and bone-related outcomes in in vitro and in vivo models. Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed and Web of Science were searched for original studies testing the muscle-derived secretome on MSCs, bone cells, or bone tissue, identifying 572 studies, of which 31 met the inclusion criteria. Risk of bias was assessed using SYRCLE for in vivo studies and a modified SYRCLE tool for in vitro studies. MISEV2023 terminology was applied. The majority of the included studies reported predominantly positive effects of secretome from healthy or mechanically stimulated muscle on MSC proliferation and osteogenic differentiation, improved osteoblast function, and suppressed osteoclast formation, with multiple in vivo confirmations. Conversely, secretome from atrophic/estrogen-deficient muscle inhibited osteogenesis and promoted osteoclastogenesis. Risk of bias and reporting limitations were common: heterogeneous dosing/reporting, incomplete reporting of purity, contaminants, and functional assay controls according to MISEV guidelines, and suboptimal SYRCLE domains in in vivo studies. The direction of muscle-to-bone biochemical crosstalk reflects muscle health—anabolic/antiresorptive when muscle is healthy or mechanically active, catabolic/proresorptive when muscle is atrophic or estrogen-deficient. These findings support exercise- and exerkine-based approaches, as well as EV-based therapeutics for osteoporosis or osteosarcopenia.

Article.Title: Licochalcone A Inhibits Melanoma Cell Survival by Suppressing HSP75 (TRAP1) and Disrupting Cellular Redox and Energy Homeostasis
Article.Authors: Lee Y.; Choi M.; Kim K.; Park S.; Bae Y.; Choi Y.; Lee S.; Nam H.; Cho M.
Article.Abstract: Heat shock protein 75(HSP75), a mitochondrial chaperone of the HSP90 family, sustains tumor cell survival by restraining oxidative phosphorylation, favoring aerobic glycolysis, and limiting mitochondrial ROS to preserve redox homeostasis. Although Licochalcone A (LCA), a flavonoid isolated from licorice root, displays anticancer activity across diverse tumors, whether HSP75 suppression contributes to its anti-melanoma effects remains undefined. This study assessed HSP75 expression in melanoma and evaluated the anti-melanoma efficacy of LCA. Expression of HSP75 was compared between melanoma and normal skin specimens by Western blotting. G361 melanoma cells were exposed to LCA, after which HSP75 expression, cell viability (MTT and trypan blue assays), intracellular ROS, the GSH/GSSG balance, ATP-associated luminescence, AMPK phosphorylation, MMP2, and apoptosis-related proteins were examined. HSP75 was also silenced by siRNA in normal melanocytes (HEMn-MP) and G361 cells, alone or combined with LCA treatment, with HSP75, p-AMPK, MMP2, cleaved PARP, and cleaved caspase-3 assessed by Western blotting. Melanoma tissue showed elevated HSP75 relative to normal tissue. LCA reduced HSP75 expression and viability while raising ROS, shifting the GSH/GSSG ratio toward oxidative stress, and reducing ATP-associated luminescence. AMPK phosphorylation rose, MMP2 declined, and pro-apoptotic markers (Bax, cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP) increased. HSP75 knockdown alone reproduced the LCA-induced changes in ATP-associated luminescence, p-AMPK, cleaved PARP, cleaved caspase-3, and MMP2, and combined knockdown with LCA further enhanced these changes in G361 cells, which were largely attenuated in normal HEMn-MP melanocytes. LCA suppresses melanoma cell survival by inducing cellular oxidative stress, reducing ATP-associated luminescence, and promoting apoptosis, with HSP75 suppression contributing to the ATP/AMPK and apoptotic responses. These findings support further evaluation of LCA and HSP75 in melanoma.

Article.Title: Recombinant Expression and Functional Analysis of GH2 β-Galactosidases Derived from Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus NSP1 and Streptococcus thermophilus RB16
Article.Authors: Shamsiyeva Y.; Kostanova A.; Tursunbekova A.; Khassenov B.; Akishev Z.
Article.Abstract: GH2 β-galactosidases are important industrial biocatalysts for lactose hydrolysis and prebiotic galacto-oligosaccharide (GOS) synthesis. Here, lacZ genes from Streptococcus thermophilus RB16 (StLacZ) and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus NSP1 (LbLacZ) were cloned, sequenced and deposited in GenBank under accession numbers QB046854 and QB046855, respectively, and expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3). A comparative study was conducted to determine their catalytic activity. rLbLacZ was found to be a typical mesophilic enzyme, with the optimal pH of 6.5 and a temperature of 40 °C, and high apparent affinity for lactose (Km = 14.02 mM). Nevertheless, rStLacZ exhibited an alkaline optimum and high thermo-activity, with optimal catalytic rates at pH 9.0 and 55–60 °C, as well as a high turnover number (kcat = 128.82 s−1) and specific activity (63.5 U/mg) for lactose. Despite different functional substrate affinities and reaction rates, both enzymes proved to have similar overall catalytic efficiency. The enzymes required specific divalent metals and monovalent metal salts to achieve peak catalytic activity. rStLacZ catalyzes the rapid and early synthesis of fast-migrating transglycosylation intermediates, while rLbLacZ catalyzes the progressive formation of slower-migrating, more complex oligosaccharide fractions. These findings demonstrate the complementary industrial potential of rStLacZ for rapid bioprocesses at elevated temperatures and rLbLacZ for the gentle processing of dairy products.

Article.Title: Integrated Multi-Omic Analysis of Paired Primary and Peritoneal Metastatic Tumors Reveals GPAA1 as a Therapeutic Target in Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Gong Z.; Zhu A.; Chen C.; Hu Y.; Wang J.; Sun L.
Article.Abstract: Peritoneal metastasis confers a dismal prognosis in colorectal cancer (CRC-PM), with median survival rarely exceeding 20 months. Here we employed multi-omic profiling to identify actionable drivers of CRC-PM. We performed whole-exome sequencing (WES) and label-free quantitative proteomics on 13 and 7 matched primary-peritoneal metastasis pairs, respectively. Public single-cell (GSE183916 and GSE132465) and spatial transcriptomic datasets (GSE225857) were integrated to dissect cellular heterogeneity. TCGA cohorts were used for survival analysis, and functional validation was performed in DLD1 cells. GPAA1, a catalytic subunit of the GPI transamidase complex, emerged as the most consistently upregulated protein in peritoneal metastases across discovery and validation proteomic cohorts. High GPAA1 expression correlated with shorter recurrence-free survival (HR = 1.72, p = 3.4 × 10−5). Single-cell analysis localized GPAA1 to malignant cells exhibiting oxidative phosphorylation and enhanced stromal crosstalk. GPAA1 overexpression promoted proliferation, migration, and EMT via AKT activation, whereas knockdown reversed these phenotypes. Our findings identify GPAA1 as a candidate driver of peritoneal metastasis in CRC, linking GPI anchor biosynthesis to metabolic reprogramming and AKT-mediated EMT. GPAA1 may serve as a prognostic marker in colorectal cancer.

Article.Title: Analysis of Ligation Activity in Miniaturized L1 Ligase Ribozyme Variants Down to 49 nt and in Split Ribozyme Forms
Article.Authors: Nitta Y.; Kato M.; Takagi Y.; Saga Y.; Ando T.; Mutsuro-Aoki H.; Tamura K.
Article.Abstract: Identifying the smallest active unit capable of ligating RNA in the absence of proteins is important to elucidate ribozyme evolution. Here, we aimed to construct an evolutionary model of the L1 ligase ribozyme. The miniaturized L1 ligase ribozyme (L1X6c2) consists of three stems: Stems A, B, and C. Mutants with shortened stems B and C were used to examine whether ligation occurred. In the mutant where both stems were simultaneously shortened, no ligation products were observed. We also constructed mutants with nucleotide deletions, measured their ligation-product signals after 24 h, and identified the structures crucial for ligation. A split mutant, formed by cleaving L1X6c2 at stem B, showed a ligation-product signal after 24 h close to that of L1X6c2, whereas another split mutant, formed by cleaving L1X6c2 at stem C, exhibited decreased activity. Although non-Watson–Crick base pairs near the ligation site did not affect ligation, the presence of G1 was important for ligation. Mutational analysis suggested that strong interactions between G1 and A51 in the G1–A51–U38 base triple are responsible for the base specificity of A51. Moreover, consecutive base pairs on each stem subtly contribute to the stability of the ribozyme folded into a compact structure to create a catalytic pocket.

Article.Title: CGRP–RAMP1/CALCRL Signaling Drives TGF-β2-Mediated Immune Evasion and Pancreatic Cancer Progression
Article.Authors: Zhang B.; Li Y.; Fan S.; Zhang J.; Zhang Y.; Wang W.; Luo L.; Xiao W.; Xie X.; Jian X.; Han Q.; Huang S.; Wu M.; Song Z.; Wen Y.; Tu H.; Li S.; Hu H.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by extensive neural remodeling and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, both of which contribute to disease progression and therapeutic resistance. However, whether nociceptor-derived signals directly reprogram PDAC cells to promote immune evasion remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized tumor-intrinsic neuroimmune mechanism driven by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) signaling through the receptor complex RAMP1/CALCRL on PDAC cells. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of Ramp1 or Calcrl did not alter PDAC cell proliferation in vitro but markedly suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in immunocompetent mice. These antitumor effects were lost in immunodeficient hosts, indicating that the pro-tumorigenic function of CGRP signaling depends on an intact host immune system. Consistently, tumor cell-specific loss of Ramp1 or Calcrl remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment, enhancing CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell effector activity. Mechanistically, CGRP stimulation promoted TGF-β2 expression and secretion by PDAC cells in a RAMP1-dependent manner. Tumor-derived TGF-β2 subsequently acted in a paracrine fashion to suppress CD8+ T-cell activation and cytotoxic function, whereas genetic disruption of RAMP1 or pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling relieved this immunosuppression. Together, these findings define a CGRP–RAMP1/CALCRL–TGF-β2 signaling axis through which nociceptive input is converted into tumor-driven adaptive immune evasion in PDAC. This pathway reveals a previously underappreciated mechanism linking neural signaling to PDAC progression and identifies CGRP receptor signaling as a potential therapeutic vulnerability for restoring antitumor immunity and improving the responsiveness of PDAC to immunotherapy.

Article.Title: Restoration of PPD-Induced Injury in iHDPCs via the OS–Mitochondrial Apoptosis Pathway: Screening and Validation of Natural Compounds
Article.Authors: Ren Y.; He J.; Zheng L.; Yue L.; He C.; Huang D.; Zhang F.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to investigate the protective effects of curcumin (Cur), resveratrol (Res), and astragaloside IV (AS-IV) against p-phenylenediamine (PPD)-induced injury in human immortalized dermal papilla cells (iHDPCs), with a focus on phenotypic endpoints that are suggestive of the oxidative stress–mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. Putative core targets were predicted via network pharmacology and molecular docking, and cellular responses were evaluated using CCK-8, DCFH-DA, JC-1, and Annexin V/PI assays in both PPD- and H2O2-exposed models. 1623 Collectively, these observations are consistent with the possibility that Cur, Res, and AS-IV may alleviate PPD-induced cellular damage, potentially through modulation of oxidative status and mitochondrial homeostasis. However, because the current experiments do not directly measure NRF2 nuclear translocation, downstream antioxidant enzyme expression (e.g., P-AKT HO-1, NQO1), BAX/BCL-2 ratio, cytochrome c release, or caspase activation, they cannot establish target engagement or a definitive causal link to the proposed pathway. Therefore, our findings should be interpreted as correlative and hypothesis-generating; direct mechanistic validation is required to confirm the involvement of this pathway. Nevertheless, the consistent protective phenotypes observed make these compounds, particularly AS-IV, promising candidates for the development of next-generation hair dyes.

Article.Title: Azithromycin Derivatives for Overcoming Antibacterial Resistance: Structural Modification and Structure–Activity Relationships
Article.Authors: Ngece K.; Paca A.; Buwa-Komoreng L.; Aderibigbe B.; Khwaza V.
Article.Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance has significantly compromised the therapeutic efficacy of many antibiotics, highlighting the need for new agents capable of overcoming bacterial resistance. The discovery of antibiotics in the early 20th century contributed significantly to transforming modern medicine and saved countless lives. However, the alarming increase in antibiotic resistance now threatens these achievements. The misuse and overuse of antibiotics have driven the continuous evolution and adaptation of microorganisms, contributing to this growing global health challenge. Azithromycin (AZM), a widely used macrolide antibiotic with favorable pharmacokinetic properties, is increasingly affected by resistance mechanisms. A number of researchers have therefore designed and developed AZM derivatives with promising antibacterial properties. This review summarizes advances in the structural modification of AZM, focusing on side-chain modification, heterocyclic substitution, molecular hybridization, and their associated structure–activity relationships. Selected derivatives demonstrated enhanced activity against resistant bacterial pathogens compared with AZM, although activity varies according to substituent position, linker structure, and overall molecular properties. Nevertheless, the activity of many AZM derivatives against Gram-negative organisms remains limited, with restricted outer-membrane permeability and inadequate intracellular accumulation representing important barriers to achieving effective antibacterial activity. Overall, the structural modification of AZM represents a promising strategy for developing potential antibacterial agents, but further pharmacological and in vivo studies are required to establish their therapeutic potential.

Article.Title: The UAP2-BRR2b Module Regulates Low-Temperature Hypocotyl Elongation by Modulating Pre-mRNA Splicing in Arabidopsis
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Chen F.; Hu Z.; Geng L.; Zhu J.
Article.Abstract: Plants adapt to low temperatures through transcriptomic reprogramming, yet how the core spliceosome maintains splicing fidelity during cold-regulated development remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP-associated protein 2 (AtUAP2) in Arabidopsis using genetic, transcriptomic, and biochemical approaches. Under normal conditions (22 °C), uap2, brr2b, and uap2 brr2b mutants showed no obvious developmental defects. Upon low-temperature treatment, however, uap2 displayed a severe impairment in cold-dependent hypocotyl elongation. RNA-sequencing revealed that UAP2 deficiency induced widespread pre-mRNA mis-splicing under cold stress. Ectopic expression of correctly spliced AtGRP7 and AtLOS2 cDNAs in uap2 partially restored hypocotyl growth under cold conditions, supporting their roles as key downstream effectors. Mechanistically, protein interaction assays demonstrated that UAP2 physically binds to the U5 RNA helicase BRR2b. While brr2b mutants exhibited a hypocotyl growth phenotype similar to uap2, the uap2 brr2b double mutant displayed an enhanced growth defect under low temperatures. Overall, our findings suggest that the UAP2-BRR2b complex operates as a functional module required to sustain spliceosomal efficiency under low temperature, providing insights into the potential connection between core splicing machinery dynamics and cold-induced hypocotyl growth responses in Arabidopsis.

Article.Title: Toxins and Antivenoms of Latrodectus tredecimguttatus: Molecular Mechanisms, Antibody Development, and Evidence from Other Latrodectus Species
Article.Authors: Rakhim M.; Abekova A.; Shynykul Z.; Koilybayeva M.; Batanova Z.; Nurolda E.; Akhmetsadykov N.
Article.Abstract: Latrodectus tredecimguttatus envenomation causes latrodectism, a neurotoxic syndrome driven primarily by α-latrotoxin (α-LTX)-mediated dysregulation of neurotransmitter release. This review examines the development and therapeutic application of specific immunoglobulins against L. tredecimguttatus toxins, integrating toxin diversity, α-LTX mechanisms, antibody production, preclinical neutralization, and clinical use. Eggs and spiderlings also contain bioactive proteins, including Latroeggtoxin-I and Latroeggtoxin-IV, although their relevance to human envenomation and antivenom development remains uncertain. α-LTX acts through receptor engagement, membrane pore formation, Ca2+ influx, and receptor-mediated signaling, providing potential targets for antibody neutralization. Conventional antivenoms rely mainly on animal-derived polyclonal immunoglobulins, whereas phage display and recombinant engineering enable fully human monoclonal antibodies with defined specificity and high affinity. Preclinical studies demonstrate neutralization across cellular, electrophysiological, ex vivo, and in vivo models, but methodological heterogeneity and variable cross-species activity complicate efficacy comparisons. Recombinant human antibodies offer improved molecular definition, reproducibility, and engineering potential, although clinical efficacy remains unestablished. Future development should prioritize standardized neutralization assays, clinically relevant post-exposure models, systematic cross-neutralization studies, and recombinant antibody combinations to achieve broader toxin coverage and safer, more standardized, reproducible, and clinically applicable immunotherapy for L. tredecimguttatus envenomation.

Article.Title: Diagnostic Yield and Clinical Actionability of Genetic Testing in Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Dumitra A.; Streață I.; Turcu-Știolică A.; Riza A.; Șerban R.; Cucu M.; Prică A.; Burada F.
Article.Abstract: Genetic testing is increasingly central to the evaluation of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet most evidence emphasises diagnostic yield rather than whether findings change clinical care. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses [PRISMA] 2020) of genetic testing across the diagnostic pathway in NDD populations, focusing on autism spectrum disorder (ASD), intellectual disability, and global developmental delay, to quantify pooled diagnostic yield and clinical actionability. A systematic search of PubMed and Web of Science, with an expanded population and outcome term set, was completed on 1 October 2026, supplemented by an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted search (Undermind) and reference-list screening. Twenty-three studies were included in a qualitative synthesis and 22 in a quantitative meta-analysis of diagnostic yield (N = 7641 patients tested; diagnostic-yield analysis comprised 23 data points, as Charouf et al. contributed separate whole-exome sequencing (WES) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) cohorts). Single-proportion random-effects meta-analysis with the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation produced a pooled diagnostic yield of 28% (95% confidence interval [CI] 21–35%; I2 = 96.1%) and pooled clinical actionability of 58% (95% CI 44–72%; I2 = 95.7%) across 16 studies (N = 1538 patients with confirmed diagnoses). A significant yield gradient was observed across modalities (chromosomal microarray analysis [CMA], 16%; WES, 36%; WGS, 43%; p < 0.0001). Actionability estimates were robust across sensitivity analyses (54–64%). Genetic testing in NDDs functions not only as an etiological tool but as an input to personalised management, including pharmacological optimisation, comorbidity surveillance, and resolution of the diagnostic odyssey, albeit with very low certainty of evidence per Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE), reflecting substantial heterogeneity and observational study design.

Article.Title: 6-Gingerol Potentiates β-Cell Insulin Secretion Without Acting as an L-Cell GLP-1 Secretagogue
Article.Authors: Intisang V.; Yameephai P.; Uppakara K.; Pathomthongtaweechai N.
Article.Abstract: The incretin hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and its receptor (GLP-1R) are central regulators of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and major targets in type 2 diabetes. 6-Gingerol, the principal bioactive constituent of ginger, has a reported insulinotropic action that depends on GLP-1 in vivo, but whether this reflects GLP-1 secretion from intestinal L-cells or signaling at the β-cell GLP-1R is unresolved. Using NCI-H716 and STC-1 L-cells and MIN6 β-cells, we examined whether 6-Gingerol acts as a GLP-1 secretagogue or at the β-cell. 6-Gingerol did not stimulate GLP-1 secretion. It had no effect in NCI-H716 cells and reduced secretion in STC-1 cells at concentrations that did not reduce viability. In MIN6 β-cells, 6-Gingerol potentiated insulin secretion in a bell-shaped manner. This effect was abolished by two mechanistically distinct GLP-1R antagonists and by protein kinase A inhibition and was accompanied by a GLP-1R-dependent rise in cAMP. MIN6 cells expressed Glp1r transcript, and Exendin-4 confirmed a functional receptor response. These findings suggest that 6-Gingerol acts at the β-cell through GLP-1R-, cAMP-, and PKA-dependent mechanisms and not as an L-cell GLP-1 secretagogue. At the pharmacological concentration used, these results suggest an in vitro mechanism rather than a physiological dietary effect, and in vivo validation is needed.

Article.Title: Mean-Centering Alters Pathway-Based Transcriptomic Comparisons of Feline and Mouse Kidney Disease
Article.Authors: Watanabe M.; Sasaki T.; Nakagawa R.; Sasaki N.
Article.Abstract: Transcriptomic similarity is used to characterize disease models, but a comparison can change when the same responses are summarized differently. We examined mean-centering before pathway averaging in 16 disease states from one feline chronic kidney disease cohort and two mouse kidney injury models, using 2016 genes detected in both species’ proteomes and 422 overlapping pathways. Among 87 state pairs without shared control samples, uncentered pathway means separated same-species from cross-species pairs with an area under the curve of 0.868; removing each state’s mean across genes first reduced this to 0.511. The uncentered value was higher in 98.6% of animal-level resamples, and the difference held across nine offset and filter settings, all four gene spaces and the 83-pair subset without shared animals. Under within-state ranking or quantile normalization, which equalize each state’s overall level by construction, the contrast fell to 0.010 and 0.001. Reference-axis projections can rank states differently from cosine because they retain amplitude, and benchmark gaps were poorly calibrated. These results identify a consequential preprocessing choice rather than a preferred species or a validated measure of disease fidelity. Because all feline states came from one cohort and all mouse states from two datasets, species was confounded with dataset throughout, and the separation reported here may reflect dataset-specific technical variation rather than species biology.

Article.Title: Association of Circulating microRNAs in Plasma with Coronary Collateral Circulation in Patients with Chronic Total Occlusion
Article.Authors: Kiseleva A.; Sotnikova E.; Zharikova A.; Vasilev D.; Kutsenko V.; Borisova A.; Ershova A.; Meshkov A.; Drapkina O.
Article.Abstract: Chronic total occlusion (CTO) occurs in 16–52% of patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and is often accompanied by variable development of coronary collateral circulation (CCC). The aim of this work was to study the associations between circulating plasma microRNAs (miRNAs) and the development of CCC in patients with CTO. This exploratory study included 43 patients: a control group—patients without significant coronary artery stenosis (n = 20), and two CTO groups with good (n = 13) and poor (n = 10) CCC based on the Rentrop classification. Libraries were prepared using the QIAseq miRNA UDI Library Kit and then sequenced on the NextSeq 550 using a 1 × 75 bp protocol. However, given the limited sample size, the findings should be considered hypothesis-generating, and further studies are required for validation in larger, independent cohorts and to establish the roles of these miRNAs in CCC development.

Article.Title: Molecular Regulators for the Wnt/β-Catenin Signalling Pathway for Bone Remodelling in Periodontitis: A Scoping Review
Article.Authors: Amir Maeraj H.; Rajoo S.; Mohd-Said S.; Nasruddin N.; Taib I.; Wong S.; Jayusman P.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that destroys the periodontal ligament, leading to alveolar bone loss and ultimately tooth loss. The Wnt/β-catenin signalling pathway is an important molecular signalling pathway that controls the expression of bone remodelling-related genes. Manipulating this pathway is a recurring theme in recent studies, suggesting a viable therapeutic target. A scoping review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines to identify the latest molecular regulators used in manipulating the signalling pathway between 2007 and 2025 from databases such as Web of Science, Ovid Medline, and Scopus. Only primary articles relevant to the signalling pathway, periodontitis, and bone homeostasis were selected. A total of 22 articles were identified, using various molecules ranging from plant extracts such as field horsetail to pre-existing drugs. The molecules function by altering the activities of targets within the signalling pathway such as β-catenin and GSK-3β phosphorylation, ultimately increasing osteoblast differentiation for bone growth that was reduced in periodontitis cases. The Wnt/β-catenin signalling pathway is a favoured target for potential therapeutic interventions for periodontitis. However, most studies are limited to in vitro methods and requires further description on the relationships between periodontitis and the signalling pathway.

Article.Authors: Liu S.; Deng B.; Li Y.; Wu J.; Xu Z.
Article.Abstract: Growth hormone has the potential to modulate inflammatory responses, alleviate intestinal injury, and preserve intestinal health. Colonic tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-2 (IL-2), and interleukin-6 levels decreased significantly, whereas the interleukin-10 (IL-10) level increased after L. lactis (pNZ8148-pGH) administration. Furthermore, L. lactis (pNZ8148-pGH) significantly increased the numbers of colonic Ki67- and PCNA-positive cells and their positive indices. In addition, compared with the DSS group, L. lactis (pNZ8148) significantly decreased CDS, serum DAO activity, and colonic IL-2 level while increasing colonic occludin and IL-10 levels. Article.Authors: Li J.; Ma X.; Si S.; Weng T.; Chen S.; Zhang X.; Ren S.; Liu F.; Li Y.; Xue F.; Xuan L.; Sun J.
Article.Abstract: Plant height is an important agronomic trait affecting cotton architecture and mechanized production. Public transcriptome data showed variation in GhLRX transcript abundance across tissues, developmental stages, and abiotic stress conditions. The homoeologous genes GhLRX2 and GhLRX19 showed relatively high transcript abundance in stems and 20-day-post-anthesis fibers and were selected for preliminary investigation. Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) treatment targeting a sequence shared by GhLRX2 and GhLRX19 was associated with lower combined transcript abundance and reduced plant height. Article.Authors: Dolnicka A.; Marcinkowska K.; Obmińska-Mrukowicz B.; Fosse V.; Raciborska A.; Śmieszek A.
Article.Abstract: Osteosarcoma is an aggressive primary bone malignancy affecting both humans and dogs, and canine osteosarcoma represents a valuable comparative model for investigating novel therapeutic strategies. Combined treatment at IC50 increased late apoptotic and necrotic populations and disrupted cell-cycle distribution. BAM15 reduced oxidative phosphorylation-derived ATP production without detectable glycolytic compensation but did not further suppress mitochondrial ATP production beyond regorafenib effect alone. Combined treatment also induced transcriptional changes in stress-adaptation-related genes, while protein analysis revealed reduced BAX and BAX/BCL-2 ratio. Article.Title: Development of an Orthotopic Patient-Derived Xenograft Model of Gastro-Esophageal Adenocarcinoma: A Single-Lineage Pilot Study
Article.Authors: Reddavid R.; Degiuli M.; Orrù C.; Giordano S.; Corso S.

Tumor fragments were then implanted into the gastric submucosal layer of seven NOD-SCID mice using a specifically developed surgical technique. Primary orthotopic tumor growth was qualitatively monitored longitudinally by in vivo IVIS imaging, whereas distant organ-associated bioluminescent signals were assessed ex vivo in excised organs at the experimental endpoint. Local tumor growth was observed in all xenografts. Distant organ-associated bioluminescent signals were detected in the liver and lungs, with an additional bowel-associated signal observed in one animal. These preliminary proof-of-concept findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of submucosal orthotopic implantation and longitudinal in vivo monitoring. However, given the small exploratory cohort and the use of a single patient-derived tumor lineage, the biological fidelity and generalizability of the model remain to be established in larger studies incorporating multiple independent tumors and comparative histopathological and molecular analyses.

Article.Title: JAK-STAT Signaling: Mechanisms and Therapeutics in Stem Cell Biology
Article.Authors: Li W.
Article.Abstract: The Janus kinase–signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway is a conserved signaling system that links extracellular cytokine signals to transcriptional regulation of genes controlling cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Increasing evidence demonstrates that this pathway plays central roles in stem cell biology across diverse systems, including pluripotent stem cells, adult tissue stem cells, and cancer stem cells. In pluripotent stem cells, STAT3 signaling downstream of leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) supports self-renewal and maintenance of the undifferentiated state, whereas in adult stem cells, JAK-STAT activity regulates the balance between quiescence, proliferation, and lineage commitment. Stem cell niches further modulate pathway activity through spatially and temporally controlled cytokine signals that coordinate regenerative responses with tissue homeostasis. Recent studies have also revealed noncanonical functions of STAT proteins, including mitochondrial STAT3-dependent metabolic regulation and unphosphorylated STAT-mediated chromatin and heterochromatin regulation that influence stem cell identity and function. Dysregulation of the pathway contributes to pathological conditions, including inflammatory disorders and cancers characterized by stem-like cell populations. Therapeutic targeting of JAK-STAT signaling therefore represents an important strategy in both regenerative medicine and oncology. This review summarizes recent advances in understanding how JAK-STAT signaling regulates stem cell biology, highlighting emerging mechanisms of pathway integration, niche regulation, and therapeutic modulation.

Article.Title: Prometheus’s Fire, Part I: The Flight of Icarus—Molecular Mechanisms Underlying Adipose Tissue Dysfunction in Obesity: From Adaptive Hyperplasia to Pathological Hypertrophy
Article.Authors: Grudniewska A.; Mrozikiewicz-Rakowska B.; Wiszniewski K.; Bik W.; Szabłowska-Gadomska I.; Kuryłowicz A.
Article.Abstract: Obesity is a heterogeneous disease in which cardiometabolic risk is shaped not only by adipose tissue mass but also by the capacity of adipose tissue to expand and remain metabolically functional. This narrative review provides an integrated, evidence-weighted molecular framework, the central original contribution of this work, for understanding how initially adaptive adipose tissue expansion transitions into pathological hypertrophy and self-sustaining immunometabolic dysfunction. We examine how impaired adipogenesis, angiogenesis and extracellular-matrix remodelling converge with mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, hypoxia and lipotoxicity to destabilise adipocyte homeostasis. We further explore how adipokine remodelling, loss of adiponectin-mediated protection and enhanced leptin signalling interact with immune-cell recruitment to establish self-amplifying inflammatory circuits. Evidence is stratified across experimental, translational and human levels; a summary table maps each mechanism to its strength of evidence and current clinical relevance. This framework explains metabolic phenotype heterogeneity among individuals with comparable adiposity and establishes the molecular foundation for Parts II and III of the Prometheus’s Fire series.

Article.Title: Recent Developments in Chemo-Photodynamic Nanoplatforms for Glioblastoma Treatment
Article.Authors: Woźnicki P.; Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) remains one of the most difficult malignant brain tumours to treat due to its infiltrative nature, cellular heterogeneity, resistance to treatment and limited drug penetration across the blood–brain barrier. The combination of photodynamic therapy (PDT) with chemotherapy within a single nanoplatform offers the possibility of integrating the photogeneration of reactive oxygen species with the cytotoxic action of chemotherapeutic agents, whilst improving their coordinated delivery to tumour cells. This review summarises the latest nanoparticle-based strategies combining PDT and chemotherapy in the treatment of GBM. The literature published between January 2025 and August 2026 was identified using the PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus databases. The systems analysed included photoreactive organic nanoaggregates, ZnO-based nanocomposites, lipid nanocarriers, dual-targeting liposomes and platforms based on covalent organic frameworks. These nanoplatforms enabled various forms of therapeutic integration, including light-triggered drug release, co-encapsulation of photosensitisers and chemotherapeutic agents, targeting of mitochondria, and targeting of glioma cells and blood–brain barrier models via ligands. The available studies have generally demonstrated increased cytotoxicity following photoactivation, and selected systems have shown synergistic effects between chemotherapy and PDT. However, the available evidence is insufficient to support the translational readiness of the currently reported chemo-PDT nanoplatforms. Three of the five systems were evaluated only in vitro, only one was investigated in an orthotopic glioma model, and several studies relied on surrogate metabolic assays or irradiation conditions of limited relevance to deep intracranial disease. The current literature should therefore be regarded primarily as proof-of-concept evidence for coordinated chemo-PDT delivery rather than as evidence of clinically applicable therapy. Progress towards clinical relevance will require platforms designed around realistic light-delivery constraints, the hypoxic GBM microenvironment, brain-relevant delivery routes and therapeutically meaningful in vivo endpoints.

Article.Authors: Chmiel J.; Kopytek M.; Dąbrowski M.; Iwańczyk S.; Musiał K.; Woźniak P.; Chmiel J.; Partyka Ł.; Ząbczyk M.; Natorska J.; Musiałek P.
Article.Abstract: Coronary artery ectasias and aneurysms (CAEAs) are present in up to 5% of patients undergoing coronary angiography. Recent studies indicated an independent association between CAEA and the risk of myocardial infarction but the underlying mechanisms have not yet been elucidated. We evaluated the relationship between CAEA and fibrin clot properties in 60 consecutive CAEA subjects and 60 clinically/angiographically matched controls enrolled across three tertiary centers. Fibrin clot permeability coefficient (Ks), clot lysis time (CLT), and levels of 3-nitrotyrosine, an oxidative stress marker, were assessed. Among patients with CAEA, 52 (86.7%) were male, the median age was 66.0 (59.5–74.1) years, and 30 (50.0%) had concomitant coronary artery disease. Compared with controls, CAEA subjects had 14% lower Ks (p = 0.036), 25% longer CLT (p = 0.001), and 21% higher 3-nitrotyrosine levels (p = 0.002). Multivariable regression analysis showed an association of CAEA with lower Ks, longer CLT, and higher 3-nitrotyrosine levels (all p < 0.05). In CAEA patients, 3-nitrotyrosine levels correlated with Ks (r = −0.31, p = 0.016) and CLT (r = 0.27, p = 0.037). With increasing CAEA peak-to-reference diameter ratio, Ks decreased (p-trend = 0.017), and 3-nitrotyrosine levels increased (p-trend = 0.002). In conclusion, we found that CAEA is independently associated with unfavorably altered fibrin clot properties, reflected by denser clot structure and reduced susceptibility to fibrinolysis. Our findings suggest that oxidative stress may contribute to unfavorable modification of fibrin clot properties in CAEA. With an increase in CAEA size, there is an increase in oxidative stress and worsening of the fibrin clot phenotype (CARE-ANEURYSM, NCT05183373).

Article.Title: The Oral–Gut–Systemic Axis in Periodontitis: Microbiome Dysbiosis, Immune Crosstalk and Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: Mochol M.; Kulig H.; Rączka A.; Lipski M.; Marek E.; Schuster L.; Dammaschke T.; Mazurek-Mochol M.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease associated with subgingival dysbiosis and altered host response. Although it is usually considered a local disease of the tooth-supporting tissues, it may also interact with distant mucosal and systemic compartments. One possible explanation is the oral–gut–systemic axis. In this model, oral bacteria, microbial products and inflammatory mediators are swallowed and reach the gastrointestinal tract. In susceptible hosts, these signals may affect gut microbial ecology, epithelial barrier integrity, mucosal immunity and microbial metabolite pathways. Human studies show links between periodontitis, altered oral and gut microbial communities, oral–gut microbial signatures and systemic metabolomic changes. Experimental studies provide stronger mechanistic support. They suggest that periodontal pathogens, particularly Porphyromonas gingivalis, may promote gut dysbiosis, barrier dysfunction, endotoxemia, inflammasome activation, T helper 17/regulatory T cell (Th17/Treg) imbalance and changes in metabolite signaling pathways. Candidate pathways include aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) signaling, suppression of G protein-coupled receptor 109A (GPR109A), short-chain fatty acid-related pathways and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) metabolism. Inflammatory bowel disease is currently the most developed disease-specific model. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), rheumatoid arthritis, cardiometabolic metabolite pathways and gastrointestinal cancer models are less mature extensions. This review summarizes current evidence and identifies the need for longitudinal studies, strain-level source tracking, multi-omics, immune phenotyping and disease-specific intervention studies. At present, the concept is biologically plausible, but clinical translation remains premature.

Article.Title: Actions of Pharmaceutical Lactones and Lactams on the Enzymes with Lactonase Activity: In Silico Prediction and In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Efremenko E.; Domnin M.; Sarapina A.; Zagidulina A.
Article.Abstract: Pharmaceutical pollutants that contain lactone or lactam rings in their structure are frequently detected in wastewater. Enzymes with lactonase activity, synthesized by the microorganisms in aerobic activated sludge, are expected to be able to participate in the hydrolysis of these pharmaceutical pollutants, but the actual activity of many lactonases towards such compounds remains poorly characterized. In this work, a systematic molecular docking study of 12 enzymes and 39 pharmaceutical pollutants (β-lactam antibiotics, macrolides, coumarins, statins) was undertaken. The binding affinity, active-site occupancy, total enzyme surface occupancy and geometric characteristics of the molecules (the distance from the catalytic nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon of the lactone ring, and the attack angle formed between the nucleophilic atom of the enzyme and the C–N/C–O bond of the substrate) were evaluated in silico for a set of hydrolases displaying lactonase activity (AidC, AaL, hexahistidine-tagged organophosphate hydrolase (His6-OPH), etc.) and metallo-β-lactamases (MβLs) (NDM-1, MIM-1, SAM-1). Lactamases exhibited favorable intermolecular interaction geometry for the majority of β-lactams. No enzyme was found that satisfied the geometric criteria corresponding to the biodegradation of macrolides. With coumarins, only Paraoxonase PON2 provided an optimal geometry of biocatalysis; however, this enzyme is absent from activated sludge but may be of interest for in vivo applications. For several statins widely used in practice, combinations with enzymes having virtually ideal geometry for biocatalysis were identified: AidC/rosuvastatin lactone, AaL/lovastatin, His6-OPH/mevastatin, and PON2/simvastatin. For the first time, several pharmaceutical lactones were identified in silico and confirmed in vitro as inhibitors of MβL and His6-OPH. Competitive inhibition of NDM-1 by lactone-containing signaling molecules of Gram-negative bacteria present in activated sludge was revealed for the first time both in silico and in vitro. The obtained results‘ may be taken into account when implementing monitoring of biological stages at water treatment stations and improve the efficiency of water purification. The revealed characteristics of MβL inhibition by macrolides may be taken into account as one of possible explanations for the effective application of β-lactams in combinations with macrolides known from multiple paratactical investigations.

Article.Title: Contrasting Effects of Chitosan Molecular Modifications on the Properties of Fish Gelatin Hydrogels
Article.Authors: Nikiforova A.; Abramov V.; Skvortsova P.; Akhmadiyarov A.; Rakipov I.; Sorokin A.; Lavlinskaya M.; Zueva O.; Holyavka M.; Derkach S.; Zuev Y.
Article.Abstract: The limited water solubility of chitosan, which necessitates acidic conditions for its dissolution, restricts its application in food and pharmaceutical systems. To overcome this limitation, we chemically modified a chitosan molecule by introducing hydrophilic groups and compared three chitosan forms—unmodified chitosan, its quaternary ammonium derivative, and a graft copolymer with poly-N-vinylpyrrolidone, with respect to their effect on the structural and mechanical properties of fish gelatin hydrogels. An experimental study combining NMR relaxometry and water self-diffusion measurements, scanning electron microscopy, and rheology revealed a distinct supramolecular architecture of gelatin–chitosan hydrogel network for different chitosan modifications. The NMR data gave information on the molecular mobility of water as a marker of hydrogel structure to elucidate molecular basis for the observed rheological properties. Unmodified chitosan maximally reinforces gelatin network and enhances its thermorheological stability. Chitosan grafting with poly-N-vinylpyrrolidone produces a fine-pored xerogel structure with higher thermorheological stability, possibly through a non-cooperative reinforcement mechanism. The quaternary ammonium derivative results in a heterogeneous xerogel morphology with weak mechanical strength and low gel–sol transition temperature. These findings establish the structure–property correlation, demonstrating that chitosan modification governs the molecular network architecture and macroscopic performance of gelatin-based hydrogels, providing molecular-level insights into the behavior of fish gelatin–chitosan systems.

Article.Title: Central Nervous System Toxoplasmosis Beyond HIV in Patients with Hematologic Malignancies: A Contemporary Narrative Review and Illustrative Case Synthesis
Article.Authors: Łanocha A.; Pawelec-Pęciak O.; Kot K.; Machaliński B.; Kosik-Bogacka D.; Łanocha-Arendarczyk N.
Article.Abstract: Toxoplasmosis is an important opportunistic infection in immunocompromised individuals, typically resulting from reactivation of latent Toxoplasma gondii infection. CNS toxoplasmosis, most commonly presenting as toxoplasmic encephalitis (TE), is rare in patients with hematologic malignancies and after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). It is nevertheless life-threatening and likely underrecognized. This narrative review integrates molecular, immunological, clinical, and transplant-related evidence on T. gondii persistence and reactivation, treatment-associated immune dysfunction, diagnosis, management, prophylaxis, and molecular surveillance. Risk reflects cumulative immunosuppression, particularly impaired T-cell reconstitution, lymphocyte-depleting therapy, corticosteroid exposure, cytopenias, hypogammaglobulinemia, and absent or ineffective prophylaxis. Typical ring-enhancing lesions, positive serology, and detectable T. gondii DNA in cerebrospinal fluid may all be absent. Diagnosis therefore requires integration of immune and treatment history, magnetic resonance imaging, molecular testing, and, when necessary, histopathology. When clinical suspicion is high, empiric therapy should not be delayed; however, diagnostic specimens should be obtained whenever feasible, and evaluation for alternative diagnoses should proceed in parallel. In seropositive allogeneic HSCT recipients, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis with quantitative PCR surveillance remains the best-established preventive strategy.

Article.Title: A Double-Edged Sword: The Dichotomous Roles of Dendritic Cell Subsets in Shaping CD8+ T Cell Immunity and Tolerance Within the Tumor Microenvironment
Article.Authors: Gao G.; Chen K.
Article.Abstract: Dendritic cells (DCs) function as a double-edged sword in tumor immunity, capable of both activating and tolerizing CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). While conventional type 1 dendritic cells (cDC1s) are well-established mediators of cross-presentation for initiating anti-tumor CTL responses, existing reviews—largely overlook the tolerogenic potential of cDC1s and the context-dependent immunostimulatory capacity of cDC2s, monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs), and plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs). Furthermore, no prior synthesis has systematically reconciled the divergent functions of DC subsets across steady-state versus inflammatory conditions, migratory versus resident phenotypes, and human versus mouse model systems. The tumor microenvironment (TME) and tumor-derived exosomes further drive DCs toward an immunosuppressive phenotype, facilitating immune escape. Here, we establish a multi-dimensional framework that dissects the dichotomous roles of diverse DC subsets in regulating CTL immunity and tolerance, resolving key biological contradictions—including recent in vivo evidence that cDC2s can cross-present immune-complexed antigens via a WDFY4-dependent pathway shared with cDC1s—an activity that complements, but does not replace, the cDC1-restricted cross-presentation of cell-associated antigens. We also provide a hierarchical analysis of strategies to restore DC-mediated anti-tumor activity, extending the DC–CTL regulatory paradigm to autoimmunity and solid organ transplantation. A comprehensive summary table categorizes DC-based therapeutic approaches by clinical development stage. By elucidating this dynamic balancing mechanism, we offer refined insights for optimizing cancer immunotherapy design and cross-disciplinary therapeutic applications.

Article.Title: CATCH-EVseq, an Ultra-Sensitive Capture Assay to Monitor Human Enterovirus RNA
Article.Authors: Germain A.; Hanson M.
Article.Abstract: The detection of low-abundance viral RNA in chronic or persistent infections remains a major challenge in virology, constrained by the sensitivity and specificity of traditional methods. One such infection, chronic enterovirus (EV) infection, has been proposed as a potential underlying factor in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME), although this hypothesis remains debated. Supporting evidence for EVs as a viral trigger includes historical spatiotemporal overlaps between ME outbreaks and poliomyelitis epidemics, frequent reports of “flu-like” illness at disease onset, seasonal outbreaks patterns, and serological findings. To address the problem of EV detection, we developed CATCH-EVseq, an ultra-sensitive platform built on the CATCH framework. By integrating high-throughput sequencing with cDNA capture using 49,847 probes targeting 3410 EV genomes, CATCH-EVseq achieved a detection limit in artificially created samples as low as one copy in a microgram of RNA for two out of three biological replicates. Additionally, spike-in controls allow for rigorous validation of the capture and sequencing throughout the CATCH-EVseq procedure. When applied to a small number of blood samples from both ME patients and healthy controls, CATCH-EVseq detected no EV RNA, either in direct assays or after in vitro viral amplification. While these results do not support the presence of circulating EV RNA in the blood of individuals with ME, they do not rule out persistent infection in other tissues or organs. Critically, CATCH-EVseq establishes a robust, ultra-sensitive framework for future investigations of low-level EV persistence in biopsies, post-mortem tissues, or other clinical contexts where chronic enterovirus infection is suspected.

Article.Title: Multiscale Interactome Analysis Prioritizes Candidate Herbs and Compounds for Diabetic Retinopathy
Article.Authors: Ahn Y.; Chae J.; Han S.; Lee W.; Park C.
Article.Abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), a leading cause of preventable vision loss among working-age adults, arises from chronic hyperglycemic injury to the retinal microvasculature; current interventions such as anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) injection are largely reactive, and mechanism-anchored herbal options remain undefined. We constructed a multiscale interactome and applied a biased random-walk diffusion model to prioritize herbal candidates, candidate compounds, and mechanisms for DR. Herb–ingredient records were drawn from OASIS; ingredient targets from DrugBank, TTD, and STITCH; and disease genes from DisGeNET. For each herb and compound, we computed diffusion profiles, correlated them with the DR profile, and assessed target-overlap significance by hypergeometric test. Eleven herbs combining high correlation (top 5%) with significant overlap (p < 0.05) were retained, led by Pini Koraiensis Semen (0.0263), Benincasae Exocarpium (0.0183), and Veratri Rhizoma Et Radix (0.0162); none had been previously investigated for DR. CASP3 emerged as a target shared by all eleven herbs, and enrichment analysis highlighted the advanced glycation end product–receptor for AGE (AGE–RAGE), TNF, IL-17, and NF-κB pathways alongside apoptosis and reactive-oxygen-species responses. Compound-level analysis recovered evidence-supported quercetin, resveratrol, oleic acid, luteolin, and diosgenin and nominated tectorigenin and cucurbitacins as novel candidates. This framework recapitulates known DR biology and elevates testable multi-target leads that warrant experimental validation for diabetic retinopathy.

Article.Title: SGLT2 Inhibition Combined with Zn Supplementation Protects the Liver-Pancreas Axis in Experimental Type 2 Diabetes
Article.Authors: Anton I.; Solcan C.; Mititelu-Tartau L.; Amalinei C.; Poroch M.; Poroch V.; Buca B.; Tartau C.; Pelin A.; Jitareanu A.; Boldeanu M.; Botnariu G.
Article.Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with chronic hyperglycemia, inflammation, and progressive hepatic and pancreatic dysfunction. Although sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors exert metabolic and organ-protective effects, their ability to preserve pancreatic architecture and attenuate diabetes-associated hepatic injury, particularly combined with nutritional interventions, remains insufficiently explored. This study investigated the protective effects of dapagliflozin (DAPA) and empagliflozin (EMPA), alone or combined with zinc (Zn), on hepatic and pancreatic alterations in experimental diabetes. Methods: Diabetes was induced in male Sprague–Dawley rats using streptozotocin (STZ) and high fat diet (HFD). Diabetic animals received DAPA, EMPA, Zn, or SGLT2 inhibitor–Zn combinations for four weeks. Hepatic biochemical parameters, lipid profile, histopathology, pancreatic morphometry, and insulin immunoreactivity were evaluated. Diabetes induced hepatic and pancreatic alterations, including elevated liver injury markers, hepatocellular degeneration, reduced islet number and β-cell density, and diminished insulin immunoreactivity. DAPA and EMPA attenuated these changes, with greater improvements following Zn combination therapy. EMPA + Zn produced the most favorable response, improving hepatic architecture, reducing VCAM-1, ICAM-1, and NF-κB expression, preserving islet morphology, increasing β-cell density, and enhancing insulin immunoreactivity. SGLT2 inhibitors attenuated diabetes-associated hepatic and pancreatic alterations in this experimental model, while Zn supplementation was associated with additional tissue-preserving effects, particularly when combined with EMPA. These findings support further investigation of combined SGLT2 inhibition and Zn supplementation as an experimental approach to diabetes-associated organ injury; however, their clinical relevance remains to be established.

Article.Title: Three Cases of Levodopa–Carbidopa Responsive Nocturnal Akinesis in Male Children of an Inbred Family in Rural Baluchistan, Pakistan
Article.Authors: Akram J.; Ghaffar A.; Usmani M.; Shareef U.; Ahmed Z.; Riazuddin S.; Riazuddin S.
Article.Abstract: After more than 9 years of follow-up, we describe three affected male siblings from a consanguineous family (PKSOK) in rural Baluchistan, Pakistan, who presented with levodopa–carbidopa responsive nocturnal akinesia associated with tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency. The affected individuals also show delayed motor milestones, mild intellectual disability, speech and psychomotor delay, without epilepsy, spasticity, cerebellar ataxia, or daytime motor weakness. The marked improvement in nocturnal motor symptoms following levodopa–carbidopa (100 mg/25 mg) treatment raised the possibility of an underlying disorder of dopamine biosynthesis. Exome sequencing of the two affected siblings (IV:16 and IV:18) revealed twenty rare (frequency < 0.001) homozygous coding variants shared between them. However, segregation analysis with the disease phenotype ruled out the potential involvement of all these twenty variants. Therefore, we extended the analysis beyond the coding region variants to non-coding variants, which revealed a homozygous variant, c.-70G>A, in the regulatory region of TH (tyrosine hydroxylase). The c.-70G>A variant has been previously reported in three studies; however, our study represents the first report in the South Asian population. Our study also expands the phenotypic spectrum of disorders associated with variants in TH and highlights the importance of considering variants in regulatory regions of TH in patients with atypical but levodopa-responsive neurological phenotypes.

Monitor genes showed near-chance concordance with metastatic tissue, and the source of the signature could not be resolved. An exploratory four-gene elastic-net panel reached a concordance index of 0.613 internally but 0.559 externally. Article.Title: Thyroid Eye Disease in the Teprotumumab Era: Pathophysiology, Clinical Activity Assessment, and an Updated Therapeutic Landscape
Article.Authors: Shooshani T.; Cherupalla B.; Durand A.; Aung M.
Article.Abstract: Thyroid eye disease (TED), the principal extrathyroidal manifestation of Graves’ disease, is an autoimmune orbitopathy. The pathophysiology involves aberrant thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) and insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R) signaling on orbital fibroblasts, leading to glycosaminoglycan accumulation, adipogenesis, inflammatory edema, and extraocular-muscle enlargement. The active phase is typically self-limited yet medically modifiable, characterized primarily by inflammation, edema, and tissue expansion, whereas chronic inactive disease is dominated by fibrosis and fixed structural change. This US-oriented review aims to provide updates in the field through 2026: (1) summarizing the molecular pathophysiology linking thyroid autoimmunity to orbital remodeling and current drug targets; (2) discussing activity-versus-severity assessment, with appraisal of the Clinical Activity Score (CAS); and (3) explaining the complementary roles of different structural and functional imaging modalities in the evaluation and management of TED. We then follow the therapeutic ladder, from conservative measures through the employment of glucocorticoids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression to the use of targeted biologics. We give particular attention to IGF-1R inhibition, including the use of teprotumumab and veligrotug, and to post-approval results, including otologic and metabolic adverse-event burden, recurrence, treatment sequencing, and the emerging efficacy of the treatment of chronic and low-activity disease. The CAS’s limited inter-observer reliability identifies additional reproducible activity measures as an open need.
