Article.Title: Scaffolds and Artificial Augmentations for Tendon Repair
Article.Authors: Kordahji G.; Yakoby D.; Kaplan B.
Article.Abstract: Tendon injuries are common musculoskeletal disorders that represent a significant clinical challenge due to the limited regenerative capacity of tendon tissue. Although surgical repair remains the standard treatment for severe tendon injuries, healed tendons rarely regain the structural and mechanical properties of native tissue, often resulting in impaired function and an increased risk of re-injury. Recent advances in tissue engineering have introduced biologically active and biomimetic strategies aimed at enhancing tendon healing and promoting functional regeneration. This narrative review summarizes current knowledge of tendon injuries and highlights emerging tissue engineering strategies for tendon repair and regeneration. Emphasis is placed on the design and application of natural and synthetic polymers, scaffold engineering, and the key biological and mechanical characteristics required for successful tendon regeneration. In addition, recent developments in drug delivery systems, mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies, and artificial tendon technologies are discussed. These emerging approaches offer promising alternatives and adjuncts to conventional treatments, with the potential to improve tendon healing and functional recovery. However, further studies are required to optimize these technologies, establish their long-term safety and efficacy, and facilitate their translation into routine clinical practice.

Article.Title: High-Entropy Alloy-Engineered ZnIn2S4 Photocatalyst for Efficient In Vitro Eradication of MRSA and Inhibition of Biofilm Formation via ROS-Mediated Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Zhou T.; Wen C.; Zhang Y.; Wang H.; Wei J.
Article.Abstract: Antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections, particularly those caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), pose a critical clinical challenge and necessitate alternative non-antibiotic antimicrobial strategies. Herein, a high-entropy alloy-modified ZnIn2S4 (HEA–ZIS) photocatalytic nanoplatform was rationally engineered and evaluated for in vitro antibacterial performance. FeCoNiCuZn high-entropy alloy nanoparticles were uniformly anchored onto hierarchical ZnIn2S4 nanoflowers via a combined solvothermal–impregnation strategy. Structural and physicochemical characterizations reveal that the intrinsic flower-like morphology is well retained, while HEA incorporation induces lattice distortion, multivalent metal states, and interfacial charge redistribution. The optimized 3%HEA–ZIS exhibits potent antibacterial activity against MRSA under visible light, achieving 98.30% inactivation and a 5.91-log reduction, with a low minimum bactericidal concentration (0.30 mg mL−1). It also demonstrates strong antibiofilm activity by inhibiting MRSA biofilm formation, reducing biofilm biomass by over 84%, while maintaining good in vitro biosafety. Mechanistic studies reveal enhanced light absorption, improved charge separation, and accelerated interfacial electron transfer, promoting efficient oxygen activation. Electron paramagnetic resonance and in situ DRIFTS analyses identify a cascade reactive oxygen species (ROS) pathway responsible for the enhanced antibacterial efficacy. Overall, this work provides insights into high-entropy alloy-engineered semiconductor nanoplatforms and demonstrates their potential as promising biomedical nanomaterials for non-antibiotic antimicrobial applications.

Article.Title: Construction and Characterization of Rabbit scFv Antibodies Targeting Fibronectin by Phage Display Technology
Article.Authors: Chiang Y.; Juang J.; Yang Y.; Leu S.; Liu J.; Tsai B.; Mao Y.; Yen F.; Chiang J.; Andriani V.; Thenaka P.; Tan T.; Shen T.; Lee C.
Article.Abstract: Fibronectin (FN) is a multifunctional glycoprotein involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, tumor progression, tissue repair, and host–pathogen interactions. Despite its biological and clinical relevance, FN-binding antibodies derived from non-rodent species remain comparatively less explored. Here, one rabbit was immunized with full-length recombinant human FN, eliciting a robust antibody response confirmed by ELISA and Western blotting. Two rabbit-derived single-chain variable fragment (scFv) phage-display libraries were constructed from peripheral blood mononuclear cells, yielding 5.5 × 107 and 5.0 × 107 transformants for the short- and long-linker formats, respectively. Seven purified scFvs displayed distinct ELISA binding profiles. Fiber-optic particle plasmon resonance (FOPPR)-based kinetic analysis yielded apparent equilibrium dissociation constants (KD,app) of 11.21–432.06 nM, with FN-L13 showing the lowest KD,app. Analytical size-exclusion chromatography indicated predominantly monomeric scFvs. Five scFvs recognized a high-molecular-weight band consistent with fibronectin in mouse plasma by Western blotting. ELISA showed preferential FN binding, with generally low reactivity toward human serum albumin (HSA) and collagens I, III, and IV, although FN-S1 and FN-L1 showed detectable fibrinogen reactivity. These findings support rabbit-derived FN-binding scFvs as research reagents for future FN-related assay development and mechanistic studies.

Article.Title: CPR-Centered Redox Interactions Between Cytochrome P450 Oxidoreductase and Cytochrome c Oxidase: Potential Pharmacological Implications
Article.Authors: Ponamarev V.
Article.Abstract: The intracellular pool of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) is a limited resource for which multiple enzyme systems compete. Among these systems, microsomal NADPH-cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (CPR, POR) plays a central role in electron transfer to cytochrome P450 enzymes and can also reduce other redox-active electron acceptors in vitro. This review analyzes the molecular basis of competition between CPR-mediated cytochrome P450 reduction and cytochrome c reduction in vitro and discusses whether this can be extrapolated to an indirect interplay between CPR and cytochrome c oxidase (COX) in intact cells. In vitro, reduced cytochrome c (Fe2+) acts as a competitive inhibitor of NADPH-dependent cytochrome P450 reduction, apparently by binding to an overlapping site on CPR. However, CPR and COX are physically separated by subcellular compartmentalization, and cytosolic and mitochondrial NADPH pools are largely separate; therefore, CPR and COX should not be considered direct competitors for a common NADPH pool under physiological conditions. Potential pharmacological implications include modulation of drug metabolism, cellular energy homeostasis, and toxicity when both systems are challenged, but these remain hypothetical and require direct flux measurements in intact cells.

Article.Title: Immunomodulatory Effects of Fractional CO2 Laser and Narrowband UVB in Stable Non-Segmental Vitiligo
Article.Authors: Frączek A.; Czerwińska J.; Załuski D.; Owczarczyk-Saczonek A.
Article.Abstract: Stable non-segmental vitiligo is sustained by persistent autoimmune responses involving tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells, impaired regulatory T-cell (Treg) function, and chronic cytokine-mediated inflammation. Although fractional carbon dioxide (CO2) laser and narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy are widely used to induce repigmentation, their immunomodulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this prospective, non-randomized exploratory study, 19 patients with stable non-segmental vitiligo received either monthly fractional CO2 laser monotherapy or fractional CO2 laser combined with NB-UVB phototherapy for 6 months. Serum IL-15 and IL-17A concentrations were quantified by ELISA at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months. Double immunofluorescence was performed to evaluate cutaneous TRM- and Treg-associated markers (CD4, CD8, CD25, CD49a, CD69, CD103, FOXP3) together with melanocyte-associated markers (MITF and c-KIT). Longitudinal differences between treatment groups were assessed using linear mixed-effects models with treatment-by-time interactions. Serum IL-15 and IL-17A concentrations decreased significantly over time in both treatment groups. At 6 months, IL-15 concentrations did not differ significantly from those in healthy controls in either group, whereas IL-17A concentrations did not differ significantly from healthy-control values in the fractional CO2 laser monotherapy group but remained significantly higher in the combination-treatment group. Cutaneous analyses demonstrated longitudinal changes in selected TRM- and Treg-associated markers and melanocyte-associated markers, with MITF showing the most pronounced increase. Several cutaneous immune markers remained significantly different from healthy-control values after 6 months. No statistically significant treatment-by-time interactions were detected for IL-15, IL-17A, or the evaluated dermal and epidermal markers. Fractional CO2 laser monotherapy and fractional CO2 laser combined with NB-UVB were both associated with longitudinal changes in circulating inflammatory cytokines and selected cutaneous immune- and melanocyte-associated markers in patients with stable non-segmental vitiligo. Persistent abnormalities in several cutaneous immune markers suggest that treatment did not fully restore the cutaneous immune-marker profile within the 6-month observation period. Given the small sample size and non-randomized exploratory design, the absence of statistically significant treatment-by-time interactions should not be interpreted as evidence of therapeutic equivalence, non-inferiority, or absence of an additional effect of NB-UVB.

Article.Title: Store-Operated Calcium Entry Inhibitors: Structural Diversity, Mechanisms of Action, and Optimization Strategies
Article.Authors: Zakharova A.; Grekhnev D.; Kaznacheyeva E.; Vigont V.
Article.Abstract: Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) is a ubiquitous calcium influx pathway critically involved in numerous physiological processes. Dysregulated SOCE contributes to the pathogenesis of cardiovascular disorders, cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases, making SOCE modulators promising therapeutic candidates. This review provides an overview of the major chemical classes of classical SOCE inhibitors that target Orai and STIM proteins. We focus on structure–activity relationships (SARs), mechanisms of action, strategies for enhancing inhibitory potency and selectivity, and discuss the limitations and side-effect profiles of these compounds. This comprehensive analysis identifies SOC channels as promising therapeutic targets and outlines future directions for rational drug design and the development of clinically viable SOCE modulators.

Article.Title: To Be or Not to Be—Thymocyte Survival and Death in the Thymic Medulla
Article.Authors: Zúñiga M.
Article.Abstract: The T cells of the mammalian immune system have a tricky challenge. They must recognize foreign antigen as “other” or “non-self” but in the context of self, while also being tolerant to the body’s own molecules and tissues. T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement occurs in the cortex of the thymus and generates receptors of relatively random specificity. The developing T cells (thymocytes) are screened in two stages, both of which are Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC)-based. The first, positive selection, occurs in the thymic cortex where cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) display self MHC + self-peptides. Thymocytes that can bind to self MHC + self-peptide then migrate to the corticomedullary junction, where they undergo negative selection. Here, they encounter antigenic peptides characteristic of peripheral tissue proteins presented by medullary antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Among the most intriguing APCs in the medulla are the mimetic medullary thymic epithelial cells (mimetic mTECs). These mimetic APCs express peripheral antigens under the direction of specific transcription factors. During negative selection, most thymocytes whose TCRs bind too well to self MHC + self-peptide die by apoptosis. However, a small proportion of autoreactive thymocytes escape negative selection and instead “alternatively” differentiate into specialized cell types that are self-tolerant and even enforce self-tolerance. The CD4 and CD8 coreceptors, which bind to MHC II and MHC I, respectively, play crucial roles in positive and negative selection. With CD8, there is an added level of complexity because there are two forms of CD8, only one of which can promote signaling through the TCR. Upon binding to MHC, CD4 and CD8 initiate signal transduction through the TCR. The strength of signal transduction through the TCR and through co-stimulatory CD28 determines the outcome of TCR-MHC + peptide binding. Signal transduction occurs within the immunological synapse and is regulated by kinetic proofreading mechanisms. In summary, negative selection involves interactions between developing thymocytes and a variety of medullary APCs. These molecular interactions occur at specialized membrane domains that bring together the components of the TCR signaling apparatus, which are subject to kinetic proofreading. Together, the regulatory mechanisms occurring in developing thymocytes and in medullary APCs generate a T-cell arsenal that is tolerant of self and active against foreign entities.

Article.Title: Normalization Strategies for miRNA RT-qPCR in Blood-Derived Samples in Obesity Research: Current Practices and Methodological Considerations
Article.Authors: Pustovalova A.; Nikolaeva A.; Kalinkin A.; Sigin V.
Article.Abstract: Reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) is widely used to quantify circulating microRNAs, but reliable interpretation depends on appropriate data normalization. In obesity research, selecting reference RNAs for measurements in whole blood, blood cells, plasma, and serum is challenging because of biological heterogeneity and preanalytical variability. This review summarizes normalization strategies used in RT-qPCR studies of blood-derived samples from participants with overweight or obesity. We examine commonly used endogenous reference RNAs, including U6 snRNA and miR-16-5p, and assess the rationale for their selection and the available validation evidence in relation to sample matrix and cohort characteristics. The review evaluates normalization practices and the quality and reporting of reference-RNA validation in obesity-related studies, with particular attention to the biological comparison being made. No candidate, algorithmic ranking, or fixed panel size is considered universally applicable. Candidate selection, the number of references, and the normalization scale should be justified for the intended comparison. The review provides practical guidance for designing and reporting validation of reference small non-coding RNAs and process controls in study cohorts with overweight or obesity, with recommendations qualified by the available evidence.

Article.Title: Dihydromyricetin and Neuroinflammation: Implications for CNS Disorders and Therapeutic Development
Article.Authors: Skinner S.; Aleman E.; Berges A.; Kim K.; Kantilal D.; Asatryan L.; Davies D.
Article.Abstract: Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a bioactive polyphenol with broad therapeutic potential, including strong anti-inflammatory activity. Importantly, DHM has been shown to cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB), enabling pharmacological activity within the central nervous system (CNS) and positioning it as a candidate for CNS disorders in which neuroinflammation plays a central role, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and stroke. Therapeutics such as DHM, which address neuroinflammation, are of increasing interest. Across CNS disease models, DHM’s effects show recurring convergence on NF-κB suppression, NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition, and autophagy regulation, alongside context-specific mechanisms involving oxidative stress, ferroptosis, neurotrophic signaling, and peripheral gut–CNS communication. This review examines the evidence for DHM as a neuroinflammatory modulator, focusing on the mechanisms by which it exerts its therapeutic effects. By doing so, we aim to support its translational potential as a natural product for improving human health.

Article.Title: Profiling Systemic IgG-Targeted Gut Microbiota Reveals Disease Activity-Associated Bacterial Signatures in Ulcerative Colitis
Article.Authors: Takahashi K.; Nakayama-Imaohji H.; Tada A.; Emmanuel M.; Mino Y.; Ishikawa H.; Kuwahara T.
Article.Abstract: Aberrant systemic IgG responses to the gut microbiota may be implicated in the pathogenesis of ulcerative colitis (UC). In this study, we investigated IgG-targeted bacteria and their predicted functional characteristics in UC. Using fecal samples and autologous sera from 37 patients with UC and 4 healthy controls, we profiled IgG-targeted bacteria under in vitro conditions using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. To correct for background bacterial abundance, we calculated the IgG+ Probability Score (IPS), which integrates the sample-specific IgG-binding rate to isolate candidate IgG-targeted taxa. Systemic IgG responses were selectively targeted at specific bacterial taxa rather than uniformly directed toward the entire gut microbiota. Active UC and elevated systemic inflammatory markers were associated with increased IPS in oral-associated commensals, including Granulicatella, as well as mucin-degrading taxa. Predictive functional profiling indicated the predicted enrichment of pathways hypothesized to be related to host-derived mucin degradation, capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis, and amino acid biosynthesis. Furthermore, exploratory Random Forest models using IPS features highlighted candidate taxa that differed among clinical parameters (UC exacerbation, Clinical Activity Index, and C-reactive protein), although their classification performance was not independently validated. In conclusion, our in vitro profiling indicates that systemic IgG in UC has the capacity to selectively target specific bacterial taxa associated with disease activity and systemic inflammation. Analyzing the IgG-targeted microbiota via IPS profiling deepens our understanding of host–microbiota interactions in UC and provides a valuable framework for evaluating candidate immune-targeted bacteria associated with disease activity.

Article.Title: N, S-Functionalized Magnetic Rice Husk Biochar for Flucloxacillin Sodium Adsorption: Regeneration and Water-Matrix Effects
Article.Authors: Pandey P.; Dhiman M.; Białowiec A.; Pokhriyal A.; Bahukhandi K.; Kaur P.; Igwegbe C.
Article.Abstract: Rice husk-derived biochars with progressively modified surface properties were investigated for adsorbing flucloxacillin sodium (FLX-Na) from aqueous solution. Four materials—rice husk biochar (RHB), nitrogen-functionalized RHB (N-RHB), magnetic nitrogen-functionalized RHB (MN-RHB), and magnetic nitrogen/sulfur-functionalized RHB (MN,S-RHB)—were prepared and characterised using morphological, structural, textural, and surface-chemical techniques. The sequential preparation routes produced materials with different surface areas, pore structures, and surface functionalities. FLX-Na adsorption increased in the order RHB < MN-RHB < N-RHB < MN, S-RHB, with the highest equilibrium adsorption capacity obtained for MN,S-RHB (118.6 mg g−1). Because chemical activation and a higher carbonisation temperature were introduced only for MN,S-RHB, the higher uptake is interpreted as an effect of the combined modification route rather than being attributed specifically to N/S co-doping. Kinetic and equilibrium data were described using several empirical models, with the pseudo-second-order and Sips models giving the highest coefficients of determination among the tested fits. The adsorption capacity of MN,S-RHB decreased from 84.60 ± 1.30 mg g−1 in deionised water to 60.30 ± 1.80 mg g−1 in a mixed inorganic/humic-acid matrix, corresponding to 71.3% capacity retention. Spectroscopic changes after adsorption were consistent with changes in the surface chemical environment, while the matrix experiments indicated that coexisting inorganic ions and dissolved organic matter influenced adsorption performance. These results show that the combined physicochemical modification route altered the adsorption behaviour of rice husk-derived biochar under the investigated conditions.

Article.Title: TLR2 Signaling in Myeloproliferative Neoplasms: Pathophysiological Roles, Mutation-Dependent Heterogeneity, and the Differential Efficacy of Ruxolitinib
Article.Authors: Pokhrel A.; Hakobyan N.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) is a versatile pattern-recognition receptor of the innate immune system that recognizes both pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and endogenous danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs)—clonal hematopoietic stem-cell disorders that include essential thrombocythemia (ET), polycythemia vera (PV), and myelofibrosis (MF)—are characterized by persistent inflammation and an increased risk of thrombosis. Dysregulated TLR2 signaling has emerged as a potentially important mediator of this chronic thrombo-inflammatory state. Findings from our group and others suggest that TLR2 may have a particularly prominent role in promoting inflammatory cytokine production, platelet–leukocyte interactions, endothelial dysfunction, and thrombotic complications in MPNs. Our findings are also consistent with evidence that NF-κB-mediated proinflammatory signaling, in addition to constitutive JAK/STAT activation, contributes substantially to MPN pathogenesis. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of TLR2 biology and examine its contribution to the thrombo-inflammatory milieu of MPNs, with particular emphasis on its potential utility as a biomarker and a therapeutic target. Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, markedly reduces symptom burden and splenomegaly in JAK2-mutant MPNs, particularly PV and MF; however, it has limited efficacy in CALR-mutant or triple-negative ET. This differential therapeutic response may reflect divergent downstream signaling pathways and may also be related to dysregulated TLR2 signaling. Furthermore, hyperactive TLR2 signaling in MPNs may help explain the incomplete ability of ruxolitinib to suppress thrombo-inflammatory responses. Therefore, combined TLR2-targeted therapy and ruxolitinib may represent a more effective therapeutic strategy for future MPN trials. Overall, however, we consider the TLR2-mediated thrombo-inflammatory response in MPNs to be an amplifier of inflammation rather than a primary disease driver.

Article.Title: The Role of SOD1 and Oxidative Stress in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Overview
Article.Authors: Gómez-Pérez C.; Ramírez-García M.; Yescas-Gómez P.
Article.Abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. The median survival time after diagnosis is 2 to 5 years. Oxidative stress (OS), driven mainly by reactive oxygen species (ROS), plays a central role in motor neuron (MN) degeneration. In this narrative review, we analyse the pathogenic role of SOD1 variants and their contribution to OS in ALS. SOD1 mutations alter the Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative damage and triggering neuroinflammatory cascades via the MAPK, NF-κB and Nrf2/ARE signalling pathways. We also discuss emerging proteomic and machine-learning biomarkers, as well as the current therapeutic landscape. Riluzole and edaravone are approved treatments, while AMX0035 was approved in 2022 but withdrawn in 2024. Masitinib and EPI-589 remain investigational. In the realm of genetic therapies, the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for SOD1-ALS, primarily due to its ability to reduce plasma neurofilament light chain levels. However, the clinical benefit remains modest. RNA interference has reached human trials, while CRISPR/Cas9 remains in the preclinical stage. Both approaches have shown promising results in experimental models. Further research into ALS pathogenesis is needed to develop treatments that integrate antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gene-editing strategies.

Article.Title: Topographic Expression of IL-1β and Inflammasome-Associated Proteins in Lesional, Perilesional, and Distant Hidradenitis Suppurativa Skin
Article.Authors: Lewandowski M.; Górska-Ponikowska M.; Jakubczyk-Słabicka A.; Świerczewska Z.; Barańska-Rybak W.
Article.Abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by recurrent nodules, abscesses, draining tunnels, and scarring. Dysregulated IL-1 and inflammasome-associated pathways have been implicated in its pathogenesis, but their spatial distribution beyond clinically apparent lesions remains incompletely characterized. In HS, matched 6 mm full-thickness biopsies were obtained from the same axilla at an active inflammatory lesion (0 cm), clinically normal-appearing skin 2 cm from the visible lesion edge, and clinically uninvolved skin 10 cm from the lesion edge. Protein abundance was assessed by Western blot. Primary topographic effects were evaluated using mixed-design ANOVA with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, supplemented by non-parametric and exploratory contrast analyses. No protein showed an FDR (false discovery rate)-significant overall site effect or cohort × site interaction in the primary analysis. In biologic-untreated HS, IL-18 showed an FDR-significant topographic effect (q = 0.0444), with higher expression at 0 cm than at 10 cm (q = 0.0469). An exploratory post hoc 2-versus-10 cm analysis identified a highly concordant IL-1β pattern: expression was higher at 2 cm in 7/8 biologic-untreated and 6/6 adalimumab-treated patients. Fisher’s combined probability remained significant after BH correction across the four proteins evaluated for this contrast (p = 0.00421, q4 = 0.0168), whereas comprehensive correction across all 12 protein × contrast combinations yielded q12 = 0.0505 and did not meet q < 0.05. Overall, 13/14 patients showed the same direction (92.9%; exact 95% CI 66.1–99.8%). IL-18 provided the clearest FDR-supported secondary topographic finding. IL-1β showed a highly concordant but hypothesis-generating perilesional-to-distant spatial pattern, whereas total NLRP3 and caspase-1 did not show robust FDR-adjusted spatial variation.

Article.Title: DeepAVPred: A Deep Learning Framework Integrating RECM-DWT and BiGRU for Accurate Antiviral Peptide Prediction
Article.Authors: Fida H.; Zhang H.; Ahmad B.; Lin H.; Ma C.; Huang C.; Fan Z.
Article.Abstract: Viral infections continue to pose a significant global health challenge. Antiviral peptides (AVPs) have emerged as promising therapeutic agents owing to their high specificity, favorable safety profiles, and broad-spectrum antiviral activity. However, experimental AVP identification is time-consuming and costly, while existing computational predictors often have limitations in predictive accuracy and feature representation. Here, we propose DeepAVPred, a deep learning-based framework for AVP identification. DeepAVPred integrates complementary sequence descriptors to capture physicochemical properties and pairwise residue interactions. We present a novel feature representation, the Residue Energy Content Matrix augmented with a Discrete Wavelet Transform (RECM-DWT). RECM-DWT characterizes multi-scale patterns in residue-energy information and complements conventional sequence descriptors by providing wavelet-derived features across multiple resolution levels. The integrated features are then modeled using an attention-based Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) network to learn contextual dependencies and informative sequence patterns. On the AVPtrain dataset, DeepAVPred achieved strong performance in 10-fold cross-validation, with an accuracy of 0.990, a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.980, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.993. On the independent test dataset, AVPtest, DeepAVPred achieved an accuracy of 0.942, an MCC of 0.886, and an AUC of 0.949. These results demonstrate the predictive performance of DeepAVPred and support its potential as a computational framework for prioritizing candidate antiviral peptides for further experimental validation.

Article.Title: A Quantum Mechanism-Centered Review of Carbon Dot-Based Theranostics
Article.Authors: Cheng I.; Contreras G.; Yeh T.
Article.Abstract: Despite advances in drug discovery, effective delivery and precise imaging still pose significant obstacles. Scientists have turned to zero-dimensional nanomaterials like carbon dots (CDs) to enable precision drug delivery. Due to their multidisciplinary appeal, there is extensive research on both the physical properties and biological applications of CDs, yet the fields rarely complement each other. This review applies a quantum-mechanistic framework to better understand CDs and unify the relationship between electronic structure, photophysical behavior, and theranostic performance. We first highlight the theranostic advantages of CDs over quantum dots, then discuss the quantum mechanisms behind a CD’s imaging capabilities, including surface states, excitation-dependent photoluminescence, and the electronic origins of photostability. Through this physical lens, we then evaluate the effect of different precursors and doping strategies during synthesis on electronic structure and how dots are engineered to load, release, and track therapeutic cargo. Photodynamic therapy and surface functionalization strategies are also evaluated. Finally, we address the significance of renal clearance and translational bottlenecks such as heterogeneity.

Article.Title: Molecular Dynamics-Guided Triage of Approved Drugs Against Escherichia coli Resistance Targets Nominates Capmatinib, Metergoline and Nilotinib as Candidates for Experimental Testing
Article.Authors: Abdelsayed M.; Boulaamane Y.
Article.Abstract: Virtual screening ranks compounds by scoring functions that correlate with molecular size, and hit lists are rarely benchmarked against compounds of established activity. We screened 2070 approved drugs against four Escherichia coli targets selected by pocket-druggability triage (FabI, LpxC, DHFR and GyrB), with each docking protocol validated by redocking its native ligand (RMSD 0.50–0.69 Å). Per target, the two top-scoring compounds and a reference inhibitor were simulated for 100 ns in triplicate (12 complexes, 3.6 μs). Docking did not recover the references: trimethoprim ranked 762/2068 and novobiocin 576/2069, while top-ranked compounds were large, promiscuous drugs recurring across unrelated targets. Pose triage failed, too: all twelve complexes retained 43–87% of initial contacts, contact-loss time separated targets, not compounds, and MM-GBSA favoured the reference at one target of four. Persistent hydrogen bonding separated the reference from the hits at three of four targets, by 2–9-fold, although the GyrB result rests largely on one replicate. Benchmarking each hit against its reference nominates three candidates for experimental testing: capmatinib at DHFR, metergoline at FabI and nilotinib at LpxC. Capmatinib ranks highest on these computational criteria, with the highest pocket retention (87%) and an MM-GBSA energy with no detectable difference from trimethoprim’s at n = 3 (absence of evidence for a difference, not evidence of equivalence). In this small panel, carrying a known active through the same pipeline was therefore more informative than docking score, pose stability or end-point rescoring. The nominations are hypotheses: no experimental validation was performed, and generality would require multiple actives and property-matched decoys per target.

Article.Title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals HER2/AR-Associated Heterogeneity and Alternative Surface Targets in Salivary Duct Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Iwasa Y.; Hori K.; Nakajima T.; Yokota Y.; Yamazaki S.; Hori Y.; Uehara T.; Takumi Y.
Article.Abstract: Salivary duct carcinoma (SDC) is an aggressive malignancy primarily treated with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)- and androgen receptor (AR)-directed therapies in the recurrent or metastatic setting, although therapeutic responses remain heterogeneous. We used spatial transcriptomics to characterize intratumoral heterogeneity and to identify alternative therapeutic targets. Spatial transcriptomic profiling was performed on four formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded SDC specimens using the 10× Genomics Visium platform. Tumor regions were characterized according to spatial HER2 and AR expression and their corresponding transcriptional signatures. Candidate cell-surface targets in HER2/AR-non-associated regions were identified using the SURFY human surfaceome and prioritized based on low expression in matched normal salivary gland tissue and therapeutic relevance. Article.Title: Enzymatic Hydrolysate of Red Yeast Rice Accelerates Diabetic Wound Healing in Mice: Association with Modulation of Inflammatory, Matrix-Remodeling, and Angiogenesis-Related Markers
Article.Authors: Du Y.; Ma W.; Chang X.; Wang S.; Zeng R.; Wu N.
Article.Abstract: Delayed healing of diabetic wounds arises from a self-sustaining pathological microenvironment featuring persistent inflammation, excessive matrix degradation, impaired angiogenesis, and insufficient collagen deposition, and current single-process interventions remain unsatisfactory. Red yeast rice, produced by fermentation of rice with Monascus spp., is a traditional fermented product with documented anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities; however, its direct extract is dominated by macromolecular and bound-state constituents with low release efficiency and poor skin permeation, which restricts its topical application. In this study, an enzymatic hydrolysate of red yeast rice (RYR-EH) was prepared by composite enzymatic hydrolysis, and the compositional changes induced by hydrolysis were characterized by widely targeted UPLC-MS/MS metabolomics. A total of 810 metabolites were detected, among which 199 showed differential accumulation after hydrolysis (179 upregulated and 20 downregulated; FC ≥ 2 or ≤0.5, VIP ≥ 1, and p < 0.05); the differential metabolites were significantly enriched (FDR < 0.05) in purine metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, ABC transporters, and the cGMP-PKG signaling pathway, a pattern consistent with hydrolysis-driven release of free amino acids, small peptides, and other low-molecular-weight constituents. In type 2 diabetic mice induced by a high-fat diet combined with low-dose streptozotocin, topical RYR-EH (2% and 5%) significantly accelerated the closure of full-thickness excisional wounds, with the 5% formulation showing more advanced closure than the 2% formulation and an effect approaching that of recombinant human epidermal growth factor (rhEGF). At the day-14 endpoint, RYR-EH treatment was associated with enhanced re-epithelialization, lower TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β levels in both wound tissue and serum, reduced MMP-2 and MMP-9 immunoreactivity, reduced Ki67-positive cellularity in the late-stage wound bed, increased Collagen I/III deposition, and increased VEGF/CD31 immunoreactivity. These results demonstrate that RYR-EH exerts multi-process reparative effects on diabetic wounds, simultaneously attenuating inflammation, restraining excessive matrix degradation, promoting angiogenesis, and restoring collagen deposition, and support RYR-EH as an effective multi-process topical agent for diabetic wound healing.

Article.Title: Gangliosides in Cutaneous Melanoma: Molecular Mechanisms, Translational Evidence Gaps, and Preclinical Natural-Compound Leads
Article.Authors: Koo D.; Kim K.; Kim J.; Yun H.; Song E.; Kim M.; Ryu J.; Kim J.; Kim S.; Lee H.; Choo Y.
Article.Abstract: Cutaneous melanoma remains lethal once metastatic despite advances in immune checkpoint blockade and BRAF/MEK-directed therapy. Gangliosides are surface-accessible sialylated glycosphingolipids that regulate membrane organization, adhesion, and signaling, representing potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This narrative review evaluated the translational readiness of ganglioside-directed strategies in cutaneous melanoma, without assuming that evidence from other GD2- or GD3-positive cancers is directly transferable. We synthesized melanoma-specific evidence on GD3-linked focal adhesion signaling, p130Cas/paxillin activity, PI3K–AKT and MAPK outputs, and distinct phenotypes associated with GD3, GD2, and GM3. We then applied an evidence-gated framework distinguishing melanoma clinical evidence, melanoma preclinical evidence, cross-tumor translational evidence, and hypothesis-generating claims. Direct contemporary clinical evidence in melanoma remains limited. Antibody, cellular, and biosynthetic enzyme strategies require diagnostic-quality antigen profiling, demonstration of surface accessibility and functional dependency, and prospective monitoring for antigen escape and neurotoxicity. Natural compounds, particularly quercetin, are mechanistic probes or formulation-enabled leads: a 2024 study reported reduced GM3/GD3 abundance and FAK/paxillin/AKT signaling in melanoma cell lines, but high in vitro concentrations and the lack of pharmacokinetic or in vivo validation preclude therapeutic conclusions. We proposed a minimum evidence package and go/no-go criteria for clinical translation, specifying experiments needed to advance ganglioside biology into biomarker-defined melanoma interventions.

Article.Authors: Ogorodova N.; Stepanova A.; Geletskaia P.; Kadyshev V.; Zinchenko R.; Kuznetsova S.; Khalanskaya O.; Monakhova A.; Beskorovainy N.; Zabnenkova V.; Ryzhkova O.; Severinov K.; Bychkov I.; Polyakov A.; Kutsev S.; Shchagina O.

WGS was performed for all patients; candidate splice variants were functionally validated using minigene assays. The total diagnostic yield was 40.2% (43/107). In 15.0% of cases (16/107), the diagnosis was reclassified by variants in alternative IRD genes (autosomal dominant, X-linked, mitochondrial, or syndromic). The majority of second variants detected in AR cases were CNVs (55.5%, 15 patients), followed by non-coding variants (26.0%, seven), structural rearrangements (14.8%, four) and exonic point variant (3.7%, one). Two recurrent CNVs were observed: a gross deletion of exons 22–24 in USH2A (n = 4) and a deletion partially affecting exon 19 of EYS (n = 4). Structural variants were mostly represented by delINV rearrangements (n = 5). Minigene assays confirmed that three novel deep intronic variants (in CHM, EYS, and CEP290) and one non-canonical splice-acceptor variant in USH2A which disrupt splicing, causes pseudoexon inclusion with premature termination or in-frame exon skipping respectively. Article.Title: Recent Advances in Lipid Nanoparticles for Cancer Vaccines: From Antigen Delivery to Personalized Immunotherapy
Article.Authors: Rachamala H.; Angom R.; Marepally S.
Article.Abstract: In recent years, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have shown great promise as highly flexible delivery systems for cancer vaccines, which enable effective cargo delivery and allow for controlling their distribution, cell-targeting ability and immunogenicity. Innovations in ionizable lipid chemistry, biodegradable formulations, RNA engineering and LNP design resulted in improvements in RNA encapsulation, endosomal escape, delivery outside the liver, and targeting of lymphoid organs and antigen-presenting cells. All these achievements led to an expansion of strategies for developing cancer vaccines from using only mRNA to personal neoantigen vaccines, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), peptide/protein vaccines, and multi-purpose platforms that combine antigen delivery and modulation of the immune system. LNPs are also studied as tools for altering the tumor microenvironment (TME) and boosting anti-tumor immunity through local delivery of cytokines and innate immune modulators. Preliminary clinical results with personalized mRNA neoantigen vaccines show strong potential for this approach. However, inflammatory toxicity, suitability for repeated dosing, off-target delivery, difficulties with large-scale production, formulation stability, personalized production schedule and regulatory issues are still significant challenges. New biodegradable and PEG-free formulations, innovations in manufacturing and lyophilization technology, and AI-based approaches in lipid screening could help overcome some of these problems.

Article.Title: Compartment-Specific Transcriptional Remodelling Defines Denervation and Geriatric Muscle Regeneration
Article.Authors: Tong W.; Yu Q.; Yang R.; Shao C.; Yang G.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Neuromuscular decline involves motor, junctional, myofibre and niche dysfunction, but whether these components remodel as a coordinated system is unresolved. Competitive animal-pseudobulk testing identified eight FDR-supported compartment–programme results; six denervation-sensitivity results remained supported after each single-gene deletion, whereas the FAP matrix-inflammatory and type IIB junctional results were gene-sensitive. During geriatric regeneration, all eight annotated broad compartments varied over time, and 26 of 34 analysis-defined biologically applicable compartment–programme tests were significant after FDR correction. The human results are hypothesis-generating, and neither RNA scores nor predicted cell communication establish functional recovery. This resource supports compartment-specific transcriptional responses within denervation and geriatric injury designs; it does not establish a conserved recovery axis across the six contexts.

Article.Title: Sexually Dimorphic Glutamatergic Control of R-Spondin 1 and R-Spondin 3 Neurons in Hypothalamic Reproductive and Metabolic Nuclei
Article.Authors: Topal G.; Yurtseven D.; Akbulut N.; Gul Z.; Udum D.; Yalcin M.; Eyigor O.

Antagonists attenuated all responses, although activation remained above control in 17 of 36 conditions. Females showed greater attenuation in selected kainate and NMDA conditions in the SON and PVN. Serum changes did not parallel neuronal activation. These findings support NMDA and non-NMDA receptor involvement and sex-dependent attenuation of RSPO neuronal activation. Article.Title: Architect or Destroyer: The Diversity of Glucocorticoid Receptor Signaling Pathways in the Brain
Article.Authors: Shkarina L.; Khaybullina R.; Primak A.; Bozov K.; Dzhauari S.; Karagyaur M.
Article.Abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs), acting through the glucocorticoid (GR) and mineralocorticoid (MR) receptors, are essential for brain development, stress adaptation, and metabolic homeostasis, yet their signaling exhibits context-dependent diversity yielding either beneficial or detrimental outcomes. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the multifaceted mechanisms through which GR integrates hormonal, metabolic, and stress signals to modulate transcriptional programs in the brain. We highlight three key levels of GR regulatory complexity: the diversity of DNA GR-binding motifs, GR-mediated epigenetic remodeling, and rapid non-genomic cascades. Clinical and experimental data reveal that while physiological GC levels are critical for normal maturation and function, excess or chronic exposure, especially during sensitive developmental windows, can disrupt neurogenesis, synaptogenesis, and myelination, predisposing individuals to cognitive, affective, and neurodegenerative disorders. We discuss promising therapeutic strategies based on selective modulation of MR/GR balance, interference with specific co-regulatory complexes, and targeted manipulation of DNMT/TET/HDAC cascades. Unlike most existing reviews—which address either (a) the MR–GR interaction as a whole receptor system, (b) non-genomic effects in isolation from genomic ones, or (c) the clinical manifestations of stress-associated disorders without an in-depth mechanistic analysis of GR targets—our manuscript attempts to integrate these three levels of GR regulation into a unified hierarchical system (binding motifs → epigenetic remodeling → the conditional nature of the boundary between genomic and non-genomic GR effects). We aim to explicitly demonstrate how these levels jointly determine cell-specific outcomes, rather than describing them in parallel as independent mechanisms. However, critical gaps remain in understanding the precise assembly of GR-co-regulator complexes in defined neuronal and glial populations, as well as the feasibility of selectively engaging beneficial GR signaling branches without systemic suppression of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis. Addressing these questions is essential for developing next-generation therapies that harness GR’s architectural potential while avoiding its adverse or unwanted consequences.

Article.Authors: Rokita B.; Adamus-Wlodarczyk A.; Olejnik A.; Czechowska-Biskup R.; Skibska B.; Kadlubowski S.; Ulanski P.; Wach R.
Article.Abstract: L-ascorbic acid is a bioactive compound widely used in dermatology and cosmetology, owing to its antioxidant properties and essential role in collagen biosynthesis. However, its poor chemical stability in aqueous formulations considerably limits its incorporation into hydrogel-based delivery systems. The components of the hydrogel matrix effectively protected EvitC during radiation processing and storage, thereby confirming the overall stability of the formulation. Neither EvitC nor hydrogel extracts induced cytotoxic effects under all tested conditions. Furthermore, the prolonged exposure of fibroblasts to hydrogel extracts resulted in a moderate but statistically significant increase in ECM-associated Col-F, i.e., collagen- and elastin-associated fluorescence. These findings support the potential of the developed radiation-crosslinked hydrogel as a stable and cytocompatible platform for the topical delivery of EvitC. The combination of favorable physicochemical properties, formulation stability and excellent biological performance highlights its potential for the development of advanced hydrogel-based skin care formulations.

Article.Abstract: Adipose-derived stem cell (ADSC)-derived exosomes are promising for regenerative therapy. Article.Title: Molecular Mechanisms of Candida albicans Adhesion to Maxillofacial Silicone Elastomers: Integrating Candidate Molecular Pathways with Material Surface Properties
Article.Authors: Hamarsha A.; Atatra M.; Watted N.; Irekeola A.; Sulaiman M.; Hasbullah N.
Article.Abstract: Colonisation of maxillofacial prostheses by Candida albicans is conventionally attributed to surface roughness, porosity, and wettability properties that explain where cells accumulate rather than why particular surfaces promote biofilm formation. This review reinterprets the in vitro literature on C. albicans adhesion to maxillofacial silicone elastomers through the underlying molecular events. Nine eligible studies identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect conducted on 31 March 2026 were appraised with the QUIN tool and mapped onto a six-stage molecular cascade: surface conditioning, reversible attachment, adhesin engagement, morphogenesis, matrix assembly, and antifungal tolerance. Three conclusions emerged. First, C. albicans senses topography through mechanically gated calcium channels and converts mechanical contact into hyphal commitment; roughness is therefore a morphogenetic cue that surface finishing can withhold. Second, the tested agents—silver nanoparticles, chitosan, thymol, and carvacrol, and a Lactobacillus brevis-derived biosurfactant—engage distinct molecular targets and are not mechanistically interchangeable. Third, most included studies evaluated silicone without salivary conditioning, whereas the clinical interface is an acquired salivary pellicle that supplies both adhesion receptors and antimicrobial peptides. All studies fell within the medium risk-of-bias band (50.0–62.5%). Pellicle-conditioned models and molecular readouts are required. The mechanistic interpretations discussed in this review are derived from the broader C. albicans literature and have not been directly demonstrated on maxillofacial silicone elastomers.

Article.Title: From Prediction to Generation: Artificial Intelligence Reconstructing the Paradigm of Protein Glycosylation Research
Article.Authors: Zhu J.; Huang S.; Zhang N.
Article.Abstract: Among post-translational modifications, protein glycosylation is distinguished by its abundance and structural intricacy. Unlike protein biosynthesis, glycan assembly follows no template; it reflects glycosyltransferase/glycosidase competition, sugar-donor availability, and organelle-enforced compartmentalization, yielding heterogeneous glycoforms that confer functional versatility but complicate analysis. Three bottlenecks persist: stereochemical control in chemical glycosylation, ambiguous assignment of occupancy sites, and reproducing native conformations of fully glycosylated proteins. Adopting the “glycan language” framework, we survey how AI addresses each, emphasizing the systems on which it has been tested. In synthesis planning, GlycoPredictor uncovered anomeric-selectivity rules such as the anti-nitrile and C2-azido α-directing effects, while Bayesian optimization discovered lithium-salt-directed stereoselective glycosylation; for site identification, ESM-2 with AlphaFold2-derived structural features improves N- and O-glycosite prediction, and DeepGlycanSite maps carbohydrate-binding interfaces. For structure and dynamics, AlphaFold3 and multimodal cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, and molecular dynamics (MD) modeling move glycoproteins toward conformational ensembles, as in the AI-assisted dissection of the MCTS1–JAK2–IFN-γ axis. In glycomics, deep learning resolves intact glycopeptides and de novo glycan topology and has defined Fc N-glycan signatures of immunoglobulin G in autoimmune and malignant disease. Because glycan language models link sequence and structure to function, they are becoming clinically actionable: they prioritize candidate variants in congenital disorders of glycosylation and stratify immune disorders and tumors by aberrant glycosylation. Remaining obstacles include scarce structure-linked datasets, encoding of branched topologies, multimodal fusion, and interpretability.

Article.Title: Dynamic Urothelial Remodeling in Diabetic Bladder Dysfunction: Disease-Course Changes, Molecular Mechanisms, and Clinical Implications
Article.Authors: Song Q.; Xie W.; Wang J.; Yuan Y.; Li Z.; Sun S.; Ai K.
Article.Abstract: Diabetic bladder dysfunction (DBD) includes storage abnormalities and voiding dysfunction, but its clinical and experimental phenotypes do not follow a uniform chronological sequence. The urothelium is a urine barrier and a mechanosensory, paracrine, and inflammatory interface. Early diabetes may cause urothelial shedding, barrier permeability, abnormal ATP release, and altered sensory receptors. With longer disease duration, superficial architecture and some barrier properties may recover, while sensory and paracrine abnormalities persist. In parallel, impaired afferent conduction, reduced detrusor contractility, and extracellular matrix remodeling may become prominent, so local urothelial changes do not necessarily track whole-bladder function. Metabolic and oxidative stress, NLRP3-associated inflammation and pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulation may contribute to urothelial injury, although evidence differs in cell specificity and disease-course localization. This review integrates clinical, animal, and cellular studies to examine urothelial barrier, sensory, paracrine, and cell-fate changes across DBD functional states, appraise the supporting molecular evidence and its limitations, and discuss the clinical relevance of urothelial biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

Article.Title: Applications and Future Prospects of Plant Multi-Omics Technologies in Precision Agriculture
Article.Authors: Tong T.; Wang Q.; Zeng F.; Ye S.; Ji Z.; Chen Z.; Wang Y.; Ouyang Y.
Article.Abstract: Against the backdrop of global population growth, intensifying climate change, and limited arable land, ensuring food security and promoting sustainable agriculture have become critical issues. The limitations of conventional agricultural systems are becoming increasingly apparent, creating an urgent need for innovation driven by science and technology. In this context, plant multi-omics technologies serve as the foundational data and technical cornerstone of systems biology and precision agriculture. Integrating multi-level data from genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, epigenomics, and microbiomics offers substantial advantages for systematically understanding and improving plants. Unlike previous reviews that mainly catalog omics technologies or focus on individual crops, this review adopts a unified discovery-to-translation framework and critically evaluates the strength of evidence across applications. This review focuses on cutting-edge applications of multi-omics in three key areas: improving the traits of cereal crops (rice, wheat and maize), remediating soil health, and innovating products such as biofertilizers and biostimulants for agriculture. We systematically explore the roles of multi-omics in accelerating breeding processes, deciphering complex agronomic traits, restoring soil ecosystems, and constructing intelligent decision-support systems. The review also examines current challenges, including the complexity of data integration and the difficulties of predicting genotype-by-environment interactions. Furthermore, it outlines future directions involving deeper convergence with artificial intelligence, high-throughput phenomics, and digital twins. In summary, plant multi-omics technology is a vital tool for unravelling the mysteries of plant life and is also a key enabler of intelligent, precise and sustainable agricultural transformation.

Article.Title: Cordyceps Polysaccharides Attenuate Experimental Ischemic Stroke Injury: Association with IL-17/NF-κB Signaling
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Chen Y.; Jiang Y.; Liao Y.; Xi S.; Li X.; Qi H.; Ma Y.; Li Y.; Fang M.; Shi C.; Gai C.; Tang Y.
Article.Abstract: Cordyceps polysaccharides (CSP) have shown protective potential in ischemic stroke, but their central inflammatory mechanisms remain unclear. This study examined whether the effects of CSP are associated with interleukin-17 (IL-17)/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)-related signaling. Publicly available human transcriptomic datasets were integrated and analyzed to identify inflammation-related pathways in ischemic stroke, and a public mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) dataset was analyzed to identify relevant brain cell populations. IL-17 receptor A (IL-17RA) knockdown was performed in oxygen–glucose deprivation (OGD)-exposed SH-SY5Y cells. The effects of CSP were further evaluated in MCAO rats and OGD-exposed BV-2 cells. Bioinformatics analyses showed enrichment of IL-17 and NF-κB signaling in ischemic stroke datasets, and single-cell module-score analysis showed that microglia exhibited the largest MCAO-associated increase in IL-17/NF-κB-related module scores. IL-17RA knockdown improved the viability of OGD-exposed SH-SY5Y cells. In MCAO rats, CSP improved neurological and behavioral outcomes, increased cerebral blood flow, and reduced cerebral edema, infarct volume, neuronal loss, microglial responses, and IL-17A/IL-17RA expression. In OGD-exposed BV-2 cells, CSP reduced IL-17A, IL-17RA, NF-κB activator 1 (ACT1), tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6), IL-1β, IL-6, and the phosphorylated p65/total p65 ratio. These findings suggest that the protective effects of CSP in ischemic stroke models are associated with attenuation of IL-17/NF-κB-related neuroinflammation.

Article.Title: Postmortem Gene Expression and the Thanatotranscriptome: Postmortem Interval Estimation, Forensic Applications, and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Akpınar Ö.; Erdem Z.; Keskiner F.; Kaya K.
Article.Abstract: Postmortem molecular changes are more complex than a passive, uniform cessation of all cellular activity. Human and animal studies have demonstrated that certain RNA transcripts remain detectable for defined periods after death and that transcript levels exhibit tissue- and time-dependent changes. These postmortem RNA dynamics underpin the concept of the thanatotranscriptome and may provide molecular information relevant to postmortem interval (PMI) estimation. Postmortem changes have been reported in the abundance of transcripts associated with apoptosis, cellular stress, immune responses, and DNA damage response and repair pathways. However, observed transcript levels may reflect the combined effects of antemortem RNA stability, selective RNA degradation, and potentially residual transcriptional activity. A longitudinal study of human blood reported a root mean square error (RMSE) of 4.75 h for a PMI estimation model based on multiple transcripts, illustrating the quantitative potential of this approach. Nevertheless, RNA profiles may be influenced by tissue type, temperature, cause of death and agonal processes, interindividual biological variability, and sampling and storage conditions. Methodological heterogeneity and the lack of independent external validation further limit the translation of these approaches into routine forensic practice. This review critically evaluates the molecular basis of postmortem gene expression and RNA dynamics, messenger RNA (mRNA) and microRNA (miRNA) biomarkers, transcriptome-based models for PMI estimation, and their potential forensic applications, with particular emphasis on the need for standardization, independent validation, and multi-biomarker approaches.

Article.Title: Preclinical Mouse Models of Rheumatoid Arthritis: Comparative Insights into Inflammatory Mediators and Immune Cells
Article.Authors: Lubamba B.
Article.Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovial inflammation, progressive cartilage destruction, and bone erosion. Mouse models are essential for investigating RA pathogenesis, defining immune-cell and cytokine networks, and evaluating potential therapies. Common models include collagen-induced arthritis (CIA), collagen antibody-induced arthritis (CAIA), human TNF transgenic (hTNF-Tg) arthritis, and SKG arthritis, each representing distinct inflammatory mechanisms. CIA involves adaptive and innate immune cells, including CD4+ T cells, B cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and neutrophils, with prominent roles for TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17A, GM-CSF, and IL-23. CAIA primarily reflects antibody-mediated and innate immune mechanisms involving neutrophils, macrophages, complement, and Fcγ receptors, with contributions from TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, GM-CSF, CXCL1, and CXCL2. The hTNF-Tg model highlights chronic TNF-driven inflammation involving macrophages and neutrophils and downstream inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β, IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2. In contrast, the SKG model emphasizes autoreactive CD4+ T-cell and Th17 responses, with IL-17A, IL-6, and IL-23 contributing to arthritis following environmental stimulation. Collectively, these models are mechanistically complementary and provide distinct insights into immune activation, cytokine signaling, and joint pathology. However, differences in immune regulation, disease heterogeneity, and inflammatory mechanisms between mice and humans emphasize the importance of careful model selection and interpretation. This review summarizes major mouse models of RA, focusing on their immune-cell and inflammatory mediator networks, therapeutic applications, and translational relevance to human disease.

Article.Title: The Tenocyte from Atom to Cell: A Critical Multiscale Synthesis Linking Collagen Chemistry, Tissue Mechanics, Cell Mechanobiology and Mathematical Modelling
Article.Authors: Stańczak M.; Kacprzak B.; Hagner-Derengowska M.
Article.Abstract: The tenocyte builds, maintains, senses and degrades one of the most mechanically demanding extracellular matrices in vertebrates, yet the chemical, physical, biological and mathematical descriptions of this system have developed in largely separate literatures. This review examines the tenocyte–matrix unit as a single causal system spanning eight orders of magnitude in length, organised around five transitions: from collagen chemistry to molecular mechanics; from molecule to fibril and fascicle; from tissue loading to the cellular mechanical stimulus; from stimulus to transcription; and from cellular output back to matrix composition. At each transition, we weigh competing hypotheses, identify where evidence is decisive and where it remains correlative, and state the governing equations. We integrate advances from 2021–2026, including single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlases of human tendons, the establishment of PIEZO1 as a causal regulator of tendon stiffness, and microstructurally derived constitutive models. We argue that tendon homeostasis is a closed-loop control problem, formalised as a mechanostat with an inverted-U dose–response, and that the recurrent pathologies of tendon-tendinopathy, ageing, diabetic stiffening and fibrotic healing are failures of this loop rather than of any single component. An open-source computational companion (tenocyte-virtual-cell) is introduced, and a prioritised research agenda closes the review.

Article.Title: A Novel Squid Ink–Quinolin Derived Compound (AEBI), Promotes Hair Growth and Enhances Hair Follicle Stem Cell Activity
Article.Authors: Tian X.; He W.; Zhou Y.; Diao X.; Fan C.; Lu Y.; Tang F.; Li N.; Wu W.
Article.Abstract: Squid ink is a marine-derived bioresource containing diverse bioactive compounds; however, the biological functions of its low-molecular-weight constituents remain largely unexplored. In this study, a novel quinolin derivative, named AEBI, was isolated and identified from squid ink through enzymatic hydrolysis, chromatographic purification, and spectroscopic analysis. The hair growth–promoting activity of AEBI was subsequently evaluated using mouse hair follicle stem cells (HFSCs) and a depilation model established in male Sprague–Dawley (SD) rats. In vitro, AEBI significantly enhanced HFSC viability in a concentration-dependent manner and increased the expression of stem cell- and extracellular matrix-associated proteins, including p63, laminin, and fibronectin. In vivo, topical administration of AEBI markedly accelerated hair regrowth, increased hair follicle density, promoted follicular maturation, and improved hair shaft morphology in depilated rats. Histological analysis revealed that AEBI treatment increased the proportion of mature hair follicles and enhanced subcutaneous adipose tissue development. Furthermore, AEBI treatment upregulated the expression of hair growth–related molecules, including Wnt10b, β-catenin, LEF1, and Ki-67, suggesting that modulation of Wnt/β-catenin-associated signaling may contribute to its hair growth–promoting effects. Notably, high-dose AEBI exhibited comparable or superior effects to 5% minoxidil in several evaluated parameters. Collectively, these findings identify AEBI as a novel squid ink–derived bioactive molecule with potential applications in the development of natural hair growth–promoting agents and provide new insights into the utilization of marine-derived small molecules.

Article.Title: Endometriosis-Associated Infertility: Molecular Mechanisms and Evidence-Based Clinical Management
Article.Authors: Chang K.; Lai T.
Article.Abstract: Endometriosis is a chronic, estrogen-dependent inflammatory disease and a major contributor to female infertility. Endometriosis-associated infertility arises from interacting anatomical and biological mechanisms, including pelvic adhesions and tubal dysfunction, reduced ovarian reserve, altered follicular and oocyte competence, oxidative stress, immune dysregulation, and impaired endometrial function. This narrative review integrates current concepts of disease pathogenesis with evidence-based fertility management. It first examines the molecular, cellular, and immune processes that support ectopic lesion establishment and may impair reproduction. It then discusses diagnostic phenotyping, infertility evaluation, prognostic tools, medical suppression, fertility-preserving surgery, intrauterine insemination, and in vitro fertilization. Particular attention is given to the strength and clinical relevance of current evidence, including surgery for ovarian endometrioma before assisted reproduction, prolonged gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist pretreatment, fresh versus frozen embryo transfer, and the use of intracytoplasmic sperm injection without male-factor infertility. Emerging anti-angiogenic, immunomodulatory, antioxidant, stem-cell, and gene- or epigenetic-based interventions remain investigational. Because neither a single treatment nor a single assisted-reproduction protocol is optimal for all patients, management should integrate age, ovarian reserve, symptom burden, disease phenotype, prior surgery, coexisting infertility factors, and reproductive priorities. Mechanistically informed clinical trials using live birth and patient-centered outcomes are needed to advance precision fertility care.

Article.Title: Functionally Characterized Platelet-Rich Plasma Promotes Endothelial Migration and Cutaneous Wound Repair
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Yang S.; Kim S.
Article.Abstract: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated as an autologous therapeutic for tissue regeneration; however, its clinical efficacy remains inconsistent, partly due to variability in PRP preparation protocols. In this study, we established an integrated framework for functional characterization of PRP by integrating platelet recovery, functional integrity, growth factor (GF) release, and regenerative outcomes. PRP prepared using a dual-spin centrifugation protocol at 92× g showed significantly higher platelet recovery while preserving functional responsiveness compared to single-spin conditions. PDGF-BB release increased in a time-dependent manner, peaking at 4 h after activation, and was positively correlated with platelet concentration. In an in vitro HUVEC scratch assay, PRP significantly enhanced endothelial cell migration in a platelet concentration-dependent manner. This migratory response was accompanied by increased phosphorylation of ERK and AKT and reduced VE-cadherin expression, indicating modulation of intracellular signaling pathways associated with endothelial cell growth, survival, and migration. In a rat skin wound model, PRP prepared under the selected experimental conditions accelerated wound closure compared with controls. Histological and immunohistochemical analyses revealed enhanced re-epithelialization, increased collagen deposition, increased epithelial cell proliferation, and reduced CD31-positive vascular area, consistent with accelerated vascular remodeling. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that PRP efficacy is governed by multiple interdependent factors. A comprehensive strategy integrating platelet recovery, functional preservation, GF release kinetics, and in vivo and in vitro outcomes provides a rational framework for functional characterization of PRP and may serve as a basis for subsequent translational validation.

Article.Title: Host–Microbe Crosstalk in Sjögren’s Disease: Epithelial Type I Interferon Amplification, Loss of Short-Chain Fatty Acid Restraint, and the Effector-Phase Focus of Validated Therapy
Article.Authors: Yu M.; Jo D.; Hwang Y.; Han K.
Article.Abstract: Sjögren’s disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disease of the exocrine glands, long framed as a lymphocyte-driven disorder in which immune cells destroy the target tissue. Genomic, epigenetic, microbiome, and single-cell and spatial studies have since shown the glandular epithelium and the microbial environment to be active participants rather than passive bystanders. This review asks whether host susceptibility and microbiome change can be joined into one continuous axis, following it from genetic and epigenetic susceptibility, through microbiome change read functionally rather than taxonomically, to the crosstalk that converts microbial signals into a host response and the cell states carrying it in human tissue. Two axes run through the whole sequence: the type I interferon (IFN) response and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) metabolism. Read against them, every disease-modifying therapy with validated efficacy so far acts in the downstream B-cell effector axis, whereas the upstream IFN axis has yielded no established treatment. Because the microbial layer and the salivary gland transcriptome or proteome have never been measured in the same patients, the model proposed here remains a testable hypothesis rather than a completed causal chain. The aim is to specify that model, the falsification conditions it carries, and the study design its verification requires.

Article.Title: Sphingolipid Dysregulation in Type 2 Diabetes and Its Microvascular Complications
Article.Authors: Wen Y.; Lin Y.; Liu Y.; Zhao L.
Article.Abstract: Sphingolipids arestructural components of cell membranes and bioactive mediators governing cellular metabolism and intercellular communication. Beyond their classical roles in insulin sensitivity and glucose/lipid homeostasis, ceramide, sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids coordinate through lipid rafts, extracellular vesicles, organelle contact sites and circulating carriers to facilitate signaling among pancreas, liver, adipose tissue, vascular endothelium and kidney. This review summarizes literature on how dietary and endogenous sphingolipids contribute to T2DM and its microvascular complications. Preclinical studies, mainly in cultured cells and rodent models, indicate that overnutrition with excess take of saturated and industrial trans fats promotes ceramide accumulation, which impairs AKT/AMPK signaling, enhancing hepatic gluconeogenesis and β-cell dysfunction, whereas S1P exerts protective metabolic and vascular effects. Whether these mechanisms are similarly dominant in humans remains to be established. Chain-length-specific ceramides generated by distinct ceramide synthases (CerS1–6) determine organelle and intercellular responses in experimental models. In human observational studies, ceramide/S1P ratios and selected sphingolipid species have been associated with metabolic risk, but their diagnostic and risk-stratification value requires clinical validation. We further discuss nutritional patterns, antidiabetic and lipid-lowering agents, and emerging nanomedicine or exosome-based strategies that restore sphingolipid balance. Targeting compartment- and chain-length-specific sphingolipid signaling may provide more precise therapeutic opportunities for T2DM and its complications.

Article.Title: In Vitro Anti-Proliferative and Cisplatin-Modulating Effects of Cedrus libani A. Rich Leaf Essential Oil on H460 and HT-29 Human Cancer Cell Lines
Article.Authors: Younes H.; Azakir B.; Zaarour R.; Hayeck N.; Borjac J.
Article.Abstract: Cedrus libani A. Rich is a coniferous tree native to the eastern Mediterranean region that is known for exhibiting pharmacological properties. In the present study, we investigated the anti-proliferative effect of C. libani leaf essential oil (EO) against H460 and HT-29, as well as evaluated its chemo-modulatory effect with cisplatin (CIS). The EO chemical profile was analyzed via GC-MS. Cell viability was assessed using MTT, while trypan blue exclusion and Annexin V/Propidium Iodide staining were employed to detect cell death. Colony biomass and wound closure were evaluated using crystal violet staining and a scratch assay, respectively. Nuclear morphology and reactive oxygen species (ROS) were assessed using DAPI staining and an NBT assay, respectively. EO and CIS individually reduced cell viability in a time- and concentration-dependent manner with combination treatments demonstrating synergistic/additive/antagonistic interactions depending on the combination ratio, cell line and time point. EO alone does not exhibit significant cell death, whereas CIS demonstrated significant apoptosis and necrosis. The combination (IC50:IC50) enhanced cell death, particularly in HT-29. Both EO and CIS reduced colony biomass and wound closure, with the combination showing higher inhibitory effect on colony biomass in both cell lines and enhanced wound closure inhibitory effect in HT-29 but reduced effect in H460. CIS and combination caused more notable nuclear alterations compared to EO alone, whereas an early increase in NBT reduction followed by a subsequent decrease was observed for individual treatments as well as the combination. This study provides insights into the antiproliferative and chemo-modulatory potential of C. libani leaf essential oil, although further studies are needed to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms.

Article.Title: Proximal Tubule-to-Proximal Tubule Efferocytosis: Gusb Prevents Efferocytosis Failure and Polyphagolysosomal Overload in CAZ-AVI-Induced Acute Kidney Injury
Article.Authors: Hasegawa K.; Sakamaki Y.; Tamaki M.; Yamaguchi S.; Shimizu I.; Kida T.; Miyakami S.; Tada M.; Otsuka M.; Minato M.; Wakino S.
Article.Abstract: Efferocytosis is essential for maintaining epithelial homeostasis, yet whether proximal tubules (PTs) can engulf other PTs and how this process contributes to acute kidney injury (AKI) remain unknown. Ceftazidime–avibactam (CAZ-AVI)-induced AKI and proximal tubule-specific Gusb conditional knockout (CKO) mice both exhibit phagolysosomal dysfunction, suggesting a shared mechanism. We investigated whether (i) CAZ-AVI triggers PT-to-PT efferocytosis, (ii) this leads to polyphagolysosomal failure, and (iii) Gusb overexpression protects against these abnormalities. Wild-type, Gusb-CKO, and Gusb-transgenic mice were treated with CAZ-AVI. Kidney injury was assessed by histology, TUNEL staining, immunostaining for Odc1 and 4-HNE, and transmission electron microscopy. PT-intrinsic transcriptional responses were quantified by real-time PCR for Ccl2, C3, Lcn2, Slc7a13, Acsm3, and Aqp8. Ultrastructural features were evaluated to distinguish efferocytosis from phagolysosomal failure. CAZ-AVI markedly reduced Odc1 in PTs and induced apoptosis localized almost exclusively to PTs, indicating PT-to-PT efferocytosis. CAZ-AVI strongly induced Ccl2, C3, and Lcn2, while suppressing Slc7a13, Acsm3, and Aqp8, reflecting inflammatory recruitment, complement-mediated opsonization, oxidative stress, and metabolic collapse. Electron microscopy revealed numerous polyphagolysosomes containing dense bodies, membrane fragments, small vesicles, and mitochondrial remnants with preserved cristae, without nuclear structures or double-membrane phagosomes, consistent with phagolysosomal failure. Importantly, Gusb-CKO mice phenocopied CAZ-AVI injury, showing Odc1 loss, robust 4-HNE accumulation, PT-restricted apoptosis, and abundant polyphagolysosomes even without drug exposure, demonstrating that Gusb deficiency is sufficient to drive PT-to-PT efferocytosis failure. In contrast, Gusb-overexpressing mice preserved Odc1, prevented apoptosis, normalized all six PT-intrinsic genes, and lacked polyphagolysosomes. CAZ-AVI induces PT-to-PT efferocytosis leading to phagolysosomal overload and oxidative failure. Gusb deficiency reproduces this phenotype, whereas Gusb overexpression preserves PT phagolysosomal homeostasis and prevents AKI progression.

Article.Title: Melatonin Supplementation During Middle Gestation Alleviates Intrauterine Growth Restriction in Piglets and Is Associated with Alterations in Placental DNA Methylation
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Han H.; Xue Z.; Yan L.; Shen Z.; Gao J.; Ji P.; Wang B.; Liu G.
Article.Abstract: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) has a negative impact on reproductive performance in domestic animals. In this study, we attempt to explore the etiology of IUGR in sows and test the potential beneficial effects and underlying molecular mechanisms of melatonin on IUGR. The results indicated that there was a negative correlation between the concentration of melatonin in the peripheral blood of pregnant sows and the ratio of IUGR, and the concentration of melatonin in the umbilical cord blood of IUGR piglets was abnormally decreased. Supplementing sows with an appropriate dose of melatonin can increase the average birth weight of piglets and reduce the proportion of IUGR piglets. Reduced representation bisulfite sequencing revealed a direct association between abnormal DNA methylation in the placenta of sows and IUGR piglets. The increased DNA methylations of key genes responsible for placenta functions downregulated their expressions. Gene downregulation caused placenta dysfunction and IUGR. Melatonin significantly reduced DNA methylation of genes related to placental function. We identified that melatonin supplementation during mid-gestation stages specifically targeted the CGI, CGI shore, exon, intron, and 3′ untranslated regions of placental genes. The results provide novel information to target the high incidence of IUGR in pigs as well as other species.

Article.Title: How the Acute Psychosocial Stress Response Ends: A Post-Stressor Transition Model of Glucocorticoid Feedback, Vagal Re-Engagement, and Frontolimbic Context Updating
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Zheng R.; Wu Y.; Zhang M.
Article.Abstract: Objective stressor offset does not mark a common onset of recovery: cardiovascular activation may be waning while cortisol is still rising and threat-related cognition persists. This structured narrative review integrates molecular, autonomic, neural, cognitive, and immune evidence on the post-stressor interval, primarily in adult psychosocial-stress paradigms. We propose the Post-Stressor Transition Model (PSTM) as an operational extension of existing recovery and allostatic accounts, not as a newly discovered biological system. Three regulatory functions organize the synthesis: updating whether threat remains current, changing cardiac autonomic influence, and regulating continuing hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenocortical output. Glucocorticoid receptor signaling, catecholamines, endocannabinoids, oxytocin, and vasopressin contribute across these functions. The framework distinguishes objective offset from system-specific extrema, physiological resolution from demonstrated adaptation, and shared timing from directional coupling. Eight propositions specify outcomes, temporal windows, competing explanations, and prespecified effect bounds. Measurement recommendations address cortisol nonresponse, respiratory influences on heart rate variability, assessment reactivity, and multirate sampling. Hormonal state and development modify candidate parameters rather than define fixed response types. No universal recovery threshold or clinically validated transition profile is claimed. The model is useful only if its additional parameters are identifiable, improve independent prediction, and withstand phase-specific experimental tests.
