Article.Title: Digital application literacy as a mediator of GAI-TPACK among non-STEM teachers after year-long professional development
Article.Authors: Dai Y.; Ye Z.; Du M.; Zhai X.
Article.Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can produce and revise instructional content through probabilistic, conversational interaction, creating demands that extend beyond routine use of digital tools. This study examined how digital technology knowledge and skills (DL-S) and digital application literacy (DL-A) relate to GAI-integrated technological pedagogical content knowledge (GAI-TPACK) among 224 Chinese primary and secondary teachers in general-subject settings. Participants completed a year-long professional development program and a post-intervention survey. Structural equation modeling showed positive paths from DL-S to DL-A (β = 0.300) and GAI-TPACK (β = 0.317), and from DL-A to GAI-TPACK (β = 0.453). The indirect effect of DL-S through DL-A was 0.137 (95% bootstrap CI [0.069, 0.219]), consistent with partial mediation. The larger point estimate for DL-A was not tested directly against the DL-S coefficient and is therefore interpreted descriptively. These findings position DL-A as a plausible practice-oriented mechanism linking foundational digital capability with subject-specific GAI integration. Because competence was self-reported at one post-intervention time point, the model does not establish causal development. The study offers a bounded operational account of GAI-TPACK for non-STEM professional development and identifies priorities for multi-wave and performance-based research.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Information Systems > Digital literacy in education; Computer Science > Information Systems > Artificial Intelligence in Education; Social Sciences > Education > Mathematics Education and Teaching Techniques

Article.Title: Optogenetic modeling of wake-like transcriptional progression in human SH-SY5Y neuronal cells
Article.Authors: Yamazaki S.; Gee W.; Valekunja U.; Reddy A.
Article.Abstract: Sleep deprivation induces widespread transcriptional remodeling in the brain, but the extent to which this response arises from sustained neuronal excitation rather than systemic confounders remains unclear. Here we establish a reductionist human neuronal model to isolate the cell-autonomous effects of prolonged depolarization. Optogenetic stimulation of SH-SY5Y cells produced controlled calcium influx and robust induction of activity-dependent genes, enabling precise manipulation of excitation history. Time-resolved RNA sequencing revealed that sustained excitation partitions transcriptional responses into discrete temporal modules, including early-, mid-, and late-peaking, sustained, biphasic, and suppressed patterns, each with distinct functional signatures. At the pathway level, these modules combine into sequential transcriptional states that evolve directionally across stimulation and recovery. Transitions were asymmetric, indicating excitation-history-dependent reorganization rather than simple reversal. Cross-dataset comparisons revealed selective concordance between defined temporal modules and in vivo sleep deprivation signatures. Together, these findings demonstrate that sustained neuronal excitation alone can drive staged, wake-like transcriptional progression, linking gene-level temporal dynamics to higher-order regulatory states.
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Sleep and Wakefulness Research; Neuroscience > Endocrine and Autonomic Systems > Circadian rhythm and melatonin; Psychology > Experimental and Cognitive Psychology > Sleep and Work-Related Fatigue

Article.Title: Improved HCV genotyping based on sequence encoding and feature integration
Article.Authors: Fahmy A.; Hammad M.; Al-Atabany W.; Mabrouk M.
Article.Abstract: Genomic sequence classification is an important task for understanding viral genetic variability and supporting genotype identification, particularly for viruses such as the Hepatitis C Virus (HCV). In this study, we evaluate the effectiveness of different sequence encoding techniques, supplementary genomic descriptors, and class-balancing strategies for HCV genotype classification under a stricter CD-HIT-EST cluster-aware evaluation protocol designed to reduce sequence-identity leakage. Four encoding methods were investigated, namely Frequency Chaos Game Representation (FCGR), k-mer encoding, one-hot encoding, and label encoding. These representations were evaluated using multiple machine learning models, including XGBoost, Random Forest, Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). To address class imbalance, SMOTE was applied, while GC content and GC skew were included as supplementary compositional descriptors. Overall, FCGR and k-mer encoding outperformed one-hot and label encoding. The best result was achieved using k-mer encoding with XGBoost and SMOTE, obtaining a macro F1-score of 0.890, accuracy of 0.922, macro precision of 0.866, macro recall of 0.925, macro specificity of 0.990, and MCC of 0.893 under the CD-HIT-EST cluster-aware evaluation setting. The statistical analysis showed that SMOTE had a clear positive effect on classification performance, particularly for the Random Forest model, while GC-based descriptors provided additional interpretability but did not show a statistically significant improvement in the k-mer-based experiment. Overall, this study demonstrates the importance of selecting appropriate sequence encodings and class-balancing strategies for machine-learning-based HCV genotype classification. The findings provide a comparative basis for future work on sequence-based classification tasks in virology and computational genomics.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Fractal and DNA sequence analysis; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Machine Learning in Bioinformatics; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Genomics and Phylogenetic Studies

Article.Title: A virulent and temperate phage cocktail synergizes with antibiotics against multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Article.Authors: González-Gómez J.; Elizalde-Flores E.; Aispuro-Leal C.; Rodríguez-Arellano S.; Gomez-Gil B.; Ruíz-Ramírez A.; Castro-del Campo N.; Chaidez C.
Article.Abstract: The rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant bacteria necessitates antimicrobial strategies that constrain resistance while preserving efficacy. Phage cocktails are typically composed exclusively of virulent phages, whereas the therapeutic potential of temperate phages remains largely unexplored. Here, we evaluate a two-phage cocktail combining a virulent (ARP5) and a temperate (ARP3) phage against a multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa clinical isolate (PaAK08). While ARP5 alone achieved strong bacterial suppression and ARP3 displayed limited efficacy, the combined cocktail sustained > 98% suppression across multiplicities of infection for 30 h. Resistance profiling revealed no cross-resistance between phages, consistent with receptor independence. Phenotypic and genomic analyses of resistant mutants identified alterations in surface-associated structures, including glycosyltransferase-linked loci, and ARP3 prophage integration events. Phage ratio optimization maintained suppression at reduced concentrations, with statistical analysis supporting additive interactions. Notably, co-administration with subinhibitory tobramycin or ofloxacin produced synergistic suppression, achieving complete inhibition for 48 h with ofloxacin. Together, these findings demonstrate that virulent–temperate phage combinations can function compatibly, expand therapeutic design frameworks, and potentiate antibiotic activity against multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa .
Article.TopicFields: Environmental Science > Ecology > Bacteriophages and microbial interactions; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Bacterial biofilms and quorum sensing; Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Antimicrobial agents and applications

Article.Title: Deployment of edge-lightweight AI vertical models in multimodal anomaly detection and energy optimization of tech-long production line
Article.Authors: Wu X.; Tao X.; Cheng Y.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Aiming at the problems that the abnormal state of high-speed liquid packaging production lines is difficult to identify in time, the computing power of edge controller is limited, and the energy consumption regulation and condition monitoring are separated from each other, a multimodal lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) system embedded in Tech-Long production controller is constructed; this realizes the collaborative optimization of abnormal operation window identification and energy consumption of the whole line. First, this study collects vibration, acoustic, and thermal signals from the bottle blowing, filling, and packaging sections; it also constructs cross-sectional anomaly characterization through time synchronization, feature-level alignment, and hierarchical fusion. Subsequently, Feather Convolutional Neural Network (FeatherCNN) is reconstructed using kernel fusion, channel compression, and 4-bit Integer (INT4) quantization to reduce model computation and storage load; thus, the network can adapt to resource-constrained Advanced RISC Machine (ARM) edge controllers. Finally, a dual-layer control chain is built, composed of continuous basic energy-saving and anomaly risk-weighted correction, so that anomaly scores influence the updates of temperature zones, valve openings, and heat-sealing parameters via dynamic weights and adjustment gains. The experimental results demonstrate that the anomaly window recognition accuracy of multimodal FeatherCNN reaches 0.931, which is superior to traditional machine learning models, deep learning baselines and various single-modal structures. The lightweight processing reduces Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) from 3.42×10⁹ to 0.58×10⁹, a decrease of approximately 83%. The inference latency of the complete model on the ARM controller is shortened from 18.63 milliseconds (ms) to 7.41 ms. Under the controlled conditions of fixed production line speed, material specifications, and statistical windows, the dual-layer collaborative control has reduced the overall energy consumption of the whole line by 26%. The results show that multimodal anomaly identification, model lightweighting, and energy-saving parameter tuning can work together in the same edge decision chain. The framework verifies the feasibility of resource-constrained controllers supporting abnormal monitoring and energy consumption regulation of the entire packaging line; meanwhile, it provides an engineering reference for edge intelligent deployment of similar high-speed liquid packaging lines.
Article.Topic: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: multimodal anomaly detection; energy optimization; lightweight AI models; edge computing; production line monitoring
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering > Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection; Computer Science > Computer Networks and Communications > IoT and Edge/Fog Computing; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Anomaly Detection Techniques and Applications

Article.Title: Ethnotaxonomy and phenotypic evidence for a zone of high common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) diversity in northeastern Amazonian Peru
Article.Authors: Vecco-Giove C.; Barrera-Lozano M.; Tuesta-Chichipe E.; Rivera J.; Pinchi M.; Ortiz R.; Tobaru J.; Blas R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The common bean ( Phaseolus vulgaris L.) is a key crop in the Americas, yet its diversity in the Peruvian Amazon Basin remains poorly documented. We examined geographic and ethnographic patterns in vernacular naming and phenotypic diversity of common beans across three biomes: the inter-Andean Marañón Valley, the Highland Rainforest, and the Amazonian lowlands. Using lexical sources, ethnobotanical interviews, and phenotypic evaluation of seeds, we recorded 152 specific vernacular names and 20 generic terms for P. vulgaris across 26 ethnic groups. Naming categories relied primarily on morphological criteria, complemented by references to origin, growth habit, culinary properties, and historical events. Vernacular name richness and phenotypic diversity exhibited a congruent geographic concentration, with the highest values recorded in the Highland Rainforest biome. These results suggest a geographically continuous zone of high common bean diversity in the northeastern Peruvian Amazon, spanning the inter-Andean Marañón Valley, the Highland Rainforest, and adjacent Amazonian regions. While the observed congruence between vernacular and phenotypic diversity is consistent with historical diversification processes, the present evidence does not establish a historical diversification axis. Linguistic and ethnobotanical evidence thus provide a useful framework for documenting and conserving common bean diversity in this bioculturally dynamic region.
Article.TopicFields: Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Linguistic and Cultural Studies; Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Agriculture; Arts and Humanities > History > Amazonian Archaeology and Ethnohistory

Article.Title: Nanobody-based lateral flow assays for the detection of α-bungarotoxin in Bungarus snake venoms
Article.Authors: Thumtecho S.; Belfakir S.; Christensen T.; Rivera-de-Torre E.; Burlet N.; Ljungars A.; Ross G.; Laustsen A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Accurate snake identification is critical for effective antivenom treatment following snakebite envenoming, but remains a major diagnostic challenge. Here, we developed a prototype lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA) designed to distinguish krait ( Bungarus ) from cobra ( Naja ) envenoming in Southeast Asia. To enhance point-of-care utility, the assay employs variable domains of heavy-chain-only antibodies (V H Hs). The V H Hs target α-bungarotoxin (α-BuTx), a neurotoxin unique to Bungarus , with negative selection strategies to minimize cross-reactivity with α-cobratoxin in Naja venom. Our prototype LFIA detected α-BuTx with a visual limit of detection of 0.5–5 ng/mL in running buffer and spiked urine and serum samples. Additionally, the assay detected Bungarus whole venom at 50–500 ng/mL in running buffer. No cross-reactivity with Naja venom was observed at clinically relevant concentrations, with signals detected only at supraphysiological concentrations (≥50,000 ng/mL). These results support the feasibility of using V H H-based LFIAs for guiding timely, targeted antivenom administration in resource-limited settings.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Genetics > Venomous Animal Envenomation and Studies; Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Biosensors and Analytical Detection; Medicine > Radiology, Nuclear Medicine and Imaging > Monoclonal and Polyclonal Antibodies Research

Article.Title: Effect of nursing care program on healthy lifestyle behaviours and quality of life in women with endometriosis: a randomised controlled trial
Article.Authors: Bursa A.; Sahin N.
Article.Abstract: This study was conducted to determine the effect of Endometriosis Nursing Care Program (ENCP), developed in line with Health Promotion Model for women with endometriosis, on women's quality of life and healthy lifestyle behaviours. This prospective, single-centre, randomized controlled trial was conducted with 46 women diagnosed with endometriosis who applied to the Endometriosis Outpatient Clinic of a training research hospital. Women with an Endometriosis Health Profile Questionnaire-5 (EHP-5) score ≥ 22 indicating reduced quality of life were included. Participants were randomly assigned to an intervention group (n = 23) receiving Endometriosis Nursing Care Program (ENCP) or a control group (n = 23) receiving routine care. The ENCP consisted of two individual 60-min sessions delivered two weeks apart. The primary outcome was change in quality of life measured by EHP-5. Secondary outcomes included healthy lifestyle behaviours measured by Health Promoting Lifestyle Profile II (HPLP-II). Data were analysed using parametric or non-parametric statistical tests, as appropriate. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Forty-six women completed the study (23 intervention, 23 control). The mean EHP-5 score in the intervention group decreased significantly from 61.8 ± 11.4 to 32.1 ± 18.7; Cohen's d = − 1.71, p < 0.001 after the intervention, while no significant change was observed in the control group ( p > 0.05). HPLP-II total scores significantly increased in the ENCP group (132.04 ± 19.81 vs 164.17 ± 18.83; Cohen's d = 1.58, p < 0.001). ENCP significantly improved quality of life in women with endometriosis and resulted in increased scores on healthy lifestyle behaviours. Structured nursing interventions may play an important role in comprehensive endometriosis care. Trial registration NCT05402943 Date of registration: 02.06.2022. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05402943?term=NCT05402943&rank=1 .
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Reproductive Medicine > Endometriosis Research and Treatment; Health Professions > General Health Professions > Health and Wellbeing Research; Health Professions > Pharmacy > Nursing care and research

Article.Title: Stochastic SEIR dynamics via graph Laplacian diffusion under transmission uncertainty
Article.Authors: Achankunju P.; Barman M.; Mishra N.; Dash S.
Article.Abstract: Epidemic spatial spread across interconnected populations depends on both mobility between locations and random fluctuations in transmission. We extend the Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Removed (SEIR) epidemic model to a network setting by introducing graph Laplacian diffusion to capture population mobility, and further incorporate stochastic perturbations in the transmission rate to capture environmental noise. Using Lyapunov function analysis, we first establish that the stochastic system admits a unique global solution which remains non-negative for all time, so that the model is mathematically well-posed and its state variables retain their epidemiological meaning as population counts. Building on this well-posedness, we then apply Lyapunov techniques a second time to analyse the long-term behaviour of the solution. The disease-free equilibrium is shown to be globally asymptotically stable when the basic reproduction number does not exceed one, indicating disease extinction. When the basic reproduction number exceeds one, the disease instead persists, in the sense that the stochastic solution exhibits a bounded time-averaged deviation from the endemic equilibrium of the corresponding deterministic system. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods are further employed for parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, applied to COVID-19 incidence data across all 47 prefectures in Japan. The proposed framework brings together network-driven mobility, stochastic transmission dynamics, and Bayesian uncertainty quantification within a SEIR model. Finally, computational experiments on a small-world Watts-Strogatz network are used to validate and visually illustrate the theoretical results.
Article.Topic: Mathematical and Theoretical Epidemiology and Ecology Models
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Mathematical and Theoretical Epidemiology and Ecology Models; Mathematics > Modeling and Simulation > COVID-19 epidemiological studies; Physics and Astronomy > Statistical and Nonlinear Physics > Complex Network Analysis Techniques

Article.Title: DashGuard: spatio-temporal deep learning for dashcam-based road accident anticipation
Article.Authors: Pullur Somasekar L.; Sinha A.; Chintaluri N.; Madasamy B.
Article.Abstract: Road traffic accidents claim roughly 1.35 million lives each year, with delayed hazard perception rather than mechanical failure implicated in most collisions. Dashcam-based accident anticipation offers a low-cost complement to sensor-heavy ADAS, yet controlled comparisons across architectures remain rare. We present DashGuard, which trains and evaluates six spatio-temporal models a 3D CNN, CNN+LSTM, CNN+Transformer, and three two-stream variants (lightweight CNN, ResNet-18, and Transformer) on the Car Crash Dataset (1500 crash and 2000 normal videos) under a consistent, leak-free protocol. A video-level 70/15/15 split prevents clip-level contamination; four-level soft labels encode temporal distance to the accident frame; and a two-clip temporal consistency gate substantially cuts false-positive alerts. On the held-out test set, the Two-Stream Transformer achieves AUC = 0.981 and F1 = 0.870, with recall of 0.991. The lightweight 3D CNN (AUC = 0.949, \(\approx \) 180 K parameters) is a viable option for edge hardware. A React/FastAPI web interface supports interactive evaluation. The results show that explicitly separating motion and appearance via two-stream attention gives the clearest gains over single-stream designs on this task.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Automotive Engineering > Autonomous Vehicle Technology and Safety; Engineering > Safety, Risk, Reliability and Quality > Traffic and Road Safety; Computer Science > Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition > Advanced Neural Network Applications

Article.Title: Integrated bioinformatic analysis identifies distinct neddylation-associated proteasome genes and immune-related features in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma
Article.Authors: Wang S.; Xu J.; Ge H.
Article.Abstract: Neddylation contributes to cancer progression, but its relationship with proteasome-related genes and the immune microenvironment in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) remains unclear. We aimed to identify neddylation-associated genes in LSCC and characterize their molecular, metabolic, and immune features. Transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Gene Expression Omnibus were analyzed using differential expression, functional enrichment, and machine-learning approaches. Key genes were further evaluated by survival, pathway, immune infiltration, and somatic mutation analyses and validated by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) in five paired LSCC and adjacent tissues. Seventy-four differentially expressed neddylation-related genes were identified. Four genes, KCTD6, PSMB2, PSMB4, and PSMD2, were selected by both LASSO and SVM-RFE. KCTD6-associated genes were enriched in bile acid metabolism, while macrophage M0 and resting CD4 + memory T cells were associated with prognosis. Lower PSMB4 and PSMD2 expression was associated with immune escape-related features. qRT-PCR in five paired specimens confirmed the predicted direction of expression change for all four genes (KCTD6 lower, and PSMB2, PSMB4, and PSMD2 higher in tumor); given the small paired sample, this provides directional confirmation only and does not establish biomarker performance. We identified a distinct set of proteasome-related neddylation-associated genes associated with metabolic and immune characteristics in LSCC. These findings suggest potential links between neddylation-associated proteasome genes and the immune microenvironment in LSCC.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Otorhinolaryngology > Head and Neck Cancer Studies; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Ubiquitin and proteasome pathways; Medicine > Oncology > Cancer Immunotherapy and Biomarkers

Article.Title: Genomic diversity, population structure, and relatedness of critically endangered Philippine eagles under conservation management
Article.Authors: Pascual F.; Perdon D.; Tablizo F.; Lapid C.; Egana J.; Mantaring R.; Punayan K.; Araiza S.; Llames J.; Abad M.; Gonzalez J.; Ibañez J.; Palmes-Saloma C.
Article.Abstract: The critically endangered Philippine eagle ( Pithecophaga jefferyi ) faces severe threats to its population from habitat loss, naturally slow reproduction cycles, and human encroachment. Thus, 38 years ago, the Philippine Eagle Foundation (PEF) was established for the conservation of the endangered Philippine eagle and its rainforest habitat. To support the PEF’s captive-breeding and rehabilitation efforts, this study investigates the genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) profiles of 20 wild-captive and 15 captive-bred individuals under the foundation’s care. Sequence reads were quality-filtered and aligned to a previously generated Philippine eagle reference genome. Identified SNPs across the 35 individuals were then further analyzed to assess population structure, isolation by distance (IBD), inbreeding, and relatedness. Population structure analysis revealed that genetic distance tended to increase with geographic distance, suggesting that the wild-captive eagles follow an pattern. Inbreeding analysis meanwhile showed significantly higher levels among wild-captive eagles compared to those bred in captivity, suggesting limited access to genetically diverse mates in the wild, and highlighting the success of the foundation’s breeding strategy in minimizing inbreeding. Finally, kinship analysis confirmed known first-degree relationships among captive-bred eagles and uncovered novel kinships among wild-captive individuals that reinforce the IBD model. These results represent the first comprehensive conservation genomics study on the Philippine eagle, providing insights into the diversity of its captive and wild populations, as well as valuable information that can guide future breeding and conservation efforts.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Genetics > Genetic diversity and population structure; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Genetics > Genetic and phenotypic traits in livestock; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Genetics > Forensic and Genetic Research

Article.Title: Identification of kinematic motifs in crouch gait of children with cerebral palsy
Article.Authors: K S.; Poojari M.; Kumar A.; Krishnan C.; Unnikrishnan B.; Joshua A.; Figarado S.; Nayak M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Crouch gait is among the most disabling gait deviations in cerebral palsy (CP). Powered exoskeletons can supply the extensor thrust orthoses cannot, but their control depends on repeatable kinematic patterns, and crouch gait is perceived as irregular. Five children with CP (8–14 years; Gross Motor Function Classification System [GMFCS] I–III) walked at self-selected speed wearing bilateral shank inertial measurement units, knee goniometers and insole pressure sensors at the heel and forefoot. Signals were filtered with a two-state Kalman filter, adaptively segmented into gait cycles using plantar-pressure events (heel or toe strike), and time-normalised to 101 points. A kinematic motif was defined as a limb’s ensemble waveform and validated using the coefficient of variation, ICC(3,1), dynamic time warping, autocorrelation and 1,000-iteration permutation testing; symmetry was quantified with the Symmetry Index. Repeatability tracked the signal measured rather than functional severity: mean ICC(3,1) was 0.76 for forefoot loading, 0.61 for heel loading and 0.29 for knee kinematics. Full criteria were met in 12 of 30 limb–signal combinations, 12 met one or two, and 6 met none. Five of the six failures were knee channels, also the only channels indistinguishable from a permuted null, yet the knee met all criteria bilaterally in the least affected participant. These preliminary findings establish feasibility in a heterogeneous cohort ( n = 5); no gait-phase classifier was trained or evaluated here.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Psychiatry and Mental health > Cerebral Palsy and Movement Disorders; Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Prosthetics and Rehabilitation Robotics; Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Lower Extremity Biomechanics and Pathologies

Article.Title: Development and internal validation of a clinical risk score for early delirium detection in older emergency department patients
Article.Authors: Sanguanwit P.; Sotakul P.; Wangviboonchai V.
Article.Abstract: Delirium is a common but frequently underrecognized neuropsychiatric syndrome among older adults in the emergency department (ED), associated with prolonged hospitalization and increased mortality. To develop a clinical risk score for early delirium detection in older emergency department patients. We conducted a prospective cohort study in the ED of a tertiary hospital from July 2024 to July 2025. Patients aged ≥ 65 years who remained in the ED for > 4 h were assessed using the Thai version of the Confusion Assessment Method intensive care unit (CAM-ICU) within 12 h of arrival. Demographic data, comorbidities, functional status, medications, presenting features, vital signs, laboratory values, and ED diagnoses were collected. Multivariable logistic regression was used to derive a clinical risk score, which was evaluated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AuROC). Among 380 enrolled patients, 102 (26.8%) were identified with delirium. Five independent variables were included in the final model: age 70–79 years (1 point); age 80–89 years, CKD stage III–V, or prior cerebrovascular accident (12 points); age ≥ 90 years (29 points); cirrhosis (24 points); and dementia (41 points), yielding a total score range of 0–118. The score demonstrated good discriminative performance (AuROC 0.79; 95% CI 0.74–0.84). Delirium occurred in 17.97% of patients with low-risk scores (0–24) and 57.65% of those with high-risk scores (≥ 25). This simple, clinically applicable risk score, based on five readily available variables, shows good ability to identify older ED patients at risk for delirium. Early risk stratification using this tool may support timely preventive and monitoring strategies in the ED. Trial registration: The trial was retrospectively registered in the Thai Clinical Trial Registry, identification number TCTR2021082700 on 25 November 2025.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Critical Care and Intensive Care Medicine > Intensive Care Unit Cognitive Disorders; Medicine > Emergency Medicine > Emergency and Acute Care Studies; Medicine > Neurology > Alcoholism and Thiamine Deficiency

Article.Title: Barriers to living walls implementation in Saudi Arabian sustainable construction projects: A PLS-SEM approach
Article.Authors: Alaboud N.
Article.Abstract: To maximize financial benefits and sustainability throughout a project’s lifecycle, the construction industry must move beyond the partial implementation of living wall (LW). While the existing literature has focused on LW drivers, there is a lack of comprehensive evidence regarding implementation barriers. This study prioritizes and assesses the LW implementation barriers in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA) building industry. Data were collected via an expert survey and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The model demonstrated robust internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability meeting the required thresholds, and average variance extracted values exceeding the 0.50 (50%) requirement. Based on the second-order analysis, the identified LW barriers were found to be formative, but collinearity was assessed and found to be within the acceptable thresholds (VIF < 3.5), ensuring the distinct contribution of each formative indicator. The path model results showed that awareness and economic barriers ( β = 0.278), integration and complexity barriers (β = 0.303), operational and behavioral barriers (β = 0.380), and resource and structural barriers (β = 0.372) significantly impede LW implementation (all p ≤ 0.001). Conversely, maintenance and technical barriers (β = 0.097) were not significant ( p = 0.227), indicating their minimal impact compared with the other model constructs. These findings provide policy guidance concerning LW adoption in the KSA and other Gulf nations, facilitating the completion of projects by removing the barriers to LW implementation and enhancing their overall success.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Building and Construction > Sustainable Building Design and Assessment; Engineering > Building and Construction > BIM and Construction Integration; Decision Sciences > Management Science and Operations Research > Construction Project Management and Performance

Article.Title: SpecLLM: LLM-based VNIR spectral interpretation
Article.Authors: Romaszewski M.; Strzoda A.; Halama M.; Głomb P.; Masłowski P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Visible and near-infrared (VNIR) spectroscopy identifies materials from characteristic spectral bands, and spectroscopists interpret spectra by features such as peak positions and intensities. Recent machine-learning and foundation models for hyperspectral data are highly effective but return numerical outputs or latent representations rather than such feature-level descriptions. Meanwhile, LLM-based spectral approaches have mostly provided raw numerical sequences. We present a method for making spectroscopic data accessible to large language models (LLMs) through compact, feature-based representations. Instead of supplying full spectra as comma-separated values (CSV), JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), or extensible markup language (XML), the proposed approach extracts summary statistics and discriminative extrema. It serialises them as either natural language or structured JSON. We evaluate prototype-based substance classification in two complementary scenes from an open-access VNIR hyperspectral blood dataset. For the selected models, compact feature representations were substantially more effective than raw numerical encodings, but less effective than a Random Forest operating on raw spectra. The natural-language format provides a human-readable, inspectable serialisation of compact spectral evidence and reduces prompt length compared with full-spectrum encodings. We also compared natural language and JSON feature representations and found them broadly comparable.
Article.TopicFields: Chemistry > Analytical Chemistry > Spectroscopy and Chemometric Analyses; Engineering > Media Technology > Remote-Sensing Image Classification; Medicine > Radiology, Nuclear Medicine and Imaging > Optical Imaging and Spectroscopy Techniques

Article.Title: Seed persistence of nine weed species in silage, manure, and slurry and implications for dispersal through organic fertilizers
Article.Authors: Nikolić N.; Massaro S.; Tagliapietra F.; Schiavon S.; Masin R.
Article.Abstract: Weed seed contamination of cattle feed can contribute to weed dispersal within crop–livestock systems when viable seeds survive digestion and are returned to fields through manure or slurry applications. However, the persistence of weed seeds from feed preservation to waste recycling remains poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate the viability of common agricultural weed seeds after exposure to silage fermentation, simulated rumen digestion, and storage in cattle manure and slurry. Seeds of nine weed species ( Abutilon theophrasti , Alopecurus myosuroides , Amaranthus retroflexus , Avena sterilis , Chenopodium album , Datura stramonium , Echinochloa crus-galli , Lolium multiflorum , and Sorghum halepense ) were incubated for one, four, and six months in three silage types (maize, sorghum, and grass) and subsequently incubated in cattle manure and slurry following simulated rumen digestion. Silage fermentation significantly reduced seed viability, although the response varied among weed species and silage types. During storage in cattle waste, seed viability declined progressively, with slurry degrading seeds faster than manure. Nevertheless, seeds of C. album , D. stramonium , A. retroflexus , and E. crus-galli remained viable after six months in manure. These findings suggest that cattle manure may be an important pathway for weed seed persistence and dispersal in agricultural soils, whereas slurry may pose a much lower risk. The results provide practical guidance for manure management strategies aimed at reducing weed spread while supporting sustainable crop–livestock production systems.
Article.TopicFields: Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Weed Control and Herbicide Applications; Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Seed Germination and Physiology; Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Forestry > Pasture and Agricultural Systems

Article.Title: Association of perioperative etomidate exposure and mortality after hip fracture surgery: a matched cohort study
Article.Authors: Hung K.; Chang L.; Chen I.
Article.Abstract: Etomidate is often used for anesthetic induction in hemodynamically unstable patients because of its cardiovascular stability, but its transient adrenal suppression raises concern about possible adverse postoperative outcomes. We performed a cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network to examine the association between perioperative etomidate exposure and postoperative outcomes in adults undergoing hip fracture surgery. Patients receiving etomidate were matched 1:1 with controls. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included pneumonia, sepsis, venous thromboembolism, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), and acute kidney injury (AKI). After matching, 6,246 patients were included in each group with balanced baseline characteristics. Etomidate exposure was associated with higher risks of 30-day mortality (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.15–1.60; P < 0.001), pneumonia (OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.03–1.47, P = 0.019), and MACEs (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.04–1.40, P = 0.014), but a lower risk of AKI (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71–0.96, P = 0.014). No significant associations were observed for sepsis or venous thromboembolism. All associations attenuated and became non-significant during extended follow-up (30–180 day). In conclusion, perioperative etomidate exposure was associated with worse short-term postoperative outcomes except for a lower AKI risk. These findings warrant prospective confirmation.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine > Anesthesia and Sedative Agents; Medicine > Surgery > Hip and Femur Fractures; Medicine > Cardiology and Cardiovascular Medicine > Cardiac, Anesthesia and Surgical Outcomes

Article.Title: Dynamic weighted federated contrastive learning for robust medical image classification under heterogeneous data
Article.Authors: Yang L.; Wu Q.; Li J.; Guan Q.; Zhao Q.; Xu B.; Yang T.; Yang L.; Zhou T.
Article.Abstract: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence technologies, AI-driven medical image classification has attracted considerable attention in recent years. However, increasingly stringent data privacy regulations have significantly restricted data sharing among medical institutions, making it difficult for traditional centralized learning frameworks to effectively exploit distributed medical data resources. As a privacy-preserving distributed machine learning paradigm, federated learning enables multiple institutions to collaboratively train models without directly exchanging raw data. Nevertheless, federated learning still faces several critical challenges in practical applications, including heterogeneous data distributions and model bias caused by non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a dynamic weighted learning method based on federated contrastive learning. Different from approaches that focus solely on local representation optimization or employ fixed aggregation weights, the proposed framework couples supervised contrastive local training with loss-feedback-based multi-factor client weighting, thereby jointly controlling local representation drift and server-side model aggregation. Specifically, contrastive learning is integrated into the federated learning framework by jointly leveraging local and global model representations for supervised contrastive optimization. This strategy effectively mitigates the distribution discrepancy among different clients and gradually aligns local models with the global model as communication rounds progress. Furthermore, during global aggregation, a loss-feedback rule is introduced to accept the candidate global model parameters and aggregation weights only when the candidate loss-feedback value decreases. In addition, a multi-factor weighted aggregation mechanism is introduced to comprehensively evaluate client contributions based on multiple factors, thereby assigning larger aggregation weights to local models that are more beneficial to global model optimization. Experiments were conducted on an osteoporosis knee X-ray dataset and a COVID–Pneumonia–Normal chest X-ray dataset under IID and different Non-IID settings. Under severe Non-IID conditions, the proposed method achieved accuracies of 92.12% and 96.27%, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 98.31% and 97.68%, and F1 scores of 90.92% and 93.22% on the two datasets, respectively. Comparisons with representative federated learning methods and the static-weighting ablation setting demonstrate that the proposed method maintains competitive classification performance and stable training behavior under heterogeneous client distributions.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Privacy-Preserving Technologies in Data; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Domain Adaptation and Few-Shot Learning; Medicine > Health Informatics > Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

Article.Title: Comparison of systemic inflammatory indices and periodontal parameters in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and gouty arthritis with periodontitis
Article.Authors: Beder M.; Yemenoğlu H.; Arpa M.; Cüre O.; Aktürk Ş.
Article.Abstract: The aim of this study was to compare systemic inflammatory indices—including the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), aggregate index of systemic inflammation (AISI), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR)—and clinical periodontal parameters in systemically healthy patients with periodontitis and patients with periodontitis and concomitant rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or gouty arthritis (GA). 66 participants were divided into three groups: systemically healthy patients with periodontitis (SHP, n = 22), patients with RA and periodontitis (RAP, n = 22) and patients with GA and periodontitis (GAP, n = 22). Periodontal parameters and systemic inflammatory biomarkers SII, SIRI, AISI, NLR, PLR and MLR were assessed. The GAP group exhibited significantly lower probing pocket depth (PPD) and clinical attachment loss (CAL) values and neutrophil counts but higher lymphocyte counts than the other groups (p < 0.05). SII, SIRI, and NLR values were significantly lower in the GAP group compared to the SHP and RAP groups, while AISI and MLR were significantly lower in the GAP group compared to the SHP group (p < 0.05). SII and NLR were positively correlated with BOP, PPD, and CAL (p < 0.05). SII and NLR were positively associated with BOP, PPD, and CAL. However, these findings demonstrate associations rather than diagnostic or prognostic utility and should be confirmed in larger prospective studies.
Article.TopicFields: Dentistry > Periodontics > Oral microbiology and periodontitis research; Medicine > Oncology > Inflammatory Biomarkers in Disease Prognosis; Medicine > Rheumatology > Rheumatoid Arthritis Research and Therapies

Article.Title: Controlled nucleation of hopfions with field pulses
Article.Authors: Castillo-Sepulveda S.; Saéz G.; Corona R.; Altbir D.; Carvalho-Santos V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract We demonstrate a mechanism for the deterministic nucleation of magnetic hopfions in cylindrical nanopillars via transient magnetic field pulses. By exploiting a chiral magnetic cylinder with engineered surface uniaxial anisotropy, we show that field pulses trigger a non-equilibrium magnetization dynamics. Depending on the pulse amplitude, the system relaxes into distinct topologically protected energy minima, stabilizing either isolated hopfions or coexisting states with other three-dimensional solitons. This approach offers a framework for manipulating 3D topological textures without requiring localized spin-polarized currents, broadening the understanding of three-dimensional nanomagnetism.
Article.TopicFields: Physics and Astronomy > Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics > Magnetic properties of thin films; Physics and Astronomy > Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics > Topological Materials and Phenomena; Physics and Astronomy > Condensed Matter Physics > Advanced Condensed Matter Physics

Article.Title: Optimizing fixation and staining to reduce cell detachment in wet-fixed direct smears, a quantitative evidence-based quality improvement study
Article.Authors: Zou Y.; Wang X.; Chen Y.; Wu Z.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Wet-fixed cytologic smears are inherently prone to cell detachment, which causes cross-contamination and reduces smear cellularity, potentially leading to false-positive diagnoses and diagnostic uncertainty. This study evaluated the effects of the intermediate alcohol step, fixation duration, and slide type on detachment to establish an evidence-based optimized protocol. We evaluated: (i) the necessity and optimal concentration of the intermediate alcohol step; (ii) fixation duration from 30 min to 24 h; and (iii) slide type (ordinary vs. positively charged). Detachment was scored semi-quantitatively using a streak-wiping method. Wilcoxon and Friedman tests were used for paired and block comparisons, respectively. The intermediate alcohol step significantly reduced detachment ( p < 0.05), with 50% ethanol superior to 75% ( p = 0.012). Prolonged fixation progressively decreased detachment ( p < 0.001), with no further statistically significant reduction beyond 3 h. Under optimized conditions, ordinary and positively charged slides performed comparably ( p = 0.811). An evidence-based strategy for laboratory quality improvement—extending fixation toward 3 h, including an intermediate alcohol step (preferably 50% ethanol) at each transition between water and 95% ethanol, and using ordinary slides—substantially reduces detachment. By preserving cellularity and helping to reduce the risk of cross-contamination, this protocol offers an implementable quality improvement tool for cytology laboratories, potentially enhancing diagnostic reliability and patient safety in wet-fixed cytologic preparations.
Article.Topic: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Physiology > Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control; Medicine > Pharmacology > Biological Stains and Phytochemicals; Medicine > Epidemiology > Cervical Cancer and HPV Research

Article.Title: Association of low parental mental health literacy with adolescent depression and anxiety: a large-scale cross-sectional study in Guangdong, China
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Wan Q.; Liu Y.; Jiang Z.; Qiu Q.; Jiang W.; Zhou F.; Kong X.; Zhao F.; Wu H.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Adolescent depression and anxiety symptoms are major health concerns, and the family environment plays a critical role. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between parental mental health literacy (PMHL) and adolescent depression and anxiety scores. Based on cross-sectional data from the 2023 Guangdong Adolescent Mental Health Survey, the study included 4,697 pairs of adolescents and their primary caregivers. Questionnaires were used to assess PMHL and adolescents’ levels of depression and anxiety, and weighted linear regression, restricted cubic splines, and subgroup analyses were employed. For every 1-point increase in PMHL, adolescents’ depression scores decreased by 0.033 and anxiety scores by 0.034 (both P < 0.05). The high PMHL group had significantly lower depression and anxiety scores than the low PMHL group. The dose-response relationship was linear. Subgroup analysis revealed interaction effects involving boarding status, mobile phone usage duration, and educational level. Higher PMHL is significantly associated with a lower risk of depression and anxiety among adolescents. Enhancing PMHL may help prevent and intervene in adolescent emotional problems; longitudinal studies are needed to verify the causal relationship.
Article.Topic: Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development
Article.TopicFields: Psychology > Clinical Psychology > Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development; Psychology > Social Psychology > Mental Health Treatment and Access; Social Sciences > Sociology and Political Science > Psychosocial Factors Impacting Youth

Article.Title: Distribution-based canonical correlation residual monitoring for industrial processes fault detection
Article.Authors: Kini K.; Harrou F.; Madakyaru M.; Sun Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Reliable fault detection is essential for safe, efficient, and sustainable industrial processes. This paper proposes a Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA)-based fault detection framework with distribution-based residual monitoring using Hellinger Distance (HD), Kullback–Leibler Distance (KLD), and Kantorovich Distance (KD). Specifically, the proposed approach evaluates residual distributions within a moving window and determines decision thresholds nonparametrically using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE), avoiding restrictive Gaussian assumptions. A key advantage is that the framework requires only fault-free data for model construction and threshold calibration, making it suitable when labeled fault data are scarce or unavailable. The framework detects faults that disrupt the CCA cross-correlation structure, including faults affecting variables in either the predictor or response variables. The proposed approach is evaluated on the Williams–Otto reactor and a Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP) under bias, intermittent, drift, and freezing faults. Additional experiments examine faults in CCA input variables, sensitivity to moving-window and KDE settings, and different fault magnitudes. The proposed approach is also compared with CCA-based Squared Prediction Error (CCA-SPE), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Support Vector Regression (SVR) monitoring under identical fault scenarios and evaluation conditions. The results show that distribution-based CCA indicators generally outperform conventional CCA-SPE and the considered PCA- and SVR-based strategies. Among them, CCA-KD achieves the best overall performance, with high detection and low false alarm rates. Overall, integrating CCA with distribution-based monitoring provides effective multivariate fault detection.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Control and Systems Engineering > Fault Detection and Control Systems; Decision Sciences > Statistics, Probability and Uncertainty > Advanced Statistical Process Monitoring; Chemistry > Analytical Chemistry > Spectroscopy and Chemometric Analyses

Article.Title: Microplastic contamination in commercially important marine fishes from the Sohar Coast, Sea of Oman: occurrence, characterization, and polymer composition
Article.Authors: Al Kharusi I.; Dutta S.
Article.Abstract: Microplastic (MP) pollution is an increasing concern in marine environments because of its persistence, bioavailability, and potential implications for marine ecosystem health and seafood safety. Despite growing global attention, information on MP contamination in commercially important marine fish from the Sea of Oman remains limited. This study assessed the occurrence, abundance, and characteristics of MPs in four commercially important fish species from the Sohar coast and tested whether MP contamination differed among species and tissues and was associated with habitat group, sex, and biometric characteristics. A total of 120 fish representing Epinephelus areolatus , Lethrinus microdon , Nematalosa arabica , and Rastrelliger kanagurta were examined for MPs in the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and gills. Microplastics were extracted using alkaline digestion and visually identified under a stereomicroscope. All 316 recovered particles were subjected to ATR-FTIR spectroscopy; 313 (99.1%) met the ≥ 70% spectral-match criterion and were successfully assigned to polymer types. Microplastics were detected in 79.2% of the examined fish, with a mean total abundance of 2.63 ± 2.60 items individual⁻1. Frequency of occurrence ranged from 66.7% to 90.0% among species. Total MP abundance did not differ significantly among species, whereas GIT MP concentration differed significantly among species. GIT–gill differences were significant only in E. areolatus and R. kanagurta . No significant associations were detected between total MP abundance and habitat group, sex, total length, body weight, or condition factor. Fibers were the dominant particle type, most particles measured < 2 mm, and polyester was the predominant identified polymer, followed by polypropylene and ethylene-propylene diene polymer (EPDM). The predominance of fibers and polyester indicates that fibrous synthetic materials constitute an important component of MP exposure in these commercially important fishes. However, specific environmental sources cannot be determined from polymer identity alone, highlighting the need for integrated assessment of fish alongside seawater, sediments, and other potential environmental sources.
Article.TopicFields: Environmental Science > Pollution > Microplastics and Plastic Pollution; Environmental Science > Health, Toxicology and Mutagenesis > Environmental Toxicology and Ecotoxicology; Environmental Science > Global and Planetary Change > Marine Ecology and Invasive Species

Article.Title: Habituation and housing interact to shape the magnitude and consistency of post-operative recovery after kidney imaging window implantation in mice
Article.Authors: Askar R.; Weidner P.; Peuckert C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Abdominal imaging windows enable longitudinal intravital microscopy but require surgical implantation, which induces physiological stress and may influence experimental outcomes. Although pre-operative habituation is widely used as a refinement strategy, its effects on post-operative physiological responses remain incompletely understood. Here, male and female BALB/c mice underwent kidney abdominal imaging window implantation following either a two-week handling habituation protocol or standard husbandry and were housed either in groups or individually after surgery. Post-operative recovery was assessed using clinical health scores, body weight, peripheral leukocyte counts, urinary corticosterone, and renal immunohistochemistry. Habituation altered both the magnitude and the consistency of post-operative physiological responses. Mean effects were primarily observed in males, including greater transient post-operative weight loss, delayed body weight recovery, and reduced urinary corticosterone concentrations. Across immune and endocrine endpoints, however, the predominant effect was a change in inter-individual variability. Under group-housed conditions, habituated mice showed reduced variation in leukocyte counts, urinary corticosterone concentrations, and renal CD68-positive cell infiltration, whereas these effects were absent or reversed in individually housed animals. Females were affected predominantly through changes in inter-individual variability. These findings demonstrate that pre-operative habituation reshapes the physiological response to surgery in a manner that depends on both post-operative housing and sex. More broadly, they identify inter-individual variability as a biologically meaningful outcome of peri-operative refinement, suggesting that refinement strategies should be evaluated not only by their effects on average physiological responses but also by their ability to promote more consistent responses across individual animals.
Article.TopicFields: Veterinary > Small Animals > Animal testing and alternatives; Veterinary > Small Animals > Animal Behavior and Welfare Studies; Veterinary > Small Animals > Veterinary Pharmacology and Anesthesia

Article.Title: ZAPP: a zero-aware photovoltaic power prediction framework
Article.Authors: Gürhanlı A.; Esen V.
Article.Abstract: Predicting photovoltaic power generator outputs is not easy, especially when the values are near zero, because even very small errors can lead to large percentage errors. We introduce a new forecasting framework, ZAPP (Zero-Aware Photovoltaic Power Predictor), that handles near-zero errors while maintaining high prediction accuracy. The model does not rely on a single unified regression model but instead attaches two refinement stages to a base regression model. The first stage, called ZeroGate, predicts whether the output should be zero. The second refinement stage, the low-power MAPE reducer, fine-tunes the non-zero outputs near the zero level without significantly affecting scale-dependent regression metrics. The datasets are divided into training, validation, and test sets in chronological order, ensuring that test data is not used during model development, threshold tuning, ensemble weighting, or calibration. Experimental evaluation included base models such as Persistence, Ridge, XGBoost, LSTM, Transformer, and a hybrid Ridge–XGBoost model. Two separate datasets are employed to strengthen the quality of the results. For the hybrid model, sMAPE fell from 60.57% to 11.07% on Dataset 1. Its final MAE, RMSE, and R 2 were 22.37, 60.72, and 0.9637, respectively. On Dataset 2, sMAPE decreased from 63.30% to 11.92%, with MAE = 52.24, RMSE = 144.60, and R 2 = 0.9559. The zero-aware correction mainly reduced percentage errors without weakening the overall regression results.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Solar Radiation and Photovoltaics; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Energy Load and Power Forecasting; Energy > Renewable Energy, Sustainability and the Environment > Photovoltaic System Optimization Techniques

Article.Title: Antimicrobial activity and ADMET analysis of novel coumarin-based pyridine and pyran hybrids
Article.Authors: Ahmed G.; Hessein S.; El haleem A.; Shmiess N.; Fouad S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A series of novel pyridine and pyran incorporated chromene moiety have been synthesized using 6-(2-(4-nitrophenyl) diazenyl)-3-acetyl-2 H-chromen-2-one 1 as the starting material. The chemical structures of the newly synthesized derivatives were characterized using different spectroscopic techniques (FT-IR, 1 HNMR and 13 CNMR) and elemental analysis. All derivatives were assessed for their in vitro antimicrobial activity against six clinically isolated multi-drug resistance strains, including Gram-positive ( Bacillus pumilis , Streptococcus faecalis ) and Gram-negative ( Escherichia coli , Enterobacter cloacae ) bacteria and fungi ( Saccharomyces cerevisiae , Candida albicans ) using broth microdilution and agar well-diffusion technique assays. The synthesized compounds exhibited moderate to good antimicrobial activity against the tested strains, with several derivatives approaching, and in one instance matching, the potency of the reference drugs. Notably, 2a , 5a , 5b , 6b , 7b , and 8a derivatives merged as the most promising bactericidal and fungicidal agents Compound 5a demonstrated an excellent activity toward S. faecalis which is equal to Penicillin G. with MIC value (3.91 µg/ml) and MBC value (31.3 µg/ml). Furthermore, compounds 5b , 6b , 7b and 8a revealed an excellent potency against S. faecalis with MIC value (7.81 µg/ml) and bactericidal activity with MBC value from 15.6 to 62.5 µg/ml Furthermore, in-silico ADMET analysis of compounds 6a , 6b , 8a , and 8b demonstrated adherence to Pfizer’s guidelines, reflecting favorable physicochemical properties.
Article.TopicFields: Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Synthesis and biological activity; Medicine > Pharmacology > Synthesis of Organic Compounds; Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Synthesis and Biological Evaluation

Article.Title: Mitigation of bacterial spot disease of pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) using diseased plant-recruited microorganisms to modulate the rhizosphere microbiota
Article.Authors: Song H.; Yang S.; Cho Y.; Choi M.; Yang H.; Seo M.; Lee J.
Article.Abstract: Plants and their rhizosphere microbial communities actively interact with each other to create optimal growth and defense conditions. It is known that when a plant becomes diseased, the plant secretes various metabolites or signaling substances that can attract protective beneficial or helpful microorganisms from the surrounding soil as a response. This is the basis of the 'cry for help' hypothesis, which proposes that stressed roots emit distress signals that recruit beneficial microbes able to mitigate the stress. Here we hypothesized that the bacterial diseased pepper plants might harbour some rhizosphere microorganisms which could be distinctively different from the healthy pepper plants. In this study, we investigated the structural shifts in the pepper ( Capsicum annuum L.) rhizosphere microbiota following infection by the spot disease pathogen Xanthomonas euvesicatoria . Through microbial community analyses, we identified specific bacterial taxa such as Rhodanobacter and Arachidicoccus that appeared to influence or contribute to community differentiation. To validate the protective roles of these recruited microbes, we applied the selected strains as targeted inoculants together with known plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB). Microbial treatments, particularly the single-strain Rhodanobacter treatment (T2) and a four-strain consortium (T4), significantly reduced the proportion of diseased leaves by 72%. Furthermore, microbiome analysis of the treated rhizosphere showed a partial recovery of Mucilaginibacter , an indicator of plant health that had been depleted under disease conditions. This study suggests that the pepper plant actively recruits beneficial rhizosphere microbes in response to X. euvesicatoria infection to support its immunity. Utilizing the plant-recruited microorganisms provides a sustainable and targeted biocontrol approach that both inhibits pathogen proliferation and reestablishes ecological balance in the rhizosphere. This microbiome-informed approach presents an environment-friendly alternative to conventional chemical pesticides in managing pepper bacterial spot disease.
Article.TopicFields: Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Plant-Microbe Interactions and Immunity; Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Plant Pathogenic Bacteria Studies; Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Plant Disease Management Techniques

Article.Title: An interpretable hierarchical deep learning framework for lung and colon cancer detection
Article.Authors: Talukder M.; Rafeh R.; Chu N.; Uddin M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Accurate and interpretable classification of lung and colon cancer from histopathological images remains challenging because of substantial inter-class similarities, morphological heterogeneity, and the limited transparency of conventional deep learning (DL) models. Most existing methods treat the problem as a flat multiclass classification task, requiring a single model to distinguish normal tissue and multiple cancer subtypes simultaneously. In this study, we propose an interpretable hierarchical DL framework that decomposes the five-class classification problem into clinically motivated coarse-to-fine decision stages. The framework initially separates normal tissue from cancerous tissue and then directs each sample to a specialized classifier for either normal tissue categorization or cancer subtype identification. Candidate DL architectures are independently evaluated at each stage, allowing the most suitable model to be selected for each specific classification task. The framework is evaluated on the LC25000 benchmark and further assessed on the independent LungHist700 dataset, which presents a distinct evaluation setting with different image characteristics and class distributions. The proposed approach achieves an accuracy of 98.50% on LC25000 and 82.01% on LungHist700. To improve model transparency, Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, LIME, and Occlusion Sensitivity are employed to highlight the image regions that contribute to the hierarchical predictions. The results show that the framework combines strong classification performance with a structured coarse-to-fine decision process and complementary interpretability techniques. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of hierarchical decision decomposition and explainable DL to provide a more transparent and task-specific approach to computer-aided histopathological cancer classification, particularly for distinguishing normal tissue from lung and colon cancer subtypes.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > AI in cancer detection; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Medicine > Radiology, Nuclear Medicine and Imaging > Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

Article.Title: Use of microstream capnography in sedation practices for pediatric patients undergoing magnetic resonance imaging
Article.Authors: A. Akgün A.; Yılmaz C.; Sayan H.; Karasu D.; Balkaya A.; Güvenç G.; Uçar M.; Çevikkalp E.
Article.Abstract: In pediatric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), there is a need for more advanced monitoring methods in addition to routine pulse oximetry to ensure safer nonoperating room anesthesia (NORA). The integrated pulmonary index (IPI) available in the Microstream capnography device provides an early indicator of a patient’s respiratory functions. In this study, we aimed to investigate the feasibility of using the IPI as an early indicator for detecting cardiorespiratory events. A prospective, observational study was conducted on pediatric patients aged 1 month to 18 years who were to undergo sedation for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The respiratory rate (RR), end tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO 2 ), oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ), heart rate (HR), complications, and EtCO 2 changes (∆EtCO 2 ) were recorded. IPI values at induction and at the end of the scan were evaluated. The primary outcome was the diagnostic performance of the post-induction IPI value in predicting cardiorespiratory events; secondary outcomes included the incidence of cardiorespiratory events and of hypopneic hypoventilation, and the diagnostic performance of EtCO 2 for these outcomes. A total of 159 patients were included in the study. ROC analysis revealed the diagnostic significance of EtCO 2 induction in predicting hypoxia and apnea. While 31.44% of all patients had ∆EtCO 2 , only 6.3% of these patients had SpO 2 ≤ 93% (hypoxia) at the same time. The induction EtCO 2 median in patients who developed hypoxia was 26 mmHg (IQR: 14–29), compared to 33 mmHg (IQR: 28–36) in those without hypoxia ( p = 0.001). EtCO 2 The optimal threshold value was found to be 29 mmHg in patients who developed hypoxia, whereas it was 18 mmHg in those who developed apnea. A total of 27.7% of all patients had hypopneic hypoventilation, and hypoxia was detected in %15.9 of these patients. IPI, EtCO 2 , and ∆EtCO 2 have a statistically significant effect on ‘induction cardiorespiratory events’. Patients with cardiorespiratory events had an IPI ≤ 6 and EtCO 2 ≤ 33. Each one-unit increase in IPI was calculated to reduce the probability of a cardiorespiratory event by approximately 46.3%. Severe respiratory complications are frequently observed in young pediatric patients undergoing NORA. Early diagnosis of respiratory complications, particularly hypopneic hypoventilation, is possible through EtCO 2 monitoring. Low EtCO 2 and IPI are considered potential risk factors for the development of cardiorespiratory events. The routine use of capnography, a method that allows continuous and noninvasive monitoring of respiration, enhances patient safety in procedural sedation outside the operating room. Intervention in pediatric patients with an IPI value < 6 who develop cardiovascular events is considered necessary. Because EtCO 2 is sampled outside the airway, continuous auscultation of breath sounds is recommended as a complementary monitor in this setting. Registry : ClinicalTrials.gov, TRN: NCT04622436, Registration date: 03 November 2020.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine > Anesthesia and Sedative Agents; Medicine > Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine > Airway Management and Intubation Techniques; Neuroscience > Endocrine and Autonomic Systems > Neuroscience of respiration and sleep

Article.Title: Molecule-aware machine learning for predicting absorption and emission of benzothiadiazole derivatives
Article.Authors: Truong D.; Hong P.; Pham P.; Trinh T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Predicting the absorption and emission wavelengths of 2,1,3-benzothiadiazole (BTD) derivatives across diverse solvents from molecular structure alone remains challenging, and conventional random-split validation can obscure whether models truly extrapolate to new chemical structures or merely interpolate solvent effects for known ones. By enforcing a molecule-aware train–test split, in which all solvent measurements of any given chemical structure are held out together, we show that champion-model $$R^2$$ falls by approximately 27–29 percentage points relative to random splitting, revealing that high random-split accuracy primarily reflects reliable prediction of solvent-induced spectral shifts rather than generalisation to unseen BTD structures. Within this framework, replacing binary with count-based Morgan fingerprints raises single-split $$R^2$$ from 0.747 to 0.941 for absorption and from 0.797 to 0.916 for emission, an improvement rooted in the ability of count fingerprints to encode the recurrence frequency of donor substructures, a key determinant of intramolecular charge-transfer character. A systematically optimised deep neural network reaches $$R^2 = 0.954$$ for absorption on its best of twenty random initialisations (mean $$0.83 \pm 0.12$$ ), the highest value reported for this dataset, yet the molecule-aware benchmark confirms that this performance does not translate to structure-level extrapolation. Comparative evaluation of graph neural networks, multi-task learning, extended descriptor sets, and ensemble methods confirms that none outperforms the count-fingerprint approach at this dataset size. Feature-importance analysis identifies tertiary amine substitution as the dominant structural driver and solvent polarity as the strongest single feature for emission (ranked first or second in all four model/encoding combinations examined, versus 8th–13th for absorption), an asymmetry consistent with the stronger solvatochromism of relaxed charge-transfer states. These results offer practical guidance for computational screening: the models are well suited to solvent selection for known dyes, whereas the design of genuinely new structures demands expanded structural diversity in the training set.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Computational Theory and Mathematics > Computational Drug Discovery Methods; Chemistry > Physical and Theoretical Chemistry > Photochemistry and Electron Transfer Studies; Materials Science > Materials Chemistry > Machine Learning in Materials Science

Article.Title: A cell-based multivariate blood test (iCAP) for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease capturing non-amyloid-β biology
Article.Authors: Qi Y.; Miller L.; D’Ascenzo M.; Berndt J.; Whitney G.; Duffy F.; Danziger S.; Peskind E.; Li G.; Masters C.; Fowler C.; N/A N/A.; Milicic L.; Vacher M.; Bourgeat P.; Doré V.; Shishegar R.; Maruff P.; Rowe C.; Villemagne V.; Porter T.; Laws S.; Rainey-Smith S.; Bomke J.; Brown B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The indicator cell assay platform (iCAP) is a blood-based diagnostic approach that uses standardized cells as biosensors to transduce complex circulating signals into cell-based gene-expression profiles for multivariate disease classification. We developed an iCAP for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease (AD-iCAP) by incubating plasma from patients with early-stage AD (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia) and non-affected controls with standardized neurons and training classifiers on transcriptomic responses. Modeling features were restricted to a predefined 84-gene panel derived independently by analyzing 5xFAD mouse plasma in the AD-iCAP. In this exploratory study, a model was trained and tested using 191 retrospectively collected human plasma samples across three cohorts. The classifier achieved AUC = 0.64 (95% CI 0.51–0.78) in an external validation set during model development (n = 82) and AUC = 0.77 (95% CI 0.57–0.96) in a blind test set (n = 23). The multivariate model incorporated 5 genes including AKT3 , GPR50 , PALLD , RGMA , and PCDH10 , implicated in AD, neuronal signaling and/or cytoskeletal dynamics. The cell-based approach is orthogonal to direct detection of circulating amyloid and tau, and these exploratory findings support further evaluation of AD-iCAP in prospective studies for combinatorial diagnostics and patient stratification for clinical trials.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Psychiatry and Mental health > Dementia and Cognitive Impairment Research; Medicine > Physiology > Alzheimer's disease research and treatments; Neuroscience > Neurology > Neuroinflammation and Neurodegeneration Mechanisms

Article.Title: Physics-constrained generative digital twin for early leakage detection in nitrogen accumulators in governor control systems at hydroelectric power plants
Article.Authors: Ustun T.; Sinha P.; Butuner M.; Koc E.; Gezer D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nitrogen pre-charge loss in hydropower governor accumulators is a slow but critical degradation process that weakens hydraulic energy storage, reduces pressure-retention time, increases pump cycling, and accelerates thermal–mechanical stress. Conventional pressure-threshold SCADA alarms can miss the early stage because oil pressure may remain inside the operating band while waveform dynamics deteriorate. This paper proposes a SCADA-calibrated physics-constrained generative digital twin for early nitrogen leakage diagnosis. Limited anonymized field-SCADA observations are used only as calibration anchors for pressure set-points, pump-ON duration, pump-OFF retention, temperature range, and the fast-rise/slow-decay waveform; they are not presented as a complete labeled leakage dataset. The evaluation uses 80,000 physics-constrained synthetic training records and 20,000 independently generated synthetic test records per run, balanced across eight degradation months. Train and test records are produced with disjoint seeds and no shared cycles or residual draws. Across five independent generation-and-training runs, Random Forest gives the best pressure-prediction performance, with R 2 = 0.999731 ± 0.000004, MAE = 0.0856 ± 0.0007 bar, RMSE = 0.1074 ± 0.0007 bar, and 96.78 ± 0.18% of samples within 1% of the 23-bar operating span (0.23 bar). The corrected health index is bounded by 1.0, and cycle-level indicators identify the Month-4 warning transition before a conventional pressure-threshold response. The framework therefore supports earlier inspection and nitrogen-recharge planning, helping operators reduce avoidable pump cycling, maintenance escalation, and the risk of unplanned governor-system outages, while explicitly distinguishing SCADA calibration from synthetic diagnostic evaluation.

Article.Title: Optimization and mechanistic analysis of high-temperature aerobic composting process for dynamic sludge in rotary drums
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhang H.; Xiao Z.; Xv H.; Jia B.; Li Y.; Diao G.; Song H.; Wu C.
Article.Abstract: This study addresses challenges in high-temperature aerobic sludge composting using a rotary drum, particularly material adhesion to the drum wall and low efficiency. Response surface methodology (RSM) was used to develop predictive models for composting period time and seed germination index (GI). The models showed high reliability (R²≥ 0.95, p < 0.001) with validation errors of 6.67% for composting period and 1.04% for GI. The optimal conditions identified were 55% moisture content, 10 mm auxiliary material dimensions, 7 L·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹ TS aeration rate, and 1.5 r·min⁻¹ rotational speed. These conditions reduced the composting period to 15 days, increased GI to 86%, and met the GB/T 23,486 − 2009 standards for heavy metal concentrations. The bioavailability of heavy metals decreased significantly, ensuring environmental safety. Microbial community analysis revealed a two-stage succession pattern, with thermophilic Bacillus and Aspergillus dominating the high-temperature phase. The process efficiency was influenced by synergistic parameter interactions. Through comparative analysis of processes, it was found that rotating drum composting achieves an optimal balance among efficiency, environmental performance, and engineering feasibility, making it highly suitable for large-scale municipal sludge valorization.
